I'm not one to write game reviews usually. This time, I feel strongly enough about this game that I want to spread the word. If you enjoy puzzles, mysteries in the line of X-Files and the MMO The Secret World, and are willing to put yourself into the game, this will be a home run for you.
This ARG uses the real world as the surface with you becoming part of a secret organization who deals with those events outside the realm of the police. As a member of the Black Watchmen, you will work alone and with other agents to solve mysteries through ciphering, internet research and more. The puzzles themselves are great and you really feel an AH-HA moment when you succeed. The community is strong and willing to help. We can't solve everything on our own.
The big selling point for me is the level of immersion. You can play the game without giving any of your information (Red) and still be a part of almost everything. If you are ok giving more personal information, then you become part of the game.  You can get phone calls relating to the game. You can have packages sent to you and even be called upon to go to locations in your area to help in the live events. The potential is huge for this game. The devs have been hands on with the community, quick to answer questions and keep everyone excited about what is on the other side of the rabbit hole.
Some are complaining about the price as it does include the first season (roughly 3 months). This includes not just the game itself, but live events and secret missions. I do feel that you will get your money's worth IF this type of game appeals to you. The more of yourself you are willing to put into it, the more you will get from it.

For anybody that's into gaming, coding, or graphic design; this is for you. This movie talks about the intricacy of coding that these developers put into their games, and the art and themes that are packed into them. It also covers three of the best rated games of the past four years or so, so that's another reason for gamers to watch it. Just remember, if you're not a fan of cussing or provocative language, and get completely outraged at peoples opinions that differ from yours, this movie may torque you off at times.
It's definitely my pick for best documentary of the year, possibly even my favorite overall movie of the year. An incredible emotional experience along with incredible cinematography combine to make it a move that grabs you and doesn't let go. I've watched it several times over (in various formats), and the journey that the three developers go through never faltered in making me reevaluate how much I appreciate the work put into things. The music by Jim Guthrie is also incredible, and really adds to the whole experience.
A must watch, either buy it on Steam (or any other format), or watch it on Netflix. However, if you want special features and a wide array of subtitle options, then you definitely should buy the Steam/Website version.  Completely worth the money I paid for it.

Review:
I had looked at this game before, but had been put of before by some of the negative reviews. I'm always cautious when people start saying things have been 'abandoned' in review... no one likes to be stuck in an unfinished or buggy game. FarSky is none of these. My wife eventually picked it up in a sale for me, and I loved it. You are just thrown in the situation and forced to experiement and try things... yes you will probably die first time out if you are timid like me. I suspect if you knew what you were doing then the first run through could actually be done in about an hour or two, but my first run through was 9 hours.. not because I needed that long, but because I didn't really ever want to leave the world; I kept wanting to perfect my base, improved my crop growing. Indeed I had all the submarine pieces collected, bar one right next to my base, and could have finished it within minutes, but kept on going for another hour or two.
Eventually I finished it, and it was a simple understated end, to a simple understated premise. I am currently taking my time playing through the survival mode and enjoying it, but the atmosphere and sense of wildness and danger are further enhanced, only now I know what not to do at least.
I have seen some people say it is a brilliant idea underdeveloped, and I empathise with that notion; I'd like more too, but perhaps sometimes being left wanting more is part of a things charm. Would firefly and fawlty towers be as good if they had gone on for 15 seasons?
Highly reccomend.

It would be a stretch to say there was ever a “golden age” of combat racing games, but Gas Guzzlers reminds me strongly of the better titles in the genre. While inferior aesthetically to say, Jak X, Gas Guzzlers is mechanically sound, possessing solid controls, easy to use weapons and a diverse range of cars. The physics engine in particular is well-implemented, avoiding the sense of weightless sliding about you get from games like Twisted Metal, nor the drunken careening into obstacles of Grand Theft Auto- unless you run over an oil slick, of course. It’s very easy to ♥♥♥♥ up driving controls and in a driving game, thus ruining the entire experience for everybody involved. Not so here. However, in other areas, Gas Guzzlers feels very much like the budget game it is. The music is ignorable at best and there is absolutely no semblance of plot, though there is amusing flavor text for each of the weapons and looks-real-but-has-a-fake-name cars. The campaign is structured like every other driving game ever, wherein you play a series of one-off races to rise through a leaderboard to the top, then becoming eligible to enter a tournament and advance to the next tier- three total. in this game’s case. You may receive a sponsorship and then gain additional funs from each win, and there are periodic exhibition events that force you to use a particular car and play a particular gametype but have large payouts. You unlock additional cars, tracks, parts, weapons and cosmetic customizations as you progress, most of which must then be purchased. There’s a fairly diverse range of tracks and arenas, and even gametypes featuring hordes of zombies in the multiplayer, if you have the “Full Metal Zombie” DLC. I was disappointed that no zombies appear in the campaign. However, barring tournaments and sponsored events, you may choose what type of event to play, allowing you to focus on a race type you are good at or enjoy over others. Also of note is the ability to select a voice pack for your driver, including a reasonable facsimile of Duke Nukem, though even his one-liners will eventually wear a bit thin. I must note that none of Gas Guzzler’s flaws is in its gameplay. If you like games that have cars with guns on them (and to my distress, many people apparently don’t) you will enjoy Gas Guzzlers. If you don’t… then why are you reading about one?

I know there are plenty of people out there that love this game, and I can see how it could be appealing if you go into it with certain expectations. It's definitely a well polished game and it has an ambitious and interesting premise.
I guess I was expecting something like an evolution simulator where the game play revolved around the pressure to adapt your organism successfully to the challenges of an unforgiving natural world. Instead, I got a bundle of cutesy mini games where adapting boiled down to collecting new body parts by dancing and singing and making buddies with other cute things.
Evolving meant slapping these body parts on my creature using a fancy Mr. Potato-head style builder and then letting it loose. It didn't really seem to matter if my creation was poorly conceived - as long as I had a mouth and legs I was golden. This game has many issues that prevent it from being fully enjoyable.  In fact, had I known about these issues, I wouldn't have bought the game.  The main issue is that the expansions do not act as DLC.  They act as their own seperate games.  They show up individually in your library.  The base game does not contain missions or maps from the expansions.  In order to play with those, you have to start up that specific expansion.  However, the animals from the expansions seem to show up almost randomly between each other.  For example, the base game appears to have almost all of the animals (fish, dinos, dragons, etc) but appears to be missing certain specific species.  The expansions have the same issue; having certain species and not others.  You can fool around in the program files and condense most of everything into the base game but you will still be missing stuff.  And, I must point out, the animal color customization button in the base game doesn't work.
As for the actual game itself, it is alright.  There are aspects of it that are annoying (each employee has their own individual giant fugly tower, there isn't much variety in animal enrichment items, there aren't many items for guests, etc) but overall if you're looking to play something mindless for a while, Wildlife Park 2 isn't the worst choice.  It is certainly not as enjoyable as Zoo Tycoon, however, and if you're looking for an exciting, challenging simulation game, I would not choose this.

It's like Skyrim with content.
This game was my first RPG. Admittedly I had no clue what was going on and picked up a bow (with all my skills pumped into blunt weapons) and expected to hit things. I've become a tad more experienced over the years. I can now fly for minutes at a time and run about ambushing Cliff Racers from behind as a form of payback. This game can make you feel like a demigod; and then strip it from you in an instant by throwing stupidly high leveled creatures at you.
Pros -
- Filled with an insane amount of lore and detail, the level of imagination is through the roof
- No laziness; at all. There is no fast travelling, no quest markers and definately no clear instructions. The player is left to their own devices to complete quests etc.
- An incredible amount of detail the player doesn't even see. When you swing at an enemy the game is calculating your skill with that weapon to determine whether you will hit; the enemy's agility to see if they can dodge; your strength to determine the kind of damage to both the enemy and your weapon; the enemy's armour points and skill; and even the amount of stamina you currently have.
-No-one likes you, you have to make your own friends. Get used to being called "scum" even after you have saved the island of Vvardenfell from the resident crazed demigod.
-The endless freedom. You are free to mess around with the game to your heart's content. You can go and murder Caius Cosades (after claiming 200 gold of course) and ruin the questline for yourself. -Joining certain factions will change other's opinions of you (Joining the Mages Guild will cause the Telvanni to like you less.
Cons -
-The combat may seem quite clunky to new players, and it can be quite infuriating if you don't know what you're doing.
-The game can be harsh and unforgiving. Save often (this could also be seen as a pro, depending on your attitude towards saving and loading)

Star Trek Online. I have almost 2000 hours on record. But I do actually have way more than that. For a while I had a really weak computer and I played the game standalone on a the DVD cover release. Back when that still existed.
Where do I start?
Star Trek Online has been through two phases, one is now gone but I'll take you through it anyway. To see how it has evolved.
When Star Trek Online was released it was driven by Cryptic and released by Atari. Both on their own site, Steam and through DVD boxes in stores. At that time the game was really weak and lacking. There was no audio dialog or fancy cutscenes and the graphics were already a tad outdate. New content was barely released because of how small the team was. But we still had a lot of fun exploration missions, you could visit every star system even if that ment just flying around the planet and looking around. You also had to pay to play back then. You could buy playing time online or buying "month" cards.
Then the big boss "Perfect World Entertainment" came a long. Now this was a good and a bad thing. The good news is that since Perfect World has a lot more resources than small Cryptic. And Atari was just a publisher, this now ment that Star Trek Online had a big team with a lot of resources. This mean the game quickly evolved in a highly positive way.
Such as missions getting better and more complex, the introduction of even more advanced audio dialoge and cutscenes. The general story telling of the game got improved a lot. There have also been way more updates and patches and they even just recently overhauled the graphics engine and it looks all quite nice. The ships have also been re-done since Beta days to make them look more realistic. Most even have brand new, made from scratch models and textures. So the graphics now compared to release are amazing.
That being said. The game is now free to play and everything ingame can be accessed without real life money. Though it'll take you ages to do that. But since the game is free, and there's something you really want I don't see a problem buying it for real money. You support the developers.
While the developers do not always pay attention to small bug reports that have been sitting on the forums or tickets for ages. They do fix serious issues. For example one time, I deleted my main character that I'd have for years and after 2 weeks I got a mail saying they managed to recovery the character. They are also good at cracking down mean players and annoying "gold sellers".
While the story driven content and graphics have been improved, togheter with general gameplay some things have been "broken" as well.
For example, most systems in the Galaxy cannot be entered unless you have a specific mission. Almost all systems have a patrol mission, where you enter.. Explore, kill some bad guys or something. But when you've done that once. You are NOT allowed to repeat the mission on the same character.
The story arc is also "shared" for all the factions in the game. Each faction has some unique missions but in the end they follow the same line of missions but it's done in a way so it's somewhat different and okay in my eyes.
They removed the exploration missions. In the old days the game itself generated a random star system, a random map and a totally random mission. So nothing was ever the same. Almost. Anyway it was a fun way to get some diversity in the game when you've done all your leveling and stuff. This was sadly removed because it did not "feel up to the game standards" but we have not seen a replacement.
So when you're done playing all the story missions and done all the patrol missions. There are also some mini missions on Starbases and some planets, but again. These are non replayable. All you got is PVE and PVP. PVE is mostly dead but if you get in a fleet you can run private sessions. PVP is somewhat broken if you can call it that. It means the "general" player can't really compet here because of how out of control DPS has gotten. But that's something you can google. Of course if you wanna' get into DPS it can be quite fun for those who love that.
But in short, Star Trek Online is an amazing game that brings the Trek universe to full scale in my eyes. You can visit and see all the locations from the show. All the starships are included in great detail along with a few new ones. The game also take place in 2409-2410. That's way ahead of Star Trek Voyager, Deep Space 9 and The Next Generation. That allows the game to have technology that wasn't in the series. For example personal shield generators and stuff like that. It works out great with the game setting and it does bring the feel of this is what Star Trek would evolve too.
There is a lot of Star Trek lore in the game to enjoy, everything from food items to a name mentioned. Or just a location or event in the series. You can also meet a lot of Star Trek Characters complete with audio dialog from their actors. Like the Doctor played by Roberto Picardo, Tuvok by Tim Russ and even Neelix by Ethan Phillips. There are also some people from Star Trek Enterprise etc.
The game also now focuses heavily on what happend in Star Trek Voyager, Deep Space 9, The Next Generation, Enterprise and even The Original Series. For example a lot of the deep episodes on the TV shows that was not really fully explained. Like Yeasterday's Enterprise.. The Temporal Cold War. More about the Tox Uthat from the TNG Episode Captain's Holiday. The small purple aliens that invaded Starfleet Command in 'Conspiracy', the aliens who kidnapped members of the Enterprise D into pockets of subspace from the episode Schisms. The Iconians.. The game takes a lot of episodes from TOS, TNG, DS9 and even ENT that weren't fully explained and expands on the storyline, even connecting many of them. You also see alien races such as the Iconians making a return.
But you don't need to be a Trekkie to play. You can still pick up on a lot of the jokes etc. There is also a lot of customization involved in the game. You have a lot of options when it comes to designing your character. It even puts the character creator in Saints Row to shame, and that's saying something. You can also customize your starship and mix parts. For example a Galaxy Class can have different nacelle's.. (Engines for you non Trek fans).
Anyway to this day, even though it's free the game gets new content quite often compared to other MMO's. The only other bad side is that the game community can be quite... Hostile. So it'll be hard to make friends and feel welcome. Try to ignore that, as some of the players including myself are awesome and nice.
In short, this is an amazing game. Especially if you are a Trekkie. And the fact that it's free, it doesn't hurt to try. Does it?

TL:DR: I like this game. Try to get it on a steam sale. Don't expect too much other than a weekend or two of gameplay (
If you're looking for an underwater survival game, and this one isn't on sale, PICK UP SUBNAUTICA!!! Subnautica is a solid title, has more to do, and the Devs are still working on it.)
The Long Story:
When looking for a game, the major points are there. Fun game mechanics, stabilty, nice design, etc. I loved playing this game. However, beware of the following:
1) No developer support. I saw comments that the developer isn't going to update this game. There was a roumor that someone else picked up the game and may be looking to either expand it or write a sequel. So far, I think that is only a roumor.
2) No modding community support. This probably ties into the first point. You're not going to find anything to update the game with from the user community. There are comments that the game might not even be able to be modified easily.
3) Not much by way of a tutorial and tool tips are far and few between. You get some tips in the dialog between Nathan and his buddy above the ocean. You're better off reading stuff online before playing. And some of the online content is just gesswork by other players.
4) Limited content. The game has three game modes (Adventure, Survival, and Sandbox), and there isn't much within them. The story is you're playing Nathan. His sub blew up. You have to survive, find the sub pieces, repair the ship, and make it back alive. That's it for story. And in game things to do is likewise very limited. Crafting, Exploration, etc.
With this in mind, I still found the game very enjoyable. However, it left me wanting more. My recomendation is to get this on a steam sale, and you should only be left with wanting more.

I put Morrowind off for years after I first purchased it, because it felt like such a step down from Oblivion and Skyrim that I couldn't get into it. And yes, maybe it isn't as action packed and polished as Skyrim, and it might not have that epic atmosphere of Oblivion. But 40 hours, 17 levels, and a few mods later, Morrowind gives Elder Scrolls IV and V a run for their money for my favorite game in the series.
The world this game is set in is enthralling. The key is to immerse yourself in it, read as many books as you can, talk to everyone and go through all of the dialogue. It begins to feel less like a video game and more like a living, breathing setting. All of your actions have reactions from the characters: take down a notorious gang, and the NPCs will talk about it.
I love the feeling of growth in this game. With each level you feel yourself getting more and more powerful. Powerful loot is rare: you'll feel accomplished when you find the right gauntlet to a set of glass armor, and you'll wear it with pride.
While Skyrim felt very streamlined and linear, Morrowind feels like you have different choices and decisions on how you reach your goal: will you kill the mage to get what you want, or will you bribe him? Each choice has different ramifications.
Any fan of the later games in the series needs to check this one out.

Anyone interested in the Elder Scrolls should play this.  arguably the best of the series  (i really miss levitation and flying so i'm particularly biased in this regard).     I must say I miss the truly massive randomly generated dungeons of Daggerfall as well, but I think most gamers today would find the interface of daggerfall unacceptable, but Morrowind's gameplay isn't so different from the later games that it would require such a large paradigm shift by the player, and for that reason alone I think fans of oblivion and skyrim would find morrowind fun...  aside from all the awesomeness that morrowind had that didnt survive to the later games.

I used to play this game on the original Xbox. I had no idea at the time what I had bought; a few friends were talking about it and said it was a fun game, but that was about it. I had no idea that I would spend many nights awake playing this game. After playing Oblivion and Skyrim, I wanted to go back and re-experience Morrowind. I never finished the main quest, which I found appalling after earning all the achievements in the other games.
Morrowind is a fantastic game, and one that should almost be played after experiencing Skyrim. The reason I say this is because of the difficulty. I found Skyrim to be much easier overall than both Morrowind and Oblivion. In Morrowind, the combat system can be very frustrating. It runs on a chance system; if you swing your weapon or fire an arrow, you have so much of a chance to hit your opponent. Once you do hit, damage is then determined by the game. In Skyrim and Oblivion, if your crosshairs are on an enemy and you attack, you will more than likely hit them. The map/directions in Morrowind are  my largest area of complaint, if I must complain about something in this game. For several quests you have to locate small caverns and burial grounds, as well as offices within forts and cities (Vivec, for example). You must read through your journal and figure out which road you need to take. There are no route markers, which make travelling somewhat difficult. And, like in Oblivion and Skyrim, there is always a mountain in your way. Also, you spend a lot of time repairing your weapons and armor. It also seems like Septims are harder to come by in Morrowind.
I do enjoy the story of this game. It is much more in-depth, and contains many challenging quests. You can spend months on this game and still have plenty to do, whereas a week with Skyrim will pretty much have you reaching for even the smallest of quests, just for something to do.
If you are new to the Elder Scrolls series and like to be challenged, then you should play this game.

Time to make a wall of text.
Morrowind was not only my second TES game (my first being Oblivion) but it is also personally my favorite. It's sad to see a lot of people be put off from experiencing this game due to things like♥♥♥♥♥graphics or a less-than stellar combat system. Certainly, the game has it's flaws, but from my perspective it trumps TES IV and V in what it does right. Morrowind is not for the faint of heart who just want to ignore any plot-lines and kill things. The game requires patience and a little bit of creativity to make the most out of it.
Being a mage sucks at first because learning spells is really expensive and magicka is a ♥♥♥♥♥ to manage in this game. Being an archer sucks at first because landing sneak attacks is finicky and whiffing all of your shots due to low agility or fatigue can be VERY frustrating. Even being a warrior sucks since melee combat can be a bit of a slog and heavy armor sucks in the early game.
But the important thing to remember in Morrowind is not to focus in one particular area of expertise, but rather try hard to excel in all of them. Quickly switching weapons and being able to cast spells on the fly makes being a diverse character infinitely easier and more enjoyable. A good warrior is bound to keep a bow around as a ranged weapon and know a spell or two to work themselves out of a difficult situation
But even more interesting than the freedom of character building is the world building of Vvardenfell. The lack of an omnipotent compass and a map that can't warp you around (gasp) make exploring the world to get things done a mandatory step in any player's journey. No spoilers, but the number of things to distract you as you journey across the island are, for the most part, all interesting and only serve to better you as a character and inform you, as the player, of the ever changing world.
TL;DR: This game requires patience, but will lead to a massive payout in story and character growth.

I'd like to provide an honest, unbiased review, but after having played it for as long as I have, I really don't feel as though I owe this game any more of my time. Still, it definitely needs to be talked about. There's a very clear and unironically ironic positive response to a game that unironically uses irony as its main draw. And, while in it's own twistedly postmodern way this may be a labor of love, it's not a labor of love that's worth even $3.
There's a lot here that makes me believe that the developer was intentionally and ironically making a poor effort to communicate to the player that the game is a joke, wholesale. It's fairly obvious from the response the game has gotten so far, on top of the overall tone of the game. It's not the work of a self-deluding "developer"--the kind of guy who pitches and re-pitches bland asset-pack games on greenlight in the hopes that he can drum up enough support to try and make an extra buck. It's a consequence of a fairly recently spawned ironic meme-y game genre, and I can't say I'm thrilled about it.
But, there's also the other side of this. There's parts I did like, and did find amusing. The first portion of the game is a quite obvious reference to P.T., and the requisite boredom of that section itself if a funny criticism. The author of THIS game, however, has a fraction of the technical skill that the Kojima team did, because half of the triggerable events I came into contact with either worked MOST (not all) of the time, or weren't, in any way, intuitive objects or places to try and activate in the first place. So, while the game itself does have some fairly clever ideas: the game's called Potato Thriller--the beginning of the main game takes place in one long, purgatory of a hallway, with the characteristic non-euclidian geometry that gives us the willies--and there's a handful of slight nods and references to other properties (the game menu is another example, and is a dead ringer for FNAF).
I'm not sure if there's a disconnect between the irony of the game's visual aspect--every piece of rendered material either seems to be bought or repurposed from a graphic pack, or has such a loosely mapped texture it's like my computer is rendering a painted tube sock full of ball bearings--or it's something else that's the problem. I genuinely want to understand how I can give the game a serious criticism without it being immediately deflected by the irony that the game seems to want to hide behind. I can say that with the right tone--this intentional badness has some redeemability. The unfortunate thing about Potato Thriller is that it mixes two very different approaches to criticism and humor, and it ends up muddling them both.
I guess, at the heart, it's not the intentional badness of the game that bothers me, or that so many other people are ironically praising a game that is itself more shrouded in irony than substantiated by anything else: it's the fact that the tone of this irony, the joke inherently acting as the heart of the game is itself broken. Moments of real humor are irregular, and the inconsistency of it actually makes me think that the developer is instead playing at being a person with a highly-refined sense of irony, instead of giving it to us. What we get as a substitute seems like a somewhat generic sequence of parts that all these games have.
On top of that, from a sheer gameplay perspective, there's very little here that I found interesting, or even redeemable. I spent what felt like the better part of two hours wandering up and down the same hallway trying to trigger some even to make progress. I'm not actually sure if there IS another part of the game, or if other reviewers are just taking the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everyone else who had trouble with it.
tl;dr Get some other game hyper-saturated in irony, like Sonic Dreams Collection. It's at least made better.

I was given this game for free to review it. I don't know why. This is the first game I've ever been given for such a purpose.
Click 'play', am welcomed by a dialogue box with two options, "Play Potato Thriller Steamed Potato Edition" and " ". Yes, the second option has no text, just a bubble you can click. I'm scared of this second bubble and I'm not going to mess with it.
Then a config box pops up. Resolution doesn't go up to my desktop resolution (1920x1080) so I keep it in the default window setting of 1280x600.
The game immediately tells you that it was made with a personal edition of Unity. It seems like this is just a project from a single dude (presumably Samer Khatib) who's doing his best. I appreciate that, indie devs have to start somewhere.
Main menu gives me STORY MODE and FRY BASKET. I assume FRY BASKET is some kind of sandbox mode, but I'm not sure. I'll try that later. STORY MODE it is.
Clicking that brings you to a separate play menu, POTATO MAN standing under flickering lights, crying(?). NEW GAME, CONTINUE, EXIT. As I'm going from the game window to the text file as I'm playing, I discover an Easter Egg on this screen where if you go to a window other than the game, and then go back to the game, you're brought to a weird level in third person (the game itself normally being first-person), and there's a nostril-eyeball-legs monster next to you (you being what I assume is an in-game representation of Samir Khatib). And a couch. And a giant pear. And a dresser. And a grandfather clock. And the only thing that I can figure that you're able to do is get killed by the nostril-eyeball-legs monster, and then kill teh nostril-eyeball-legs monster. Aaaaand that's it. Welp. Hit ESC to go back to the play menu.
It opens with a cinematic. Laptop and radio on a table, surrounded by chairs. The radio is giving you the news as told by (presumably) Samer Khatib and Samer Khatib's vocoder'd voice talking to each other as news anchors. It's obviously supposed to be funny, and it kinda is. As for visuals, ehhhhh. The laptop, for instance, isn't even on the table. It's floating a good four inches above it, just hanging there in mid-air.
As others have said, pressing 'ESC' brings you back to the play menu. Which is a shame, because during a cutscene I instinctively pressed the standard 'skip this' buttons, which includes ESC. I got about three minutes into the game - which is apparently just PT in a room that doesn't cycle and instead of being scary it's supposed to be weird like an episode of Spongebob. There's parts after that where you get karate chopped by POTATO MAN, but I don't know what they are, and I'm not willing to sit through the first bits again just to find out.
There are minigames. I use the word 'games' loosely, here. These are the FRY BASKET games. I played the first one, wherein you are POTATO MAN and you're supposed to go socialize with the PARK DEVILS, which are little devil guys, and you're in a park. And you socialize by going up to them and they kinda yell at you, and you have to go up to each one, and then the minigame is over. This is the only one I tried, for reasons which should be obvious.
POTATO THRILLER isn't really a 'game' per se. It's more like an interactive school project. It shows that the creator understands the basics of the engine, creating shapes and textures, animation, minor physics effects, minor lighting effects, event triggers and that sort of thing. If this were a project in a class, it'd probably get an A, unless that class was Game Design. Because again, it's not really a game.
Is it scary? No.
Is it silly? Yes.
Is it weird? Spongebob.
Is it good? If my friend showed this to me as his first thing he's ever made, I'd be impressed and I'd laugh at the jokes, and I'd hope he would continue to make games because it shows he has potential to make actual games eventually. Which this isn't.
Is it worth money? Nah.
However, if you're thinking about starting a career in making games, you could learn something from this game. Learning the basics, having an example of what a display of those basics looks like, recognizing that this should be a stepping stone to a better game later. That sort of thing.

ABOUT THIS GAME
Heroes & Generals is the ultimate WW2 game – a free-to-play Massively Multiplayer Online First Person Shooter set in WW2, where Germany, the United States and the Soviet Union fight for victory in one grand persistent online war fought by players across the world.
No matter if you play as Infantry, Tank crew, Fighter pilot, Paratrooper, Recon, or as a General taking strategic decisions – everything you do makes a difference in the war.
There is a great variety of authentic weapons and vehicles accessible in the game such as the effective US M1A1 Thompson submachine gun, the legendary German Panzer V Ausf G. ‘Panther’ tank, the excellent Soviet Yak-9B fighter plane, and even a bicycle! The arsenal is constantly growing as updates for the game are released regularly.
In Heroes & Generals your team always has your back. Every single player makes a difference, but you win, lose and make friends as a team. With a growing and welcoming community and a focus on teamplay, Heroes & Generals wants to bring players together and have them make friends from all around the globe.

Howdy,
My first & only steam review so bear with me, i simply want to post something on the current state of Heroes & Generals for those who have yet to play it and who might be tempted to put money into this so called FPS / RTS mix.
H&G is a Free to Play - Pay To Win, FPS/ RTS game in a ww2 setting, sounds fun right ? well it was... it was a great game that i enjoyed playing for over 3k hours and put in some RL money (a regret in hindsight)... unfortunatly this game is being developed by a studio / company that i can only describe as incompetent.
Reto (developers) used to have an active productive community that designed maps, layed out roadmaps, proposed balances to weapons and vehicles and weighed in on how people would have loved to see this game progress, Reto however went in the opposite direction... the "silent majority" direction (also known as the easy money grab direction).
After 3 years the same old bugs still remain unfixed, player options are limited (squad 2.0), the grind has been made infinite unless you buy gold, broken tank system, constant inbalance of weapons (buff / nerfs of weapons after every patch),RTS is broken, etc..
and with their most recent update they broke their own sound system.. i kid you not, RETO have implemented a feature called sound occlusion which is a fancy word for directional sound effected by enviroment...and its a sad joke... you cant tell where people are shooting from or even hear someone when someone is firing a MG42 right next to you...
for me this was "one feature to far"... the feature that broke the camels back if you will.
So my advice to potential H&G players would be... try it out !

Firstly, I received this game for free from Black Shell Media in order to review it. I only managed to get about maybe 10 minutes into the game.

A light hearted parody jab at the 'Silent Hills PT', 'Potato Thriller' tries to walk the line between spook and spoof. The end result stumbles drunkenly as it goes and ultimately falls on its face just shy of the finish line.
The game is intentionally broken in many ways to deliver its jokes which typically hit the mark.  It's the places where the game is broken without intent that pulls the experience down burning away all the goodwill it earned.
Game design structure is important to keep in mind even when dealing with horror parody games.  The pacing of the experience is rough which leaves the horror jump scares feeling unearned.  While the jokes hit well enough but are either cut short or drag on to long turning a laugh into a disappointment.

Gas Guzzlers takes me back a few years to the days when video games were fun first and realistic last. I got it on a whim when it was on sale, and I've gotta say I'm happy with what I payed. At the time of this writing I've only clocked in about two hours, but it was two hours of explosive combat driving with the right amount of humor to leave a smile on your face. This game isn't bogged down by some stupid plot to explain why everyone attached guns to their cars, and there's no slow-moving rpg elements as you build your cars. No, this game is just full-fledged arcade histaria as you blast your way through the pack of cars while Arnold Swartzeneger laughs and screams out cheesy movie quotes. It's a fast-paced game that gives you some challenge, even if it does rely on rubber-band physics. It'll keep you playing on the edge of your seat. If you enjoyed games like "Full Auto", "Twisted Metal," or other similar games, you will enjoy this.

A Weekend With The Black Watchmen ARG
The world is overflowing with mysteries and conspiracy; some are visible to all, but others are less obvious, hidden beneath a layer of secrecy, lies and the occult. If you go deep enough down the rabbit hole you are bound to discover some disturbing things – things almost too plausible to be true. Blood rituals, human sacrifice and experimentation are mainstays of the silver screen, there’s no way that they could be taking place beneath our very noses, or could they? There are agents worldwide investigating these disturbing reports and this weekend I joined them to get to the bottom of some shadowy people and their dealings. This is how I became a member of The Black Watchmen.
I initially mistook The Black Watchmen as just a game, but it is much more than that. I am now part of a secret reconnaissance cell partaking in undercover investigations. My basic training involved learning to crack codes – binary, hexadecimal and rot13 enciphered messages – a cinch given my degree in computer science, but things soon became more difficult. My fellow agents and I were tasked with investigating the disappearance of an antique collector – and that’s when things took a decidedly more sinister turn. The case files we were given, drafted by the first agent on the scene, consisted of nothing but seemingly innocuous images of books, dolls, crucifixes and bottles. The keen-eyed among us were able to identify a rot13 enciphered code in one of the images, which we were then able to decipher manually. The code pointed towards a pastebin link with details of an antique script called “Folio 13″, the kind a collector would love to have in their collection, but how did it tie in with his disappearance?
A Google search for “folio 13″ and “Cipher MMS” lead me down a rabbit hole of religion, conspiracy, secret societies and the occult. I was suddenly in over my head, reading up on ancient Jewish sects and Pope John Paul’s teachings – certainly nothing that could be attributed to the disappearance. I was over thinking things, going way too deep and missing an answer that was right in front of me. The organisation that penned the document wanted it back and was willing to go to any lengths to get it.
As the case was solved I gave myself a pat on the back and put my feet up, but my respite didn’t last long. The agency had heard word that a clinic tied to rumours of human experimentation had reopened its doors and I had been asked to investigate its staff members for any signs of illegal activity. By cross-referencing each staff member’s employment history I was soon able to establish a link between them and illegal human experiments – all those years of Google-fu were finally becoming useful.
With a link established it was tie to go deeper and find out exactly what was going on at the clinic. An undercover team was dispatched after closure to bug the building for remote monitoring. And then silence. The agency ceased contact until Sunday when all agents abruptly received an email informing us that the alert level had been “raised to 3″. With urgency we made our way to our usual channels of communication (IRC) and began to converse about what could be happening, and there it was. In our game clients was an image coded in braille.
The image was surprisingly complex, containing not only the braille code, but a map that could be uncovered by applying various filters, and behind that were words which turned out to be street names. Some very intelligent deciphering later we had uncovered a restaurant in Portland called “The Fried Onion”.  Initial reconnaissance of the location yielded no results, but now as the restaurant opens for business, we have agents on route for a face to face with forces unknown.
Now we wait

Long story short, this isn't a game for you if you don't plan to give out your cell phone number, actual address, and from what I've researched, most of your time in order to experience all of the game's content.
If that
something you're into, however, then this is probably going to be quite the experience.
The idea behind the game's mechanics is very interesting. It teaches you to think outside the box, analyze details carefully, and especially do your homework and deeper research into the subject in mind. In order to truly rise above the ranks and reach the top (so to speak,) you'll need to give out information such as your phone number, address, and to quote the game, "You may be contacted via phone calls, at all hours of the day or night, receive packages from the mail, and experience real world interactions with our assets in the field." Now, let me go ahead and say that this is not
in order to experience the game. But if you expect to fully complete the game without giving this information out, good luck with that. The fact that I have to give my personal information out in order to get a full 100%, however, I don't. First of all, I'm recommending this game because *I* like it. That may seem obvious, but the reason I say it is that this game is most definetly not your "typical" game, and I can totally understand that a lot of people will hate it. If you don't like doing challenging puzzles where you have to look outside the game itself to find the answer, if you really don't like being part of the online "community" of a game, and if you don't have a certain tolerance for bashing your head against puzzles and skin-crawling creepyness in storylines, this game is not for you.
Awesome Thing #1: Permanent ARG
----------------------------------
The concept of a permanent ARG is really interesting. Basically the client is only part of the game, the *real* game is the overarching plot being run by puppetmasters (they are evil and sadistic and we love them).
I'm crap at explaining this, but it's a really cool overal effect of a kind-of-real-world story going on. If you know what an ARG is and/or have participated in them (for example, the ones that were done around events/releases in The Secret World, which were run by some of the same people as this game) then you have some kind of familliarity with how it works. I dunno, google it I guess.
Also, get used to googling things. And going off on tangents and chasing red herrings and having a really weird and sometimes frankly disturbing browser history.
Awesome Thing #2: The Community
--------------------------------------
I've been around this game and its community since the first kickstarter attempt, and first, let me say it's pretty hard to separate the two, and that's a good thing (usually). Unless you are some kind of puzzle solving supergenius, you *will* get stuck at some point, and many members of the community are totally willing to help without being too spoilery. There are also real world missions (yes, really, this has already happened in Alpha and in previous games) so it's actually requred for the community to find someone in a city where the clue leads to go pick up some dead drop somewhere. It is awesome when you get to be a part of something like this, even if it's just watching a webcam feed to see if/when an agent shows up...
Neutral Thing #1: Hard Puzzles
--------------------------------
The solo puzzles can be pretty hard (judging by some of the alpha and beta puzzles) but this version of the game starts you off pretty easy, and there's always the community to help. Check the forums, check IRC etc.
I really like the challenge of the puzzles. I like think-y games more than action games. This is a think-y game x 1000. I get that a lot of people won't like that, but there it is.
Sometimes the leaps of logic required can be a *liiittle* too far, in my opinion, but it's generally pretty fair, if hard.
Neutral Thing #2: Creepy♥♥♥♥♥♥br>-------------------------------
As for the creepyness, well. It just is. Some of the subjects in the puzzles involve illegal medical/psychological experiments on humans. One previous mission (may or may not be linked to in this game) involved tracking a serial killer. Some folks might find these things too disturbing, and I get that.
Me, I like spooky games. This one is spooky. If you don't like spooky, maybe not a good fit.
Not So Awesome Thing: Missing Out
--------------------------------------
My main complaint for the game is that partly because of my own bad timing/luck I've missed a bunch of the cool things that happened during testing. You really need to keep up with the game and be connected with the community (which may not be convenient for a lot of people, myself included some of the time) or you can miss things. Which leads to being confused as to what the bleep is going on when you try and jump back in to chat/forums, and some dissapointment at missing the coolness that went on while you were away...
Other than that though, this gets a thumbs up from me. I'm really excited to see where this game goes, and I hope it gets extended for more than one season. And that we don't get too many (fictional!) agents killed.
...And that I get kidnapped.

Well, it is a Star Trek themed MMO...
+ Tribbles
+ NPCs to fill your party
+ Crew/party customization
+ Freely re-customize your character from the hubworld
+ Graphics Engine.  While the graphics and performance are passable, the amount of options, and the way they're instantly applied without any negative impact, is very nice.
+ For a free2play game, it doesn't seem especially pay2win or pay2fun.  Only a handful of vanity items, many of which are already available for free.  Though I haven't reached endgame, so who knows how it goes.
+- Small single-player semi-unique quest zones
+- Graphics and performance, passable but not impressive
+- You can freely customize your uniform, but most equipment doesn't have a visual impact
+- Fully auto auto-attacks, this helps prevent the staring at hotkey timers problem that most MMOs suffer from, but target switching can fail between kills
- Global chat is cringeworthy
- PvE queues have cooldowns
- Difficult to locate quest objectives
- Can't tell which doors are openable
- Uninteresting, overcomplicated skill tress, which just provide stat boosts
- The bridge of your ship is just a novelty, and not an integrated part of gameplay
- PvE Qs don't seem balanced at all, joining low level players with max level players
- Selling items is a nonsensical mess, and can't be done directly from the inventory
- While there are occasionally dialogue choices, they don't seem to have any impact
- For a game so old, there are still quite a few bugs, typos, and general unintuitiveness
- Seperate sets of controls for Ground and Space.  These would be better as an optional feature, since for the most part, these modes function identically
- Almost all quests are identical.  Read a wall of text from an NPC, warp to an area in orbit around a planet, read another wall of text, fight in space, read another wall of text, beam to the ground, read another wall of text, ground combat, read another wall of text.  Every time.  Read another wall of text.

This is a game I wanted to like, but just couldn't.  To start with, I love Zoo Tycoon, even as an adult, so I figured that I'd enjoy this game.  And there are details about it that I DO like even better than Zoo Tycoon -- such as needing to wait for animals to gestate and training the animals.
But the controls are just so totally cumbersome that it's agonizing.  It's WORSE than the old controls to the original Zoo Tycoon.  There is no way to add gridlines on the terrain, so digging holes to place sea creatures in is a nightmare.  The zookeepers, trash guys, etc, all have these annoyingly small, diagonal zones -- which means you're placing workers every other exhibit.  The customers make me want to feed them all to the lions, because they're constantly demanding more plants, more food stands, more decorations, etc... even if it's only been 10 squares since the last food stand and they're three steps from a decoration.  Oh, and the decorations are (a) ugly and (b) extremely limited, so there's no satisfation in prettifying your park.
Having played through almost all of the missions now, I would not recommend this game.  I wish it was better, but it's just not.  Oh, and the fact that I CAN play through almost all the missions in a couple of hours also should warn people how easy it is.  It's just too bad there's so little satisfaction in winning.  :(

The Bots are really fast if you want it. Very smart if you want it. They make you feel like a little baby trying to play the game if you want it! But they can be very stupid if you want it too. [There's a big variety of configurations that you can apply to the game before entering the action.]
The graphics are very good. Not to argue about. And looks pretty modern even after so many years.
Sound effects and music not so addictive like the UT99 ones, but close enough to make you feel fine.
Cons:
The Campaign looks boring if you don't like some of the game modes. But you can always go to the Instant Action mode. It gives the game the replay factor that every FPS should give.
The Multiplayer mode is dead. (It's not because there are no people playing this game anymore, but Epic Games just has unplugged the servers after years and years of service. There are a mod somewhere that allows you to play in that mode if you want to search for it) But back in time, when you could play this mode, the number of custom servers with tons of custom maps and mods to download were so big that the wait until all the stuff to be downloaded and you finally enter the server was so absurd that you were disencouraged to play there anyway.
It's a game that came out before the Steam, so there are more players with versions of the game out of here than the Steam players (but if you really want to play with friends in multiplayer mode, the mod that allow this, allows you to enjoy the game with all the people around the world too ;) )

I played this at some point, pretty sure as a PS3 demo. Bought it now from a Black Friday sale for $5 here on Steam. Barely worth $5. It seems super short and limited in event location, even with the different types of races.
*Note; playing with PS3 controller [via SCP Controller].
If you're used to ATV Off-Road Fury controls, or even other MX vs ATV games - throw that out the window. The right joystick for rider control does more turning than the actual steering stick. There's virtually no preload. Heaven save you if you go off a jump a little sideways; there is virtually no correcting it and you probably won't land it. Yes, it's more realistic, but for a game it's super obnoxious. Yeah, you can make a game last longer if you have to keep re-racing.
Racing and completing Cups doesn't mean as much if you don't reazlie you are. After the 3rd heat you just go back to the race menu and select a new one. You can find your way to the garage and see what else you can buy every now and then, but no where is there a satisfying "New Unlock" splash-screen, or any kind of notification at all. For a racing series, that's actually super disappointing. Alot of the fun of these types of games is winning/unlocking new vehicles and equipment. Without that, the whole game just feels like tediously limping through each race.
Good luck with the multi-vehicle races. The second a trophy truck touches you, you're either rolling through the mud or are bounced into the trees.
Stunt controls are odd, and a little lagged. So I don't do much of them yet.
Some positives:
The addition of real-time ruts that stay in the dirt for the whole session is nice! They don't disappear 10ft behind you like some games.
Graphics are ok, but the ground texture loses resolution the second you get near it, especially the hills.
Overall, No, I would not recommend this. Either go back to Unleashed and enjoy retro graphics, or wait for a new version.

Never before had I felt the rush if battle like this. I have overcome many trials, many tribulations, fought 100 men with an army of 25 and rose victorious. But this, this... this is something different. As my men prepared for the siege on Derchios Castle, Lord Artimenner stood by my side and said to me, "Sire, no matter the outcome of this battle, I wish you to know I will fight with you to the end (Relationship with Lord Artimenner increased from 45 to 51). We gathered around and laid out the plan. We knew that many of us would not make it back, but we also knew that once we get through the outer defences of archers and crossbowmen, we would be through the wort of it. As long as we survived the outer defences, the castle was as good as ours. We were outnumbered, with 150 of us against Count Grainwad and his 200 trained soldiers. To make matters worse, Count Grainwad was my father-in-law. Relation aside, I was content to take his castle, and with it, the remnants of Swadia. The next morning, after the ladders were complete, we marched towards the castle. Men all around me fell to the ground, as if pinned to the ground by the arrows that pierced them. I drew my bow and began returning volleys of arrows as my men climbed the ladders. I managed to thin the numbers of the archers by a substantial amount, and began my journey up the ladder. Although that ladder had to have been only about 30 feet tall, I felt as if we were climbing it for hours. The tension and whispers flowing within the remnants of my soldiers were high, but I would have none of it. "Stop your talking and return fire", I recall saying to one of my men, who was talking to another about his wife and child he had left back at home, in the village of Tadsamesh. Once we arrived at the top of the ladder, we saw it. Dozens upon dozens of corpses and men screaming in pain as the last morsels of life drained from their gaze, some of them mine, but most of them Grainwad's. The arrows flying all around my head only made me more angry and viscious. That's when I spotted him, Grainwad, commanding a squad of archers to fire at my direction. I felt an arrow pierce my side, but it had done little more than a slight poke, thanks to my armor. I drew my cleaver from its sheathe and ran towards Grainwad. He put up a good fight, but soon he fell to my feet and begged for mercy. I would deal with him later, however, as I had to continue to command my men to finish the remaining Swadian pigs. Derchios Castle was mine. Unfortunately, Grainwad managed to escape before I was able to apprehend them. I would get him eventually, I told myself. I knew my journey wad far from over, a few petty castles weren't going to win the entire realm. I began to set my sights on Dhirim. Soon, Calradia will know my name, and tremble in fear when it is mentioned. Soon, I would be king, and Calradia will only consist of one kingdom, my kingdom, Pugglingtonia, and I will rule it, me, king, King xXx_Booty_Smasher_xXx

The follow up to the original Mount and Blade game. Just like the original, it's a realistic take on the time when Kings, Queens, Knights and Lords ruled over lands everywhere. There are no dragons or magic spells (unless you download the mods for those types of things), just good old fashioned Medieval Times. Without the plague obviously.
This one has some minor gameplay changes such as hitboxes feeling different, and some balancing changes from what I can see, however, this is by far the superior game. Not only can you take the same pathes you did in the original game when it comes to ruling land (become a lord for a kingdom, help someone who believes they are the rightful ruler rebel against the current king, etc) but now you can finally start your own kingdom. There's also many new features, such as the ability to open your own shops in towns.
Definitely pick it up as it's a game you're going to sink many, many hours into.

Metal Slug 3 is absolutely one of the greatest action arcade games of all time. This is the best game in the series, with the biggest and coolest bosses, and it has an extra-long final mission that is absolutely epic. If you like run and gun action, this is one of the best to ever do it. You can’t go wrong.  *However*…this isn’t a great port at all. It’s barely even a competent port. You're gonna get slowdown, input lag, online lag, and washed-out visuals. You’re given some filters and fake scanlines to supposedly make the visuals more authentic, but the effect doesn’t look very good. It’s really disappointing. In fact, of the four Metal Slug games that DotEMU has ported to Steam, Metal Slug 3 probably looks and plays the worst.
Now listen, none of these issues are necessarily game-breaking. If you decide to get this version of the game, you'll certainly have fun - there's a two-player mode, you can change the difficulty, and you can skip right to your favorite missions. So, you’re not going to have a bad time or anything - just remember that this is an arcade game, which means that A) it's designed to eat up your lives/quarters, and B) it’s really short. As long as you're aware of those two facts, you'll have a total blast.
But even as good as the game is, I still can't recommend such a bad port. There are so many superior ways that you can play Metal Slug 3 in any number of Neo Geo collections or compilations. Plus, you're being asked to pay 8 bucks for the pleasure of playing a crummy, sloppy port. That's just criminal! If you're interested in this game, you should absolutely play it...but not like this. Go track down a good Neo Geo collection or Metal Slug compilation for the console or handheld or your choice, and you'll have a much higher quality experience.

When I hear “bunch of misfits” I always think of these guys here. They are united by one goal, they are brave, they are weird, they are human, robot, mole and a smelly old man. They are ... Lionhearts!!! This is one of the wackiest game i've ever played. I can't express how crazy and absurd (in a good way) are the story and characters. I write this review with a huge grin on my face. In almost every cutscene I laugh my♥♥♥♥♥off.
You are the Lionhearts, a bunch of misfits, who are trying to save their kingdom from the evil king Forge. He wants to unlock the power of the Book of Rule, so it's up to our heroes to steal the book from him and use it to undo all the bad things. Let me introduce the Lionhearts (drum roll): Q – big robot that like to drink tea and he always have a cup in his hand; Jonesy – a mole, often mistaken for a rat and everybody likes to make fun of him; Rexus – short  and smelly old man, that put a spell to locked the book's power. He have some sort of jedi powers and he is blind as a bat; finally the character you control Roman. He always wear a red scarf around his mouth, like he is in the wild west. Truth to be told the game kinda feel that way. The story is complete bonkers and I love it. It will take to very different places and you will meet a whole bunch of insane characters, more crazy than our heroes. King Fogre is also insane. He sends his son Stig to lead his army againts the Lionhearts and he is … to say it politely, not very bright person. I don't want to spoil more. One last thing. In every cutscene you will see amazing stuff.
The gameplay is straightforward. It's a third-person shooter and you play only as Roman, but Jonesy and Q are always behind you. They help, but you will do most of the shooting. You can give them three command – guard an area, return to you and defend you. They have their health bars, but if some of them die it's not instant game over. You will see them in the next level if the story dictates that. I try always to make them run over a health pack, but it's not that easy.
The weapons are great. You have some standard like submachine gun, sniper rifle and bolt action rifle, but the others are amazing – Gurnar personal mortar who looks like a tuba and fires granades, rocket launcher that can fire up to four homing rockets and my favourite and the most unique ever created in any media – land shark gun! (появяват се думите една по една и една акула) You fire it at some target and the shark start “swimming” and then it start to eating enemies. It will follow you around for a short period of time. The ammo for all the weapons can be acquired in two ways. The first is by killing enemies they drop different types (they also drop health packs) and the second is by going into “The Grunt & Polewart”. It's a pub. There also you can change your weapon, fill up your ammo and health. What better way to get them and drink a beer.
The secondary weapons are also insane. Sticky bomb that makes enemies run in panic when it's on them. It's funny to see them running around and screaming. There are more. Guy Fawks Traitor bomb – turns enemies againts each other, Knockout bomb – giant boxing glove that punches enemies from a distance, Portable Black Hole and finally the best from the secondary – Tropsy Turvy bomb. It turns the world upside down and enemies fall to their death. If the weapons were all standard the gameplay would be kinda boring.
The level design is okay. There vast open spaces, but earlier levels feel kinda empty. Yes, you will shoot constantly, but there isn't something interesting sights to see. But later levels are much better. Most of the buildings can be destroyed and for such an old game, it's interesting to see it. You will see snowy villige, shooting bad guys near the beach or in a trenches and so on. The levels have this weird mix setting between middle ages and steam punk. Really interesting design. There also hidden tokens spread around the levels and when you find them you will unlock things like big head, big hands, another difficulty and so on.
After every few levels there is a turret section. They are 2-3 minutes long and don't overstay their welcome. They are fun and challenging enough. And speaking of difficulty this game is not easy. The enemies are not Storm troopers. They are accurate and they will shoot on sight. I died quite a few times, so you have to use all your tools to survive.
One of the best things here is the voice acting. It's simply amazing. When you combine it with the great writing, you have fantastic recipe for laughing a lot. All actors have british accent. Some sound more scottish, others more english. They all do amazing job. Even the side characters are greatly voiced. My favourite character is Rexus. He is more goofy and with him are the best scenes.
The soundtrack is also good. Typical orchestral tracks, but some have this military vibe and feel like you are in a war. Others are more ambient, but nothing is more satisfying that to kill enemies accompanied by scottish bagpipes. They will lift your spirit up and you will fight more agressively!
The things I don't like here are not many. The graphics are not a problem for me. The game came out in 2003, so you can't expect to look great. The biggest problem is the lack of enemy variety. You will see all the time the grunt with bolt action rifle, sniper rifle or the guy with submachine gun or granade launcher. There are few flying like zeppelin and the really big enemies (they are tough and fun to fight), but they are few and far between. The other problem that people may have is with the gameplay. It's repetetive, but I like it. The crazy guns and funny cutscence is what kept the game become stale.
The game is made by Planet Moon Studios, which also made another underrated cult classic – Giants: Citizen Kabuto, a game ahead of it's time. It's like their faith to make underrated games. If you didn't guess by now, I love AnD. Everything is over the top! The characters, the guns, the enemies. It's funny as hell, you have crazy weapons, hilarious cutscenes, it runs great on a modern PC and on top of that you have a freaking jetpack! Instantly 10/10! Bad joke aside this is a refreshing idea to spice up the gameplay. It adds verticality. Some enemies have it too and it's fun to fly around and try to shoot each other. Or just grab the homing rocket launcher. You have it in almost half of the game and it's amazing! It's not an expensive title, so go now and buy it. I had hell of a good time with Armed and Dangerous.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Bugs- They don't fix many of them. Not even gamebreaking ones.

The Elder Scrolls III Morrowind is one of the best purchases and games I have ever played in my life. I had first played Morrowind back in Middle School on the old Xbox system and fell in love with the world, the mystery, and the open endedness of the game world. After wanting the game really bad, I decided to purchase it on Steam and it was a wise decision. Morrowind gives the player the ability to truly do whatever they please, create the character of their dreams, and explore an enormous world with amazing characters, creatures, and cities to explore. The Elder Scrolls III Morrowind is certainly one of the best Elder Scrolls games I have played out of the entire series and I wish more of the game would have the same feel as Morrowind. I would certainly recommend Morrowind if you love a good RPG, but also if you love open ended exploreation and the ability to go anywhere and do anything you please. Out of 5 stars, I would give Morrowind a 5.
Also included in this purchase is the official expansion packs for Morrowind as well. The first expansion pack The Elder Scrolls III: Tribunal takes the player to a new location called Mournhold the capital of Morrowind Proper. The expansion is exciting but after a few hours of exploring it does get boring as it is possible to discover everything you can in this expansion. The city does add more quests to the game which is exciting but the quests are certaintly not easy and may take a while, but that is what makes the expansion great. Of course if you purchase Morrowind on Steam you will automantically get this expansion, but out of 5 stars, I would give Tribunal a 3.
The second expansion pack is The Elder Scrolls III: Bloodmoon, which adds a large island territory called Solstheim which the player can travel to and complete new quests to stop the Bloodmoon prophecy from taking place. The island adds even more beautiful scenery, creatures, and towns and cities to be discovered. It is certainly an entertaining expansion as the player is exposed to new landscapes different from those of Vvardenfell and it adds yet another good 15 hours to the already massive game. Of course if you purchase Morrowind on Steam you will automatically get this expansion, but out of 5 stars, I would give Bloodmoon a 5.

the cell stage is based on the feed and grow mechanic. you eat, grow, upgrade and the cycle continues. to be honest i think that this stage couldve been a bit longer or exiting as after the first few minutes the stage becomes repetitive and boring, but not so bad that its unplayable. the ai is decent, not the best in the game but its supposed to be that way.

easily my favorite stage in the game, the creature stage adds a lot of new mechanics and takes you to the surface of your world (eg: lv-420 which is mine). you can befriend or extinct whole species and modify your creature, new and improved with legs and arms. further on in the stage, you can create a team or clan to help you with your tasks. there are a lot of features to unlock for your creature like wings... my favorite. the ai has improved from the last level again, following evolution.

from here, this is where my intrest in the game plummits. the tribal stage is similar to age of empires but you can befriend or terminate tribes. when you do this you will get a totem to add to your pole. theres not really much to say now. the ai is about the same as last stage.

well isnt it surprising that this stage is like the civ games. you create a city, you send out boats, cars and airships to get resources and to claim or destroy other cities. i cant tell how good the ai is.

SPACE!! THIS ISNT SPORE WORS (the spelling of wars is intentional) if the're going to put this effort into the game they might aswell just make the game the cell and creature stage because there so much better than the garbage that insues. id play the sims or simcity if i want a civilation simulatior.

while this isnt really a stage i thought i would talk about this. this is a great time killer which gives you all the unlockables to create what ever you wish. people who buy the expansion packs can make extrodinary creature with this tool, and people call it that, a tool, one of the best tools in games.

overall i think that spore was overhyped in its production which led to people discarding the game, me personally didnt follow the game in production and i was still disaapointed with the trio of the final stages. if your going to buy this game do your self a favour and dont play the final 3 missions. play the first 2 only, unless your curious, spore get 3.5 stars out of 5

There are a bunch of classes to unlock, but the unlock screen also suffers issues, whereas you have several sub-menus but going back goes to the main menu, so you need to do a ton of clicking for no reason. Some "lock" icons do nothing while others show something, again making the UI a mess, cluttered, and unintuitive.
So to the game then; Again more UI issues (tiny blocks around the screen everywhere, hard to see, unhelpful and terrible) when you get dropped in your base. Pretty much empty. You learn few controls from the hint screen but most you have to look up (at the main menu, yeah, can't ingame, great again). Entering "the dungeon" 2 enemies spawn; wizards or bats. You can only attack left or right for some reason, feeling horrible and hitboxes are a pain. Overall this seems like a Binding of Isaac clone in execution, just with just 1 axis rather than 2 (or diagonal) and any (ranged) powers (you know; that class-stuff?) are so expensive you can use them twice ingame and never again. I've tried a wizard and both my fireballs went the wrong way since control is so horrible, and no way to regain mana at all that I saw.
Drops are horrid too, again the extreme tiny text doesn't help, no idea if the new gear is better worse than the old (and to replace you need to manually drop one than pick up the new identical looking one rather than having a replacee that would make sense). I found a key but couldn't actually use it on the keylocked door :/, got a raw bat, cooked it, then had no idea how to eat it (or if that would do anything). All in all, it's rather painful to play.
In one playthrough I visited someone in my base and then had no way to remove their upgrade screen, so had left the room to get rid of the screen (difficult!). But from then on ever time I clicked interact that screen popped up again and never left, and eventually I died behind it.
Talking about dying, it says to press ENTER but that doesn't work. Respawn just dumps you on the main menu to restart over.
Progress is saved inbetween games I think, considering people I met last game ended up in your safehouse, which you can't return to after going in a dungeon and offering upgrades and all (I think). FarSky is easily one of my favorite games of all time. Beautiful scenery and well-chosen music give this game a perfect atmosphere, especially when using headphones. In fact, sound plays a huge role in this game, as learning what noises each critter makes can save your life. Rushing water can tell you when a hunter is charging at you, the chirping of dolphins can reassure you when your nervous, and a whale's song still draws me to the windows of my base no matter how many times I've heard it.
However, audio can only take a game so far without good visuals, and FarSky has some of the best visuals I've seen. Screenshot opportunities abound, and within 10 minutes of gameplay I was able to snap one of a whale swimming above some giant seaweed while a school of manta rays attempted to get out of the way.
Then, night begins to fall. Hunters begin to awake, and the peacful ocean floor becomes their hunting ground. As the ocean becomes dark, you have the choice to either face the oceans predators, or stay in your base until dawn. That's a lot of how this game works; it's a risk versus reward system. You can either stay where it's safe, or gain resources to advance.
Of course, with this being an underwater game, you will find various things to help you throughout your world. Mineral deposits, wrecked ships, treasure chests, and much more rarely, entire underwater bases. The bases are yet another example of risk versus reward. Since most bases you'll find (besides your starting base) are flooded, you'll be faced with a choice to either use some materials to fix up the base and claim it as your own, or just salvage what you can and move on.
When you start, you are given only the most basic of supplies, and you have to swim a bit before you even get to your base. Once you do, the biggest concern in this game is hunger. Hunger is more likely to kill new players than anything else, as you need to play a while before you have a stable food source. You can either take the time to grow your own food, or risk attracting predators by killing fish.
While this game has many strengths, it also has a few weaknesses, as follows:
One last thing: There are some people who say this game needs a higher difficulty.The way to do this would not be to challenge the player's skill, but to challenge their mind. A harder version of this game should employ strategy rather than merely how powerful your equipment is or how well you can aim.
Overall, this game is a gem that merely needs to be polished a bit more. Come for the gameplay, stay for the beauty.

Two minor flaws - AI in onslaught mode is very dumb and FOV is somewhat narrow. Everything else is just what you would expect from an Unreal game.

I have to say, in the beginning, I was
skeptical. The game's menu and overall initial attitude made it look as if it just another hastily put together project by a teenager with Unity assets. However, upon actually getting into a game, my view completely changed. Sure, some of the reflections still looked a little overdone and typical of a generic racing game, but that's where any similarites ended between the two. The rest of the game is top indie-quality, by which I mean no condemnation; rather, I say it because it's got more charm and heart put into it than a AAA title of the same name could with the budget the developer had.
They definitely squeezed everything out of the engine they used. Visuals are top-notch, and the game is
with
of options, only lacking borderless windowed support, but not something most independent games have anyways. Plenty of modes (Deathmatch, CTF, Battle-Races, and then just straight-up vanilla racing, with a few explosions added in for good measure) plenty of guns (chainguns, rocket launchers, mortars, and even the legendary railgun from Vigilante 8), and plenty of cars to fill them with (parodied versions of Ford offerings, Pontaics, Mazdas, and even a Lambo), with multiplayer support included, too. I have to say, in my experiences with studios I've never heard of prior to buying a game, only rarely have I ever seen a multiplayer game play so smoothly, much less a racing one. Hardly any issues, besides the fact that the Steamworks invite system doesn't seem to properly work with this title. Even so, the game has enough variety in servers to quickly refer a friend to the one you're joining, or a direct-ip input option to refer them directly to your server.
This game had everything I was looking for in a quality game in the same vein as the death-race games of old, and I
it to anyone even considering the game if you had any interest in the genre; it's the bee's knees.
