Of all the games I play, this is one of the most enjoyable. I love being able to control an army, give strategic orders, and seige castles. The base game is great in it's own right, though as of this review (Sept 2015), the game is beginning to feel a bit dated. The mod community has kept this game alive and running strong as well. I recommend it for the vanilla experience, and when you want to try something more, take a look at the available mods. There are plenty out there that change the game either with just a few minor tweaks and additions, ranging all the way to complete overhauls that feel like a different game, or even an expansion.
PROS
1. Create and advance your commander either as a mercenary, bandit, or noble lord of a faction.
2. Raise an army, and level up troops into an unstoppable force.
3. Become King/Queen of a faction, then command other lords to assist you in battle.
4. Smooth gameplay, well polished. Good soundtrack.
5. Balanced troops, for the most part. You can make any army work with the proper tactics.
6. LARGE mod community ensures there are tons of new and exciting ways to experience the game.
7. ALL the below listed CONS have been addressed and resolved with various mods. No reason not to try it.
CONS
1. Base game can feel repetative at times.
2. Difficulty sliders top off at normal, and can sometimes make the game feel a bit too easy.
3. Limited to 150 troops shared between armies, if you do not modify settings.
4. AI can be a bit derpy at times. By default, enemy troops charge straight into your forces with no tactics.
TL;DR
Do I recommend this game? Yes. Absolutely yes. I also recommend mods to bring the game a little more life if you feel something is lacking.

This game attempts to give us Minecraft underwater, and comes up with some interesting idea of its own, but sadly falls short of being an enjoyable game.
This is Minecraft with an emphasis on the mining, not the crafting. Base construction is little more than expanding a pre-existing building. Mining consists of holding down a button while numbers pop up - unless you get an extractor to do it for you. So what's left to do? Well, explore, and that's something this game does well. The underwater landscape is pretty and full of life, and it's quite enjoyable to bounce around, uncovering more of your mini-map.
Your aim is to find and mine enough materials to build the best items, so you're able to get deep/far enough to find all the parts of your submarine. This is fine, but makes the game essentially one long grind. Chances are you'll die of starvation your first time. Want to kill that fish with your giant Big Daddy drill? Nope, tough, go craft a knife, which is tricky to kill things with at the best of times. Knife not cutting it? Your only other option is a harpoon gun, which you have to craft ammo for. Up until this point, the predators of the sea prove to be quite a challenge, but from this point on, it's smooth sailing. You could build up your base if you wanted, but there isn't really anything to be gained from it. Then it's just a case of Slenderman-style collecting until you're home-bound. And then there's a sandbox mode... though I have no idea why you'd want to do that.
In short, this is a fun little romp around an underwater area, but honestly there's not much 'game' here. Mine the stuff; Shoot the stuff; Find the stuff; and you're done in a couple of hours.

There are a lot of people who compare this game to Zoo Tycoon, and for good reason. It's basically the same premise, after all. This game cannot be faulted for being less realistic than the ZT series, because it is, and that does add a little depth to the simulation.
BUT.
The interface is far, far more clunky than ZT's, and some of the design decision are questionable. For example, each zookeeper you hire requires you to build him a special Zookeeper's Hut, which is a three-story-tall eyesore. And he can only handle about two enclosures, so prepare to build a lot of them. Also, some of their claims about number of animals are specious (You can't have Rabbits AND Bunnies.), and the overall assortment of things to customize the look of your zoo is FAR smaller than ZT (No flower beds? Really? And the entire list of statues I can build is 'Bear' and 'Panda bear'.)
All in all, I think ZT2 is a far better game, and kinda regret this purchase.

The best zoo-tycoon game in my opinion. The WP series features heavily on realism, unlike the Zoo Tycoon series, although that series is good too. Animals look realistic, as are their AI behavior. It takes a while for babies to be born, unlike ZT where it apparently happens instantly. Food don't magically appear out of thin air to feed your animals. like in ZT. You need to place the proper facilities to make the food.
WP 2 also focuses more on those rare/unknown animals, unlike ZT where they feature mostly well known/popular animals. I like this idea, because it lets people who play this game learn about animals they've never seen/or read about before. For example, there's the frilled sharks from the marine expansion. I doubt many people who aren't shark fans would know what they are.
The map isn't really set up like a grid (ZT again). You simply 'paint' the paths along the ground for your customers to walk on, which makes your zoo look more realistic if you're using stone or dirt paths for instance.
One thing I do like in ZT over WP2 though is setting up your habitats for marine animals. It's very easy to do in ZT but I find it frustrating to do the same in WP2.
Both zoo series are good, but if you want more realism in a zoo game, then WP2 is the way to go. With 150+ animals, realistic AI, along with loads of plants and attractions, etc, however, you should buy it anyway.

This is a great and relatively short game!
I quite enjoy perspective-based puzzle games (although there don't seem to be too many around).  This game was no exception.
It had a beautiful and simple aesthetic, and was quite colorful.  The sound/music (mostly an ambient, atmospheric humming sort of sound), didn't distract from the puzzles, and sounded excellent.  Thankfully, the character's walking pace was quite quick.
The character is controlled simply by clicking where you wish to go.
The puzzles were, on the whole pretty good.  Sometimes the amount of things that were moving when rotated things was a bit much, however.  Occasionally, the puzzles felt as though I just solved them by trying a bunch of different things out.  Also, sometimes the puzzles hold your hand a bit, which can be either good or bad, depending on the difficulty and your prowess at this game.
After completing a majority of the levels, I found myself just grinning at the overall cleverness of the level.  Most of the puzzles were satisfying to solve.
Overall, this was a great game, and I'm glad I impulse bought it! :D

I jumped in on this after seeing Kripp's promo video for the game.  It looked interesting, and I wanted to see what it did better than Duelyst and Hearthstone.  I went 3-0 in my casual games and went 7-3 in my first arena run.  So after 13 games, here are my thoughts.
It's interesting, but unfinished.  A lot of non-blocker UI bugs, but nothing that is too distracting.  There is a LOT of room for quality of life UI improvements.  But there essentially was a built-in deck tracker buried in a menu in-game, so that's nice.
Overall I thought it was fun, but in 2 of my 3 losses I got utterly crushed by Lernaean Hydra (an OP legendary card).  In Arena, a mode where you randomly draft your deck.  The design of this card is so bad that it really just put me off, echoing similar poor design choices in Hearthstone.  Seeing this card, I just said to myself, "Do I want to play another digital CCG where my non-combo opponent can win the game on one top deck when I'm at full health?"  The answer ends up being, no, I don't.  There are too many games to play out there.  We don't have to be forced to play games with bad design holes like this, even if they do have a good aesthetic.
Currently, this is in beta, but it has a fully functioning cash shop from what it looks like.  Personally, I consider a game with a cash shop released.  The beta label is there to shield developers from criticism while accepting cash from consumers for an incomplete game.  But that's really my own personal hill I like to die on, and doesn't really factor into my review.

Awesome underwater survival game.  After playing through both Adventurer (easy) mode and Survival (hard) mode, I can say this game can be tough, but is mostly fair.  Simple crafting system, three depths that offer completely different ecosystems (fish/predators, ores that can be mined, even the seaweed rewards and appearances vary on depth).  A bit of advice if you do buy this game, on Survival mode, focus on building yourself a nice self-sustained farm first.  After you have hundreds of potatoes and carrots, you have the means to heal yourself for a long time, which is nice since one death is game over.  Other than that, save some gold then once you get copper and manganese, you can build a little army of harpoon turrets.  Every time you steal crystal which is one of the most valuable resources, krakens will come after you, which are the toughest monster in the game.  Those harpoon turrets will make quick work of them, combined with a spear gun of your own.  Took me 6 hours to fully explore the map on hard mode, but it was well worth it.

Wonderfully irreverent humor and surprisingly solid if not deep puzzle mechanics. While I would call Hunie Pop a casual game there was nothing casual about it's development. Great art and a fun fully voiced cast put it way above similar games that rely on sex appeal to hide bad gameplay.

HuniePop is hilarious, in a 'what the hell am I doing with my life' and 'I hope no one ever finds out I play this game' kind of way. I am simultaneously embarrassed for myself and wholly too amused to care whenever I boot this game up!
The art style is bright, clean, and aesthetically pleasing to those that enjoy an anime style. While the ladies themselves do nothing for my libido they're likely considered hot to the majority of players- and I get to enjoy the numerous variety of hair and clothing styles that you can earn for each of them.
Gameplay is very simple, match 3 or more of the same tokens to achieve affection points for your lady of choice. There are 12 girls total, and each date you go on fills a heart meter and escalates the amount of points you need to succeed when on your next date. Throw gifts at her to make her happy, and ply her with alcohol and food to sway her opinion of you further. Date a lady four times and she'll spend the night. There are perks that can be unlocked by talking to the ladies, and you can buy specialty gifts using game currency.
Lastly I should probably mention that if you're an achievement hunter this game could be 100% with a moderate amount of time and a bit of effort!
Play for the puzzles, stay for the shoulder boulders.

Overall rating: 9/10

This here is a warning to others about problems I suffered. First off, the game drops to like 10fps when you full screen. There is a workaround for it, but I shouldn't have to do so and I've played other games using the same engine version without this problem.
Secondly, the controls. I have a Dual Shock 3 and it sets my left stick as the movement. This along with the fact that the game is only 4 way directional and your character runs everywhere they go makes even navigating the game world a chore. All too often I pass up my destination by a tile or two or it detects slight movement in an adjacent direction. This means when I'm holding right but move it even slightly up, it will now register as only 'up' being pressed since there's no diagonals. The worst part about it all is that there's no key or button binding options at all and users will have to resort to external solutions a second time just to make the game tolerable.
This is all a real pity because of what I did play, the battle system looks well thought out. The graphics are great even if the sprites are a bit small in-battle, but they are well animated. The extreme briefness of the intro is right up my alley. All of this means nothing though if the base controls and display have to be modified outside the game program making for a frustrating and inconvenient experience for most.

This game is quite nice - and rather short. Is this a negative? I am not quite sure due to the battle system. I am not quite sure if I would have enjoyed it that much when it would be double the length. The game mechanic does a nice twist to the common turn-based RPG battle system. Every attack (determined by the weapon you choose every turn, you will have a handful like some game series heroes) will take some time to do - leaving you open or defending you the time doing so. The same goes for your enemies. Knowing when to strike, when to defend is crucial. Sounds nice, works nice but can get stale over the time.
The story isn't that big of an impact - though it is nice to experience (similar to a bed time story. You enjoy it, maybe learn a thing or two, and can move on.)
You get roughly 2 hours to 6 hours playtime. Replay-value isn't that high I'd say, so people want to squeeze every playtime hour out of their dollar, this could be the wrong game. You get a really nice little game for a really nice price. Nuff said.

The system is extremely simple. You pick a weapon that blocks as much damage as it Def stats says it does, then after a number of tick equal to its Spd, you deal damage equal to its Effectiveness (minus enemy armor, of course). Same for the enemy, repeat until one side runs out of life points. There's pretty much no randomness involved, it's about picking the right strategy and luring the enemy into making a mistake.
This results in an extremely neat and satisfying combat. Truly one of the most rewarding and engaging combat system I have
seen in a RPG, and I do not say that lightly. And on top of that, the story is interesting, surprisingly less predictable than I'd have thought, and there are man great characters.
Given the cost of this game, it'd be a crime not to try it if you have any interest whatsoever in classic RPGs.

It can sometimes be hard to work out how to progress, but the unusual and fun battle system, the non random encounters where it's possible to avoid enemies, and the cute running animation mitigate this and sometimes all you have to do is experiment until you understand.

Just a few days ago I remembered playing a game called "Have a nice day" or something along those lines and thought "Damn, this game was fun, I'd like to see a game like that again".
Then I saw a review of Gas Guzzlers Extreme by some cynical british dude while it was actually on sale on steam. It pretty much looked like the game I remembered, but with decent graphics.
So, I kinda had to buy it and I enjoyed it a lot so far =)
It could use a few more weapons, but to be honest, I couldn't think of anything really missing. The basic weapon roles are filled (machine gun, shotgun, rocket launcher).
I'd like to mention one more little thing, because it's something I haven't seen in a while: If you kill a car in a race, it actually is out of the race. It's not reset after a short delay or any of those shenanigans, you can enjoy watching it burn where you shot it lap after lap =)
And you can win a race early simply by wrecking all opponents.
So, I guess my point is: It's more a shooter with you sitting in a car than a racing game with the occasional shooting.
Car handling is decent and enjoyable, but obviously not realistic in any way or form.
I'd give it a 8/10, highly recommended if you want to shoot a driver if he dares to drive ahead of you.

As Cryptic Studios released the game 2nd Februar 2010 they had an idea of how to make a good Star Trek Game. I played in Alpha and Beta and ordered several copies preorder to gain a lot of ingame stuff that was different on every copy of the game. They did not make it perfect at start, it had its flaws, but hey were working on it to make it better over time. I really enjoyed playing the game. You had exploring missions. Yes at some point they repeated themselves, but that is how close you can get in a game to a Star Trek feeling. The ingame store had updates from now and then and I bought some stuff, like the Defiant Retrofit (Now T5). You could speculate how a game that demands monthly money to play it can have an ingame store that requires money again, but it was another time and technically you could unlock almost anything by playing. The design was  attracting a casual playing older/wealthy player base anyway. Prices were not too high and any unlocks were always account wide forever.
This all changed as Arc Games purchased Cryptic Studios and everything went downhill. The chinese company turned the game really quick into a typical chinese pay to win game. With the release of the T6 Ships around 80% of players left, for obvious reason not being willing to pay real money for them. Only other way to get these ships was brainless grinding and playing every day. Didnt take long for the famous chinese shop in shop system appeared in which you could buy stuff that only was unlocked on one character for the double price. Yes I actually calculated everything. Ofcouse you can grind everything out, but getting a T6 ship from the Zen Store without using money will take you around 150 days with one character, depending on the dilithium exchange prices and you having enough unrefined dilithium.
Anyway we went enough on the pay to win part now, lets get to the gameplay. Well every patch breaks more stuff than they can fix. This is not Cryptics fault. They actually work hard I think, they just dont get any money to repair and improve stuff in the necessary amount. Arc Games is sucking everything out. The warp out animation is broken for months. An animation Cryptic originally changed 3 times at release till it satisfied them. But look here, shiny, shiny new ships. Give us your money is Arc Games answer to that. There are several issues in the game right now. Game breaking graphic bugs and never ending glitches can be expected while you play. Be sure the server disconnects you around 30s per map you are moving.
Now lets get to the part if you really have to pay money. Yes and no. Technically you can play with your free ship, but the enemies are getting stronger and stronger and standing a chance with a T5 ship against the Vaadwaur proves challenging, against Na'kuhl it is suiciding through the missions.
If this still didnt convince let me you tell you that, besides having bought multiple keys for ingame items at release, I am a Lifetime Subscriber. We get free Zen every month, only reason why I still play btw. As I went back into the game after a break I had the problem I couldnt claim the T5 I bought some time ago on any other character. Wait there is a player support that I asked immediatly to get a message some days later, I just need to dismiss it on the character I own it and reclaim it there. The ability to become (at least for a few hours a day) the captain of my own "enterprise"

Things i didnt enjoy as much:

Micro transactions needed to remain competative (unless you have the time to invest)

I don't know exactly why, but i love this little survival game.
It doesn't feature a lot of content and is rough around the edges, but it made me clock way more hours than i thought i would.
The Story mode (Your submarine broke, you're stranded on the bottom on the sea surviving while you find the 9 scattered pieces of it) gives for around 6 hours of play without rushing (once you know the rules you can rush it quite easy) Once you finish it you unlock the 'Survivor Mode' (AKA Hard Mode) or you can play it on Sanbox mode.
The survival aspect isn't on the hard side either. Food is a bigger issue early game and the predator AI is quite simple and predictable once you get to know it. Then as usual you have the crafting part which works pretty much as every other game. There's harder games out there if you're looking for a challenging survival experience. Far Sky falls more on the easy side of the survival genre.
The ambience is what got me most of the game. The visual style got me from the first moment and I loved diving deeper to more haunting scenery. It also quite translates the loneliness feeling of being underwater.
On the bad side, I feel like this game would fully blossom with modding capacity and it could have been polished a bit more. But it's still a gem in it's actual (and definitive. The dev has stated a sequel might happen but development on this game is done) state.
So TL:DR a not fully polished gem that is worth more than meet the eye.

Say what you will about it's graphics, or about the game being quite imbalanced compared to a lot of games... The artistic style, character customization, in game factions, the world design, and especially the storyline are all of once in a lifetime type of quality. I won't spoil the storyline just say it's... Amazing, say what you will about lots of the NPCs in it seeming boring or whatever, the faction/main quest specific characters are fascinating, and to me, that's what matters more.
My favorite fictional universe of all time, the TES universe... And the best storyline I've seen anywhere, the playable races are a lot more diverse, and interesting than the typical human/orc/dwarf/elf thing, and other than World Of Warcraft is one of the few in-game universes that avoids the if you ask me, overused common tendency of using orcs as the villains. You can be nearly anything in this game, and to me the way Morrowind was done, was the perfect mixture of fantastical fantasy with gritty realism.
Some people oooo and ahh over raw graphical power, and though I somewhat care about graphics, artistic value is much much more important to me. Imagine you can play one game with okay graphics but an epic mind blowing art style, or a game with super realistic graphics, but it's heavily based off of uninteresting bland things in real life or something, I'd choose the first any day of any week.
In spite of the graphics being quite outdated, the art style also has this... Type of grim and serious quality to it- in spite of it deviating very far from reality, which I also like.
Things a lot of people dislike about Morrowind: It's not a very player skill oriented game, combined with the fact it's primarily first person/though you can use third person to marvel at your characters epicness.  A lot of players have a heavy disdain for primarily first person games, that prioritize character skill aboce player skill, personally I like it though. Without spoiling anything I can tell you, out of all TES games, Morrowind is more like a fantasy game with some mild science fiction elements, and that's also a huge part of the reason I like it so much.
Yes, a game that, in a lot of ways resembles medieval times, but has some sci-fi elements thrown in there, and it does it very VERY VERY well, even if that may sound strange to you.
Yes features in Daggerfall were removed in Morrowind, though I feel like it's the perfect balance, between Daggerfall, and games after Morrowind, because Daggerfall has extremely outdated game mechanics... And yes, the graphics of Daggerfall shallow as it may sound, did turn me off. Unlike Daggerfall Morrowinds graphics in spite of being quite old fashioned now, are good enough that I'll always be content with what it has to offer... And the art style which I keep going on and on about is amazing.
Other than Daggerfall, it's also the only TES game with multiple vampire bloodlines you can choose from, for some people this wasn't a big deal, for me it was a HUGE DEAL. Another nice thing about Morrowind, is it's less about platform jumping skills, or twitch action skills or aiming skills, and more about conversing your resources properly to succeed and survive... The AI of the guards however... Is very bad, and easy to take advantage of... And while I admit this is a glaringly huge problem, there's so much good about Morrowind I can easily overlook that.
There's a chance we will disagree, some people like their heavily fantasy games to be more based on real world stuff, or don't care for the mild hunts of sci-fi Morrowind has in it, and I've even chanced across a few people, who haven't been captivated by Morrowinds factions or storyline like I have, though if you ask me, it has the greatest storyline I've ever heard of, even compared to movies and stuff.
Some people won't like the fact that you will start out very weak, and have to repetively train your character, and use some cunning to get out of that situation, then you eventually become so powerful you as a player don't need a whole lot of twitch action skill to succeed, although this is something I actually like, and don't mind. There's also a huge amount of mods for the game, so you can have nearly anything you want in the game, I'm not gonna lie and say literally everything, but probably almost anything you could think of.
I think it'd be fair to say, Morrowind is less skill based and more strategy based, then the TES games that came after it. Morrowind isn't for everybody, and I'm telling you of the most common complains about it so you know beforehand. That all said I give Morrowind a 10/10 or 11/10 or something like that, one of the greatest games of all time, and if you ask me, hands down the best single player game there is.

Car combat games are criminally underrepresented on PC, so Gas Guzzlers Extreme was a game I was very happy to play. This game has multiple modes that allow players to options to choose from weaponless racing, weoponized racing, or straight up deathmatch car combat. The wacky named cars and drivers, deep voiced announcer, and cheesy dialogue all pay excellent homage to classic car combat games of the past such as Twisted Metal and Carmageddon. There are lots of vechicles to choose from and many ways to customize your vehicle with choosing between various mounted guns, paint jobs, and rims that anyone who enjoys making their game avatar their own will very much enjoy the features. Although Gas Guzzlers Extreme sufferes from some weapon balancing issues, predictable A.I., and a lack of an on screen radar, I found the game to be one of the best examples of a modern car combat game and a great appeal to old fans of Twisted Metal and Carmageddon.

Oh man....this is as adrenaline pumping a racing game as I have played. In addition to the kick♥♥♥♥♥soundtrack, the cars are beefy in an arcadey way, the tracks are fun and often challenging, and the guns....oh man the guns!
So, there are a few different race modes (all the racing standards really), but in addition to all the standards, there is also deathmatch. DEATHMATCH! That is balls out crazy bad assedness! There is also capture the flag (which is pretty much deathmatch with an obvious objective added).
The campaign mode (so far as I have gotten) involves moving up through the rankings while buying new cars, upgrades, weapons and of course tricking out your cars as well. Each race features three modes to choose from (typically standard race, battle (with guns), and elimination). It's as simple as that.
You can select a cheeseball voice for your racer and s/he comments throughout. I chose Arnold, and get some laughs out of it.
So, in addition to the guns (THE GUNS!!!!), there are also pickups such as smoke, oil, mines, etc....flapjacks happen to be one of them lol...that you can then drop to mess up the other drivers. There is also nitro for that extra boost. You obviously have a myriad of ways to destroy your fellow racers, not the least of which include good old fashioned ramming. You can also pick up buffs like shields and double damage along the way. All are obviously single use or timed (depending on the type of pick up).
Multiplayer features all the modes in a seven race round robin of sorts. They are team oriented, and if you play with somebody you know, you can definitely incorporate tactics into the matches to increase your odds of winning. There weren't a ton of players online when I played last night, but it was still a ton of fun and the game populates the matches with bots to fill them out if you don't have all 8 players to fill a server. The bots are actually pretty solid players as well lol.
I would say this may go down as my fave racer. It is intuitive and easy to grasp, but still rewards practice. It has fun tracks, cool guns and upgrades, and no small amount of humor involved (outside of the voices, you might have a blow up doll or president bust passenger in your car, you might find penguins on the track, etc....).
Definitely must own, must play.

Talisman: Prologue is a single player game. No AI to play against, but it doesn't really need it, because the gameplay is designed around quests with a 1, 2 or 3 star outcome based on how many moves it takes to complete the quest. (3 being best). Each character has about 6 quests each, most of them tailored to the characters abilities.
There's a nice selection of characters, not just the base ones, and I'd quite like this quest based version of Talisman, BUT it seems to be fixed, and obviously so, which I find quite irritating, because I know the first two attempts on certain quests are going to be less than 3 star outcomes before I even start, and when you get the one that's going to let you win it's obvious that this is the one that's being rolled in your favor. At times it just feels like a complete waste of time, spending 42 turns rolling when you know it's for nothing. I'd prefer to win and lose based on randomness in the rolls, rather than it being stacked for or against you at the start.
My other peeve with this is if I have 8 strength and my enemy has 2 WHY did you let it still roll like it has a chance. What a waste of time to sit and wait through that whole scenario with only one possible outcome, with no way to skip it and no option to just auto win those rolls. This on top of the obvious outcome fixing is really frustrating.
Saying all that I wish, once again, that Steam had a neutral option, because even if I've been  annoyed when I'm done with a game session, I don't hate the idea of starting it up the next time. So do i recommend it, I've no idea, I'm so confused :P I selected yes since I will play it through, and I've played worse games. I really didn't want to select either yes or no though.
So if you'd like to play through the quests and sample the characters and maybe get an idea of which one might be right for you, this is for you.
If the obvious fixing and waiting through pointlessness will annoy you more than you'll enjoy the quest element, I'd avoid this and just buy the Digital edition.

I was excited about this game when released. It does use a talisman board and characters and provide solo quests.
However the quests are not very interesting, primarily being "use this ability a bunch of times"  or "go to this space."
It has only a few classes. The interface has a number of issues that were fixed in Talisman digital edition to help speed up and streamline gameplay but on a turn with no events I had to click three or four times to progress.
It might be helpful for teaching the classes and rules to someone new to Talisman, especially with some of the shorter quests. In the prophetess track, for example, you have to use her special ability thirty times which starts to show you when it is helpful and when it isn't.
Some of the missions might help familiarize players new to Talisman or new to this edition with the Board.
On the whole it reminds me of bad Talisman games of old when the game was decided but we'd be rolling repeatedly to land on a specific spot just to get to the actual end.
A pretty major strike is that you can't (as far as I can tell) take a break from a game. Since most of the missions are time consuming and it is a slow moving board game, being able to save and come back to the game would be a plus and is available in Talisman digital edition.
Ultimately if you are considering this, I would instead suggest getting Talisman Digital and just play with a single AI opponent to start so you can get a handle on the rules. I'll probably play it some more because I want to like it. Maybe somethign will change my opinion but it doesn't seem likely.

Mount & Blade: Warband is a game that defines the whole concept of what a perfectly shaped sandbox/RPG medieval game should be like, mixed with loads of action and epic adventures.
Start either as a peasant or a noble man with a fully selective character customization and background history at your own choice, participate in tournaments, travel and discover the vast variety of what Caldaria has to offer you.
Warband will be an unforgettable realistic experience that will mark in you the true hardships and living ways of the medieval age.
What makes this game so great after all?
It isn't just a 1st person game where you can travel around doing quests, Mount and Blade: Warband goes way beyond that by offering players a battle system where you can command your army while simultaneously giving your men orders during the heat of battles.
In this game, both your character individual life and his relationships among all other NPC's are equally important to how well you can manage your army expenses and food variety in order to achieve success either alone, or within a faction.
A never ending adventure! If you are not looking for trouble, trouble will come to you as time passes by and factions envolve with each other by declaring full-scaled wars against each other conquering castles and other key locations that will drastically change the game economically and militarily.
Be either a good samaritan with your army of justice and fight off bandits and free entire villages from rebel control, a evil masterless soldier with a thirst for blood and wealth in the middle of the Caldarian disgrace, or simply a trader travelling around buying cheap and selling expensive, Warband will give you a fair challenge with very balanced rewards and consequences in whatever way of life you decided to take.
The game difficulty is well balanced, and instead of making things harder just by simply increasing the units stats that you are facing against, the AI gets a lot more rational and fast even during the campaign map as well with the in-game combat, they will almost act as real human players!
Remember that I have mentioning about your character individual role in the game? Get a good relationship with lords by doing quests or freeing close family members from enemy heavily guarded dungeons, and who knows if you can freely marry their daughters unless you convince them with your persuasion skills to run away with you!
The medieval atmosphere and music has never been so good as it is now; If you enjoyed the previous Mount & Blade game, you will fall in love with this one.
Mount & Blade: Warband will be the game that you will be happy to be hooked into to, a fair balanced game between adventure and RPG with a vast variety of content and diversity in all of its aspects.
Some negative aspects.
Bugs, Glitches and some graphic reading failures
Despite being unusual, you will encounter some glitches that will make some of the game items to disappear, or to find everything in a black screen when you return to the world map. There are also some in-game bugs that makes everything blur and unable to see around, although, I found out this can be fixed if you simple minimize the game and open it again!
Some crashes might happen too, but those are rare to encounter.
Conclusion
I would rate this game with a 79 out of 100, or 4,0 out of 5,0, a never ending sandbox game that will make players fall in love as they experience the life and atmosphere of what a true medieval age game has to give!

LAST EDITED 8/23/17 for the Escalation update
So, this is the second time I've played, and quit, Star Trek Online.  Since the Escalation update promised, among other things, a complete rebalance of the game, I figured that I should give it another shot, to see if it was worth my time and effort.
It wasn't.  If anything, the rebalance has only exacerbated the problems that made me quit the first time.
The biggest problem is... basically everything past level 50.  From 1-40, you're given a new ship every 10 levels or so, to help you keep pace with the increasingly-stronger enemies.  These ships have stronger hulls more weapon slots, more and better bridge officer seating, and sometimes new capabilities, like subsystem targeting, heavy weapons, hangar bays, sensor scanning, or cruiser commands.  This works well - until you hit level 50.
You don't get a new ship at 50.  You can possibly get a new ship with dilithium, but the selection will be extremely limited.  At 60, there's no new ships available to you at all unless you either join a fleet, open lockboxes, pay the cash shop currency, or if you're extremely lucky, you might be able to get a new ship from an event - assuming, of course, that one is running, ships are available, and you get into it early enough to earn your way to a ship.  Even if you do get a Fleet ship, they're stripped of unique consoles and other equipment, and you still need to get a Fleet Support Module from the cash shop to even be able to purchase it.
This is a problem, because the game is now balanced around you having a T5-50 ship at level 50, and a T6 ship at level 60.  Many enemy groups are designed so that, at level 60, they'll summarily obliterate anyone attempting to take them on solo in anything less.  This is especially noticeable with more recent enemy groups, like the Son'a and Vorgons, who can endure minutes on end of player attacks without their shields breaking, and in return can obliterate a player almost instantly.
As a result, Space combat around 45+ quickly becomes an unfun mess, where you cannot hope to keep up with the situations the game expects you to.  Many missions can develop into a 'zerg rush' situation - where you fly in, deal a little bit of damage, and then die immediately, only to respawn and do it again and again and again until you finally manage to win.  This isn't fun; this is a chore.  This is the game telling you that you cannot legitimately win, and that the only reason why you can win is because it refuses to let you lose.
Worse are Small Craft missions.  Many of these force you into near-unwinnable situations against overwhelming enemy firepower.  Situations like "survive the attacks of three enemy fighters while also working under a time limit to destroy 3 noncombatant units that will reset your mission progress if they are allowed to survive for too long."  What makes Small Craft missions so bad is that it is exceptionally hard to find equipment upgrades for Small Craft - weapons and shields in particular.  Weapons and shields for normal starships cannot be equipped on them.  You work hard to make your main ship as good as it possibly can be, only to have it taken away arbitrarily, and forced to use a small, weak, fragile craft that you cannot easily equip - that's not fun game design.
Ground combat is better, but only by comparison.  There are fewer situations where you're just outright killed with no recourse, and even if you are defeated, your Bridge Officers can sometimes revive you.  You also don't have the spawn-camping problems that can occur in space missions - ground missions are typically designed so that you do not respawn close to enemy combat zones, unlike space missions where you can sometimes wind up dying, and then dying again within seconds of respawning, before you even have full control over your vessel.  It's also easier to find level-appropriate shields, weapons, and armor for ground combat, since you don't have to worry about replacing a ship every 10 levels.
I'm sorry, but I can't recommend this game under it's current status.  Until either the monetization is let up to the point where I can compete up to the endgame, or combat is rebalanced so that it's not necessary to have absolute top end gear just to survive level-appropriate content, this game isn't worth the money it's asking.

Helen's Mysterious Castle is a surprisingly decent dungeon-focused RPG.  The combat is turn-based and single party and uses a "tick" system which gives it some tactical chops but can become repetitive since it's mostly about finding the winning pattern for a certain type of enemy and then repeating it when you come across it again.  Bosses fights are mostly well-done and require some planning.  Thankfully, the game is short enough to avoid becoming too repetitive (around 5 hours or so) and the difficult scales well until the last area of the game, which is mercifully short.  A big plus for being able to see enemies on the map so you can avoid them when you feel like it.
The dungeon design was much better than I expected from a 1.99 RPGMaker game.  There's some clever hidden paths and shortcuts and dungeons are more than a series of connected hallways.  The only downside to dying is being booted out of a dungeon, though your character moves quickly and it's easy to get back to where you left off, so you don't have to worry about lost progress to a fight gone bad.  You can also save everywhere and that always rules.
Helen doesn't level up, but you get experience that you can put toward leveling items and they serve as the primary means of doing damage, avoiding damage and healing.  This is also the rare game that makes a good case for a limited inventory, since all the items you find can be useful.  It's nice to play a game where treasure chests aren't random crafting garbage or "sword you already have+1".  There's even a neat little treasure room set-up that makes dropping and reacquiring items simple and easy.  It's a surprisingly smart system where there's a room filled with chests you've found throughout the game.  Drop an item anywhere and it reappears here if you want to pick it up again.  It's simple and useful and I can't understand why more games wouldn't use such a method to keep track of treasure.
Story is pretty minimal until the last part of the game and is bland and generic for the most part.  Being bland and generic is okay when there's not much talking and most of it is light and comedic but once "cut-scenes" start being more than about a couple of exchanges long, the mostly mediocre writing becomes annoying and you're just skimming dialogue.  That said, for the most part it's okay in a bland way and can be somewhat humorous at times.
On the downside, there's the typical RPGMaker clunk.   You can't customize controls without third-party software, can't change the level of in-game music (it's really loud at low universal computer settings), the controls when moving around are kind of stiff and event flags can be kind of finicky at triggering.  There's one area in particular when I had to "sit" on a chair next to a table to trigger an event, which I didn't realize you could do since I figured the chair was a a solid object.  I figured out what to do after a while but there's a few areas of the game that have this "I know what to do, but I can't quite figure out how to trigger it" problem.
There's also a bizarre widespread bug where you have to enter a double door building by the right door instead of the left one, otherwise the game will crash.  This is really annoying since it happens immediately after a boss fight.
All in all, I went in with no expectations for HMC and was quite surprised there was a solid, little game here.  If you can put up with RPGMaker clunk, there's a decent game here with some good ideas that could have really benefited from a larger scope.

I'm a big fan of the Metal Slug series. I played a lot of different Metal Slugs in a lot of different arcades as a little kid, and I've played through Metal Slug 1, 2, X, 3, 4, and 5, with 3 and 5 being my favorites.
However, I'm not a big fan of this particular emulation, and I think I've seen much better ones for PC elsewhere.
First, for an $8 emulation of a really, really, really old game, it really doesn't handle its settings very well. There were some keys I couldn't map, and the graphics menu was buggy and so it took more time than it should have for me to adjust the graphics settings.
Second, and more importantly, there needs to be a "Disable suicide attack" option. I understand that it's a mixture of the auto-fire command and the jump button in-game (jump + attack is the suicide attack combo in a vehicle, so you basically cannot try to jump while holding auto-fire), but frankly, I have suicided my vehicle far more times in this version than in literally any other version of Metal Slug I have every played. And that includes this same company's version of Metal Slug 3 on the iOS, which, incidentally, doesn't share the same issue with "every vehicle of mine will suicide charge into a random wall" that this version has.

Of all the games I play, this is one of the most enjoyable. I love being able to control an army, give strategic orders, and seige castles. The base game is great in it's own right, though as of this review (Sept 2015), the game is beginning to feel a bit dated. The mod community has kept this game alive and running strong as well. I recommend it for the vanilla experience, and when you want to try something more, take a look at the available mods. There are plenty out there that change the game either with just a few minor tweaks and additions, ranging all the way to complete overhauls that feel like a different game, or even an expansion.
PROS
1. Create and advance your commander either as a mercenary, bandit, or noble lord of a faction.
2. Raise an army, and level up troops into an unstoppable force.
3. Become King/Queen of a faction, then command other lords to assist you in battle.
4. Smooth gameplay, well polished. Good soundtrack.
5. Balanced troops, for the most part. You can make any army work with the proper tactics.
6. LARGE mod community ensures there are tons of new and exciting ways to experience the game.
7. ALL the below listed CONS have been addressed and resolved with various mods. No reason not to try it.
CONS
1. Base game can feel repetative at times.
2. Difficulty sliders top off at normal, and can sometimes make the game feel a bit too easy.
3. Limited to 150 troops shared between armies, if you do not modify settings.
4. AI can be a bit derpy at times. By default, enemy troops charge straight into your forces with no tactics.
TL;DR
Do I recommend this game? Yes. Absolutely yes. I also recommend mods to bring the game a little more life if you feel something is lacking.

Hello, I enjoy Helen's Mysterious Castle very much.  It has a distinct Chrono Trigger feel (even though it is completely different though) and has a fantastic intuitive feel.  5 stars!

This game is an absolute blast to play!
Helen's Mysterious castle offers an interesting spin on turn-based combat by introducing a "wait" system. Each weapon or spell has a "wait" stat on it that decreases the time you have until the enemy's next attack, ensuring that you have to pay close attention to every battle instead of just mashing the confirm button to move onward. The amount of swords, shields, bows, and spells you collect with varying wait stats offer a plethora of options in combat.
The plot honestly took me by surprise by starting off as yet another "the amnesiac hero is on a quest to discover who they truly are" story, yet there are enough twists and turns throughout the story combined with simple yet enjoyable characters that it manages to be a memorable tale by the time you get to the end. If this game ever gets a sequel, I'd love to know more about the events that lead up to the first game.
I'll admit the game is a bit short. But with what I just wrote combined with the replayability added via multiple endings, Helen's Mysterious Castle will be the best two dollars you ever spent.

I would argue that Helen's Mysterious Castle provides the best value you can get for $2 USD in the entire Steam catalog. If you're familiar with Cave Story, then you're already familiar with how a simply presented game on the surface can provide much more than you've bargained for.
Helen's Mysterious Castle has all the fundamental things that make up a good game; an intuitive and unique easy-to-learn combat system, a developing story with humorous characters, proper difficulty scaling as you progress, and some minor exploration to unlock more equipment. The store page implies the game to be a bit difficult, and it can be if you aren't thinking proactively in battle and levelling up your weapons as you progress. Fortunately, I never found myself having to grind just to get past a part in the game. It's difficult for any game to find that "challenging but not unfair" feel, and I think Helen's Mysterious Castle nails it well.
Right off the bat, it's easy for a player to notice several small things that seem off-putting or otherwise incomplete, such as Helen's lack of proper dialogue or inability to read. This isn't the developers being lazy;
Any backtracking (which is completely optional in a casual playthrough) is helped with quick shortcuts to-and-from towns and areas that are unlocked as you complete them, so there's no need to trek all the way through a dungeon just to get to the next area if you've already done so before. The only reason you'd backtrack in this game is if you missed an item or equipment in a section and want to go back and get it.
It's easy to quickly judge and dismiss any RPGmaker game, but the experience I felt from Helen's Mysterious Castle is a significant cut above what you'd expect to feel from an RPGmaker game. I'd easily recommend this game to anyone looking for a fun RPG to play, especially if you're on a budget.

In it's own right a non-offensive game with a combat system that is pretty cool the first two hours or so, but does get repetitive. Since it's all based on visible numbers (no real status effects, delays or anything to speak of), there is no real strategy involved. You just get the best gear that you can and there will always be a 'best' approach to combat, with no reason to deviate from that.
Narrative is nothing special, either.
The real problem, though, is the technical execution. A few points in short:
- No usable Fullscreen mode (dev even recommends to play in windowed mode on this very store page)
- No possibility to load in-game or way to get back to main menu (in fact no pause menu at all). If you want to load a previous save, you have to Alt-F4 and restart
- Gamebreaking bug after a few hours that the dev is incapable of fixing
All of these issues are inacceptable for a commercial release, even if it is cheap. For an 'okay' game, I am not willing to put in a lot of research to get it running myself. Perused the Steam forums to verify that the dev is not able or interested to resolve the issues with the game, then uninstalled.
EDIT: I did file a request to receive my money back, however, since the gamebreaking bug occurs more than 2 hours after starting the game, that is not possible. This is, of course, not the fault of the developer, you just have to deal with the fact that Valve apparently can sell a defective product created by somebody who doesn't know what they are doing and not reimburse the cost if it doesn't feel like it.

I would certainly have to recommend this game. It's not very expensive and it manages to have some fun and clever gameplay for an rpg to mix things up a bit. While the game outwardly has a very cutsy and sometimes silly demeanor, there does seem to be a hint of some more serious things going on. What I can only describe as the "Wait" system has been very well implemented and adds a certain amount of complexity and strategy to battles despite the limited number of actual moves. Personally I felt it was kind of nice that there is little random chance and most things are a direct result of your actions. Another thing that was kind of nice was that it was not random battles and battles only started when you touched an enemy on the map. The developer also managed to utilize experience in a very interesting way that didn't really make the game feel grindy. The art direction and hud as well as the user interface are all very efficiently designed.  The only things that took away from this game for me was that it can be a little jumpy when you move, the game does not appear to be very long(Though for the asking price I can't really call this a fault), and I unfortunately experienced a  game breaking bug pretty late into the game. However, as far as I can tell this is a rather rare thing to happen so I can still freely reccomend this game. For all it's faults it does enough right in unique manner that I think it is certainly worth a try, especially for the price. One of these days I'll probably go at it again with a new save and see if I can get past that bug. I'l probably shelve it for the time being however.

While the concept of the game is nothing new, it has definitely been brought up to modern times. Lots of humor brought into the game, be it computer player names, or the included voice packs. (Hail to the King, Baby!) Also, why wouldn't you want a game that includes a Reliant Robin look-alike!
It's an amazing arcade racer, with the expected handling and control that you'd expect from such. Think Burnout Paradise, but now you have shotguns/miniguns/RPGs/grenade launchers/railguns/nukes to blast the competitors out of your way. Power-ups are scattered around the race tracks, and can definitely help you catch up if you're behind, or to keep the competition in the dust.
While the game is a blast to play, it does quickly get repetitive, as there's only a dozen or less tracks for each mode, and that's not including when you drive the opposite direction. With exception of a few game modes, you're locked to your weapon of choice from your garage, or sponsor for the duration of the race, so make sure it fits your preferred style of destruction! In-game money does seem to be a very moot point, as you are rewarded with exuberant amounts (assuming you place first, and have the sponsor bonus cash), and upgrades honestly don't cost much, and only take a single race or two to be purchased. As for buying cars, by the time it's released to be purchased, you already have enough winnings to not even hesitate purchasing it, even with buying every upgrade for every vehicle as soon as it's available.
Game modes include:
Classic Race: No guns, no power-ups, but boost is included.
Power Race: No guns, but you do have power-ups. Driving skill of the track, and power-ups are the key to winning.
Battle Race: Same as above, only with your guns now.
Knockout Race: Same as battle, only the last player of each lap is eliminated, and the race continues until only one person remains. Taking out opponents can quicken that final lap, as they do not respawn. Neither do you either.
Deathmatch: Set in an open area, weapons are scattered around the playing field, and you can switch between the ones that you have collected during your current life. First to the set score wins.
Last Man Standing: Same as above, only you don't respawn.
Capture the Flag (Team): Also set in the same open arenas, there are two flags that need to be captured. Only one player from each team can take a flag, and in order to score, the flag holder needs to collect the second flag from the opposing team. First team to the set score wins.
Team Matches: Any of the above modes can have set teams, and the team that reaches the score, or highest ranking of the race wins.
Owning the Full Metal Frenzy DLC, the two vehicles are just plain remodels of two existing cars, with the same stats, handling, and performance. Dominator, Demolition Derby, and Domination Derby are great modes, but that is all the DLC brings, as Zagreb is very small, and the flags spawn in 2 of 4 places and alternate back and forth, unlike other maps that have several spawn points. The Cowboy arena is also very hilly, and hard to get your sights set, as well as for this arena, the computers are more prone to running away and hiding, rather than trying to fight you, sometimes forcing the clock to run down, as they boost from health pickup to health pickup.
All in all, it's a great fresh game, with great influences, pushing it in all the right directions, and steering away from poor decisions of it's inspirations. Grab the demo, enjoy it, then purchase it! I do recommend buying it when it goes on sale, as $10 is a fair price for this game, not $25, especially with how minimal the DLC bring, and their high price for what they include.

If you are coming from Oblivion or Skyrim, expect some big changes. Morrowind is much more alien, in both good and bad ways. In my experience, I have found Morrowind to be much more immersive and challenging. You start as an outlander in the game, expect to be treated like it. You have to earn your way to the top, you are not seen as special. You will need to prove yourself to guilds, houses, and people. Your actions have consequences, and joining one faction may lead to exclusion or outright violence from another.
Do not expect to find the best tier simply because you are a high level. High-tier loot are not included in randomized chests and containers, rather they are hand placed throughout the world. You can come across glass or daedric weapons and armor as level 1, but they are often guarded by the most difficult monsters and men.
Morrowind does have its faults. The combat system is based upon a dice-system, and the graphics have definately aged. But the flaws are easily overlooked when you dive into the heart of the game.

Metal Slug 3 is my all time favorite game in the series.  It's also my favorite platformer/shooter ever.  Having said that, this port is poorly done, and I imagine that the original developers of this masterpiece would cringe if they saw what it has become here.
While the original gameplay still shines, there are a few head scratching flaws with this port.  The game slows down with heavy action on the screen, but it can also slow down or temporarily freeze in relatively calm areas.  The aforementioned slow down is also accompanied by music that speeds up or slows down(not intentionally).  I've noticed this during stage transitions, and it's very annoying if you're a die hard fan of the original version, or even the well done original Xbox or Xbox 360 (outside of the sprite smoothing in the latter version) versions (not to mention the Anthology version, of course).  The music itself is also of a lower quality than the original.  This is noticeable in several areas, and it seems like an emulation issue.
If you've never played a Metal Slug game before, these issues may not bother you.  If you have, or if you're looking for the most faithful version of this, I'd suggest that you look elsewhere.  Perhaps SNK will one day upload the true version of this game.

I only have a few hours under my belt, but I feel like I pretty much have seen enough to base a fairly accurate review upon. I did not do story mode yet, just sandbox, so this is all about sandbox mode.
You start out with just your extraction tool and your base that you immediately have to decide where to place on the ocean floor because your oxygen is running out. Since the world is procedurally generated you might get lucky and find a whole bunch of gold and coal deposits close by, or you may have to really search for a decent place to create your base that will not have you getting lost constantly, racing back home all the time to eat and refill your 02.
An annoying thing common with this game and others like it within the survival genre is the fact that you have to constantly keep eating millions of calories like you are a sumo wrestler with a tape worm. Seriously devs, how much do you eat in your offices while making these games? You must all be super high and have the munchies because every single survival game focuses so heavily on eating everything in sight. My character feels like John Goodman at a chinese buffet.
There are no tutorials to hold your hand, but crafting is pretty easy to get the hang of within one or two lives and you soon realize you need to hoard materials to craft stronger equipment to breathe longer and go to farther depths to get more resources to make better equipment to go out farther and deeper to get more resources to craft stronger equipment to go out farther and deeper to get better resources so you can craft better equipment so you can I don't know, save the princess or something, I wasn't paying attention.
The game is fun, well made, visually pretty, has that same kind of almost hand painted look to it like the long dark has, so its very easy going on graphics cards, I by no means have a gaming rig, just a GTX 750 ti and the game runs perfectly, I'll bet even my integrated AMD radeon graphics could run the game just as well.
I recommend it as long as you are into this type of genre, and I would recommend throwing it on the wishlist and holding out for a good sale.

Gameplay-wise, no issues - swimming is smooth, using items is smooth, expanding your base is fine.
My major gripe is the progression into the 'next level'. Once you figure out how to get to the next level, there is a huge content gap between each 'level'. There are other games out there that ease you into the immersive crafting/collecting of content (and have more content to play with as well).

Star Trek Online is a solid piece of proof that Perfect World Entertainment ruins everything it touches, particularly with paywalls. I've never been particularly picky about heavily monetized games as long as they do it right. But this game? It outright paywalls you out of the endgame by making any tier 6 ship obtained only through the cash shop (yes, including fleet ships). What's worse is that the best ones you have to leave up to chance by buying keys for one of MMO's cursed items: lockboxes. You can get tier 6 ships from events, but good luck with waiting for an event that even gives them out.
Sadly, I wish that was the only bad thing I have to say about this game. The combat ranges from fairly easy to completely unfair. There have been missions where, despite bringing friends, PvE enemies resort to the cheap and much-loathed tactic of spawn-camping, shuttle missions come to mind but plenty missions where you're in your ship of choice are just as guilty. The game itself has no protection against spawn-camping, so your only hope of winning a solid chunk of missions in this game is via Zerg Rushing. This game is called Star Trek, not Starcraft. Also, I've said it before and I'll say it again: When designing combat, one of the biggest questions you want to make sure your players don't have to ask is "What killed me?". This game completely disregards that, even to the point that the damage report menu that you can view if you die in space combat bugs out and is unviewable half the time or just doesn't work.
The game is riddled with bugs and glitches that Cryptic has never bothered to fix, either. I can typically ignore bugs if they're hard to encounter, but it says a lot that I can barely do anything without a mission-breaking bug causing me to have no choice but to reset. This game came out seven years ago, there's absolutely no excuse for such things to keep happening.
I wanted to like this game, I really did. But no game should be this stressful from lackluster developers and greedy publishers to play. I can't care about a game if the developers and publisher behind it can't be bothered to care, either. If you want a good sci-fi game, please save yourself some sanity and look elsewhere.

The puzzle aspect of the game is fun, and the art direction is decent in the way that the characters don't look like a 10 y/o painted them. However the "content" of this game is... incredibly shallow. The characters don't actually have any personality. You know how good writing is "show, don't tell"? This game is all about "tell". The guiding fairy basically announces a girl's archetype and there's all there is to it. They have no backgrounds, no stories to tell, you're just supposed to reveal their height, weight and cup size in conversation (seriously, what?). The way the dialogue is written, the game *has* to be happening inside the protagonists's dream with all characters being manifestations of himself, because there's no way any real conversation between two humans would proceed like that.
Bonus points! You know what makes the Japanese girl happy? If you gift her chop sticks! And the latina girl? Sure, gift her a sombrero. That's just.. waow.
Now, personality of the girls is probably not what you're getting this game for. But even in that aspect, the game is lacking. Each girl has only 4 images, unlocked one by one after each successful date, and frankly, only the last two are ever interesting. You'll get more material for free on the internet.
So to summarize:
As a Bejeweled alternative: OK
As a visual novel where you can flirt with characters: Lacking
As stimulating material: Lacking

Whilst anyone who has played the two new games will feel somewhat at ease with the controls and mechanics, Morrowind is a much older school RPG than Oblivion or Skyrim and buyers must be aware of that before purchase. You dont always hit with a weapon if you are not skilled in its use, despite the cross hair being on the target, or potion making will fail despite having the correct ingredients for example. There was a time last year that i was looking for the perfect CCG/TCG on steam that was free to play.  i played a lot of them and here's my opinion on why Hands of the Gods got it right.
it didn't feel generic and or basic like Star Crusade, Hearthstone, Shadowverse, Magic Duels, and SolForge.
it wasn't overly complex like Faeria (still a good game in its own right) or Infinity Wars.
Chronicle: RuneScape Legends was unique, but didn't feel tactical (maybe it was but hard to fathom).
Eternal Card Game and Shardbound are downloaded, but i haven't played them yet so i can't comment.
Which leaves us with Duelyst which was/is a great game; tactical yet quick to understand, and very unique with units on a grid.  Hands of the Gods shares similarities with Duelyst, yet it is unique enough to be different and fun.
The Negatives: It feels like its in a very early stage.  the artwork is temporarily placeholders.  some cards are not consistent with the others in its family which is stated by the devs as a bug, the cards lack information like how much tiles it can move, and if its ranged, how far it can hit...
Overall, this game strikes a very good balance of tactics, difficulty, uniqueness; it just needs to be ironed out more.  Also earning new packs is easy, you get a quest everyday, and also if you level up any of your 7 leaders that you can play, you get like credits to purchase a card pack as well.

Like all these card games, they claim it is skill based and yes there is some, but especially in arena type games it has so much random that even the best skilled players can lose because of the leader and cards that they can make their set from.
I really want to like these games, and enjoyed this at the start, but it is the same as all the rest and soon gets very annoying.

U dont lose many ranked points in that case but it s frustrating for sure.
Update1:
The gameplay itself has potential as i really like turn based strategy where positioning matters. I will change to thumbs up for it beiing able to become a solid cardgame.
Update2:
Developers comment that i should focus on quests makes no sense. Quests take hours to do and are even slower when you lose a lot. And there is no question you will as free to play player.
I pay only money for games cause they are fun and i want to do so. But here i would just have to pay money because it is frustrating otherwise.
Twitch Streams are a sad excuse and will probably not get you more than 15 gems (which can't even get you one 10th of 1 card pack!). They just do it to push their twitch ratings.
I am really at my limits of frustration and will probably stop playing this game for now.

Please ignore my pitiful play time. I've been playing on the 'Creepy and Cute' parts pack, where I have 50+ hours.
Pick it up in a sale. Not worth £15, but certainly worth £10 or less. Simply the technology in Spore is really quite incredible. All the creators are hugely detailed, and the combinations of creatures, buildings and vehichles is extraordinary.
Gameplay wise, there's 5 stages.
Cell Stage: Control your cell, eat food, don't get eaten. Seemples. Topdown, swimmy thing. Probably the second or third strongest stage.
Creature Stage: Ascend onto Land, and into proper 3 dimensions! Control your creature, meet new species on your to sentience! Either the first or second best stage. Probably on par with the Space stage.
Tribal stage: Contol a tribe of your now fully evolved creatures, and become the dominant species. Not too terrible, just the weakest stage. Just a bit repetitive, and the AI gets a bit ropey around here.
Civilization Stage: Contol your vehicles, and become the dominant empire. Probably the second worst stage, just repetitive.
Space Stage: The finale to Spore, you get to explore space! Unfortunately your spaceship doesn't have any effect on how it plays unlike vehicles in the civ. stage. Empires consisting of other creations are quite nice, and each one (including your own) has a Philosphy and Archetype. Wanderer, Warrior, Shaman, Trader, Scientist, Zealot, Diplomat, Ecologist, Bard or Knight.
At the end of each stage, you get either a Red, Blue or Green card. Red cards are for carnivores who kill and pillage. Green is for herbivores who ally and befried, while Blue is a bit of both. Depending on your card selection, you get one of 10 archetypes. Each one gets a ability, and more depending on how many cards you get. Personally, I prefer to choose an Archetype from the Spore Wiki, and aim to be one of them, and evolve from cell to space. Zealot is the best, fanatical frenzy is the bomb.
Overall Spore is an excellent game. However, it feels emptier the bigger the game gets. Cell stage it's all small (literally), but your just one cell, it's very personal. As you progress to packs to tribes and eventually cities and spacefaring empires, your little critter you made just isn't...important anymore.

Spore introduces an amazing idea to replicate how life starts off as a single cell, and then evolves to dominate the universe and beyond. The millions (maybe billions) of choices to make in the game, such as creating your creature, making a village hostile or peaceful, or dominating your home planet through military means, is truly amazing. The evolution stages in the game each have their unique touch to it, making the player hooked on to the game for countless hours. Whether its taking down an Epic creature, or making peace with other nations, the game is remarkably fun.

I rate the game Star Trek Online 3/5. OK. And by "OK" I mean not that bad but not that great either. I can recommend it to some but I personally don't want to play any more of it. I don't have the patience for it and I'm pretty sure I don't have the time either, not when there are so many other great games out there to play and so many other amazing game worlds to visit.
Essentially, Star Trek Online is a fun, highly detailed, hugely expansive adventure game with a very friendly community which is also severely hampered by awkward controls, an obtuse interface, repetitive game design and occasional bugs. This game requires a lot of patience and a lot of time.
+Good (at least adequate) graphics made to run on many different systems.
+Great character customization options (if the options can be deciphered).
+Lots of game options and settings.
+Truly expansive game with HUGE numbers of missions and locations (many of the space stations and such have the exact same layout unfortunately which gets highly repetitive).
+Large ship variety each of which have many subtle and non-subtle nuances about how they fight and what their load-outs can be.
+Free to play and not pay to win with an unusually friendly and helpful community which is always wanting to have new players to join in a game which mostly focuses on cooperative fights against computer controlled characters/events. There are lots of things you can buy with real money if you want to though. You can go up against other players too but most of them are extremely high-level and so have totally overpowered weapons and ships and shields who have been playing for years.
+There's a lot of stuff to see if you just want to fly around and look at stuff in your ship but that can get boring too. Afterall, you don't HAVE to do missions unless you want to see everything the game has to offer. But there is a lot you can see regardless, this being an at least partially open-world game. Lots of stuff for groups of friends to do also.
+/-You can play as the federation, Klingons or Romulans. I only played as the federation as I heard that the Klingons and Romulan factions don't feature campaigns or missions that are as well developed. Unfortunately the Borg and others are not a playable race. While there is a lot to see and do, the game will not let you do whatever you might be able to imagine. (I had hoped for a short while when I first heard about this game to be a good-guy rogue borg cube (we will assimilate some of you if you, you know, want to be assimilated) and I couldn't. Boo hoo!
+/-Classic, largely orchestral star trek music (which might not be for you if you don't like that very much or find it boring like I do) which can get repetitive over time and usually has a self-righteous feeling to it.
+/-Adequate though authentic sound effects.
+/-The game has levels to keep missions difficult and challenging and to reward you with leveled-up equipment as you progress. However, while thoughtful, as this increases replayability, this feature is implemented in a potentially buggy manner. If you enter a mission with a high-level friend and then that friend has to leave then you might be stuck in the mission and will need to find some way of escaping without being destroyed and thus automatically restarting the mission at that high level. You need to escape somehow and then re-enter it for the level to switch back to where your lower-leveled character is so you don't get almost instantly destroyed by high-level NPC enemies. The enemy difficulty leveling should ideally occur in real-time if possible. Still, this is not an issue which necessarily comes up a lot unless you have friends who are all very high level when you are not.
-Awkward controls even with the detailed keyboard and control re-mapping options. This game will make Just Cause 2's controls seem intuitive and streamlined. It might even make the controls in Mirror's Edge feel streamlined. System Shock 2's controls are easier. FreeSpace 2, a detailed space fighting sim, has easier controls than the space battles in this game.
-I mean, the game simultaneously seems to want you to use it like a menu and a 3d game which is usually obtuse. It is difficult to figure out how to do ANYTHING. Equipping a weapon or any other item is needlessly difficult. Indeed most menus, statistics and controls are needlessly obtuse and confusing giving this game a frustratingly long learning curve. I believe IGN's review said it best when it said something like how everything that is usually simple in a game is complex and everything that should be complex in a game (like traveling from one star system to another at warp speed) is oddly simple. This mostly just involves little, irritating things but all these little things combine to make a frustratingly difficult learning curve and this is the number one reason why I don't want to play this game anymore. Also, I have other games I'd rather play as a result despite this game's wonderful community. Even the interstellar map of the galaxy, for example, is hard to understand. Homeworld, this isn't.
-Occasional glitches and bugs throughout.
-The game's friendly AI is mediocre at best and the game's enemy AI is really bad. That's not the worst thing so far as fights are concerned though. The worst thing is that there simply isn't a lot of tactical depth to this game. Stay out of enemy weapon range (or line of sight if you are running around on the ground or a space station or inside a ship) and hit the enemy with your own weapons as quickly and as often as you can. Most tactical depth beyond basic maneuvering consists of figuring out which combination of abilities, special powers, shields and weapons to use at different times and against different groups of enemies (which is often not a very straightforward matter (which is fine in itself). However, this layer of tactical depth is often implemented in an extremely confusing manner which has a long and arduous learning curve to figure out (unless you have good friends (like I did) who will take an enormous amount of time to tell you what to do.) Unfortunately, once you have a combination of abilities, powers, shields and weapons selected, battles would have become a simple button-mashing frenzy if it were not for needing to wait for each item and weapon to recharge between each shot. You can opt to fire one weapon at a time though or fire them all at once in salvos (which is almost always best anyhow). Regardless, after you've decided on a loadout and inventory, the battles themselves get boring FAST.
-Maneuvering, either with your character or with your spacecraft feels cumbersome and restrictive, even with all the myriad ways of customizing your controls. The AI doesn't do much better though (and your own AI team mates and NPC characters have a nasty tendency to get stuck in corners or in tight hallways causing many of the game's areas to have uncharacteristically (uncharacteristic for the world of Star Trek even) large hallways and open spaces.
-You probably have to really love star trek to want to play this game. At least this is the way it was with me. The game world is a messy hodge-podge of every star trek episode and movie ever made and while this can be great for people looking for nostalgia and gives you a huge variety of enemies to fight the world can seem like a real chaotic mess unless you are fairly familiar with most star trek episodes and movies which have ever come out. The game tries to introduce you to things though but this game requires a LOT of reading text boxes to find out what's going on, almost from one minute to the next.
--The game world attempts to control overcrowding and lag issues by having different "instances" or sort of sub-space like parallel universes running at the same time. To actually join your friends and see them you have to figure out how to join their particular "instance."
