Helen's Mysterious Castle is a quaint and short game. Very short. About six hours short. But that's not why I'm not recommending the game. I'm not going to recommend the game, despite the very cheap price point, due to the fact that it doesn't feel fleshed out.
You start off the game with almost no idea of what to do. How do controls work? Where are my menu options? What key presses do I need to do? How is my controller mapped? I probably spent half an hour going, "Ok... wtf?" You kind of run into that through out the game, as it does a poor job of explaining itself to you. The only thing it really goes into depth with is the combat system. If it didn't, I would have instantly refunded the game.
Furthermore, the story isn't very compelling.  You start off as an illiterate mute. You can't read any signs and can only respond with either "?" or "!". That's not engaging for me. The illteracy is fixed later via plot progression, but then you realize it was done that way to pretty much artificially inflate the length of the game. Some exposition of the story as you go wouldn't have ruined the game. For sure how it starts out would have had to change, but hey, how you start out is terrible anyway.
Otherwise this game is very much a classic JRPG. You know what? If it wasn't for the fact that this game was grind heavy, it probably would only be a couple hours long. This game is bad. Dont' buy it.

Such a marvellous little RPG!
General Overview:
It's not a very long game, nor is it too challenging if you know what you're doing. The game mechanics work really well, being turn- AND Wait-based. Wait-based? Yes! The Wait gauge telling you how long you have to "wait" until you can execute your move. Being fast usually means hitting less hard, but being quick can result in the opponent doing some serious damage.
Story:
The story is a bit lacking. Took me a while to figure out I was a monster, living with monsters that look like humans. The game is pretty linear, and so is the story, but it can be difficult to figure out just where to go and what to do next. There's not much character development either.
Inventory:
Your inventory is limited to eight items, be it weapons or gear. If you collect an item, that you later wish to drop, just drop it. It is "collected" by one of the NPC's and you can easily get it back. The weapons and spells are pretty cool, but the Heal-spell is a bit of a let down. It decreases a level every time you use it outside of a battle, meaning you have to upgrade it again.
Leveling:
You don't level. Your character, Helen, doesn't get stronger. The EXP you earn are instead used for leveling and upgrading weapons and spells. That's a pretty interesting and unique idea for a game made with RPG-Maker! Throughout the story, you'll be able to find Health Bonuses, boosting your Max HP with a few HP. The steaks you get when you die, help a bit too, but only to a certain extent.
Visuals:
This game looks wonderful! It's made in RPG-Maker, but it looks so much better and more customised than any other RPG-Maker game I've played before. The characters look cute, you can actually open cupboards and every monster is represented by an overworld sprite and a portrait.
Music:
Standard music, but nice tunes. In the credits, all songs are credited, which leaves me to assume they come from the free music database. That doesn't make them any less fun to listen to though! ^ u^
Controls:
Really easy to use. Just use the arrows to walk and Z and X for other actions, hold Shift to run and you're good to go. Don't accidentally hit the F12 key to make a screenshot, it brings you back to the Title Screen... That happens to some people, you know >///>
Overall Opinion:
A wonderful, short, fun and exiting RPG to play, that can be challenging at times, but never too much to make you stop playing it. I've read some reports of the game crashing, but I haven't even encountered a glitch, other than the music not always starting when you reload.
Get this game, it's fairly cheap and a lot of fun to play! It also comes with seven Trading Cards!! ^ u^
It's a cute little RPG. Worth it, especially if it's on sale.

I have man-months of time invested in this game!  Bought it a long time ago and played it to death.  Got it on Steam for a fraction of what it used to cost, and so far I've managed to avoid getting completely sucked in again.  But beware!  This came can get as bad as the original Civilization!  It's a huge time sink!
Each of the 5 "stages" of your creature's life are separate games, and they don't really build on one another all that much.  But your actions early in the game DO affect the type of creature you will end up being in the final stage.  That is, how you act early on will be remembered by the game, and when you get to the last stage all the other races in the game will know if you were carnivorous and agressive or herbivorous and passive, for example.  This will affect how they treat you, based on their own traits as well.
The 5th stage is when you become a space-faring society, and this is when the game becomes a huge time sink.  Your goal is to fight your way to the central core of the galaxy you are in, but to do that you will need to be very strong, and this takes time.  While you build up your might, you are setting up trade routes, terraforming planets around stars that might be many jumps distant from your home solar system, and shuttling comodities between all these far-flung worlds in an attempt to keep your economy pumped up.  It's a lot of work, but it's fun.
Grab this one when it's on sale and give it a shot.  It's different than most games you've played before - at least until you get to the last stage.  Then it's similar to a turn-based game like Civilization, but in space with lots more control over what you are doing.  It's still a lot of fun, but it's not a game you'll beat over a weekend unless you REALLY play a lot!

Oh man, this game was bloody great.
Helen's Mysterious Castle is an RPG Maker 2000 game, but don't let that deter you. The gameplay is so unlike any of the other RPG Maker games on Steam that you won't even realize it was made on such an engine (unless you once tinkered with the program yourself). Instead of having a party, every battle is one on one. Along with that, you can avoid battles by walking around enemies, although this can be a tad difficult with the grid-based movement in the world.
The combat is a mixture of Turn-Based and the Active-Time-Battle system you see in many Final Fantasy games, with a hint of Pokemon in the sense you can customize your movesets. Every item you pick up is either an active or passive item, and you have 8 inventory slots + a bank which holds found items that you've dropped from your inventory. I could explain this more and talk about the surprisingly complex mechanics , but essentially everything is deliberate in the game. Enemies have AI that react to what you do, which becomes much more important towards the end. There is no noticable RNG, as critical strike chances and missing attacks is not an issue in this game. You see the stats of your enemies attacks, and the stats of your own as you fight. It makes for this very flow-like combat system that is surprisingly addictive, but never too easy. In fact, later encounters become fairly difficult. Towards the end of the game, regular enemies are hazardous and you can't simply brute force your way through.
The writing and storytelling of the game is decent. A majority of the characters and NPCs in the game are memorable, and the game manages to pack in enough plot twists to keep you on edge and surprise you as you continue into the castle. It's definitely a game of wonder and discovery, but it's never overwhelming. The game world is large enough to be interesting and explorable, but small enough so that travelling around is never a chore, and it has many shortcuts unlocked throughout the game to make travelling that much easier.
I'm sure my writing here is starting to seem like an incohesive mess, so I'll just end it like this. The game's super cheap (2 Canadian Dollars is a hell of a deal) and it kept my attention for 7.5 hours straight. That's playing through the story, and unlocking every item and secret, and completing the bonus dungeon. In that time it never felt it was dragging on, but at the same time, the game never leaves you wanting more (although I do recommend completing the post-game bonus dungeon as it has some of the best fights in the game and gives access to unique equipment). Helen's Mysterious Castle achieves an almost perfect balance of everything. Difficulty, Content, as well as Humour and Story Depth are presented as professionally as an RPG Maker 2000 game can be, and it's an extremely good example of how a whole can be so much more than the sum of its parts.

Pros: Story, Sound
Cons: Gameplay, Graphics, Controls
Spore tells perhaps the grandest story of all: the story of life.  Even the mightiest space empire must begin somewhere, be it from peaceful, vegetarian cyclops or militant, five-legged blobs.  The sounds and music match well: the bubbling of the primordial soup, the cheerful gibberish greetings, and the whoosh of nuclear-powered rockets.
However, the gameplay is far too simplistic, easily divided into two choices throughout every stage: friend or kill.  Spore never reaches the level of any game based on a single stage (e.g. Pacman, Diablo, or Civilization).  The graphics look amazing up-close, but all practical views are from faraway.  Controls are absolutely terrible, lacking any kind of consistency between levels.
Despite its lofty ambitions, Spore wallows in shallow waters.

The comparison with Minecraft is bound to be drawn, but honestly I find this more akin to farming-based games like Farming Simulator, Harvest Moon and Rune Factory. The crafting system is simple and utilitarian, it's not voxel-based, and there's no terraforming - resources are 'node' based, and you exhaust them with your hand-drill or with automated gathering devices you can find or make. The game is very focused on the procedures of sustaining oneself and surviving - producing food, collecting resources from the automatic gatherers etc. This lends itself well to a relaxing, "project-based" style of play: make the gear you need to descend that ravine to the crystal node, loot and repair this derelict base you've found, etc. I also appreciated the little touches that reflect the setting; one of the important nodes is soil, which on the sandy seabed is rarer than you'd think.
The main objective is to collect nine parts of your escape submarine, but the real meat of this game is expanding steadily across the ocean floor, figuring out where to base oneself in order to harvest from the nodes and gather from the shipwrecks without overextending yourself and running out of oxygen or daylight hours. Given the undersea setting the number of predators is about as diverse as you could hope for - multiple types of sharks, jellyfish, shoals of barracuda and lantern fish. They're not easily aggro'd during the day unless there's blood in the water, but at night they will happily tear you to shreds. They do, however, prove lucrative to hunt later on for food & this can prove quite exciting, especially with the prospect of the blood attracting more.
The main portion of the game took me about 7.5hrs to beat, and I've spent almost that amount of time again in the Sandbox mode (no submarine parts, just expansion). Beating the main section once unlocks a Hardcore mode - more aggressive enemies, one life etc - I don't really enjoy those types of games, but you may well do. In any game mode you collect gold coins in chests lying about, and these are used when starting up a new Sandbox-mode game to buy starting equipment.
Where this game falls short is the amount of content - more infinite sandbox games have spoiled us for sheer size, and given this game is much shorter than Minecraft or Terraria, that's also less time before you've essentially 'seen everything'. If, like me, you really enjoy the undersea setting you won't mind (it has more depth than a lot of the 'biomes' of similar games to make up for it having far fewer) but I still found myself wishing there were more things to find aside from shipwrecks - undersea ruins, maybe? The depth of technology, too, is a little shallow and while that's a product of the setting a few more branches on the tech tree like hunting gear or fish-husbandry would have gone a long way. Still, for one man and one year's worth of work, it's solidly made and satisfying to play.
Overall, this is easily worth a solid 7 out of 10, an 8 or 9 if you're really into the setting. You'll get your money's worth, particularly if it's on sale, but without modding or multiplayer you'll eventually move on.

The objective of HOTG is to be the first knock your opponent's Summoning Stone from 25 life to 0 life. To do that, you have to assemble a 25 card deck and summon creatures and play spells. There are 7 pantheons to choose from, namely Roman, Greek, Chinese, Norse, Aztec and Egyptian. Each pantheon allows you to choose a leader that has a special 2 mana cost power similar to Hearthstone. You choose your favourite leader and 25 cards and you're ready to play. There's no original world to work with as all the characters come from real life superstitions. You will start with some beginning where Zeus was killed and his sould was resurrected by Anubis to prevent the war between the Greek gods and the Egyptian gods. Ares leads the charge.
Gameplay-wise, HOTG is very similar to Hearthstone and Duelyst. If you start second, you get a mana potion card that gives you 1 temporary mana point if you cast it and you start with 2 mana crystals. By default, you can only summon creatures and gods in the 8 squares surrounding your Summoning Stone. Once summoned, they are exhausted. Normal creature cards are called Beasts, Zombies and what-not and special unit cards are called Gods. There is a small delineation between the 2 as some powers can only affect Gods and others only affect the other types. E.g. Zeus' power gives +1/+1 to a God only.
Conclusion, you can try it to see it for yourself but it's not playable. I would not recommend it in its current state. The P2W features are also a major turn off. My guess is that Hi-Rez Studios is testing the waters after Duelyst got sold to Bandai Namco America.
Note: Made by Hi-Rez Studios, the makers of SMITE and Paladins. Oddly, you get a feeling that the developer comes a little too slow to the picture by copying other mainstream successes. SMITE comes after DOTA and League of Legends. Paladins comes after Overwatch. It would be better to design something that is yours.
1. Easy to pick up
If you've played Duelyst, it's pretty similar. It's not hard to pick up.
2. Points for Trying to Jump In
Duelyst seems to have fallen so I guess HOTG is trying to fill the possible vacuum.
1. Pay To Win
You still have to pony up cash for an optimized deck.
2. No Defender Advantage
Unlike Magic the Gathering, defenders are at a disadvantage here. There is summoning sickness and your units can be targetted.
3. Snowballing
This is linked to point 2. Unlike Duelyst, where your General can attack to clear units, once the board is cleared of enemy troops there is almost no way to comeback. You will get into a scenario where overwhelming forces simply clear anything you summon.
4. Temp Art
Sadly, this is more like an alpa than a beta. So many cards have temp art on them that you can't help but notice them.
5. No Chat with non-Friends
You can't chat with your opponent so that way they can hide the fact that you are playing with an AI.
6. Low Player Population

This is an example of a dating simulator done extremely well, almost perfectly in fact. Huniepop combines a masterfully constructed match 3 game with classic dating sim mechanics to create a challenging series of conquests.
Pros:
The match 3 has not one, but three point systems in place all of which impact the gameplay.
The gift system is very well balanced and varied, allowing for many different strategies.
The voice acting is superb. This is were huniepop really shines. So many games in this genre come off with hokey or overdone voices, these girls sound like normal girls would.
I can not praise the script enough, both for humor and eroticism, as long as you are not easily offended.
The art is classic anime style, and nicely done. Momo in particular was very well drawn.
Cons:
The only two drawbacks to this game are its length, being that the entire game can be cleared in a matter of a few hours if one were so inclined. The other being its balance of road to reward, as the finale for each route is just a single (albiet very sexy) CG.
In conclusion:
This game is very much worth the price, I highly recommend it.
For the developer:
Wonderful job. Please continue making games. My only advice is keep releasing uncensored versions as well, and beef up the ratio of gameplay to rewards.

I just got a new computer so my hours played are shown as a little low. Before I played directly from the original game client that launched with the game. I've as since, downloaded the game through Steam.
I've been playing STO since the very beginning, I've always been on and off(that's what she said), and I suppose having a lifetime membership has helped in that regard.
After a number of updates, the ground combat, skill system, and crafting have went through a number of improvements, and I enjoy them how they are now. You can play ground combat like a shooter or traditional mmo, but feels good to mix and match now and then.
Space combat is the real treat, and plays differently depending on how you equip your ship and what type of ship you use. Large scale battles can be a very nice spectacle to behold.
The story of the game starts off about 30 years after the last original timeline movie(Star Trek Nemisis),  and the original timeline events spoke of in the 2009 movie, as such, Romulus has been destroyed.
Each story sequence helps explore different aspects of each of the different show storylines. It's also been great to hear Star Trek Alumni reprise their roles.
I'm still having fun in Star Trek Online, and will put hundreds more hours into it. You don't have to spend real money if you don't want to, but if you're spending time in the game, it might be nice to give something back every now and then.
Star Trek online is a great game for fans of the franchise, unless they don't like space battles or the idea of ground combat. But keep in mind, there are also a few diplomatic missions as well and puzzle solving.
That's it from me for now.
-Live long and prosper.

This is probably the most fun racing game I've played yet.   It has replaced Grand Tourismo 3 A-spec as my favorite racing game, and that was a game that I got 100% gold on all races and tests.    The controls of GGE are sublime.  At first a seasoned racer might think the controls are a little simple, and that the simulation is not realistic, but this completely falls by the wayside as the game increases in complexity and speed.   When you start getting the faster cars, and onto the harder tracks, the game assumes an incredible speed, and you begin to be amazed and start thinking things like "did I really just pull that off?!"   All in all, this game sets the standard for a Car Wars road racing video game.   There is no other game better.  The game also as an incredible amount of songs.  The game is light hearted and all the cars, upgrades, race tracks and gameplay are whacky jokes.   For example a M3 BMW is a "Bummer 3M"  And a Shelby GT500 is a "Lord Shaggy 500 JT"    Recently I've tried some other racing games, and frankly the "learning curve" on the controls has been tedious and annoying.   I put that in quotes because I know how to drive a car fast, and I've been playing racing games for a long long time.  A game should be good enough that you're not fighting against the controls.   GGE delivers, the controls are sublime.

Spore tells perhaps the grandest story of all: the story of life.  Even the mightiest space empire must begin somewhere, be it from peaceful, vegetarian cyclops or militant, five-legged blobs.  The sounds and music match well: the bubbling of the primordial soup, the cheerful gibberish greetings, and the whoosh of nuclear-powered rockets.
However, the gameplay is far too simplistic, easily divided into two choices throughout every stage: friend or kill.  Spore never reaches the level of any game based on a single stage (e.g. Pacman, Diablo, or Civilization).  The graphics look amazing up-close, but all practical views are from faraway.  Controls are absolutely terrible, lacking any kind of consistency between levels.
Despite its lofty ambitions, Spore wallows in shallow waters.

Honestly I didnt think I would enjoy this game as much as I have been so far with my exp playing this quirky game.
For a $2 game you can expect a pretty dam good experience with this retro JRPG style game despite it throwing you in the game with no explanation whatsoever. It's most likely a short game given its price. But as you go along with the game the story slowly but surely unfolds itself both subtlely and obviously as you progress through the game.
But what I really made an impression on me is that you can tell the devs had fun making this game as its evidently clear with its plot twist trolling and pun intended humor. Not to mention what surprised me was its refinement system and simple yet intuitive turn based battle sequence. Also the OST tracks are quite memorable and the MC is a cutie. (When you open the item menu keep an eye on her every couple seconds. You won't regret it)
Generally you see "EXP" as the numbers to indicate when your character will lv right? Welp not for this illiterately challenged elf girl. The "EXP" gained from defeating foes is soley used to refine the equipment you find via the item menu.  As your Eff(Atk) and Def is soley based on the gear you chose to use during combat.
Elf girl herself doesnt gain any stat boosts at all other than HP boosts you find lying around or free steak when your defeated (yay).
Now the combat system is different but intuitive in its own little way compared to the generic turn based combat. I'll over glorify it alittle. This games combat is all about momentum and how well you can control the flow of battle with some slight predictive insight on how the enemy will react to the equipment you decide to bust out in battle.  As each equipment has a "Wait" count to it which is the amount of numerals it will take for the equipment used to take effect. That applies to the enemies as well. Refinement generally reduces wait count on said equipment so be sure to grind for EXP. You will be fine as long as you know simple subtraction. Some monsters are trickier than others especially with feints.
Now although I already pointed this out, I am enjoying the game in my current 1st playthrough. Also F4 to toggle full screen.

Pretty solid VN so far. E-mote does indeed make it look really smooth. There's a lot of body movement for VN characters (think hands, arms, boobs) and facial expressions as well. It's very lively and aims to be funny. The dialogue may seem a little bit childish at times, though. This game is comparable to Go! Go! Nippon! in a way that they both tell you some informational/interesting stuff about Japan's culture or history inbetween character interaction, but it doesn't go as deep. For example, it doesn't tell you how to get to certain places, how much certain things costs, where to get a Suica card, etc. The main focus are the three girls.
What's nice, though, is that it has multiple text options as it says in the description. If you're learning Japanese, this is extremely useful. What's even better is that the 3 main girls are fully voiced, so you can hear them talk Japanese and at the same time have the text in the chat menu display in English or Romaji and the additional text (in the top left corner of the screen) display in Japanese or hiragana (or any other combination of the 4).
However, if you're not learning Japanese, or you're already extremely good at speaking/reading it, the price might seem a little too high. Overall, as somebody who recently started learning Japanese, I do recommend this game and I'm very sure I can learn quite a few things from it.

"Combat is stupid and doesn't make sense"
Many things are die rolls, yes, owing to its blend of tabletop rpg with 3d real-time environment, which of course makes the early game painful. But the farther you go, the more skilled you become, the more powerful you actually feel, having overcome that piddling early-game crap. Some enemies will always worry you, and then you'll fight them, whether because they're the objective or you just can't get away, but you'll come out on top and actually feel victorious. Had that happen just yesterday afternoon, in fact. Took that dude's heart for alchemy experiments back at the house, later.
Melee combat 'misses' aren't - that's the skill of the person or creature you're fighting negating your lack of. I.e., you are swinging, and they are 'avoiding' it. Could it have been conveyed better, via popup or animation? Yep, likely, though for quick weapons, popups would get annoying.
So, how, as a programmer, do you convey that? Think of it this way:  would you stand there and take it if you saw some fresh-off-the-boat peasant swinging a sword made of laminated insect chitin at you? Betting not. Betting you'd dodge, sidestep, or otherwise evade it and commence pounding said transient's face, if such were in your skillset. It isn't animated, it doesn't taunt you, "Attack was dodged!" It gives you a quick, easily digestible sound cue, as if to say, "keep swingin', this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥'s well armored and bouncy to boot!"
"Gaw, dad, my feet hurt"
As to fast travel, I miss it too, having spent copious free hours in Oblivion and Skyrim prancing all over the map, but nor is it completely absent, as you suggest. There are several methods and many npcs who offer travel between set points, after which it's up to you to discover where to go.
"The menu is funky and all up in yo face"
Menu windows are resizeable and moveable, and by clicking the corner square, their related hud elements can be disabled.
Honestly, if the single-column, no-graphical-representation-until-and-unless-you-select-the-thing inventory lists of Skyrim are somehow better in your eyes (oooh, I can zoom in on and flip it around!), I'm not even sure what to tell you, except to refer to your flawed 'combat is stupid and doesn't make sense' argument, already refuted.
"Lol we're not even on Morrowind, just some dumb tiny I don't even"
Vvardenfell is an island (and quite a large chunk of) the land that comprises the province of Morrowind. Vvardenfell would objectively be a terrible name for a piece of entertainment software. You will visit the capital city of Mournhold on the mainland in the expansion Tribunal, if your rustles are still jimmied.
I know, I know - single player games or campaigns in otherwise multiplayer games (looking at you, CoD) seem lately to top out at 8 hours, max, but it's important in a game like Morrowind to give yourself a chance to see everything it has to offer.
All in all, I'd encourage negative reviewers to dig deeper, and for those on the fence to hop down and grab a shovel.

Star Trek Online is for trekkies seeking to captain their own ships. As a hardcore player/trekkie this game does that but the problem is it takes a lot of its time on space battles and on hostility against other races. Sadly, it's an MMO and we can't avoid combat as one of the main parts of the game. It would be great to explore other options such us being medical officer to being a captain of a medical ship. Having a science vessel and focus a lot on scientific journeys. Grab a battlecruiser and go head to head with the Klingons on PvP (spoilers: sadly because of the new seasons it will decreasr the number of it anymore). However, in my opnion, the story is great and explores the events and ideas which CBS decides to ignore in the television and movies, the events after Voyager. Despite the limitations of its engine, STO still provides good storylines and dialouges during your journey on become an admiral. The endgame content is also great which will make you busy and have fun. Unfortunately, if you hate doing everything over and over again, it's a grind system you'll hate. You have to grind a lot of things just to get decent stuffs especially in reputation system which kinda annoying. But for me it's still great how they put everything you want in game for free you just have to grind for it (both in good and bad circumstances). The gameplay is good and understandable. If you are a new player it provides you with enough knowledge on how the game works through tutorial story arcs (I find the Romulan tutorial arc the best intro to the game since it tells a good story while teaching you how things are done).
I find a lot of complains in graphics and cash grabbing. In my opnion the graphics are optimized for low-end devices (i compared the holodeck and tribble server graphics which holodeck did lowered some graphical standards which is really helpful for players with no luxury of higher-end stuff). On the note of cash grabbing i can say that it's totally based on the person on how he plays. Before the new dawn season i was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off because how bad my toon having crap ship and equipment. Turns out it was my fault for not being careful on making a skill build. After new dawn, which made a new skill system, it really improved my toon a lot. I had more skills more skill bonuses and such. Even with non-epic weapons i can still do pretty huge impacts on pves and pvps. Last but not the least, yoy can pretty much get everything for free (on the bright side you can have all the ships in the game in  the tribble server if you want to).
Overall this game is 8/10 for me

This game is a subtle mix between modern chess and modern card game. Distantly related to Duelyst, Hand of the Gods is in fact a unique tactical masterpiece.
I have been playing it for several weeks, when it was closed beta on Steam. And I can assure that HotG is improving at each patch, even though the game is still in infancy.
Is it F2P ? Patience is required to get all legendary cards. But this is true for all online CCGs. One game mode is better than Free to Play: Arena (draft) is in fact free. Devs are so generous with in-game currency that you can play Arena virtually forever. And that’s great because Arena is fun, because Arena gives cards and because in Arena everybody is equal. Sore losers can’t complain they lose to wallet players.
While growing, the community is still small. But fear not ! Contrary to real-time PvP games (shooters, Mobas…) a turn-based game doesn’t need to split its worldwide players between 3 to 5 geographical locations. In addition team-based PvP games require more players online to gather teams. HotG is 1 vs 1. Also HotG has nicely avoided what I call the Smite syndrome. A very serious game disease which multiply the game modes, splitting the community and increasing the queue wait time to 3+ minutes. And often much more. Hi Rez has learned his lesson from Smite and HotG has only 3 game modes. Consequently, wait time is around 1 minute, which is great.
Bottom line, Hand of the Gods is not another CCG and not another tactical game such as XCOM. HotG has a unique gameplay, offers epic characters (it’s cool to be a god) and is F2P. Give it a try ! But be warned that the game is hard to master: the combination of cards and two dimensional board makes it easy to make mistakes. The winner is the player who makes the fewest mistakes !

I, like many of those who bought Haven Moon, have been a fan of the MYST series since its inception, and I fully understand how the designer of Haven Moon feels about the worlds and culture given to us through the creators of MYST.  With that said, I cannot recommend Haven Moon.  Yes, the graphics and rendering are excellent, and the music is atmospheric, if limited.   However, there is not much to hold this game together.  There is no culture or back story.  It's just a series of tasks to achieve a promised ending that I found to be anti-climatic.  I won't go into it because I don't want to issue any spoilers, but really, the end was an extreme letdown for me as was the alternate ending.  The games just stops in the same manner that it just starts.  It's more a segment of a larger game than a freestanding game of its own.    I found the islands to be far too similar with the exception of Cannon where the storm is raging, but even here, the interiors were very much the same.  Also, I guess I'm too much a fan of MYST, but I expect to be able to interact with objects in a setting where here, they're just decorations.  I also found that the controls were problematic, and although the movement didn't make me sick as it did others, I found it bizarre that using the arrow keys would not allow me to turn, only go sideways and backwards through a scene.  I love the puzzles of MYST and Obduction because you can ascertain what you have to do.  Here, there are things that have to be done that are totally cryptic and must be found by sheer luck as I did once or twice or by tedious repetition.  Where sounds must be used as clues when combined in games withing the MYST series, here, it's just find the sound and look for a few pixels with which to interact.   On the whole, it took me 4 hours to complete, and I really didn't feel as though it was worth the $15.  I wish I'd done what others said to do and waited for a sale, but I needed something to take my mind off of life for a little, and Haven Moon certainly didn't do that.   There's just too little here for the excellent,  but far too similar artwork to save.

The moment you emerge from the teleporter at the beginning of Haven Moon the developer's love for Myst is obvious.  The soothing ocean waves...the breeze...the peaceful isolation.  It's all there.  From an aesthetic standpoint, Haven Moon delivers.  Everything looks pretty and all the gold thingies are nice and shiny.
Haven Moon places you in the role of an unnamed person who finds themselves transported to a mysterious moon.  Upon arriving is a letter from someone named Ektor Turren, who reveals that they are the last survivor of their civilization.  He tells you that he spent his lifetime stockpiling treasure and encourages you to find it.
And that's it.  That's the story.  It's probably the weakest element of the game, with very little actual notes to read.  I wish more had been done to flesh it out.  For example, you never do find out why Turren's civilization was destroyed, although there are some strong hints.  I would have liked to know about the planet Menra and its people.  But everything is done in such broad strokes that when the end of the game comes (there are two endings), it's hard to really care about the choice you make.
But the puzzles are the real star of a game like this, right?  Those on display in Haven Moon are fairly logical, based around gathering clues from the environment or trial and error fiddling with the machinery.  Although at one later section the game does commit the sin of pixel hunting (something Myst never did).  At the very least, it would have been nice to have some slight visual clue to tell you when you were looking in the right place instead of just having to scroll your mouse over every little thing hoping the cursor will turn green.
And that's another thing: interaction with objects in this game is kinda odd.  When you move your mouse over something, it turns green but then locks you in place so you can't move.  I imagine this was done to help people realize they found something to interact with, but it just feels awkward having control taken away from you.  You have to look away from the object before you can move again.  It's also weird that for certain things you can't go backwards.  For example, if you move a lever one space too far you can't just pull it back one.  You have to pull it all the way to the bottom then back up, which is just unnecessary.
The controls are another oddity, with the default being left mouse button to move forward and right mouse button to go backward.  Fortunately, you can change this in the launcher to something more suitable to your tastes.
Overall, Haven Moon is a decent game in the vein of Myst.  It has the potential to be better, but a weak story coupled with odd movement and interaction controls holds it back.  The game was made entirely by one person, so I can't fault it too much.  But as a lover of Myst myself, I can't help but want a little bit more out of this game.  At five dollars on sale, it was worth it for me.  So give it a shot if you have a craving for Myst-like games.

The graphics made the game easy to look at and the areas below 250m were beautiful. There are a lot of pretty lights and the creature designs get very creative.
The story is that you crash a submarine and it breaks to pieces and you have to put it back together. That is all there is to it. I may have missed something, but it did not explain who I am, or who the person is guiding me through this survival disaster. There is no putting the submarine together, it just happens. There are bases scattered in various areas with little explanation and it actually defeats the purpose of building your own base, which is a big part of sandbox games. The point of building the sub is not so you can continue whatever mission you had to complete, which would have made the game very interesting, but so you can float to the surface and be rescued. (none of this is a spoiler because the whole story is literally handed to you in the first 5 mins of the game). If you just build a water scooter, you can swim up to the surface but it blocks you with an invisible wall at 30m which just killed the immersion, and explains why building the sub to complete your mission is a much more intersting story prospect.
Depth of gameplay
There jus isnt much to it. I will compare it to minecraft for this one. In minecraft, you make your own story because there is none. You mine resources for armor and weapons because they always break. You build multiple homes in different locations because it is beneficial. This game has none of that. You make an armor piece and you respwn with it when you die. When you die, you don't reload. You just magically reapear in your first base. All your droped loot is marked on the map and stored for easy access when you go back to it. It is really hard to get into this game because it honestly felt like the game was rushing me to beat it.

The suspenseful sound track that plays when you attack a certain preditor is okay, but the ambient music more than makes up for it. My only complaint is that it didn't play enough in game. And the game only took about 2 hours to beat and I was taking my time with it, so if it played the same ambient track on a loop, I would not have gotten tired.
This game is not hard at all. I feel like survivor mode (unlocked by beating normal mode) would be kind of hard because there are more preditors, the sub parts arent marked on the map, and you only get one life. I'd try it but honestly, I'd either die and move on, or reach a point and get bored from always having to roam the ocean floor in a grid trying to find these parts, which even though they are engulfed in giant obvious glowing lights, only become visible when you get close.
Overall I can't recommend it for the above reasons as well as two other reasons. One is that it is not worth $14.99 USD and the other is that the dev gave up on it already. Even though people still buy this game, the developer got lazy and the odds of another update, more content, or even just paid DLC are probably zero. I will not be buying another game by this developer, and I will steer anyone away from this game that I can.

I first came across HMC a couple of years ago, and I'm so happy that it made its way to Steam.
You are Helen, a girl of indeterminate age who can't speak or read...and that's kind of it! The story reveals itself as you make your way through the titular mysterious castle, and while an RPG that drops you right into gameplay without a cutscene or whatnot can be disorienting, it does allow you to get right into the battles, which is where HMC really shines.
I'm a fan of JRPGs that:
a) require more than mashing A to win
b) have defending be a viable strategy
c) have grinding/buying a ton of healing items not be the solution to everything
...and HMC meets all three criteria. Battles are duels - you (Helen) v. a monster. As you explore, you can find a massive array of weapons, with each weapon having three stats - Effect (how much damage the weapon does), Defense (how much of your opponent's damage the weapon can negate), and Wait (how long it takes to use the weapon). Each enemy also has its own set of attacks, which makes battles a kind of back-and-forth dance: the monster is getting ready for a big attack! Do you put up a shield to block it? Or use your longsword to both attack and block some of the damage? Or spam a ton of quick, weak attacks so that you beat them first? Or charge up your healing spell so that it comes out right after the attack connects?
Another thing that makes HMC unique is that Helen herself never levels up: you still earn experience points after battle, but they're instead used as a kind of currency to level up your weapons, to increase Effect & Defense and/or decrease Wait. The only way Helen can get stronger is through HP upgrades, which are found through exploring - these optional upgrades, as well as the veritable arsenal of weapons you can find, gives the game a great amount of replay value.
The story is genuinely funny at times, although ultimately it's not much to write home about. The game itself isn't particularly long, too - it can easy be finished in an afternoon. Regardless, Helen's Mysterious Castle is a delightful little JRPG, and two dollars is a steal for a game this fun. Buy it whydontcha

I've noticed that the reviews for Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim tend to be about why that game is the best Elder Scrolls game and the others are terrible in comparison. I really enjoy all three of them (sorry, Arena and Daggerfall, you're just not very enjoyable by today's standards), so I figured I'll give reviews for each that focus on what's unique about each of them, and what kind of players that will appeal to.
Morrowind has easily the most vocal proponents of any of the three. They are very passionate about it, and insist that the latter two were disappointments. There's a pretty simple reason for that. It's easily the most chaotic of the three. What I mean by that is that you have far and away the most freedom and choices with Morrowind, but also easily the biggest negatives of the three games. Players who love chaos in their games tend to be the most vocal about what they want, so that's why you see Morrowind fans being the most passionate.
For the positives of Morrowind, the aforementioned freedom is the biggest one. It doesn't funnel you into rapidly progressing through the main questline right away, and in fact discourages it through tying a need for certain levels in different skills to the ability to even receive many of the main quests. You are also free to decide which factions appeal to you, based on which skills you emphasize. Unlike Oblivion and Skyrim, you can't decide to progress all the way through the questlines of every faction. Several of them are incompatible with each other, so deciding which factions suit your playstyle is up to you. Morrowind also has the largest selection of spell types, armor types, weapon types, and even skill types (you can cast spells to blind enemies, use spears as your main weapon, and have all sorts of options not available in Oblivion and Skyrim). Another big draw is a beautiful soundtrack that really puts you in the game emotionally. The enchanted items also tend to be much cooler and more abundant than in later games. The recall and mark spells also provide a nice way to teleport out of danger or when you are overburdened. The environment is pretty cool, with swamps, ash storms, green plains, volcanoes and lava, and all sorts of other different types of scenery and climate.
For the negatives of Morrowind, you have to be prepared to be much more frustrated with this game than you will with Oblivion or Skyrim. Many areas don't scale to your level, and so sometimes your freedom can be deceptive, as you can't realistically go to many parts of the island for a large chunk of the game without dying almost immediately. There is no fast travel to locations you've already visited, so you waste a lot of time walking the same roads over and over, or constantly paying for transportation between cities. The combat, magicka, and stealth dynamics are also much worse than in later games. Your magicka doesn't replenish on its own, so you have to either sleep, take potions, or wait far away from civilization (you can't use the wait function within a large radius of every town or city). Sneaking is a lot more difficult in this game, but less nuanced. A large portion of it is entirely luck based, regardless of how high your sneak skill is. The barter system is also fairly frustrating, with items costing exorbitant sums while merchants only have a small pool of gold to buy things with from you, so it takes forever to build up the large sums needed for many items.
And now, let's talk about the biggest negative of the game, which also happens to be the biggest negative in any of the games: the combat system is terrible. Instead of your weapon skill determining how much damage you do, it determines (although somewhat loosely) whether or not your attacks connect. And even then, they will frequently miss. So you'll stand right in front of an enemy, swinging your weapon over and over, and very few of them will connect. Your fatigue affects it as well. A similar thing goes for spells, where every spell has a rather large chance of failing to cast, while still draining your magicka. It's the single dumbest decision Bethesda made with any of the Elder Scrolls games.
This game is definitely worth it, although if you first play it after playing Oblivion or Skyrim, you have to change your expectations, because it is a lot less polished or refined than those two. If you love chaos/anarchy in your games, this will be your favorite. If not, it's still a great game to play, it just takes a lot of getting used to.

Haven Moon is well-intentioned and it certainly has some virtues (it's fairly easy on the eyes), but it suffers badly from "single-developer syndrome":  I've seen it plenty of times in the puzzle/P&C/adventure genre -- bad puzzles escape the QA process when there is no QA process and no other developers to serve as sounding boards and critics.  Haven Moon unfortunately commits many of the worst crimes of point-and-click puzzle games of this sort (Myst-like):  Pixel-hunting -- a cardinal sin in 3D games, mandatory incorrectly-hinted large search-space guesswork, "precise" maps that actually represent inaccurate geometry upon which puzzles depend, buggy and badly-hinted puzzles, nearly silent but crucial audio "clues", and visual hints that are nearly impossible to pick up on when one's display gamma is a bit too high.
I personally found the navigation to be nauseating when played on a computer (there's no vertical intertia), so I used my TV, which was absolutely fine for splendid 3D puzzlers like Obduction and Quern, but the increased distance and TV-style gamma/color made some of the puzzles' hints difficult to detect, especially when they must be "hunted" down.
Pixel-hunting was to some extent an acceptable game mechanic in the days of 2D, when screens were fairly static and one could reasonably spend a finite amount of time looking for the "hidden object", but it's a poor excuse for a "puzzle" when you have three full degrees of freedom and no static screens.  Myself, I far prefer being given an object that is completely visible and the problem is figuring out how it works, what its purpose is, and what it affects.
If this is the sort of game you prefer, try the aforementioned Quern & Obduction, which are very tight in the puzzling realm (turn the music off on Quern, though).  Perhaps the Haven Moon developer will collaborate with others on his next effort.

Helen's Mysterious Castle is the best one that's ever been made, and probably that will ever be made. Hands down, no contest. The combat is extremely complex. What starts as rock paper sicissors evolves into a game of ai exploitation as you learn to turn the enemie's own strategies against itself. The feeling of having to figure out the game and its story on your own is a whole lot better than having a "hey listen, hey listen" tutorial bot nagging in  your ear every 2 feet. The gameplay or combat system is where the game REALLY shines, it's a 1v1 match (every time) and is all about strategy and timing, it is fun and incredibly addictive, in addition everytime to defeat an enemy you gain XP, but not to your character but to your weapons and gear so most of the game (until you are full of beef) you are basiclly in the same hp status. The graphic yes are not the most stunning when looking at todays modern games, but is still charming to view. This goes for the music as well Its not distracting but still very catchy and grand to listen too. If you are still reading this then ill wrap it up, Basically if you are into challenging rpgs and are looking for a good time then PLEASE by all means give Helens Mysterious Castle a whirl.

The Ship: Murder Party is a fantastic game. Single-player plot - The single-player story begins with an introduction from Mr. X. He tells the passengers of his wish and warns that those too weak to play his "game" may be of use to the sharks, but not for him. The player assumes the role of Charlie Panther, second class passenger. After (easily) dispatching his quarry, Charlie hears a young man whisper to him from a nearby third class cabin. Upon investigating, he is greeted (and complimented on how well he killed his quarry) by the young man who introduces himself as Jimmy the Bellboy. Jimmy explains that "Mr. X don't like no loose ends" and that he is planning on destroying the boat after the hunt is over—along with whoever wins. Jimmy then offers to get Charlie off the boat for $100,000. However, before he can start gathering money, Charlie has to deal with his own hunter. Jimmy suggests he find someone who looks just like him so he can fool his hunter. Charlie notices someone who could definitely pass for him at the museum, so he steals a tranquilizer syringe from the sickbay and injects the man with it, causing him to instantly become unconscious. Charlie returns to Jimmy, who in turn tells Charlie's hunter that he is in the museum asleep, therefore taking the target off Charlie's back. With Charlie safe (from his hunter, at least) Jimmy sends him to the Vesuvius bar on Deck B, where Bruno, the bartender, has him steal wallets from rich customers and give him half of what's in them. This works for a while, but the guard become suspicious of their plot, and Charlie is forced to leave. Jimmy then directs him to the Fence, a portly British man in Deck B's restaurant. The Fence has Charlie steal several treasures (including the Holy Grail), paying him more for each returned. He then has to escort an ambassador around the ship to complete his "mission". After the ship is picked clean, Charlie returns to Jimmy, who has been injured by an assailant who was soon jailed. He tells Charlie that he wants the man dead, and if Charlie does him in, that he will take him off the boat for $25,000 less. Charlie gets himself arrested by pulling a weapon in front of a guard and is hauled to the brig. Inside the brig, Charlie meets with a very large muscle-bound convict, who hints to Charlie about the whereabouts of a knife hidden in a Bible. The convict is shot dead by the guards, however, as he begins to become insane with rage as he talks about Mr. X and the Bermuda Triangle. Charlie finds the shank in a bookshelf and stabs Jimmy's assailant. Upon being released from the brig, Jimmy is ecstatic that his assailant is dead and gladly takes $25K off Charlie's escape price. Charlie is then directed to a Japanese Yakuza, who wants the captain of the ship dead for having an affair with his wife. After killing him, Jimmy tells him that the captain is still alive. After killing the captain, this time for real, Charlie is directed to Miss Tweed, who wants him to kill some kidnappers who took her dog. The player then meets with them, but upon seeing that he does not have the ransom money, they kick the dog off the ship, presumably to its death. After killing the kidnappers, Charlie returns to Mrs. Tweed, who sobbingly (due to her dog going overboard) gives him the money. After, Charlie returns to Jimmy who gladly accepts the reduced price, but tells him to do one last job, in which he has to go to the Radar room of the ship, and put the radar itself out, so when in the water he can't be spotted by the crew. Returning to Jimmy on the Boat Deck, he wishes him good luck, and that the two can maybe see each other again. As Charlie floats away in his escape boat and Mr. X flies off of the ship in a helicopter, a massive explosion tears through the ship, separating it in two, and starts to sink. It is then revealed that Mrs. Tweed's dog survived, as it pops out of the water. The screen suddenly goes black, which might have meant Charlie was hit by debris from the explosion. Charlie then wakes up in a hospital lying on a bed with a nurse treating him. Mr. X's voice is heard on the nearby speaker saying "Welcome ladies and gentlemen, welcome one and all..." Each player is given a nickname by which they are identified. This is done to make it more difficult to tell players apart from NPCs, who have similar names and look the same as normal players. Each player is assigned a quarry, whom he or she must murder. The last known location of a player's quarry is always revealed to the player. However, the appearance of the quarry is only revealed if the player converses with the quarry. Multiplayer - There are several different weapons with which to eliminate one's quarry. Different amounts of money are rewarded for a kill depending on how difficult it is to use the weapon and how many times it has been used. If a player murders an NPC or anyone other than his or her quarry or hunter, a cash amount - dependent on the server settings - will be deducted from his or her bank account. Players with less than a certain figure, set by the server, in their bank account will be kicked from the cruise. Various weapons can be found scattered all around the ship, such as flare guns, fire axes, firearms, knives, swords, crowbars (which state "to be used by a free man" - a reference to Half-Life's storyline), even secret traps provided just for killing your quarry, like falling lifeboats, saunas, freezers, even a deck that turns into a 60 degree angle by command, among others. If a player is seen pulling out a weapon in front of a guard or a camera, or spotted by eyewitnesses, then they are sent to jail. There is an "eye" symbol in the player's HUD that tells them whether they are being spotted or not; if they are watched by security the eye turns red; if not, the eye is green. The meter for trespassing counts down and the player is fined when the countdown is complete (and, if they run out of money to pay the fines, go to jail). Guards can be bribed to overlook weapons. Everyone has eight needs similar to The Sims. Such needs are eating, drinking, sleeping, socialising, maintaining proper hygiene and using the bathroom. Some of the needs would cause impairment, such as lack of sleep would cause the player to fall asleep on the spot. Other needs could become fatal, such as thirst and hunger. If the player does not fulfill these needs, he or she will die, resulting in a loss of $1000. Needs are sated by going to restaurants, taking showers, talking with other players, etc. This forces players into situations where they are vulnerable to attack, and also attempts to prevent players from camping. 8.6/10

Spore is a brilliant idea for a game with decent graphics and great options for diversity. It also has decent execution, for the most part. However there are two major flaws that taken together are essentially fatal. The game does not autosave at any time, and the game crashes ridiculously often. Spore wants you to invest many hours into carefully planning your creature's physical, social, and technological evolution, but it doesn't care to prevent crashes that erase your entire civilization, right down to turning your planet that was possibly a spacefaring race back into a planet of burgeoning protozoa. What this means is for a player to experience the game meaningfully, they will be stopping to manually save every 30 minutes or so, completely removing themselves from the experience that is essentially the point of the game. If you can train yourself to do that and accept frequent crashes and still find the experience deep and engaging, you may get a chance to actually enjoy the relatively fun and diverse game world.
In short, Spore is a decent game experience that is destroyed by its easily patchable technical issues.

TL;DR: Great game. Story is interesting, gameplay is deep, graphics suck, but the art design is solid. 9/10, buy it now.
Let me start by saying that I will NOT be comparing this game to Skyrim or vice versa. Skyrim is an excellent game, and so is Morrowind. These senseless, nostalgia-driven reviews tearing down Skyrim and jacking off Morrowind are just that: senseless.
Story:
This is an Elder Scrolls game. The deep, detailed lore provided by this franchise can rival epics such as The Lord of the Rings. But for Morrowind specifically, you are the Nerevarine--or at least, you will be. A child born on a certain day to uncertain parents, you grew up to do something to get yourself thrown into the Imperial City Prison. By order of Uriel Septim VII, you were shipped to Morrowind and set free, with instructions to report to one Caius Cosades in the city of Balmora. Should you choose to do so, you will start an epic journey spanning the whole of Vvardenfell (a large island very close to the mainland of Morrowind) to fulfill the Nerevarine Prophicies and destroy Dagoth Ur, a maddened god who threatens to take over all of Morrowind and eventually, Tamriel.
But if that doesn't suit your fancy, you can run off into the sunset and slaughter small insects.
Gameplay:
You start by selecting a race, which provides you with a few bonuses to your skills. A Nord will get +5 proficiency in heavy armor as well as a strength bonus, a Dunmer gets +5 proficiency in light armor as well as a speed bonus...the list goes on. Afterwards, you'll select a class that further defines your playstyle through stats--you can play as an assassin, warrior, rouge, witch hunter, and more. Should none of the classes suit your fancy, you can make your own. You'll also be prompted to select a birthsign, which gives you bonuses to some stats on top of your class and race bonuses.
After creating your character, you are swiftly thrown into the wide world of Morrowind. With nothing to hold you back, you can either roam the world and seek adventure, or continue with the main questline.
Combat seems odd at first; you use your weapon to attack enemies, as expected, but an invisible dice roll determines whether or not your weapon actually impacts with your enemy's body. It seems strange and archaic for a 3D game, but it is actually one of the deepest combat systems I've encountered in an RPG. You are more likely to hit your target based off of A) how much fatigue you have, B) how much fatigue your enemy has, and C) how proficient you are with the weapon you are using. A warrior trained to use blunt weapons will generally hit his target each time, provided he has high fatigue and has practiced with his hammer--but if you give him a dagger, he will hit nothing, as he is unskilled with short blades. It seems to make sense, and really isn't that bad once you get used to it.
Lockpicking is much the same. You equip a lockpick, and whether or not it succeeds is completely dependent upon your Security skill and the quality of the lockpick you're using.
Morrowind's magic system is stunning. The player can combine from about 140 magical effects together to make just about any spell imaginable. This carries over to enchanting, where these spell effects can be bound to an item--such as a sword--to cast a combination of spell effects on either the target, user, or everything around the user. Using the spell system, you can leap over entire cities in a single bound (take that, Superman!), walk on water, destroy all monsters in a 500-foot radius, fly with the speed of 100 Cliff Racers, and much more. For some, the magic system is the pinnacle feature of Morrowind.
There's so much more I could cover about Morrowind's gameplay; however, Steam only allows us so many characters in these reviews. Play the game, and you'll understand just how overwhelming it is. On to the next section...
Graphics:
The first Halo game is older than Morrowind by about a year. If you can't run Morrowind, I feel pity for you. While the graphics are at their core bad, the art design is amazing. Morrowind is filled with strange and uncanny creatures. Most of them are insect-like and alien, as if they were pulled straight from a science fiction game. They do not look out of place, however; their aestetics are fitting for the ashy world of Morrowind. The weapons look like weapons. They're gritty, sharp, and look like they can do damage--which indeed, is what they do. The Dwarven ruins are clearly the rusted wastes of a once-great power, now fallen to time, leaving only their hostile automated machinery in their place.
Yeah, it's a fantasy RPG with alien-like animals, and robots. I love every minute of it.
Overall:
Morrowind is a spectacular RPG that rewards the patient, adventure-seeking gamer. I implore you to buy this game. My rating for Morrowind is 9/10.

TL,DR:
This game is somewhat between your ordinary survival game and an "interactive experience" in the likes of Proteus and Dear Esther. Looks gorgeous, plays nice and easy and performs smooth but has a very limited gameplay scope. Consider it an anti-stress game to grab ONLY during a sale.
There are gameplay elements, of course, and there is also a goal to be achieved here (in case you are playing the Story Mode), which is to gather the materials required to construct a submarine, with the (ironic) purpose of taking you back to the surface.
So, this is where you may be put off a bit, as this is what you WILL do (I can almost guarantee):
-Gather Iron to Construct all the different crafting tables.
-Hunt for some shipwrecks to get some crafting materials and also, to find some seeds and vases to grow your own potatoes and carrots.
-Find some gold ore to be able to craft better helmets that allow you to go deeper in the water, so you can find some more crafting materials that combined with gold will allow you to craft better helmets that allow you to go deeper in the water, so you can find some more crafting materials that combined with gold will allow you to craft better helmets that allow you to go deeper in the water, so you can find some more crafting materials that combined with gold will allow you to craft better helmets that allow you to go deeper in the water... you get it
-Find a knife so you can kill as much fish as you want without being worried with ammunition as you were until now with your harpoon, and also, so you can cut down algae and some "power algae" that provides you with a nice power orb (required for your submarine).
-When you finally get your best helmet (and matching oxygen tank that will allow you to stay more time in the water), you can now access the depth at which the rare material spawns (and also where the most beautiful parts of the game).
-Get the material, escape the furious Kraken(s) that where supposedly guarding it and craft the submarine to get back to the surface and win the game.
All I described above WILL be the thing that you will do in Story mode, for almost exactly an hour. There is a sandbox mode, which is basically the same but does not end the game when you get to the surface.That is where the survival ends and the "interactive experience" starts as you may explore the seemingly infinite randomly-generated underwater surface.
Still interested?
As much as I like the game, I cannot recommend you to buy it in full price, but at the time I write this, there is a very tempting 80% discount, making it 3€. Grab it like that, and then you will get your money worth.

Haven Moon, as the description and reviews suggest, is a Myst-style point and click adventure where you find yourself on a mysterious and abandoned island and read about the world through text you find left behind. Your objective is to figure out how to activate teleporters on the island chain. The game is relatively short, shorter than Myst, and I would say something between 2-3 hours for an experienced adventure player or maybe 4-5 for someone new to the genre. Puzzles are environmental, not inventory based. There are a few puzzles which require finding hidden switches, but mostly the game is about using your brain and I feel all the puzzles are tough but fair.
If you're going to play the game, I recommend giving it a chance and really thinking through your options before looking up answers to puzzles. Try fiddling with switches, thinking about the next thing you want to, and writing down what you find. Pay attention to any information you get from letters. Play with sound turned on, because directional sound cues are important for several puzzles. If you think through everything, you'll get through the game.
The game is beautiful (it really nails that old timey Victorian brass, books, and spiral staircases feel; great architecture in general!) and the score is lovely to listen to. If there are drawbacks, I think they mostly stem from the game's scope. It was made by a single developer. Most of the areas in the game are shown in the screenshot carousel. There are limited configuration options. Controls are a little wonky. Movement is a little slow. And as I said it's a fairly short game for the $15 asking price ($10 in the current sale). But I think if you're wiling to forgive the rough edges, you will find a very solid contribution to the genre.
I played version 1.1 and left some pretty detailed feedback for the developer, so I'll update my review if any of my suggestions are implemented.

I always look forward to another Myst-like point & clicker with exotic landscapes and atmosphere.  Haven Moon delivers on this.  The visuals are gorgeous, the music is right, and the puzzles are logical but not diabolically hard.  Knowing this came from a single individual as his first game is astonishing:  my hat is off to you sir!
It is short (I was not ready for it to end!) and the gameplay is very linear.  I wish the inter-island travel (and there's a lot of it) didn't drop back to a load screen each time; it kind of breaks the mood a little.  I would love to have heard more ambient music in the outdoor areas.  However, I can't wait for the next game from this developer.

A clear spiritual successor to the Myst franchise, this game does a good job of immersing the player in the game world. However that immersion felt broken somewhat by loading screens and repetative travel between the islands that make up the game areas.
There are hints of a great story, but I would have liked to see it more fully fleshed out.
I felt that the puzzles were fair for a game in this genre with a good mix of straightforward, subtle, and complex elements. I would caution that the progression is very linear, so the frustration factor sets in quickly if you get stuck.
Overall, I think Francois Roussel did an impressive job recreating the ambiance and spirit of the Myst games, particularly as a solo developer. My biggest complaint is the game is quite short (less than 4 hours gameplay for me) which makes the full price feel a bit steep and hard to recommend, but fans of the graphic adventure puzzle genre will find enjoyment in Haven Moon.

Review TL:DR: A nice card/board game with some interesting abilities and pretty decent visuals for what it is. Don't go in expecting to have everything immediately (as with all card games or similar.) Each class feels different with a playstyle to fit most players. Try it; IT'S FREE!
Firstly, pay-to-win?: No, not as much as other card games. No names but we all know who I am pointing at. Everything can be obtained via little playtime if I'm being honest. You have a few ways to gain the currency needed for a pack.
1) Quests: pretty self explanatory.
2) Wins: 10 currency per win. 30 for a pack. Similar to other CCG type games.
3) Leveling up your heroes. You get 100 currency for leveling up your heroes, this doesn't take much time at all.
4) Daily login rewards.
Clone or no clone? While this game takes things from other games that are similar it does a few things differently. Games are usually quick, good for a little play session. There are interesting mechanics like that of Athena (GOD) and Bellona (Hero).
Gameplay: Each player chooses 1 of 7 classes, more to come too! Your objective is to destroy your opponents 'summoning stone' on a board-game style battlefield. Each has 25 hp (Health points) and when it reaches zero. DING DING you win, or loose. You can only summon creatures ADJACENT to the stone with a few exceptions. A lot of the game is deception and out maneuvering your opponent. No just mindless hitting face because there are mechanics to stop that! Such as the 'protection' or melee/ranged system.
Balancing: honestly it's pretty good; each class has it's own 'broken' cards but that's normal in a CCG. Classes have to have powerful abilities to make it exciting, and boy is it. All these crazy abilities CAN be played around as a lot of it is board positioning.
Final thoughts: A very good attempt at a CCG/Board game style game with it's own charm thanks to the SMITE IP! I mean, it's free... Give it a go!

What they did is make 5 half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥mini-games, each one a different game genre, and combine them into a single game that progresses & evolves your creature through each mini-game. None of the 5 mini-games is much fun on its own. Just when one of them seems like it's about to get fun, you're done with it and have to go on to the next.
The cell stage is so short and limited that it could be a Flash game. In fact, I have played many Flash games that have much more depth and enoyability than this mini-game.
The creature stage is actually pretty fun the first time through, but slogging through the unlocks is not even remotely fun a second time, even if you make completely different choices.
Tribal stage is a really simplistic RTS that you beat in minutes.
Civilization stage is almost a 4X, except there's no "explore", "exploit", and not much of an "expand" among those 4 Xs, and diplomacy is barely a thing (though I admit I wouldn't know, as I just conquered everyone).
The space stage is a more complete 4X, except you have to slowly fly your ship to any civilization/colony you want to interact with. On top of that, your one ship is the only unit you can ever really control. This portion of the game never ends - you just keep flying your ship around and doing the same boring stuff forever. The galaxy is pretty massive, which is good, but the limit to how much you can do in it, along with the tedium of flying your ship around, pretty much eliminates the appeal of the large scale.
The lesson here is when you make 1/5th of 5 different games, then smush them together, you don't actually get a whole game. Sorry Maxis. The only way an idea like this could work is if each of the 5 mini-games was fleshed out and felt like a full game on its own.

Honestly, while this game may have been all the rage when it was released, it has definately not stood up well to the test of time. I wanted to see what all the long time Elder Scrolls fans thought was so great about this game, and all I can say is, not much.
The fighting mechanics are rather dull, which could be a description of both Oblivion and Skyrim as well, but they have at least been refined to feel more fluid over time.
It is a massive world, but your character is painfully slow, especially when you run out of stamina, and there is no form of fast travel.
The set pieces, while interesting, are few and far between. Everything in general is just rather dreary, which is fine for setting the mood, but it needs to look good too. Having to slowly jog through large amounts of rather uniteresting areas is a miserable experience. This is even after I installed several mods to make the game look a great deal better.
There's a number of other smaller issues that I could go through, but just what I've written here so far makes this game almost entirely unenjoyable. I tried, I really did, and the only thing I've taken away from this experience is respect for how much better the sequals are. Any love for this game is purely nostalgic, which is fine, but there is no reason to invest any time in it today when there are so many much better games out there to play.

When I was young, I obtained a copy of Morrowind. This being my first real RPG as a child, I tried it for a bit and was immediately baffled by combat system. I was confused and refused to play it for a while, yet something nagged at me.
I eventually returned, wiser and with a greater amount of patience for reading, and eventually, something clicked as I began to progress through the game. The world within Vvardenfell felt like a living world with NPCs going through their daily lives (though you'd need to fill in the blanks yourselves due to AI limitations), fiiled with lore that was implemented (to a good extent) in the main quest which kept me interested in playing to see how it pans out while the completion of questlines created a sense of accomplishment that NPCs will acknowledge and may even praise (unlike in Skyrim where only key NPCs and guards will recognise the compeletion of the Main Quest, ruinning that experience for me and Oblivion whereby the constant stares led me to lock my main character in Sheogorath's Palace). Guild progression also requires a certain level to advance to the next rank which was a far more immersive experience than being a dual-sword wielding warrior with minimal magic skill who became Archmage in Skyrim.
Despite the bugs (that can be fixed with patches (official and unofficial)), it never stopped being fun for me to wander out in search of a cave to kill bandits only to notice an NPC standing out in the wilderness, quest in hand. It helps that there were no quest markers and that all you had was a journal that gives a desciption of nearby landmarks (though this can get annoying at times with the vague directions).
The design of the world and its inhabitants were interesting but for me, what kept me in wasn't how odd the landscape was (unmodded, of course) or how weird this Nix Hound was. What kept me in was a sense of progress and accomplishment as I performed quests, levelled up, discovered the odd object that made me wonder if I was sequence-breaking. The thrill of exploration is everywhere in this game (unless you run into cliff racers at level 1, then it's a re-enactment of your favourite Tom and Jerry sequence)
If you want to try out an RPG for the first time and don't feel like trying out other RPGs, Morrowind is a good game to introduce yourself to the franchise and genre.
