If you're an MMO fan, this is for you.  If you're a Star Trek fan, this is for you.  There's just SO much content for a Free-to-Play game.  The soundtrack is sublime.  The Cryptic character creation (present in Champions Online, as well) is the hands-down, absolute BEST around...even with a 6+ year old engine.  The duty officer system, R&D system, and (in the later game) the Admiralty system provide alternate ways to advance your character (which, IMHO, definitely add to the RPG aspect of the game).  The Foundry (player-generated content) allows for even MORE free content.  Finally...the space battles are SO much fun.  The action is engaging...not quite frenetic, but definitely keeps you on your toes.
Weak points, now.  The ground game is probably the weakest point of the game...if you don't like MMO-style combat, you'll be uncomfortable here.  There is the option to switch to an FPS-style control scheme, but it's not really a full FPS...hovers somewhere between MMO and FPS combat.  You'll die a LOT more in ground missions than you will in space stuff.  Also, while it is certainly not pay-to-win, you'll probably need to spend a little money at some point to fully enjoy the game (remove credit cap, ship upgrade tokens, etc).  Endgame can get kind of grindy, having to repeat the same space battles to earn marks.  But...if you enjoy those battles, you might not even care.  Crafting isn't very engaging.  It's just another thing to grind...certainly doesn't have the depth and entertainment value of other MMO's.
Bottom line...this game is fun.  For a F2P, there is a LOT of content to explore.  The storyline is engaging, and the combat is action-packed and entertaining.  Engage with the community, toss a little money at the game to support it, and above all...don't be a jerk.

ART: 5
I wasn't a huge fan of the art unfortunately, would have liked to have seen a little more detail put into the environment, also Vinty's character compared to the others in the novel.
MUSIC: 6
The soundtrack changed throughout various scenes being appropriate to the environment/situation where the scene was heading.
STORY: 6.5
I enjoyed being back with Vinty and her cute yet clumsy approach to everything, traveling through Melbourne and experiencing culture shock compared to living in her home town. This story felt more like a bonus episode rather than a sequel, never the less I still enjoyed reading through the novel.
OVERALL RATING: 6/10
This visual novel brings in a more realistic approach to an everyday life story which is unique compared to other visual novels, but lacked keeping me engrossed. It was also interesting to see the actual camera footage being taken in Melbourne and being integrated into the game. Vinty's personality was one of the main things that kept me going. Although it was a short visual novel, it's worth picking up if it's on sale.

For a puzzle game, this is actually one of the best I've played in awhile. No matter how you challenge yourself, the game remains difficult yet reasonable at the same time. It takes components of dating sims - such as improving personal traits, gift-giving and even dating - into a realm of puzzle-solving that I've never ventured before.
Every time you win, the score needed to win goes higher, the points become harder to obtain, and the combos become more elusive. You have to choose either to let the difficulty climb, or better yourself to stay on top, and you're rewarded either way!
It's certainly not perfect - it's a dating sim that is heavily biased in favor of the player, while the puzzles are biased against you - but that brings the challenge and replay value to a balanced level.

Spore is an interesting concept that suffers from lack of consistency throughout its gameplay and lack of replayability.
The beginning of the game shows you all of the greatness of spore - creating your race, consuming other beings, and swimming around in a cesspool of creative and dangerous creatures. As soon as you evolve to the point of being able to go on land and interact with multicellular beings, the game's attraction begins to diminish. Now you're fighting with other races, using a mixture of "evolved" traits that can be changed at any time and generic attacks, and utilizing an overly simplistic mechanic to communicate and befriend them. Next  thing you know, you evolve far enough that you can create weapons and buildings and you're playing any other generic RTS. All the cool racial choices you've made thus far in order to survive become completely cosmetic and useless. The game itself doesn't take very long to progress from cell to this world dominator phase.
I cannot recommend purchasing this game at full price, or even while it's on sale. If you've realling been pining for it, get it while it's on sale. But even so, there are many games that are more deserving of your time.

Ember Kaboom strikes me as a beginner's attempt at their first game. The visuals are very simple, everything contained to a single screen height, linear design, very basic interface and controls. The other thing that comes to mind is the developer had a SNES growing up. The momentum Ember has while running is a sloppy attempt at Mario's running physics, and most of the enemy movement patterns are ripped straight from Mario (from the goomba-like mice to the  Boss Bass narwal) with some Donkey Kong Country animal friends for good measure.
That said, is it any good? Not really; it's pretty bland, not laughably bad nor entertainingly good. It does show a decent amount of variety level features, different types of platforms and bouncy mushrooms, and the environments are always changing. That said, there isn't much pulling the stages together either. There are 12 levels with 3 stages each, each stage has nothing to do with the next one. There's at least one new gimmick or enemy type per level as far as I saw (I did 6 of the 12 stages), and stage names or early platforms will generally tell you what you need to know about a given stage's hazards. Aside from that, the level design is very basic and straightforward, occasionally hiding a 1 UP but nothing to explore otherwise.
The major compaints I had were the ice physics, general controls, and lack of features/polish. Normally you have momentum when you run, it's lost if you stop. On ice however, you go full speed in the last direction you hit, but if you jump without holding a direction you lose momentum almost immediately. The movement is not very good to begin with, but this just compounds the poor controls. The core gameplay simply isn't very good, it's all about moving forward, you can't attack aside from jumping on most enemies' heads, and you die in one hit. The levels are packed with some "not a coin but might as well be coins" swirly-thing that, when you collect enough, you get a 1 UP. The overall time is shown at the end of the level but it doesn't record it or have a leaderboard that I could see, so why bother? There are no graphics options, no key rebinding (stuck using arrows for movement and space to jump) everything is just bare bones. There are a lot of cosmetic improvements that could be made; such as adding a world map for the level select, more detailed and better animated sprites, the story has almost no impact on the game (it doesn't tie into the levels, the same animation is shown at the end of each stage, etc)
Not a terrible game, it is playable but not much fun.

Having won the game in a giveaway I was curious to see what it was like and if it could succeed where other indie platformers had failed to impress. Yes. The answer is yes, it did.
Ember Kaboom is a platformer where the best way to enjoy it is to try and keep your momentum going, making adjustments on the way to avoid hazards in your path. The option is always there if you want to try a slower pace though. Jumping challenges are fantastic as you'll navigate falling platforms, temporary bridges and using enemies themselves to bounce across gaps.
Variety is the spice of life and this is an area the game excels at. The game constantly changes the style as you move through the levels without straying too far off course, so in one stage you're using bouncy mushrooms to soar high, then you'll be riding a goat to outrun a giant snowball and then dropped in the ocean for a leisurely swim. The two narwhal levels do tend to hurt the pacing somewhat though.
The only major overall issue is that the game is pretty short, requiring only an hour to burn through all the stages it has to offer. That said, I can see this as a game people would like to revisit for some simple platforming fun.

A relatively short but very well made game inspired by Myst.
Like many other gamers I've never forgotten the experience of playing Myst for the first time. It was one of the first games to come out on CD-rom and like The 7th Guest was used to promote the sale of CD-rom drives. The combination of a beautiful and carefully designed 3D world with interesting lore and difficult puzzles was unlike anything I had played before. It has inspired many games that came out afterwards and will probably continue to inspire developers for many years to come.
The influence of the Myst games is unmistakable but this game doesn't recycle any of the plot or puzzles from these games. The designer has created his own little world (well, moon actually) with it's own lore and original set of puzzles. The game focusses on the manipulation of devices rather than on cryptology or advanced math puzzles that you'll find in the Myst games. In order to solve Riven I needed several pages of notes for all the different puzzles. For this game I only needed one sheet of A5. Since it was developed by just one programmer it shouldn't come as a surprise that the scope of the game is much smaller than that of any of the Myst games. But luckely that which is there is of high quality and the puzzles might be a lot easier, they're no cake walk either.
The world has a distinct steampunk look with lots of brass, wood, marble and iron. A lot of care and attention has been given in the overall design of the different islands you visit and everything looks and behaves very realistic. This is only let down by a relatively low level of antialising (probably a limitation of the engine used) so you'll notice jagged edges and interference patterns while playing.
The interface is clean and simple. While you can use the arrow keys or WASD keys to move around, there is no need since you can play the entire game using only the mouse. Left clicking will move you forward and right clicking will cause you to step backwards. This is very similar to interface of RealMyst. There are a couple of items that you'll pick up and they are displayed as small traslucent white icons at the bottom of the screen. The cursor changes from white to green when you can interact with an object and you can turn handles and valves by either left or right clicking. Useable objects are automatically taken from your inventory when you click the correct object. Puzzles are locked when you've solved them, which is helpfull since you won't loose time trying to manipulate things that no longer need manipulating.
The story is told primarily through a number of notes left by the man who built all the buildings and machines. Unlike Myst and Riven there are no audio or video clips. Very much like Myst you'll have to make a moral decission at the end of the game which will lead to the good or the bad ending. I wish that some of the books in the library you find where readable so you'd be able to get to know this world and the man who created the machinery better. But I can see how that would be too much to ask from a one man development team. I can only hope that a possible second game will delve deeper into the lore of this world. There is enough background story given so you'll understand how these islands came to be and where the inventor went but it leaves me wanting to know more.
The sound design is also very good, featuring ambient noises when you're outside and subtle music when you enter certain buildings or visit certain places. One of the puzzles relies on the use of sounds and some of the machines use sound to let you know when something is or isn't working.
Once you've completed the game there is not much reason to hang around or replay it. While the islands look nice, they're small and there isn't much to see or do once you're done with figuring out how everything works. The notes hint about the existence of a nautical vessel (a boat or sub) and you'll find a harbour on each of the islands. But you won't find this vessel, since the inventor used it to visit an unkown location that you won't be able to reach.
I haven't been able to find out if the developer is planning on creating a sequel, but I honestly hope he does. With a bigger budget and maybe some more programmers and designers by his side a sequel (or prequel) could be much bigger and contain more puzzles and background lore. There is no reason why there shouldn't be many more islands or even a big land mass on this moon. And since the inventor was able to transport you from earth to this Haven Moon, there is no reason why you shouldn't be able to visit other moons or planets.
Despite the short playing time I have to say that I'm really impressed by this game. I enjoyed solving the puzzles and discovering the different islands. I think that the current price of €15,- is fair for what's offered and I'm glad I could help support the developer by buying it. If you find this too expensive for a 4 to 5 hour game than you should definitely get it whenever it is on sale.

TO GET WASD MOVEMENT: the keybind menu is in the Unity launch window.  The Unity launch window is that first window that opens after you launch the game from steam, where you then hit the "Play" button to start the actual game.  To add WASD movement, just click the "Input" tab, and then double click the appropriate cell in the "secondary" column for the direction you want to move, and type the key you want to  use to move in that direction.  There is no keybind section of the ESC menu while in game.  WASD has been around for decades, it's a little frustrating to me when a game does not enable this by default.
Hold down the SHIFT key to sprint.
The game defaulted to 1024x768 screen resolution for me, which was pretty blocky, so if you start the game and it doesn't look like the store page video did, you can increase the screen resolution in the Unity launch window, before the game starts. The game looks pretty good at high resolution, although the framerate is a little choppy when spinning the view.  I don't have framerate problems in other games.  Maybe this will be improved in a patch.  It's not bad enough to bother me so far, just enough that it looked slightly jittery when I turn the view around quickly.
The game appears to have four "islands" total, so it does not seem to be only the one island you see in the promo video--there appears to be more content.  The puzzles (that I've seen so far) do seem like the old myst puzzles.  The music is nice, and the game has a pleasant, relaxing atmosphere.  The default control is to move forward with left mouse button, and backwards with right mouse button, however you interact with things in the world with left mouse button too, which I find a little irritating, because it causes you to move around while you are trying to click on things, but this is a minor beef.
This game is apparently the work of a single dev, so as with Banished, Beseige and numerous other single-dev games, this effort deserves some props on that score alone.
The ESC menu has a "Readme" button that contains credits and a short message from the dev, a "Restart" button to restart the game, and a "Quit" button to quit to desktop.  There is no save game, load game or options in the ESC menu.  There is some quick reference info on the default controls.
Thumbs up from me at this point, however if I come across serious issues with the game, I'll come back here and revise this review.

I wrote a review for Viking Conquest so i figure I might as well make a review for this though there's really not much for me to say. This is a game set in a medieval environment where you start as a freelancer and get to fight for or against 6 different factions who have very different troop trees and ways of fighting. Wide variety of different weapons to play with and if Native gets too boring or easy for you there's a wide variety of mods like Floris, Nova Aetus, Gekokujou, Brytenwalda, Pendor, Perisno, Light and Darkness (the only mod with a story that I know of so far), and many more. There are also several good mods that are still in development like Silverstag and L'aigle (this is a mod that takes place in the Napoleonic Wars) that you can count on being good once they're complete. If medieval combat sounds interesting to you then this is the game for you.
Two things of note is that while most computers that aren't 7-8 or more years old can run Native, many mods improve the textures which is great if you have a relatively more modern PC (not a gaming rig, but something that's decent by the standards of around 4-5 years ago) but a computer that could barely run Native might not be able to run a mod that's more graphically intense like Floris. Also, spears are rather weak in this game since the face-hugging AI will get right up next to you making it practically impossible to hit them (you can try thrusting your spear in a slightly different direction from the enemy and then immediately re-direct the thrust to the enemy once the spear is moving). I can see this being annoying to spear fans and HEMA enthusiasts but...nothing can be perfect. Although, in Viking Conquest, spears get a new overhand thrust (you can do it the same way you'd do an overhand swing with a sword, by moving the mouse up before clicking the attack button) that will hit an enemy no matter how close they are.

Quick review;
Getting the negatives out of the way:
-The game suffers from audio problems.
-Navegating the menus sucks
-Leaderboard navegation sucks
-I've had the game crash on me before (and heard other people tell me the same thing).  It's only happened once in the +50h I've spent on this game, however so it wasn't an issue that presisted.
Recommended to anyone who is likes action-packed games.  This game has it all and it is the best an action-platformer shooter can offer you.  MS3 consists of 5 levels you must complete, with their own unique bosses.  While the game only has 5 levels, there are branching paths on all levels (except 5th) to expand it's replay value.
Level design is creative and variable because of the way the player has to interact with the environment to progress alive.  This is further explored with the variety of weapons available to use (and their mechanics).  This is reinforced with responsie controls and fuild movement.
The game offers a good challenge and new players will probably get bodied on their first runs.  The developers knew this so they added various ways you can die (each with their own unique animation).  This game's visuals are up to par with Castlevania: Symphony of the Night in terms of quality.  An extensive amount of detail added to animation, backgrounds and characters.  You will probably notice something new every time you play through this game.
MS3 is worth the purchase for <$10, if you haven't already played it.  It's got action, humor, great animation, responsive controlls and amazing level design.

This game is an awesome concept that's sabotaged by some horrible execution.  I really like the idea and the aesthetic, but there's too many problems to be able to recommend it.  The game mechanics center around the idea of "CALENDULA" being a haunted game that's buggy and deliberately unplayable.  The problem is that there's a number of actual, non-fake bugs that range from frustrating to nearly gamebreaking.
If you're going to make a game designed around solving fake problems, the presence of so many real ones is inexcusable.  There's definitely some cool stuff in here, but as it stands, this feels like an unpolished mess.

After reading a bried review of CALENDULA, the mysteries it proffered seemed like something I couldn't pass up. I've been a horror fan for quite a while and was hoping the "game that doesn't want you to play it" might offer a unique take on what an experience of horror could be. What I found was a sense of isolation, being pushed away constantly and only catching the briefest glimpses of what it meant to understand something we can't really truly understand. While the game is primarily based up the recurrence of puzzles involving the title menu and briefs vignettes in the first person coupled with weird/distrubing imagery, it all forms a neat little circle. I could expound theories for a while about what it all means but I'll stick to this: its entertaining to actually enage in as a player, its imagery is disconnected enough to genuinely chill at times and it seems a welcome place for interesting theories about story. My only sticking point would be length I suppose, as I got through it in little over half an hour (I could see hitting upwards of two depending on your ability to guess puzzle elements) and aside from replaying to mine story ideas/theories, its puzzles will just become routine. Still, I think it is well worht your time to try out and if you're in a dark enough room, it'll disquiet you something fierce.

This game was not at all what I expected. Or rather, it wasn't nearly as deep or well designed as I expected. I thought it would something along the lines of IMSCARED mixed with a little The Stanley Parable, but it turned out to be a very simplistic puzzle game which comes down to basically manipulating the exact same mechanic in a slightly different way to "solve" each puzzle.
As a reward for solving each puzzle you are treated to an extremely vague and incredibly brief cut scene. I got the impression that they were supposed to be very psychologically evocative and make me work to figure out the puzzle behind the puzzles, perhaps with an undefined sense of dread. This atmosphere was not effectively built up however, and the ending, while tangentially related to the cut scenes in retrospect, was pretty unsatisfying even if it was meant to be a metaphor or if we were meant to carry over the anticipated feelings of dread and anxiety from the gameplay over to the ending, neither of which I think was successfully executed if that was the intent.
I got this on sale for 4.19 US, and I would probably agree with another reviewer's comments that if the game was free, I might suggest a playthrough just because the "puzzles" are relatively nonstandard and the intended thought process behind the cut scenes and ending is at least intriguing. However, since the game is not free, I finished it in about 40 minutes, and found it to be generally unsatisfying regardless of price, I would not recommend this title.

The game is not intuitive, the hints aren't given that well, and overall it's a repeat of the same 4 screens or so. Largely dull and not a satisfying experience. It's definitely the weak version of Pony Island. Even for an hour of a good game, I would not have minded the price, but it just wasn't that. I tried.

I'm about 7 hours into Gas Guzzlers Extreme as I right this. As a lover of Rogue Trip on PS1 I have been hunting for a game like this for some time. I went through a couple indie games before I got to this one and it's exactly what I was looking for: Cars with guns.
The career mode reminds me of Need For Speed Underground 2 in many ways... but with guns. It does take some getting used tot and the default key bindings are rubbish, however once you're up and going and shooting and racing it's a really great game. I love that is has a plethora of ahievments to unlock that actually feel meaningful to get (similar to Counter Strike: Global Offensive). The graphics really are top notch. If you don't have the specs to play this game at max settings you're really missing out on some great stuff.
It's challenging and rewarding as a PvP race game. I don't like the Power Race mode (cars WITHOUT guns, boring eh?) and I'm not a massive fan of the Deathmatch/Last Man Standing/Capture The Flag modes either. They are fun to play around in but the lack of a minimap of any description is just killer, it's like playing a FPS game without a radar. It's fun, but it's not as fun as the races.
Haven't done a lot of multiplayer just because there aren't really many people playing it as far as I can tell. One thing I like aobut the career mode is that you progress, you upgrade and unlock, you have to think about where and when to spend your money (not that there's a real shortage of it), and that isn't present in multiplayer. All cars are the same and all upgrades are unlocked, which is fun in a sandbox mode kind of way but it is much more satisfying to have earned those things yourself.
Would love if I knew some more people playing the game because I think there's a lot of great things to explore and experiment with. No regrets buying the game at all and will certainly continue to play it.

A relaxed smile-inducing kinetic VN that you can get through in 90-120 minutes if you read faster than a snail; the main character Vinty is the big selling point here, mainly because she's more likable and sympathetic than 90% of protagonists in your average VN.
The story is simple, but it moves briskly and never feels like it bogs down in introspection (another major pitfall in the wider genre). The setting is unique too; how many games are set in Melbourne? If you're planning a trip then you could do a lot worse than preparing by giving this a playtrough; it's cheaper than a guidebook, and it includes lots of good tips for how to get around the city and places you might want to visit. The youtube video links are a nice touch too; they're a really creative way to bring the story to life.
If you're on the fence, I'd check out WIthout Within 1 which is free (apart from costing 15 minutes of your life to finish), see if you like the sense of humour- chances are you'll fall in love with Vinty and want to see what she gets up to next. I'm totally in line for the next installment- it'd be cool to have her take us on a tour of Hong Kong!

The "adult" content is censored on Steam, but there is a patch you can download to uncensor it.  The music is excellent and very catchy, so it may be playing in your head the next day. I own about 300 games, of which 30+ of them are RPG Maker games. I happen to like the RPG Maker genre.
DarkEnd is among the very best RPG Maker games that I have played.
I spend more than 100+ hours playing this game, and enjoyed it tremendously, and that is why I decide to write a review of DarkEnd to share my experiences.
In DarkEnd you can play as one of 4 different Primary Characters, and each of these 4 character has a very unique and intriguing storyline. You can also select a Secondary Character from the remaining 3 characters. The storyline is quite complex and convoluted and you normally would not know who is good or bad until the very end. Each of the character has their own unique reasons to go into the DarkEnd, and the outcome is also different and unique. Playing this game is like reading a detective novel for me, and each stage of the game give me a better glimpse of the story.
There is also a lot of replayability because when you finished the game, you can play NG+ and select a different starting character. All the items and gold get carried forward to the next game, but all the quests resets. I like this system very much. There are also lots of optional side quests, and optional dungeons that spawn randomly too.
On the negative side, there are some minor gramatical and syntactic errors. However, I personally not mind these errors, and did overlook them because I like the stories, the plot twists and the interesting game play.
I had a good time playing DarkEnd and for me, its worth the money spent. I love this game and would highly recommend it.

I bet most people would describe Acro Strom as "Wipeout and Mario Kart had a baby". There has recently been released some amount of anti-gravity racers but there aren't many hoverbike games, which in the end are quite different things. You don't use air brakes here, and genereally the game is more arcadey and generally it does not feel like it wants you to train it every day for many hours to become a better pilot, as is the vibe that I get from most anti-gravity racers. This game feels to me that it prioritizes having fun (instead of the "simulation-level skill needed in order to race in these speeds"), via really-easy-to-grasp mechanics and fantastic sense of speed, nice music and personal presentation. This game really feels that it could have been in the arcade right between Hydro Thunder and Crazy Taxi, and I mean this in nothing but in a good way.
I have been looking for racing games with one criteria: Let me feel the high speed. I want to go fast! Personally I don't get the sense of great speed in for example any simulation type of games. I want to go faster! And in my research there are only a handful of these kind of games available on PC. Acro Storm manages to be one of those.
The game being in pretty early development there is not too much content and as per usual with EA titles, don't buy this game if you are expecting to get many hours worth of content or if you are impatient or if you can't stand of any inconveniences (such as lack of tutorials, little bit weirdly acting powerups, little bit "messy" HUD, not rebindalbe keys etc.) Let's just say that there are pretty rough edges, but the good core is there already. I would describe the current state as a "sample" of the fruits of the development this far, and I am generally very cautious about EA products, I only buy them when I feel I want to support the developers for what they are doing.
Nevertheless, the game already offers nice kicks from speed and shows alot of promise with it's personal style.
Now, why do I recommend the game as of now?
+That feel of speed.
+Piloting (Or is it driving? Surely not flying?) feels pretty good.
+Nice music (even though not particularly my favourite kind, it fits in the game/atmosphere well)
+Personal look
+Tracks and environments are nice (and promising in regard to future tracks).
+Price is really fair at this point.
+Support the developers for doing this hoverbike game (because hoverbikes are preeetty cool don't you agree?) which is a rare genre and not doing a 16-bit roguelike platformer or a open world survival game. In the end, if you buy early access titles you don't just buy the game for what it is now, you buy it with a promise that it will get better, and you will buy it because you want to give your support. Also it is already fun to play, so there is that thing too!

This is a game with a lot of promise. It's also a game that's still in it's infant stages, so I'll cut this short and sweet.
As it is now, Acro Storm has the potential to be a really nice little addition to the futuristic racing genre and a VERY welcome addition to the "Hover Motocross" sub-series.
The game itself is a futuristic racing game with Mario Kart style power-ups, which comes out feeling like the lovechild of Jet Moto and Rollcage. At the time of this writing there are four racers, three bikes, four tracks and about nine or ten power-ups.
Of the four characters, there's one human man and three alien women. I found myself using the guy most often simply out of complacancy. The designs on them are kinda cool, but the modeling work could use some refinement. the bikes offered are all very beautifully crafted and distinct with the added bonus of allowing you to customize it's color using color sliders. None of the bikes or players felt very distinct, which can be atributed to the game's infantile state, but it gets the job done as far as having distinct options when it comes to the bike you ride and the♥♥♥♥♥you look at while playing.
The racing feels solid for the most part though, paradoxically, the basic turning feels too stiff while the drifting is so loose, it feels more like strafing half the time. The power-up system, while absolutely bewhildering in presentation, is adequately functional once you figure out what the power-ups actually do. While it could use several dozen buckets of Elbow Grease, I'm already loving the gameplay style this game is trying to go for.
The levels themselves are located in an arena circuit, an arid canyon, a frozen outpost and a seaside industrial facility, all in varying levels of completion and polish. The tracks really vary for me. The canyon track, being the first one developed, is really quite fun to race on and the easide industrial facility track is really fast and surprisingly challengng. The ice outpost track, while incredibly fast, is also a bit....bland...Everything looks the same along the track to me, which makes races seem to drag on forever. The arena circuit is also pretty boring, being just a simple circle. It need more going on in it.
When it comes to music....the main menu track is pretty bland and uninspired....BUT WOW, DO THE RACETRACK THEMES SHINE! Each track has it's own distinct theme with it's own distinct style. From a Breakbeat/Techno track that feels like it came from a PSX racing game on the canyon stage to an absolutely stunning Trance anthem in the ice outpost, the music grabbed me from the word go and I have to admit, I oftentimes fire up the game and get in a few laps just to listen to the music! Not only do the tracks help accentuate the races, but the varying genres help to build upon the enviroments to give them their own personal flair. Keep this up and I may start begging for an OST!
Overall, I'd say this game needs a LOT more work, but then that's why it's Early Access. I'll be excitedly waiting to see what the next update brings us because this is shaping up to be the beginning of a beautiful racing game.

A sequel to the free game Without Within, Without Within 2 gives more content to it's price.
Again, this tells the story of a protagonist who has Calligraphy as her job. But now, she is on her trip to Australia, where she will see her favorite, and the most famous, Calligrapher in action.
This tackles all about people in general. About how they managed to get on top. But little do we know that most of these people did
, including dirty tactics just for them be rich and powerful. As another human who strives to live every day, this is unfair because these kind of people just got a "free ticket" to riches and such. But I know that most rich businessmen, and probably most of us right now, strived hard to earn money and buy what we want. This is what I like about this VN, as it teaches us (probably) to work hard despite hardships in real life. This is what being a human being is all about.
- Cute artwork as always!
- Decent music to accompany the transition of the VN.
- Improved storyline that adds more humor and decent tension.
- A new character that is gives a major plot to the story.
- There is definitely something charming in this VN. There is a button that shows you a video (though it sends you to YouTube)! A plus point for me.
- It lets you explore Australia a bit more, accompanied by the Video buttons. It gives you a certain feel about the area. What I liked is the Sky Deck. A really unique perk done by the creator. Kudos to them!
-
- How the Visual Novel starts is very underwhelming. They should have replaced it with something more humorous and excitement-enducing for the story to improve.
- This is just me, but they should introduce more of Australia! I was fun seeing the Yarra River and all that. I wish they should add more to be honest.
- This time, there are no more choices unlike the prequel. Choices are always good in a Visual Novel, as they add more content and diversity. They should have included it still and just improved it.
Overall, the videos are really a unique part of this VN. I really like it. This VN also teaches us a lesson, that whatever happens to us, never drag other people down just for your own good. Selfishness is a bad trait of us humans. We human beings are generally helpful to others in need. But sometimes it becomes too much, but that doesn't give us a reason to avoid helping people. We still help them to enable them to perform on there own two feet.
I recommend Without Within 2 to anyone.

Well, The best way to put it is 'Flatout, but with guns instead of the windshield cannon thing'.
The gameplay is fun, and you have the option of racing with or without guns, or playing a small number of arena modes. Getting a kill in a race is incredibly satisfying, mostly because when someone dies in a race they are COMPLETELY out of the race. If you can ram them hard enough, you can even kill opponents in races that don't have guns, and there's even an achievement for it. Sadly, the weapon classes are limited to shotguns, miniguns, and rocket launchers. The good news is that there is some good variety within each weapon class. There's plenty of vehicles available, including a Reliant Robin and a DeLorean, and all vehicles can be upgraded (however, some vehicles can be upgraded further than others). The vehicles seem to just scale though, and it's more a case of 'what's better' instead of 'what would work best for me', which is a bit dissapointing. You can also choose from 4 sets of voiceovers for your driver, 3 of which that are silly, and 1 that is just Duke Nukem (possibly unlicensed, but I don't care). The sponsor system is cool; you can only have one sponsor at once, you only get bonus money from your sponsor if you have the sponsor's decal equipped, and sponsors might abandon you if your performance gets sloppy. Sponsors will also invite you to special sponsor team events where you are given a car and a weapon, and you are put on a team led by your sponsor with the objective of defeating a team led by a rival sponsor, with a sizable cash payout if your team wins. Standard career events are randomly generated based on what tracks and gamemodes you have unlocked, with optional secondary objectives that offer bonus cash if you complete them. The game's humor is good, and it's crude, but not completely tasteless, with subtle refrences in all sorts of places.
This game made me realise that Full Auto 2 would have been more than just mediocre if it was more like Flatout 2.

This is a troubling review.
Firstly, the few hours I played Calendula, I enjoyed my time with it.
It's certainly far more different compared to other games out there, and is certainly all the more interesting for it.
Compared to gems like Pony Island, however, Calendula ultimately comes across as a shallow experience, meant to be had once. It's not a long game either, with most achievements taken in within an hour or 2.
Its biggest failing, though, is that it could've been something good, but ultimately settles for mediocrity, namely with going for a theme that is beaten to the ground, compared to its opening premise, which easily showcases the best parts of the themes it runs with. A pity, then, that it decides to discard those in favor of something more cheap, that seems profound, but ultimately isn't.
Puzzles are fairly straightforward, with the exception of one particularly obnoxious puzzle. Though even that one can be solved with some patience.
Overall? A 5.5/10 from me.
P.S. That soundtrack is amazing.

Great game! Not giving DarkEnd a chance simply because it's an RPGMaker game is just unfair.
As a classic RPG lover, the grinding and learning tactics the hard way is the most enjoyable part. Reminds me of DarkSouls!

While it won't win any RPG Maker awards, DarkEnd is an OK attempt at a traditional dungeon crawler.
The positives are mostly in design.  The world creation and levels are decently thought out.  It plays well with a controller, my case a Logitech RumblePad.  It has a very old school quest hub system that harkens back to pen and paper D&D.  I loved its use of lighting.  It created a rather unusual fog of war which normally isn't seen in RPGs today.
There were two serious drawbacks that keep it from being a great game.  First, it is grindy, even on Casual level.  After a while it, I felt bored playing it.  It was fight after, fight after, fight with very little story telling. It needed more story to break the monotony of battle.
The biggest drawback is questing.  After unlocking all the overland characters, you find one NPC that spams crafting missions.  It totally ruins the experience of completing the side/major quests.  Should have split them into at least two groups.  The other aspect is its randomness prevents completion of some quests as they don't trigger during exploration.  This forces the player to redo previously beat content where you are often so over-powered that it drags.
If you like grindy RPGs, this is at least worth a look for at most a $5 spot.

I’ve played and beaten the non-steam version of this game a while ago. Overall a solid RPG. Recommend it for people who like to enjoy the challenging turnbased RPGs.
DarkEnd is somewhat similar to the instant-classic Etarian Odyssey series. Light on story but rather focused on gameplay. The battles are really harsh for unprepared party and could get wiped easily by simple blunder.
What I really like about this game is the boss battles. Most RPG maker RPGs I have played have rather simple boss battles. The bosses are only just stronger. All you need to do is use your strongest skills and heal when it is needed. It is not so simple in DarkEnd. Each and every boss, except the first one, has a catch and require special tactic to beat them. Since every spell and skill have cooldown and warm up timer, you have to think carefully which skill to be used at which moment. Spamming the strongest spell/skill without any strategy will only get yourself killed in DarkEnd.
Optional bosses are also very challenging. Since you cannot save in the dungeon, it can be a really tensed situation when you try to challenge a rare optional boss in the randomly appeared sub-level.  I wish the developers should give the game some achievements to make challenging boss battles even more worthwhile.
The story is nothing revolutionary. There are some interesting plot twists and lore which will be revealed late in game, but the story itself is pretty simple. The characters are well developed, especially Griselda and Lucion. However, the localization is a real let down in this game. Even as a second language user myself, I found some dialogues in game very cheesy and ridden with awkward grammar.

Graphically, the game exactly of what you can expect of RPG maker games out there. I noticed the game used the stocked RTP materials mixed with some custom work. The pixel sprites are neat and colorful and some scenes in game are simple beautiful.  The characters’ portrait arts are nice too.
Verdict : Have you ever played any of Etarian Series?  Do you like them? Do you like very challenging RPG? If your answer is a “Yes”, buy this (at least at the discount period) and you will enjoy this difficult but very rewarding RPG experience. A solid 7/10 game.

To put it simply... This game has less depth and refinement than many FREE community projects, from the official RPG Maker Forums.

If you are expecting an epic RPG where a young hero braved an adventure along with colorful people to vanquish evil, you are looking at the wrong place because, in DarkEnd, you will find no such thing.
-Story-
The core story is very simple. Once, there was a king, who led mankind to prosperity with his magical talents. However, he wished for more power, the power to rival gods, and after messing around with “Primordial Darkness”, the element of creation, he was driven mad and unleashed the destruction upon the land; the DarkEnd. A hero stood up and destroyed the Magus King and stopped the DarkEnd. However, the same mistake was repeated once again due to mankind’s nature. You are one of the four chosen heroes to stop the DarkEnd, once and for all.
Although the core story is simple, the game becomes very interesting due to the fact the game uses minimalistic story-telling to reveal the backstory of heroes.  You can choose a main protagonist and a supportive character out of four given heroes. Each hero has his/her own reason to stop the DarkEnd and the game reveals them with relatively smooth pacing.
The character development was quite unexpected as the band of heroes seemed very stereotypical at first. However, they evolved very quickly as the game progressed. There is a distinct personality for each hero and their unique dialogues help this.
-Gameplay-
The gameplay is the meat and bone of this game. Like many dungeon crawlers, this game’s primary gameplay is pretty straightforward. You have to go inside the DarkEnd, floor by floor until you reach the end. There is a town which serves as the “main base” where you can heal, restock items, and buy/sell equips.
The battles are unforgiving and very exciting. I’m currently playing with Valiant difficulty (Developer’s recommendation) and I have to say this is probably one of the most challenging RPGs I’ve ever played.  Even a typical battle with normal mob can make you break cold sweat.  Challenge a rare monster or optional boss without preparing and you’ll get the “gameover” screen in your face very quickly. The difficulty, however, is never unfair.  With enough preparation and reasonable strategy, every battle can be won. There is no need to go grind and overpower your characters.
The game’s skill tree called “Corridor of Origin” is very unique. In the base town, you can go to a alternative realm called Corridor of Origin, where you can light up the crystals (akin to Sphere Grid in FFX) to earn various skills. Each character has a unique Corridor which allows you to set up multiple combinations of skills for your main and supportive heroes.
The best feature of this game is randomly changing dungeons.  There are massive amount of sidequests, sub-dungeons and enemies, which changes every time you reenter the dungeon.  Replay value is very high since you have 4 heroes with unique story line for each and randomly changing dungeon.
-Graphic and Sound-
The pixel art in the game is very pretty. The game is mostly gloomy and dark, but some of the scenes are simply pretty for a 2D sprite-based game. The character portraits are also very beautiful. Although the cut-scene graphic may be a bit choppy, I have no problem with them. In fact, they reminded me of cut-scenes from old Genesis RPG; Phantasy Star.
The music is no less thrilling. The game made use of wild range of captive music from cool, calming ones to upbeat and exciting ones. The battle themes are very catchy and memorable. I found myself humming battle tunes after a few hours.
-Conclusion-
Story - 8.0/10
Gameplay- 9.0/10
Graphic&SFX – 7/10
Replay Value – 10/10
Overall – 8/10
DarkEnd, in my opinion, is a nice throwback to olden day’s gameplay-driven RPGs. The game gives me the distinct atmosphere of games such as Etrian Odyssey, Diablo 1 and Dark Souls. So if you are a fan of such kind of RPGs, DarkEnd is worth a try.

Dark end is a 2D RPG developed by Kosdots Games and Published by KISS ltd. The game follows the journey of a main character and a secondary character which are both selected at the start of the game from a choice of 4, the game offers a variety of difficulty levels to suit all players from those just interested in the story so do not wish for a hard game, those looking for the usual RPG experience and those in search of a game that will drive you insane with how hard it is. The game takes place after a great and powerful man lusted for power to rival even the Gods, he found power but unleashed the DarkEnd, the man was defeated but as time passes man forgets and the darkness now returns, choose your hero and fight the darkness. You journey to the frontier to fight the DarkEnd, to progress through the DarkEnd you must complete individual floors and leave through the portal but in order to use the portal you need a key, the keys can be found in chests or dropped from enemies and the floor boss, through each level you will encounter enemies and rare enemies. As expected the rarer enemies are well rarer and will put up more of a fight and give you more exp as a reward for killing them. You should not underestimate rare enemies they can be deadly and in the event your party dies you will have a game over and have to start from the last time you saved and that is only at the frontier, don’t lose all your progress out of pride. Do not fear you do not have to do the whole game in 1 run there are serpent gates which act as a checkpoint once activated you can then travel back to the point you left from the frontier after resupplying of course. The levels you progress through may change if you die and start them again they can change in that they have a boss rather than a chest or they can change all together. The game features several very catchy songs as all good RPG’s should. Each character can act each turn at the beginning you are given the option to fight or flee, each character can attack, defend, use magic or use a special the magic attacks use mp and the special attacks use Ep which is generated by attacking and getting hit, not all characters have a special to start with, magic and other abilities can be unlocked using the upgrade system which involves choosing to kindle various crystals. Each floor will differ if you have to repeat it such as loot and if a key spawns in a chest or you have to fight the boss for it, when you characters health is low you can use a potion or a heal spell. All spells and specials have a cool down so be sure to time their uses correctly and choose the right target an enemy with a fire weakness might well die in 1 hit to a fireball and an enemy with a fire resistance almost certainly will not. Spells initially have a warm up period as well meaning at the start you ca’t cast a fireball and destroy the enemy turn 1 but as you upgrade your spells the warm up will no longer be required.
Dying in DarkEnd can be very frustrating especially if you are having a good run maybe you found some good loot and then you got cocky and a rare enemy destroyed you, but if you didn’t want a challenge you should have chosen a lower difficulty. Dying and retrying is how you learn anyway, although it can be sad to lose a good run it just encourages you to try again and not make the same mistakes.
The combat of the game can be very strategic with you having to time your magic and special attacks to when they are best used for example an attack that provides a stun effect might keep you alive long enough to use a magic that was on cool down next turn.
The DarkEnd is split into floors of 5 on the 5th floor you will encounter a boss and also get some story, after the set of 5 floors you will then enter a new area with new music, new enemies(far harder) etc.
The art style of the game is just lovely with the majority of the game having the usual 2D RPG look but during tutorials and cut scenes the looks of the characters truly show the time taken to create.
Overall from playing DarkEnd I highly recommend it to any 2D RPG fans it has a beautiful look, charming characters, good combat and a catchy soundtrack what more do you need?
The only negative is the game has a small resolution meaning if you are a graphics snob this probably isn’t for you.
I rate this game highly and would give it an 8/10 for a small indie game it is excellent and is currently in my top 10 games of the year.

Having played Skyrim first in the Elder scroll series, I wanted to play another game. after checking around, Morrowind seemed to be the best choice. so I bought the game on steam and began playing it, I was so used to the hack and slash battle mechanics in skyrim and the objective markers that I felt lost in the game. I stopped playing it for a while and tried again. this time i got a better understanding of how the game works and why it is so great compared the the other elder scroll games. sure the graphics might be laughable, but there are mods to fix that. the part that stood out to me is the gameplay itself.
Compared to Skyrim and Oblivion. this game isn't a hack and slash game. it isn't about what weapon you have that has the highest damage. there is a lot more at play in the combat system. it is more of: what is the enemies level, what is your level, what weapon is being used, what is the stamina or amount of stamina remaining, who has a higher stat in a certain skill being used now? etc, etc. so spamming the attack button will not do justice, you have to pay attention to your skills and stats.
compared to Skyrim and oblivion's gorgeous landscapes, morrowind is the one that felt out of place in tamriel. and that is the best part, Giant mushrooms, Necthes, scribs, kagotis, kwamas, cliffracers, trama roots, and so much unusual plant and wildlife gives the island of Vvardenfell a unique otherworldy atmosphere, compared to the viking inspired lands in skyrim and the european design in oblivion. I even played arena and daggerfall and they don't even compare to morrowind either.
the story is also the best part, you were sent to vvardenfell on the emperor's orders and from there you are given no objective marker, your map is blank. this leaves so much room for you to explore and search for other towns, cities, caves, tombs, dungeons, and other places. so much so that exploring vvardenfell at an early level feels like a dangerous journey and as you level up it becomes a brethtaking adventure. compared to skyrim and oblivion, this game also has amazing locations such as the city of vivec, the ghostfence, red mountain, balmora, mournhold, the clockwork city, solstheim before it became the dunmer refugee island seen in skyrim, and much more.
Just playing this game every now and then I find something new, and it is even better when you have mods available to make the game look 10 years younger and adding so much content. there's even a mod called "Tamreil rebuilt" which is literally adding to the game's land by recreating the entire continent of morrowind, with quests, locations, npcs, weapons and more(I recommend downloading it. even if it is still incomplete).
Overall. this truly is one of the best games of all time

To start this off, I'd just like to say that this game is flat out amazing. It's that in depth RPG you always dream about, but are never able to find. The level of choices and possible outcomes, the different roles and characters. it really is an amazing game. The game just sort of flows along by random chance, things shift differently every time you play. It really is one of the best RPG's I've had the chance to play.
While the game is older and it doesn't have the greatest, most up to date graphics in the world. It's actually still very pretty. And the way it looks and the way the game plays has that great classic RPG feel to it. All the menus and such have that great oldschool feel to them, really giving the game a great feel to it.
The game is kinda difficult to learn at first, things change rapidly and you can get attacked at any time. It really is a trial and error sort of game. You're gonna lose soldiers, you might even get captured for a time. But then you start to learn it, and you have even more fun.
The combat is very satisfying, the way the different attacks and blocks work is very emjoyable. The focus and thought that you have to put into every battle is really alot of fun. The AI might seem a little odd at times, but hey, it doesn't have to be perfect.
The level of politics in the game is amazing as well, you can build reputation with entire kingdoms, or just a small town. Once people like you and you are respected, you can start to own towns/castles/kingdoms/etc. The constant changes in who is at peace or war is interesting as well. The sides always change up to create interesting shifts in the gameplay. You can go to loved by two united kingdoms to being loved by one, and hunted by the other.
So, do I recommend this game? completely, it deserves to be played more than it is right now. If you like an in depth RPG, this is your game, so have fun :)

Metal Slug 3 (MS3) is a 2-D side-scrolling platformer game developed by the company DotEmu with emphasis on action-oriented run & gun gameplay.
+ Remastered version from the year 2000 resolving some technical faults of the original.
+ In comparison with its predecessors of the MS series the levels are less linear, offering a few alternative paths through a stage.
+ Each stage has its own atmosphere and iconic art style of the MS series.
+ Two player cooperation contributes to the fun and appeal of the game.
o Solid sound effects.
- Very short game that can be finished in less than an hour.
- Irregular slowdowns in single- and multiplayer.
+ The run & gun gameplay is identical to the other parts in the series.
+ Easy to learn but hard to master combat mechanics.
+ Different weapons and power ups with their own advantages and disadvantages.
+ In comparison with its predecessor Metal Slug from 1996 the overall level of difficulty is higher.
+ Challenging boss battles with extensive attack patterns.
+ Various enemy types with well crafted animations.
o Level of difficulty and number of continues are adjustable.
- Four characters that only differ from each other in appearance.
- Lack of coherent story telling.
- No voice acting.
DotEmu successfully converted this classic run & gun game to the PC with a few beneficial changes. MS3 remains true to its origins with a rock hard nature and all guns blazing from every part of the screen.
Nothing beats the Metal Slug series on old arcade machines, were you had to pay for every time you died.

When reading this review, please bear in mind that I am reviewing the Agents of Yesterday DLC, not the full game.
Star Trek Online: Agents of Yesterday is a brand-new DLC for Star Trek Online. It consists of 6 missions if you choose to create a character from the Starfleet of the 23rd century, and also about 4 other missions towards the middle of the game whereby you become a Temporal Agent.
The storyline takes you to various different locations and various timelines, most notably: the JJ Abrams Timeline (or the Kelvinverse) where the U.S.S Kelvin was destroyed in battle (presumably). In this timeline, you assist the U.S.S Yorktown against Na'Kuhl Raiders who are trying to destroy the timeline hence creating a weapon against the Federation. One of the many Steam games I've played that makes me wish there was some kind of in between rating I can gave other than the Caesarish "Yea" or "nay." Since I must, I have to lean more towards wanting to enjoy the "game," but it simply wasn't for me.
Many will point out the heavy borrowing from the Pony Island concept and they're not wrong, but it's not a reason alone to dislike Calendula. Yes there a many completely original games out there, and there have and always will be games that borrow concepts from those before it. It's not a big deal, because so many great games take these concepts and do something great with them. Sometimes it's a new twist. Sometimes it's an incredible story. There's a myriad of things you can do with a borrowed concept to elevate it. Calendula did so very little to try.
The atmosphere was fun and the puzzles were pretty decent. Other than that, it's incredibly short (50 minutes without much brain stuggle,) and it doesn't have much plot or heft to hold the package up. Not a regretful playthrough at all, but I have a hard time recommending it.

My overall rating for Without Within 2: 97/100
Sequel about Vinty's adventures and tries to be the caligraphy star finally made it to my playlist and I have to say, that it succeeded over expectations. This time, we will travel to Melbourne, Australia, in order to meet our idol and learn to be a professional artist. The plot in the end is a bit surprising, but I think the goal was achieved. Lets see it in detail.
GAMEPLAY
+ Classic visual novel
+ Chapter timing and animations
+ Real world footages
- Sometimes videos were too often
Invertmouse made a good progress and learnt from his mistakes, that occured in the first title of this series. Visual novel stylisation and chapter timing was great. Also, Vinty's comments were hilarious. I was really surprised, when I saw real Melbourne footages, it is something that draws a player into the game. But it has to be used cautiously, too often may disrupt the player's mood.
CHARACTERS
+ Vinty
+ Excelia
+ Grace
o Other were just an episodic character
Vinty's comments and jokes were mentioned in the previous section. I like "the eyes joke" and how she was a little bit under- or overestimating situation. Excelia started as a proud and cocky star, but both characters learnt something. Excelia, that the fame is fragile and Vinty, her biggest talent is hidden within her heart.
I loved also Grace, she is the type of character, that may change the world, by pushing other persons in the right way. Brilliant. Other characters made just an episodic appearance, which was expected and not bad at all.
VISUALS
+ Same as Without Within 1
I have to say, there were no glitches, drawing and anime style were cute and bright.
SOUNDTRACK
+ More lively songs
Compared to the predecessor, this title has more song, that are fitting in the story perfectly. Good work!
SUMMARY
I am pleased, that even independent developers are able to create deep, funny and original game with surprising elements. The saying "less is sometimes more" pays here for one hundred percent. For the price is this game perfect and a must for every visual novel collector.
Strongly recommended.

If you're like me, you're very skeptical of racing games. Especially ones that include weapons against your opponent. Hell, we haven't had great ones come to mind for years (Carmageddon, Diddy Kong Racing, etc). So what makes this one stand out?
Everything. This game spoils you with some seriously cool graphics, gameplay, and humor right from the get-go.
*WARNING - THIS IS NOT A DRIVING SIMULATOR - TURN AWAY AND GET ASETTO CORSA OR WHATEVER IF YOU WANT THAT KIND OF GAME*
What kind of cool graphics? Well, let's just say this game isn't going to run smoothly on your old 2009 PC. I'm fervently against graphics-over-gameplay gaming, but this is so beaufitul and the way it plays is so much fun that I can't wait to run it when I get my GeForce GTX 770 in (planning on running two of them, but I'm getting off-topic). So I guess I'm kinda griping and praising the game at the same time, with saying it's "necessarily beautiful" and if you don't have a PC that's capable of running it without horrible lag, it's going to affect your gameplay a TON (perhaps even unplayable).
Where do I begin about the gameplay? You drive a car, shoot opponents, win, get money. It's not that easy, though. There are different types of races available that you need to get to know to advance yourself in the "Career Mode". Tons of tracks. Tons of cars. Tons of weapons. Tons of playability when you mix and match all three. As I write this, I'm only 4 hours into the game, and I'm blown away. I picked this up for $10 on a sale, but I would be happy paying the $25 had I known about it's existence prior to clicking on the "Weeklong Deals" button.
The humor? It's all around. If you don't have a good sense of humor, well, you're just a stick in the mud and aren't going to have a good time with the game. Yeah, it's a little juvenile in some of it's humor, but that's what makes it great. Your opponents have names such as "Jack Kass, Luke Likesheet, and Alotta Fagina" (you giggled at at least one of those, didn't you? ;) *snicker*). Currently, I'm driving a car that's sponsored by Buttwesser. Yes, Buttwesser. Once more... Buttwesser.
9.5/10 - This game is going to get a lot of playtime from me.
P.S. - Haven't tried the multiplayer, but holy crap that would be awesome.

I guess part of my negative review/experience was failed expectations. A game making use of real evolution as a game mechanic would be awesome, and educational! This is neither.
It's not just that though. I feel like the pre-civilization stage was too short, and after that, it's just a really poor RTS. Evolution was the game's hook, but over the course of the game (and far too quickly), they funnel it into a generic, boring version of games you've played before.
For comparison, E.V.O. (for the snes) wasn't even close to being a realistic game about evolution, but at least it stuck to its guns and built its gameplay around that. It might not have been the best game in the world, but it's a lot more charming and coherant than this game was.
If you're like me and want a game that uses real evolution as a game mechanic, you'll have to look elsewhere. Too bad it's such a super niche genre.
The best I've found is a game that in alpha right now. Species: Artificial Life, Real Evolution. And there are a few other little applications scattered across the Internet as well, but they get abandoned all the time.
One day we'll get a good evolution game...
...one day...

Let me just start this by pointing out one thing that could have excused the lack of content to the game if it were not true: This game is done, it is not in alpha or beta. What you see is what you get. Which is quite sad, because I myself was under the impression that the game was still in the works when I played it. It just has that sort of feel, that there's plenty to the game but there could have been more.
It's, sadly, nothing overly special. Your submarine is busted, and parts of it are scattered across the ocean floor. Some of which are in areas that are far too deep for you to reach without making better equipment. Which is good, as it gives a sort of progression to the game, and therefore makes it so you can't just go getting all the pieces and beating the game right off the bat.
It's decent, and puts you in a underwater environment, setting it in a playing field not often explored in a sandbox game. The jumping (Or, swimming) system is decent too, having about seven extra 'jumps' you can take while underwater makes traveling a bit less boring. The combat is alright, so long as you're use harpoons when it comes to predators. Since the predatory fish (Baracudas and sharks, primarily) tend to charge the player, knives won't really work against them. A few good harpoons in the mouth, on the other hand...? Now that'll make them regret coming after you.
Was... Interesting. But a bit short. With only 3 sets of materials to craft from, it feels pretty lacking. Especially the last equipment set, which only serves to give you a bit more protection than the prior sets of gear instead of letting you delve deeper in to the unknown (unlike the prior sets). Which is a real shame, considering the next part I'd like to touch on.
This aspect of the game was probably my favorite part. The first area of the game seeming pretty bright and lovely, which as you go deeper becomes darker, but lit up with luminescent plants and even glowing fish. Giving the deeper sections of the sea a sort of magical feel, but also makes them feel very foreboding as the denizens of the deep don't take too kindly to you coming in to their home.
All in all, the game is decent to play, but it's not likely you'll play it much after initially beating it, which takes only a few hours at most. A good game to get when it's on sale, but it's certainly not a good idea to buy at full price. Especially when taking in to consideration you could get quite a few good games that are finished and on sale for the price you could buy this one at full price.
Were the game still in the works, I could recommend it... But it's just too lacking when it comes to being a completed project.

As a straight survival game, FarSky has a good balance between challenge and playability.  I like to explore and I like combat, and I had fun playing it.  I usually only build what is useful and necessary in sandbox games, so the simplicity of the bases and equipment was not a negative for me.
I most enjoyed Survival mode, available upon completion of the initial Adventure mode.  The increased difficulty of Survival mode made the game quite challenging and required careful resource management decisions.  It was most satisfying to earn my way back up to the top of the food chain.
Survival Advice:  At your first opportunity, make two underwater scooters to alternate between.  Move extractors around.  One can always open the inventory screen and heal at leisure, so carry ample food and bandages.  Predators only attack when there is blood in the water (or at night), so hunt with caution or while carrying serious firepower.  Enough harpoon cannons around your base can tranform threats into food.  There is no easier target to hit than one heading directly at you.

A solid 2D-RPG & Dungeon Crawler, make by a passionate indie studio "Kodots Games" & definitely one of the best traditional RPGs made by RM Engine..
In DarkEnd, You'll play as a pair chosen from 4 unique characters, both gameplay & story-wise, tackling through ever-shifting dungeons.. Battles within these places are of endurance type & how you approach each battle is up to the player with freedom of equipment & accessory choice, flexible skills system, so adapting to each encounter is the key to survival..
The opening scene may "seems" generic, but in-game atmosphere & minimalistic story-telling will keep the player intrigued while on the 10-15 hour ride per playthrough, with the brilliant execution of the plot-twists & Informations that answers some questions, while raising some other.. When the player has followed through with the stories of all 4 characters, you'll have your every answers..
& DarkEnd has the most interesting Boss fights.. There's never a dull moment when fighting the bosses, there're many unique twist & turns in these fights, not at all like modern immunity bosses or HP tank bosses..
All in all, DarkEnd is a reminder of everything we loved about playing a traditional RPG & a refresher of how they can be better.. If you're an avid RPG player like me, who's thinking modern RPGs has lost some of the glamour nowadays, You'll enjoy this little treat..

There's a lot of hate revolving around this game and the TES series in general.
It boils to the people who think Morrowind/Oblivion/Skyrim is the best of the series, in this review I will debunk these statements and their arguments.
Statement 1:
"Skyrim is better than Morrowind, Just look at the combat. Also it looks better!"
The combat is outdated to say the least, back then dice roll combat wasn't uncommon and generalised. The TES series began as a former DnD variation, it kept its roots until Oblivion.
For all the remaining arguments about Skyrim being supposedly "better" one word can be said.
Mods.
Morrowind Overhaul fixes the graphics and several bugs and other things, it even requires higher specs than Skyrim's Ultra HD textures. The combat can be fixed too.
Everything Skyrim did well Morrowind did mediocre. Skyrim had great exploration but shallow quest lines, NPC characters, rare items, shallow cities, copy pasted dungeons and the overal dumbing down of quest journals and using quest markers.
The thing is Morrowind did pretty bad on the exploration process and combat. Thats it. You can fix Morrowind by mods easier than Skyrim. I'm not saying its impossible but Skyrim tends to crap itself very fast with mods and load orders.
So, lets take this in a nutshell right?
Skyrim did what Morrowind could not, but Morrowind can do better what Skyrim does with mods, while Skyrim can not.
Now the great argument comes, the argument every person hates because it happens so much in the gaming industry and it has taken a lot of beloved series.
Dumbing or Casualizing. In a short nutshell dumbing down or casualizing is done to games to broaden the game's audience so more people buy it. In even a tinier nutshell, more monies for the developers/publishers.
Comparing Morrowind to its sequel "Oblivion" is a big point, Oblivion improved a few things as far as exploration but the rest was somewhat the same. But then it hit Morrowind fans.
Quest markers, Item devaluation and Holding your hand in Quests and NPC's.
A little ♥♥♥♥ing floating thing that tells you where you need to be and your character magically knows it.
This removes any part of difficulties of quest where you had to ask NPC's where you needed to go or what you needed to do. Now it just ♥♥♥♥ing points you into the direction.
Quest markers could have been tolerated if they were the only dumbing down part since it was expected and could not be avoided but it did not end here.
Imagine this, you're doing the main quest and you thought to yourself; "What would happen if i'd kill the Protagonist right now?" Well? In Morrowind you could considering you were powerful enough but after he died the game would tell you that the fate of the world is doomed and that loading a save is a good decision if you want to complete the main quest.
Well they removed this in Oblivion. If you still try the game simply doesn't let you, it will hold your hand and stop you. Unkillable characters make the game feel very plastic and overall reduced playability or free choice.
They did this because 9 year old brainless little♥♥♥♥♥♥♥killed people by mindless decisions and they complained. "This game is too hard! Reloading a save sucks!" Well maybe you need to think about what you do and take some ♥♥♥♥ing responsibility. Jesus christ.
Another point is item devaluation.
Reducing one rare item's value for the sake of making it easier. "Wow I got this super rare item" And their first thought? "I wonder for how much I can sell it!" Morrowind items were valuable, not every single ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥d merchant could buy it.
Well in Oblivion you can and in Skyrim it got worse.
Thats it boys, the dumbing down and negatives and positives of the last 3 TES games.
In one last nutshell;
Morrowind: Great game, has a few weaknesses but fixable by mods. 9.5/10
Oblivion: Core gameplay is good but it has attributed to the dumbing down of the series. 8.5/10
Skyrim: An ok game, very dumbed down to appeal to everyone. Weaknesses can be fixed by mods but harder to fix than Morrowind. 7/10
Morrowind is a must buy for every game, a milestone of a decennia.

It's hard to say that I recommend this game, but since it's free to play, you're not out anything if you download it and hate it.
I've played this game off and on for years, but I finally just downloaded it via Steam. I did have some trouble opening up the game the first time; the game froze on the loading screen. I just opened the game in safe mode. (Options > safe mode). That fixed the issue.
Here is a bit about me, which will impact my review: I would call myself a fan of Star Trek, but I'm not a hardcore fan. I've watched all of TOS, some Next Gen, and I haven't watched Voyager or DS9. Therefore, a lot of the references go over my head (since many of the enemies are ones that I'm not super familar with) but that hasn't hindered my enjoyment of the game. If you're a hardcore fan, you may love this game, or be super frustrated by the way it throws the Federation into war against almost any alien race that moves. If you're into gaming, you'll probably be frustrated by the controls, which don't always respond well.
There are three playable factions in the game: Federation, Klingon, and Romulan. I have enjoyed Federation the most, the other two don't seem quite as well developed, or maybe it's just my personal preference.
I have played through most of the new expansion that lets you create a 23rd century captain. The levels have been pretty underwhelming. The story is okay, and some of the voice acting is good, but I've encountered many bugs that range from humerous (including seeing my character in her undies) to frustrating (getting stuck on a panel and having to re-start the level). The rest of the game, from what I've played, has fewer bugs, but expect to have to restart a level or two while you go along. The 23c addition is great for me, being a TOS fan. It's enjoyable to see the costumes, the retro-styled spacedock, and having the chance to hang out with some TOS characters. The levels have their problems, but the nostalgia is strong and makes it fun.
Other reviews rave about the space fighting and hate the ground combat. I'd have to disagree. The space battles get very tedious, and they don't require much skill unless you're fighting a ship that's significantly higher in level than you are. You can set all of your weapons to autofire, so you just have to steer your ship in circles while you wait for the enemy to die. Yes, the ground battles are clunky (especially in terms of how combat works) but it's great to see alien landscapes. The levels are very controlled, you don't get to go and explore the world on your own, and most levels keep you boxed in by rock walls or buildings, but the designs of the planet surfaces are fun to see.
Missions themselves range from well-written and engaging to extremely boring, tedious, or frustrating. It's worth playing through the bad episodes to progress to the good ones.
My federation character is level 53 (out of 60) and I didn't spend any real world money. Believe me, the game wants you to. If you want a great ship, you'll have to pay for it. You can also pay for special costumes (including ones seen in the movies and tv shows), pets, weapons, lock box keys, and more. My advice: sink a lot of hours into the game before you decide to buy stuff with real money. Some of their ships and other goodies are hideously expensive, so invest wisely.
While my review sounds very negative, the game is worth a go, since there is some good content to be found, it's free to play, and most Star Trek fans will find something to enjoy.
