I have been a fan of the "Star Trek" TV show for many years. If you're a fan of the TV show, this game will give you a lot of nostalgia and will make you feel like you're part of the Star Trek universe.
PROS:
- You will get to choose your own new starship around every 10 levels, or basically with a new promotion (until level 40).
- There are LOTS of missions and some of the stories are pretty long and interesting. You will have to accomplish multiple tasks (even puzzles) to progress further in your story.
- You get to choose your own uniforms, which includes the colors and looks.
- You get to travel through many sectors of space with beautiful views of stars, nebulas, and planets if you choose to approach a particular solar system.
- You get to choose what alien race you will be, hence deciding your organization as well. Will you choose to side with the Federation, the Klingon Empire, or the Romulans?
- Get ready to immerse yourself with popular characters from Star Trek, such as Worf and Sela in later stories!
- Leonard Nimoy, aka Spock, sometimes narrates the prologues of what's happening.
CONS:
- The graphics sometimes get glitchy and there are times where when the character is talking, their mouth movements do not match the speaker.
- The background music tends to get too repetitive, and personally feel like there should be additional background music, especially when exploring space.
- You will do a lot of tasks to get dilithium (you can refine up to 8,000 a day) to save up for an exchange with Zen (currency that you can also buy with real money).
- You cannot get a T5 or a T6 ship simply for leveling up. You will either have to save up your dilithium for Zen, or you can just buy the ships themselves whenever they're on sale.
- You will not be able to progress further in the game once you're over level 50 with just a T4 ship, so get ready to face that.
- You can't choose to be a Cardassian in this game. This is strange to me since they played an important role in the Star Trek shows.
Overall this is a highly enjoyable game, even for those who do not know much about Star Trek.

I recommend Morrowind only if the game and both DLC don't set you back more than $10, and you are a massive Elder Scrolls/open-world fan.
Morrowind has been lauded as the best game of the TES series by some. I started with Skyrim, which is my favorite game of all time, then played Oblivion, Morrowind and a bit of ESO. Morrowind is, in THIS series #2 in my opinion, and Oblivion was shockingly bad for me. Expect nothing and you will have fun.
Morrowind is old now. I remember when the game “Pong” was new and how awesome Space Invaders was when it came out but that doesn't mean I still play them now. Morrowind's graphics are archaic, and the landscape is rather empty and a bit “angular”. On the other hand, I like the theme and the visual aesthetic – especially the architecture. I also like the concept behind the main quest, but after playing newer games, the quests leading you into the story don't build interest or motivation to continue. Granted, I'm used to faster-paced, modern games, but the side quests feel like mere time killing devices that provide time to get stronger before the end.
NPC are horrifyingly random and lifeless. Important dialog is written, so npc only speak only random, ambient lines. Everyone in the game, from nobles, to guards, to beggars, keeps saying over and over "I could kill that Guar (type of beast). Those boots are ruined." No dialog at all would have been better. The written dialog options were okay, but even after a quest is completed, you'll have the old dialog options littering up the dialog window, so finding the options you actually need is frustrating. You may as well not talk to anyone at all and use Google to navigate through your quests.
Morrowind combat is nothing like more recent Bethesda games. It's based on the roll of a die; not the player's actual gaming skill. In a word, it's rubbish key-smashing until you kill something or run out of potions and die. I will go so far as to say that such a combat system never belonged in a video game at all. I didn't expect I'd be buying the Elder Scrolls version of D&D.
Magic using is brutal...just an awful, horribly painful system. Magicka does not regenerate without sleeping long enough to recover it, and your pool of magicka is very limited. Perhaps by the end of the game you'll have built up a big enough magicka pool to use your spells, but by then...who cares? The only way to play as a mage is to cheat with mods that regenerate your magicka... or to spend days trying and failing to make magicka potions. It's clear that magic was made to be used as a backup to other forms of combat or...running away?
I have many complaints about this game, but the theme, open-world, and game aesthetic are strong. With a ton of mods Morrowind is enjoyable for a few hours at a time. Just wait until it's on sale.

I don't know why this game is so addictive.  I honestly think it's because it's so short, not in spite of it.  The first time I installed it, there was a bit of a learning curve (no tutorials, but I don't recall this game even sent me wiki-hunting).  Once I figured out what I was supposed to be doing, finding all the submarine pieces went pretty quick.  I "won" the game, said, "That wasn't bad," and uninstalled to pare down some of the "wall of text" that was my games list.
A couple of months later, frustrated with balance issues in an Early Access sandbox game, I just wanted a sandbox. game. that. worked.  Where the enemies were probably going to murder me, sure, but only if I wasn't smart enough to avoid them.  Where the equipment worked as planned and had clear crafting goals.  And that was only as grindy as I wanted it to be, because I was really, really sick of spending ten hours looking for the most basic components and getting slaughtered by the equivalent of slimes spawning every three seconds.  In short, I wanted something casual where I didn't feel like lighting my computer on fire an hour in.  So I reinstalled it, "beat" the game again (I seem to stick with Adventure Mode with this game, not Sandbox), had that brief feeling of accomplishment, and uninstalled again.
Yeah, I went through that cycle three more times before I finally just left the game right where it was.  Now whenever I want something short and simple I don't even have to walk away from--at this point I can fix a submarine in 90 minutes--I fire this up, noodle around for a bit and call it good.
Cons:
It's short
There's not a whole lot of variation in crafting materials, things to build, or things to kill
There's no tutorial (that I can remember--at this point, if they've added it, I'm long past looking for it)
Pros:
It's short
There's enough rarity built-in to get you out of your base without being a ten-hour grind
A tutorial wasn't really necessary
TL;DR:  Don't go into it expecting a five-course meal, but if all you want is a candy bar, it's pretty satisfying.

Mix in a big bunch of "design yourself" stuff, and you get the picture. A more in-depth explanation would spoil it. There is nothing like it really.

SCREW DARWINIAN EVOLUTION! THIS IS HOW IT SHOULD WORK!
In all seriousness though this is a cool game to play. The point of the game is pretty much the very definition of evolution: you adapt to your environment, adjust your creature's physical traits according to the other creatures, and stay alive long enough to proceed in the game. Note, the game is pretty much a watered down example of evolution (I mean come on, do I really need a pair of eyes on the back of my butt?), but that doesn't mean it's a bad game.
The game consists of five stages; cell stage, creature stage, tribal stage, city stage and finally the space stage. Your strategy in surviving will depend on which stage you reside in. In each stage your creature will evolve and have access to new 'parts' and abilities. The abilities come in handy, but they ultimately depend on your route (e.g., if you become an onmivore, you have the ability to call surrounding creatures to help fight, or if you go war-like in later stages you have access to better weapon stats for your spaceship).
Speaking of spaceships, I have to applaud this game for allowing creative users to work to their fullest. There is a wide range of creative options that allows you to create vehicles, buildings and creatures to your liking. This creativness also helps give a type of identity to your species, or it just gives you the right to say I made the coolest airship blimp ever.
The way the game works is also interesting. It pushes the player to adopt different strategies and each playthrough almost demands you take a different strategy. The difficulty will also determine your gameplay (easy=you're a god, normal=mixture of difficulty with fun, hard=you will die just by walking by a random nest). The difficulty almost makes you pick certain characteristics to, for example hard will encourage you to go more millitaristic while easy will allow you to play more peacefully.
The only fault I have with this game is that the ending can take awhile to accomplish (yes, there is an ending). The 'final enemy' goes between passive and aggressive tactics that make them unpredictable and inconvinient, as you will be exploring space and then all of a sudden you recieve an alarm indicating they are attacking you. Also, for a game that takes a lot from scientific concepts such as evolution the game can get pretty silly. Like I said before, do you really need eyes on my butt, or a third arm just for giggles?
I definately recommend this game if you enjoy something with creativity. If you like games that are different from your everyday shooter I would also recommend this simply because very few games are like Spore, giving almost complete control over a species and your path.

In my experience, a solid 7/10.
Star Trek Online is a pretty damn solid MMO, especially if you're a Sci-Fi fan like me. Its combat is pretty good (especially the space combat which is fantastic and could almost be counted as one of the game's best features, in my opinion), the character customization options are also pretty good (especially for Federation players who get a metric ton of playable races to choose from ranging from Vulcans and Humans to the parasitic Trill and the warlike Andorians and telepathic Betazoid). You can even customize your star ships! Many (if not most) of the available ships have alternate parts you can use to replace the default stock parts (ex. all the Federation ships I can think of have alternate engines and saucer sections you can choose from) and different paint-jobs you can apply to further differentiate yourself from other players. You also custom-name every ship you acquire (Federation players can even give their ships their own custom-made registry numbers [ex. the Enterprise's registry number is NCC 1701]).
A lot of reviews will highlight the number of microtransactions in the game, but I think they blow it way out of proportion. Does STO contain microtransactions? Yes. A few of the cooler ships available in-game are behind a microtransaction paywall (ex. the Federation Constitution-class is a replica of the original Enterprise and is available for a fee), however, the vast majority of the most powerful vessels in STO cannot be purchased via microtransaction.
Are there better MMOs out there? Certainly. But this is, by far, the best Sci-Fi MMO I've ever played. STO's free-to-play model is fair to those who pass on microtransactions but accomodates players who don't mind shelling-out some cash to gain access to some of the ritzier playable races, outfits, ships, and bridge layouts.
I highly recommend Star Trek Online to any fellow Trekkies out there who're looking for a decent Sci-Fi MMO since you get to rub-shoulders with awesome characters like Spock, Worf, Sela, Seven-of-Nine, and Tasha Yarr. There are even a few instances where you'll fight allongside iconic ships like Voyager, Defiant, and at least three different Enterprises!
If you're a Trekkie, give it a whirl and I don't think you'll be dissapointed.

I started with Skyrim and wanted to see where this crazy Elder Scrolls open world stuff really got started. I was not disappointed when I started playing Morrowind. The game is a bit dated, graphically and gameplay-wise, but I think it offers a lot of fun times and interesting ways to play.
Pros:
-text based dialogue gives more information and options that aren't limited by voiceovers
-intricate magic and leveling systems allow for truly amazing customization
-main quest is really interesting so far (I'm about 30 hours in)
-the lore is vast, making it seem like a living, breathing world despite the aged mechanics
-the creature designs are simply amazing... creepy and intimidating...
-varied map makes the world seem even bigger than it is (in-game fast travel options add to immersion too)
-in game strip club with some swag moves
-score by the same guy who did Skyrim's soundtrack (and SW KOTOR and Bounty Hunter)
Cons:
-lack of tutorials means you have to either experiment for endless hours or get help online with gameplay mechanics
-some stock dialogue gets repetitive
-soundtrack is limited... you will hear the same explore tracks over and over again
-graphics are dated (though I really enjoy the oldschool feel)
-difficult to tell what you can and can't do in-game... some enemies look tough but get killed easily and vice-versa
-those who know what they're doing can totally break the game and become godlike (Is that a con? Still not sure...)
Basically, this game is really cool. Even if it were worse than Skyrim or Oblivion in every aspect, it's still really unique and offers a lot of cool exploration. I suggest looking up videos about why Morrowind is the best TES game. They'll do it more justice.
I definitely reccommend this game to anybody who wants to see a little more of Tamriel.

I spent probably hundreds of hours at least in this game before picking it up on Steam just to support this game a second time due to not just how many hours it has provided me in entertainment, but the exceedingly high quality of those hours of entertainment. I've never found a game environment as engrossing as this one.
A little disappointing (in the philosophical sense) that the construction set didn't make the cut. But from a practical point of view you really don't need it. Anything you could conceive of doing has probably already been done by the modding community. Plus I think you can probably still download it from somewhere. Download and install and off you go.
The world and culture of the Dunmer is brought to life masterfully in this game. Their capital, Vivec, is probably the most impressive city in any of the Elder Scrolls games. House Redoran is the best, and if you don't agree, then die n'wah! The story is great, lots of twists and turns but it all fits together really nicely. There's so much lore, and so much of it is accessible through in-game books if you choose to read them. The exploration is absolutely top-notch. There is so much to explore on the (huge) isle of Morrowind and none of it suffers from the "sameness" problems that cropped up in Oblivion and Skyrim. Everything you explore is unique and interesting. You really never know what you're going to find. It could be that little doorway built into the side of a hill is just a house, it could be the entrance to a mine or an ancient crypt or a Dwemer ruin, or it could be the site of a system of teleporters that will whisk you around the map. The only way to know is to check it out. There is so much to find in this game I guarantee you won't even come close to finding it all without the help of tools and wikis. If you had a lifetime to search for it maybe. There are underwater ruins, hidden valleys, secret notebooks, reclusive hermits, and mysterious temples. For someone who enjoys exploration it's wonderful, absolutely the best non-procedurally generated world I've ever had the pleasure of exploring.
This next bit may sound like I'm just trolling, but hear me out: This game also features some of the best house customization of any of the Elder Scrolls games, despite being completely not intended for it and in fact not even being able to properly "claim" any particular house as your own. But that shortcoming turns out to be an advantage, as you can choose basically any house in the game to be your home. You cannot move the furniture, unfortunately, but you have a huge assortment of choices to make simply by merit of there being thousands of potential houses in the game. And once you've picked out a place to live, the decoration options are the best of any Elder Scrolls game to date. There are no object physics -- another shortcoming turned to an advantage. You can place whatever you want, wherever you want, with no fear of the physics engine suddenly launching it into space, or at least across the room, because someone accidentally bumped it (or sometimes even for no reason at all) Not a problem in Morrowind! Your house will always look as grand as the day you laid it out! And the most important part... the part that's really bothered me in later games is that there's no dynamic lighting. I don't know if it's because the lightmaps have to baked into the level or something, but I can tell you there sure is plenty of dynamic lighting in Morrowind! You can light your whole house as you see fit by placing lights and lanterns and torches and candles wherever you want them. And not just plain old white lights either, we've got every color of the rainbow for you here in Morrowind! Some of them flicker, some of the glow, some of them pulse. There's an incredible variety of lighting available in Morrowind, and you can bring it all home with you to choose as you see fit! One thing you will pick up early on if you like the house decorating aspects of the game is to pick up every damn light source you can find! By theft if necessary.
Oh, did I forget to mention that many of these houses you can choose from have occupants already? Well, that's easily fixed. You've got a sword, right? Seriously though, it really is some of the best customization of a house, and yeah sometimes you do have to kill the (usually unimportant, once you've tackled their quests) owner before taking it over, but damnit, none of my houses have ever looked as good nor have I spent as much time customizing them as I have in Morrowind. You can use the mark and recall spells to substitute for the lack of fast travel, and while some people prefer to abuse the fact that you can mark any location you want to recall to by using it for actual fast travel or when they want to travel back to a merchant while heavily overburdened, mark also allows you to set your home as, well, your actual "home" for the purposes of recall. And in this way your home becomes more of a home than any of the actual buyable homes in the later games.
The graphics are not so good. It's still pretty in places, but it's dated, has polygons and fuzzy low res textures. The faces and character models in particular are butt-ugly (and I say this fondly because I love this game) but seriously they're pretty hideous, even compared to Oblivion's potatofaces. The combat is pretty awful. Each weapon is best at either bludgeoning, slashing, or piercing, but they still provide you the option to do any of the three styles of attack for no apparent reason, even going so far as to let you have an option to "always use the best attack for the current weapon" which while making perfect sense from a game mechanics point of view simply takes away even that small element of skill and decisionmaking and makes the already bland combat even more uninteresting as you simply click click click until you or the other guy dies. Your skills level up as you use them, and this seems like it would make sense but in practice is a bit goofy. It leads to silly stuff like bunny-hopping around everywhere to raise your jump skill. (Yes there's a jump skill) It's easily gamed and abused, but whatever it's still fun. The magic, while also extremely easily abused, is easily the high point of both the combat and skill systems. You can not only enchant your own items in this game, you can also create your own damn spells! Both for combat and for practical use. There are some limitations but it's definitely not enough to prevent abuse of the system. It is a whole blast of fun once you figure out some of the stuff you can do, but it can also be pretty game-breaking, so if that bothers you, you might want to avoid the magic and enchanting system entirely. You can do things like giving yourself permanent flight (I don't consider that abuse though I just consider it awesome), complete magic immunity, super-speed, or even permanent perfect invisibility that allows you to engage in combat and steal items with absolutely no repercussions at all. Godmode, basically. Used non-abusively though, it's pretty fun to be able to create your own spells (and name them!) and it allows you to create some pretty wild and crazy effects.
If you're a fan of the Elder Scrolls series, or western RPGs in general, this is probably the best one you'll find. If you can get past the graphics and some of its more obvious flaws, everything else will more than make up for it -- I promise.

SCREW DARWINIAN EVOLUTION! THIS IS HOW IT SHOULD WORK!
In all seriousness though this is a cool game to play. The point of the game is pretty much the very definition of evolution: you adapt to your environment, adjust your creature's physical traits according to the other creatures, and stay alive long enough to proceed in the game. Note, the game is pretty much a watered down example of evolution (I mean come on, do I really need a pair of eyes on the back of my butt?), but that doesn't mean it's a bad game.
The game consists of five stages; cell stage, creature stage, tribal stage, city stage and finally the space stage. Your strategy in surviving will depend on which stage you reside in. In each stage your creature will evolve and have access to new 'parts' and abilities. The abilities come in handy, but they ultimately depend on your route (e.g., if you become an onmivore, you have the ability to call surrounding creatures to help fight, or if you go war-like in later stages you have access to better weapon stats for your spaceship).
Speaking of spaceships, I have to applaud this game for allowing creative users to work to their fullest. There is a wide range of creative options that allows you to create vehicles, buildings and creatures to your liking. This creativness also helps give a type of identity to your species, or it just gives you the right to say I made the coolest airship blimp ever.
The way the game works is also interesting. It pushes the player to adopt different strategies and each playthrough almost demands you take a different strategy. The difficulty will also determine your gameplay (easy=you're a god, normal=mixture of difficulty with fun, hard=you will die just by walking by a random nest). The difficulty almost makes you pick certain characteristics to, for example hard will encourage you to go more millitaristic while easy will allow you to play more peacefully.
The only fault I have with this game is that the ending can take awhile to accomplish (yes, there is an ending). The 'final enemy' goes between passive and aggressive tactics that make them unpredictable and inconvinient, as you will be exploring space and then all of a sudden you recieve an alarm indicating they are attacking you. Also, for a game that takes a lot from scientific concepts such as evolution the game can get pretty silly. Like I said before, do you really need eyes on my butt, or a third arm just for giggles?
I definately recommend this game if you enjoy something with creativity. If you like games that are different from your everyday shooter I would also recommend this simply because very few games are like Spore, giving almost complete control over a species and your path.

HuniePop is gracefully unapologetic in it's presentation and it's character. Having originally peeked at a copy which I didn't own for laughs, I was treated to an actually really hilarious set-up for what turned out to be one of the most fun and hilarious games I've ever played.
HuniePop is an example of really knowing it's audience. Anyone willing to spend time with an open mind gets to experience this gem of a game on Steam. The gameplay is your standard match 3, it's straightforward enough for someone who's totally useless at puzzle games to get into and learn how to kind of pass everything but you can ramp the difficulty up if you want that.
HuniePop's selling point is the humour. It's seriously funny if you have that kind of sense of humour. It's dumb, it knows it's stupid but it doesn't care. Just watch the intro sequence, if you laugh. It's probably for you.
Pros:
Character designs are broad and fun. Beli best girl.
Gameplay is straightforward enough for anyone to get into but has a ramping difficulty curve if you need that.
Not all of the game is thrown at you. You have to figure out how to get into bits of it.
The item system is initially somewhat confusing but you can easily figure out what setups are good for you if you put some thought into it.
It's seriously funny.
It still has some subtlety to it despite this. There are a few things about characters that poke fun at public perception in a very clever way.
It won't break the bank for price.
Cons:
Don't expect depth from the characters. They've very caricature and stereotypical.
It's very dumb. Though this is a minor point.
Very minor: There's a tiny amount of tinkering to unlock the blocked away parts of the game though it's simple enough and there's a walkthrough in the forum area.
Once you've smashed everything, there's not that much replayability.
In short, it's really good for what it does and it's a welcome addition to Steam in my opinion. It's funny, has it's own charm and have had some serious laughter over it.

Anything you could conceive of doing has probably already been done by the modding community. Plus I think you can probably still download it from somewhere. Download and install and off you go.
The world and culture of the Dunmer is brought to life masterfully in this game. Their capital, Vivec, is probably the most impressive city in any of the Elder Scrolls games. House Redoran is the best, and if you don't agree, then die n'wah! The story is great, lots of twists and turns but it all fits together really nicely. There's so much lore, and so much of it is accessible through in-game books if you choose to read them. The exploration is absolutely top-notch. There is so much to explore on the (huge) isle of Morrowind and none of it suffers from the "sameness" problems that cropped up in Oblivion and Skyrim. Everything you explore is unique and interesting. You really never know what you're going to find. It could be that little doorway built into the side of a hill is just a house, it could be the entrance to a mine or an ancient crypt or a Dwemer ruin, or it could be the site of a system of teleporters that will whisk you around the map. The only way to know is to check it out. There is so much to find in this game I guarantee you won't even come close to finding it all without the help of tools and wikis. If you had a lifetime to search for it maybe. There are underwater ruins, hidden valleys, secret notebooks, reclusive hermits, and mysterious temples. For someone who enjoys exploration it's wonderful, absolutely the best non-procedurally generated world I've ever had the pleasure of exploring.
This next bit may sound like I'm just trolling, but hear me out: This game also features some of the best house customization of any of the Elder Scrolls games, despite being completely not intended for it and in fact not even being able to properly "claim" any particular house as your own. But that shortcoming turns out to be an advantage, as you can choose basically any house in the game to be your home. You cannot move the furniture, unfortunately, but you have a huge assortment of choices to make simply by merit of there being thousands of potential houses in the game. And once you've picked out a place to live, the decoration options are the best of any Elder Scrolls game to date. There are no object physics -- another shortcoming turned to an advantage. You can place whatever you want, wherever you want, with no fear of the physics engine suddenly launching it into space, or at least across the room, because someone accidentally bumped it (or sometimes even for no reason at all) Not a problem in Morrowind! Your house will always look as grand as the day you laid it out! And the most important part... the part that's really bothered me in later games is that there's no dynamic lighting. I don't know if it's because the lightmaps have to baked into the level or something, but I can tell you there sure is plenty of dynamic lighting in Morrowind! You can light your whole house as you see fit by placing lights and lanterns and torches and candles wherever you want them. And not just plain old white lights either, we've got every color of the rainbow for you here in Morrowind! Some of them flicker, some of the glow, some of them pulse. There's an incredible variety of lighting available in Morrowind, and you can bring it all home with you to choose as you see fit! One thing you will pick up early on if you like the house decorating aspects of the game is to pick up every damn light source you can find! By theft if necessary.
Oh, did I forget to mention that many of these houses you can choose from have occupants already? Well, that's easily fixed. You've got a sword, right? Seriously though, it really is some of the best customization of a house, and yeah sometimes you do have to kill the (usually unimportant, once you've tackled their quests) owner before taking it over, but damnit, none of my houses have ever looked as good nor have I spent as much time customizing them as I have in Morrowind. You can use the mark and recall spells to substitute for the lack of fast travel, and while some people prefer to abuse the fact that you can mark any location you want to recall to by using it for actual fast travel or when they want to travel back to a merchant while heavily overburdened, mark also allows you to set your home as, well, your actual "home" for the purposes of recall. And in this way your home becomes more of a home than any of the actual buyable homes in the later games.
The graphics are not so good. It's still pretty in places, but it's dated, has polygons and fuzzy low res textures. The faces and character models in particular are butt-ugly (and I say this fondly because I love this game) but seriously they're pretty hideous, even compared to Oblivion's potatofaces. The combat is pretty awful. Each weapon is best at either bludgeoning, slashing, or piercing, but they still provide you the option to do any of the three styles of attack for no apparent reason, even going so far as to let you have an option to "always use the best attack for the current weapon" which while making perfect sense from a game mechanics point of view simply takes away even that small element of skill and decisionmaking and makes the already bland combat even more uninteresting as you simply click click click until you or the other guy dies. Your skills level up as you use them, and this seems like it would make sense but in practice is a bit goofy. It leads to silly stuff like bunny-hopping around everywhere to raise your jump skill. (Yes there's a jump skill) It's easily gamed and abused, but whatever it's still fun. The magic, while also extremely easily abused, is easily the high point of both the combat and skill systems. You can not only enchant your own items in this game, you can also create your own damn spells! Both for combat and for practical use. There are some limitations but it's definitely not enough to prevent abuse of the system. It is a whole blast of fun once you figure out some of the stuff you can do, but it can also be pretty game-breaking, so if that bothers you, you might want to avoid the magic and enchanting system entirely. You can do things like giving yourself permanent flight (I don't consider that abuse though I just consider it awesome), complete magic immunity, super-speed, or even permanent perfect invisibility that allows you to engage in combat and steal items with absolutely no repercussions at all. Godmode, basically. Used non-abusively though, it's pretty fun to be able to create your own spells (and name them!) and it allows you to create some pretty wild and crazy effects.
If you're a fan of the Elder Scrolls series, or western RPGs in general, this is probably the best one you'll find. If you can get past the graphics and some of its more obvious flaws, everything else will more than make up for it -- I promise.

There is a trend in video game series  that I have been seeing in recent years, and it disturbs me.
This trend is the simplification of the "series formula" with each sequel.
Unfortunately, the Elder Scrolls series has fallen victim to this trend.
However, there is another trend where video games become more "familiar" to modern players with each sequel.
As the first  Elder Scrolls game was released on floppy disks, I believe that Morrowind hits the sweet spot between these two trends. Sure, there are a lot of features that Skyrim and Oblivion players would be lost without (such as the compass), but it is still a fun medieval fantasy RPG.
Also, I highly encourage you to check out the mods for this game. You know what? Check out the mods for all games developed by Bethesda.

In Oblivion, you are an assistant to the hero prophesied by the stars and the dream of a king, and go on to greatness as foretold. In Skyrim, you are a natural hero born with dragon blood and the innate ability to speak the language of dragons, and go on to greatness as foretold. In each game, along the way, you are seen as the savior of many guilds, groups, and towns, even if they are in conflict with each other in some way.
In Morrowind, you are placed in Vvardenfell by order of the Emperor because you match a supposed prophecy. With the Daedric prince Azura's assistance to enact her revenge, you're thrown into the position of fulfilling said prophecy under guidance from the Blades, and by going to the hard work of convincing everyone you really are the prophesied one. You don't know if you really fit the bill, but you'll be damned if everyone else won't believe it.
You climb your way up the ladder of each guild or ruling house you join, fighting your way to the top each time. It's a long, hard road through many cracked and broken pathways, but you clamber up the pile of corpses you made with One-Clan-Under-Moon-And-Star wrapped around your finger, and an ancient Dwemer hammer in your hand. You reap what you sow.
This is a sign of how different this game is from its successors and predecessors. A story which questions deification, worship, and prophecy; a world wracked by cataclysmic blight storms and the threat of a mortal-turned-insane-god; gameplay that greatly encourages a close eye to character building and leveling; and a plot which culminates in the death of gods and the destruction of that which deifies mortals. This is why Morrowind is so much different than its peers.
Is the gameplay to everyone's liking? Of course not. Those unexperienced with character building, and those without the patience to take in the world around you, won't find much to enjoy in this game. That's the key word. Patience. It's encouraged, and rewarded in spades. Don't play this game if you started at Oblivion or Skyrim. There's very little chance that you'll find this an enjoyable experience.
For those with the open mind and the patience, this is an incredibly worthy experience that will suck you in and never let you go. Play this only if you know how to manipulate chance and skill to your favor, and how to make your way through a harsh, unforgiving, and challenging world.

In my opinion: The best Elder Scrolls game available. Its almost the polar opposite of titles like Skyrim. Morrowind encourages exploration and flatout tells you to deviate from the main story to become more experienced and come back when you think you're more prepared to progress. There is no fast travel, only Striders which are basically buses. And there are no quest markers. The game instead gives you directions which you then write down in your journal. Personally I had a much better time trying to figure out how to get places based on hints and directions than just walking mindlessly towards a beacon on my map. This game is flawless, a masterpiece. Granted it does take an hour or so to get past the "terrible" graphics. And you may one to get an HD overhaul mod or two. But with the previous set aside, RPG/Adventure games can't get any better than this.

I loved the concept of an underwater survival/crafting/sandbox adventure, and this game did a little more than merely scratch the surface of that; but is FAR capable of doing so much more.  The art design, the music, the crafting system all work to create a tranquil gaming experience.  The storyline is basic - survive, repair and return - you decide how/when/where to do that.  There are a variety of aquatic life forms - both flora and fauna - to delight the eye and add to immersion; but insufficient to encourage re-playability without the player's own ingenuity.   The cooking/farming and crafting are entertaining, but expanding those skills falls short of really essential.  That all being said - its a game I return to time and time again, and still thoroughly enjoy!
There are mysteries to unravel - decisions to be made, and not just the ones mandated by the story mode.  Nuances of the environment(s) to explore.  The game is more than just "find the pieces", but we (the player) have to make it so; being able to mod it would go a LONG way toward extending re-playability. As a single person team, it would also go a long way toward removing the governors from this project allowing this game to truly do the genre justice!   There is SUCH awesome potential laying fallow here for a phenomenal game!
Would I recommend it?  Yes, with a disclaimer.  Its beautiful, entertaining, marginally challenging but requires a lot of player innovation to prolong the fun.  If you take your time there IS a pearl in this oyster, albeit a small one at the moment.  Here's hoping it grows...

Star Trek Online is a very *typical* free-to-play MMO, in which all of the best items and ships require real money represented by "Zen." It's a little pay-to-win in this way.
However, despite this, the game is very playable without these special goodies and for the amount of time that I have poured into this game (~250 hours), I think it is safe to say that I have rather enjoyed myself. It's a good game, but honestly, I would really only recommend it to someone who is a big Trekkie or looking for a casual MMO to put some time into. The story missions get fairly interesting and very little grinding has to be done to complete most of the content. Grinding is really only for the endgame stuff, which is to be expected with MMOs.
One of the highlights of this game is the content creator, which allows for players to enjoy user-created content in the form of arenas with waves of enemies and unique missions, many of which have been inspired by the television franchise to create some very fantastic stories. Many of these "plot heavy" missions can be over an hour long and in a series.
The story content is the "questing" of the game, and it will easily take you to max rank (50 as of this review). Some of the missions get repetative, and others have some tremendous difficulty spikes (*cough cough* The Reman series). The misssions are set up in different "series" in order to separate plot lines.
Player customization is pretty nice in this game as well, allowing one to choose several races and offering many slider options to make a unique character. They also offer a multitude of outfits and colors as well as ship designs and patterns in order to customize your vessel.
For Trekkies, the game offers much of the rich universe of Star Trek, allowing one to dabble in many unique storylines concerning the the rise of the Romulan Republic (yes, the destruction of Romulus is canon in this game) ,the resurgance of the Borg, the Dominian, and the appearance of the Iconians.
To conclude, Star Trek Online is what one may expect from a free to play MMO. To really excell or to easily excell, one might have to put in some grinidng or some cash in order to get all of the fancy ships and equipment. But, the game is very playable without spending a penny. I recommend this to any Trekkie or for one looking for a casual MMO without breaking out the wallet.

Ever think that Skyrim would be a lot better without the clunky combat system and the inability to hold any titles that have any power beyond giving you a cool name and a suit of armor?
Mount & Blade: Warband is perfect for you then! Apart from the combat, which is still super clunky, this game manages to do what Skyrim could not: make there be a purpose behind becoming the head of the magic college, or the Companions, or the Dark Brotherhood, etc. In this game, you play as a completely customizable character that is thrust into the world of a time period in history. Depending on the background you choose, your character will have varying degrees of difficulty gaining enough renown to have your own territory and build larger and larger armies. Each battle you win, or lose, gains, or loses, you renown and experience. See that city sitting on the hill? Want it to be yours? Done. If your army is big enough, and equiped well enough, then consider it yours! Just be prepared to face the consequences, cause the king who owned that piece of land is going to want it back.
To sum everything up, this game is really clunky, but is really detailed and is for the people who think Skyrim could have had a lot more stuff in it.

Spore is a game that promised, well, the galaxy.  It delivered something far more modest in comparison.  That said, for its current sale price it's well worth it.  I played this game when it was new, and I still liked it then.  Don't go into it expecting a top notch version of each of the genres its stages represent.  The game is like a tour through various game genres as your creatures' society evolves and eventually makes it into space.
The number one problem I had with the space stage was that it was suggested you could create something akin to the Federation in Star Trek.  That is not the case: you can create individual alliances but those are not permanent and require some attention to maintain.  You are the universe's only space nanny, having to personally go with your ship to aid your allies or they may get angry with you.  It's not as bad as I'm making it sound unless you try to make a huge alliance, which is where the game's faults become clear: it's decent at many genres but not great at any of them.  There are also a few mods for the space stage as well, but as far as I'm aware nothing so complex that it fixes the primary issues I had with it.
The level creation for the Galactic Adventures expansion does add another layer of possibliites onto the game, as well.
All of this said, I absolutely reccommend the game, especially at its sale price.  Just don't expect something spectacular; instead expect something unique. If you aren't particularly picky with games and like the genres the game represents, there is a lot of fun to be found.

Review based on the current beta build at the time of this review.
A game that could have been better, the graphics aren't bad and the era is one not often seen in flight games.  I had written an initial "not recommended" review but retracted it when they released a beta patch adding a new flight model and some other changes in order to give it a 2nd chance.  However it must be said that there is  still more wrong than right with this game.
JET FLIGHT: You have two choices of which are flying like a car, or flying with a buggy "simulation" mode in which aircraft controls don't function properly.  For some examples: applying right rudder has 0 yaw effect and will roll your plane over toward the left, or how banking can have little or no effect on turning.
HELO FLIGHT: Large improvement over pre-beta.  Helicopter flight actually felt decent and the bindings were an improvement from before.  The main bother here is the dodge mechanic which lets the helo suddenly jerk left or right.  It doesn't look so bad in cockpit view but out of cockpit it looks ridiculous.
WEAPONS: Very auto-aim based, get in the general proximity with the sight and watch the bullets fly from your jet as if they were coming from a turret in the nose.  Missiles can be adjusted to varying degrees of accuracy, generally not an issue.  Bomb view is limited to straight flight when in simulation, no rudder control due to the bug for fine adjustments.  Applying rudder or banking will pull you out of bomber view.  This game would strongly benefit from the option to use a mouse for the door gunner while using a flightstick for the helicopter as well.
AI: Not much to say but if you control any aircraft during mission the AI will no longer function on that aircraft for the remainder of said mission.  (That aircraft will just keep flying straight.)
STORY: The story really had no draw to it, you hear the narration of some letters from the main pilot and to the main pilot as well as the general briefing for missions but they lack any emotional draw and just didn't engage me as a player.  On another down note to story there is almost no radio chatter during missions to draw you into the story and it creates a very hard separation between the missions and the cuts between them.  What little chatter there is is comparable to the the movie Sharknado and the cuts during missions feel just as dry and out of context as the cuts inbetween missions.
Overall the gameplay in simulation is undesireable due to the current bugs with no sign of developer feedback.  Unfortunately while arcade works better I have serious issues calling games with the "flying car" model of flight a flight game in this day and age.  Air Conflicts Vietnam is a game that has or had a lot of potential that just isn't coming through.  Is it redeemable, I'd say yes... however it will take more than I believe they are willing to do at this stage considering they have mentioned work on an expansion.  In its current state this game comes off as dry, repetitive, buggy, pretty  much uninteresting, and I just can't recommend it.

I really wanted and still want to like this game.  Cutting to the short, it just is too repetitive and random.
The game is centered around an elegent rock, paper, scissors scheme in which certain units do better against others or via a combination of sequential attachs.  Large battles are segmented into regions.  When one region buckles, the battle is over.  Or, at the end of a few rounds, One side can retreat.  Certain cards influence battles and between turn moves.  But, that is really it.  Smaller battles are the same, but one region.  Leaders and unit return come into play as does initiative.  Ultimately, this is rather dull after 50 or so reiterations of the formula.
You can take regions and influence countries, but there is really little impact or value.  Taking and holding a capitol (for a random number of tuns) knocks out a power.
Cards create some random events.  Some can be quite the game changer while others seem to serve little purpose.
I wish the game allowed custom starting positions, playing anyone other than France, or more reason to control territories.
It just feels like more could be done.
I would say, buying this on special for $10, it seems a fair value.  At regular price, I think this is not going to feel like a good purchase.

Games like this make me wish Steam had a more granular way of rating games, rather than just giving it a thumbs up or thumbs down.  Buttttt, that being said I can somewhat recommend this game.  I bought the game on sale for $10, and it was OK for that price.
Pros:
-Engaging gameplay, it was fun to figure out the systems and how to beat them. The battles are simplistic but fun, and allow a number of different tactics.  The strategic dynamic is also neat; as the French you have raw strength and skill and can smash army after army; however the nefarious British can continually bring in new enemies to beset you.  It's like fighting against a flock of ducks; you are trying to quickly smash the ones in front of you before the entire flock can swarm you and pull you down.
- music is surpisingly listenable
- the game seems bug free, and does a reasonable job of conveying the rules to this complex board game.
Cons:
- The UI design is terrrrrrrible.  Adjusting and combining armies is a giant pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ and in general the strategic map seems blithely unaware of the last 30 years of game design.
- Once you've played a few games, there is not much need to play more. This is alright for a $10 game. If I had payed the full $30 I would be much more bothered by this.
- The AI is competent at the battles, but is largely out to lunch when it comes to the strategic map.

So I tried this game, and after 2 hours I decided to get a refund.
I was an avid player of the original board game that this video game is based on, and maybe that tainted my experience with the video game.  TL;DR: 1) unclear / vague rules and game procedures leaves you not knowing why somethings are happening, 2) differing rules compared to the original board game results in less control of your units, and 3) no sandbox campaign / strict alliances means less complexity and intrigue.
1) Unlcear / Vague Rules and Game Procedures
The battle's are performed without any visible dice.  You can't tell what the "rolls" are, you just know the final result. This makes it extremely difficult to determine what your odds are for performing certain actions over others --- how are you supposed to tell if it's a better idea to fire with your infantry vs charge with your cavalry if you don't know what the dice rolls and modifiers are?? Units also end up in "disorder" randomly - it can happen if they attack or get attacked, and it's unclear what that stance does to their battle modifiers -- is it minus 1 dice on attack and defend? Don't know.  Commanders are also not allowed on the front lines, yet their ranking somehow impacts your troops battle performance. Again, it's unclear what a Commander ranked 12 vs a Commander ranked 3 will actually do to your troops battle performance.  This becomes important when you're deciding to rally troops who fled their flanks, because rallying lowers your commanders rank for the next battle phase, which impacts your overal troops performance....but you never know what that impact really is, so you can't tell if it's worth rallying a unit or keeping the rank high.
Battles are a big pile of educated guesses. You honestly end up assuming certain things based on how you feel this should be. For example, a Cavalry unit should get a bonus against charging artillery units...right? So you charge your cav against artillery, but you don't actually know what it means, or what the modifiers are. Very frustrating.
2) Differing Rules Compared to Original Board Game
I used to play the board game for hours and hours and hours with my friends. Fantastic game, made better with a few tweaks we'd make to the original rules that enhance the exprience.
The rules of this game are so much more different than the rules of the board game though, and ultimately this was the reason I requested a refund.  Here's a a few examples:
a) you are limited to just 4 units per flank in a battle (in the board game, no such rule exists).
- This isn't a huge problem, but it ultimately turns what would have been massive battles into small skirmishes where you line up your top elite soldiers to mow down the enemy who are forced to come at you in a tunnel 4 at a time. The board game allowed you to use your numbers more effectively so that you can swarm and overwhelm elite units, which frankly is more realistic.
b) units have this weird level / rank number that somehow impact their battle strength, and depending on their performance in a battle, they can rank up (in the board game, no such rule exists).
- In the board game, you have militia (-1), regular infantry (even), elite infantry (+1) and skirmishers (+1 fire, -1 charge), and each have specific battle modifiers that I've written, that stay constant throughout the game. This made it very clear what your expectations of those units should be in the battle field. You decided to hire cheap militia instad of investing in regular and elite infantry? You might pay the price because each roll with your militia is a -1, and if they're charged with for example an elite infantry at +1, that's a difference of 2..which makes a big difference especially in long protracted battles.  In this game however, you can't tell what a level 4 infantry vs a level 2 infantry do. Is that the dice roll modifier? You don't know, because you don't see the dice rolls.  The board game also allowed infantry to "square" against cavalry, which is a formation that repels cavalry charges more effectively, giving you a increased battle modifier if charged by cavalry.  However, you remain in square and require a full turn to get out of one, and firing out of a square lowers your modifier.  So deciding to square when cavalry charges requires some thought of the consequences.  In the video game, you can't decide if your infantry squares or not, it's literally automatically decided for you, and I can't tell if there's any rhyme or reason to when they square vs not squaring and taking the charge head on.  Again, you end up just clicking through a battle assuming and hoping things happen positively for you. Very frustrating.  In the video game however, your units do rank up, but it's not clear what needs to happen for them to rank up (ie., how many kills or battles fought before a unit ranks up? No way to tell). I like this change, and it's easily implemented in a video game, but again, because everything else is so vague and unclear, it ruins this feature.
c) there are so many cards in the video game that aren't in the board game, and cards become the new "political action points" that the board game uses.
- if you want to conquor a new territory, you need to have a card that lets you get a minor nation/territory to join yours. Which sucks, because your dependent on the card draw. In the board game, you have political action points that you can spend on annexing territories. That annexation is also not guaranteed as is in the video game. For example, you can spend a point to annex Venice, but you make a bad roll that leads to Venice fighting back, which leads to a small rebel army being raised to fight your annexing force. Very fun stuff, but the video game has none of that nuance.  In the video game, you march an army in, play the card, and the territory is yours - boring. There are many other negative impacts to the over reliance on these cards in the video game that would take me much longer to explain.
3) there are 4 (or 5) different campaigns you can play in the video game, and alliances are somewhat locked (in the board game, there are many scenarios with locked alliances, but also sandbox games where anything can happen..French and Brits ally against Austria? It can happen!)
- this basically ruins the intrigue and political side of the board game. You can't convince anyone of an alliance. I know it's difficult to program AI, but I mean that's a core function of the board game, trying to convince other leaders to join your cause -- before you back stab the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s while they fight your enemies for you. None of that exists in this game.
Maybe my expectations were way too high, but honestly the game needs a lot of work, particularly at this price point of $30+ CDN. I will watch closely to see if further updates are made to improve the game, and if so, I might dive back in. I really want to relive this board game.

I remember years ago when I first purchased Ecco the Dolphin for my Sega CD. The gameplay was simple, move the dolphin from the beginning of the stage to the end of the stage, avoiding or destroying obstacles in your path. But, it wasn't the gameplay that intrigued me the most about the game, it was the ambience - the sheer joy of being able to immerse myself within the superior graphics (of the time) and excellently composed music to create what felt to me the ideal oceanic environment. I still have the soundtrack on MP3, for when I wish to isolate myself within once again.
When I purchased this game, I had high hopes that it would create a new dream of ambience, despite all of the negative reviews that I had perused, the simple gameplay mechanic really wasn't what I desired the most - in fact, it falls extremely short in depth of every other sandbox game that I have ever played. Yet, I was extremely disappointed after playing this game to realize that all of the potential for beauty that was promised was nothing more than an illusion designed simply to entice dreamers like us to waste our money on a poorly crafted attempt to make quick cash.
The music was engaging, until it became repetitive. The graphics were good, until I realized there was no way to interact. The extremely limited availability and flexibility of creation components destroys the "sandbox" quality of the game. The overly simplified equipment upgrade mechanics destroy the gameplay. The collision detection is broken. The interlude and story sequences are poorly written. There is absolutely nothing about this game that I can honestly compliment other than the fact that it had wonderful potential if the developers had not given up on it so early, but even then I just can't bring myself to admire those who choose to be lazy. I will *not* be purchasing another game from this developer ever again.
I do not recommend purchasing this game based purely on disappointment that I have suffered, the empty promises, and poor overall quality of something that should have been a wonderous achievement.

Original review:
"No time to explain, n'wah, buy the game!♥♥♥♥♥♥ that cliff rider is coming, bai!"
Maybe back in the days when I wrote that review, it was just an inside joke, a horror and nightmare that people who have played or heard of Morrowind would only get. Looking at it now, maybe it's a bit unfair to leave it as it is, especially considering how I feel about Morrowind and how much time I've spent on it, long before I got it on Steam.
Morrowind....
It'd be hard to capture everything about the game, and it'd be twice as hard to put it into words, but I can at least try, not just for my own satisfaction but for every possible person that might come across this review and actually stop to read it.
Morrowind.
The third game in The Elder Scrolls series, released back in the distant 2002. A lot of words could be used to describe it, for me personally it'd be just one - fascinating. For me personally, Morrowind is the kind of game that years later, playing Skyrim, I realized how much it has affected me - I'd always compare Skyrim and its mechanics and story to Morrowind; many people may not find it fair, but it's deep within me, and I'm sure that many people who feel about Morrowind the same way have done it, more than once. I also admit I teared up twice - once when I realized that the Morrowind main theme is incorporated within the Skyrim OST and once when I got to visit Solstheim... The latter one, especially, woke up a deep feeling of nostalgia, turning the camera around and looking at the Red Mountain, wishing I could just jump on that boat and set foot there once again.. set foot back home.
You see, Morrowind is a masterpiece, not only one of its time, but a masterpiece that will stick along for years... It's no lie that it's old now. It is, indeed, and its graphics might not be as welcoming as they used to be back then, but the world and story it has to offer, it's something I'm yet to find in another game.
But enough fuzzy warm feeling of nostalgia, let me tell you why I believe this would probably remain one of the games that I'll always come back to...
Morrowind is a timeless RPG, one that will take years for others to catch up on. While some may disagree, I believe everything from the details of the atmosphere of the game, through the sandbox mechanics that allow you and encourage you to do everything you think of, all the way to the combat system that I've seen people complaining about, all this is polished nearly to perfection.
Morrowind is unforgiving, it won't hold your hand, it won't tell you what to do, it won't make things easy for you. It's a combination of detailed conversations, exploration and thought that is required to reach your goals. One wrong turn along the way and you'll find yourself in a cave full of Daedras, and if you manage to overcome the odds, your reward will be there waiting for you.
Morrowind will make your imagination go nuts. You want to be a deadly wizard, using spells no one has ever heard of, well then, be one! You want to be the most powerful being walking this earth, Gods' demise, unmatched by no power, divine or mortal? Be one! You are allowed to do nearly everything in it, you just need to find your way to do it.
Morrowind is frustration, trust me, not once or twice you'll walk into enemies severely overpowered than you are and they will kill you, over and over and over again. Cliff racers will haunt your dreams and mudcrabs will give you the most challenging fights you've ever experienced... Maybe except for that ebony beggar dude, ♥♥♥♥ that guy seriously.
Morrowind is the land where you are no one. Brace yourself for being treated and called any kinds of names, from the popular 'outlander' to the so annoying 'scum'. Question is, would that break you or would you reclaim the destiny of the Nerevarine, Protector of Morrowind?
Morrowind is .... perfect, in its imperfection.

I enjoyed it a lot, although Napoleonic Era is admittedly my least favourite military period.  It's good on strategic level but really shines on tactical (battles) level.
It can be challenging but is never unfair. Battles can change rapidly from "I've got this" to "Now I'm fukked" and back to "I've got this" in a minutes. I recommend playing it on hard or at least normal level on "ironman" (I've played "Into Russia" on hard and managed it at first try, although I got lucky a number of times). I also recommend reading a manual (at least part about battles, as it is important to know the modifiers behind the rolls). It's a bit shame that you can't play as England here, but it makes sense from the gameplay asymmetry perspective. Interface is allright, graphics & music too, no bugs experienced. Thumb up.

There are a few grievances but this is a fun little board game. I've played nearly 140 hours and enjoyed every moment of it.
It has surprising depth under the guise of simple rules. You will know if you either read the manual or play a difficult campaign.
The game has a lot to offer. It's casually fun, and if you are looking a challenge, playing the last scenario in emperor difficulty will likely be the hardest gaming experience you've ever had. It has tons of replayability.
This game would have been really great if the Dev was able to fix those grievances(British amphibious landing, enemy retreat indicator and direction; pretty much the only complaints I have about the game), but alas it didn't sell well enough for patches.
Still this is the game I've poured most time into among Napoleonic games; I own many Napoleonic titles and this one was among the best. I played VG:N far more than  I played Napoleon Total War.
Recommended if you like board games and like fun battles. Not recommended if you are looking for some deep diplomacy and complicated mechanics.

I really like this game, even though I should by all counts hate it. It very much feels like a board game, not just asthetically, but in the ruleset as well. The dice rolls aren't shown, but it's very obvious that there's a lot of random at play. That being said, the combat system doesn't feel dictated by the random, although it certainly is frustrating to miss repeatedly even when you have a +14 modifier.
Started out feeling good about the game, a couple hours in and I was tepid, but as I perfected my strategies for the battle system and figured out the more advanced tactics (I think), I came to really enjoy it in the end.
Strategic mode is where it unfortunately falls a bit flat. The AI is somewhere between ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and cheesy. Since the only province that actually matters is the capital, the AI will enevitably just bunch 3 armies of 20 guys on vienna and berlin. Diplomacy point system is interesting as a system to keep threats out of the coalition, but your only sources of diplomacy points are conquering nations (at which point you really don't need to keep anyone else out of coalition, since a bunch of your soldier's just became available to reposition), or a rare card draw. And since points for you are so raer, any card that gives points to Britain is almost certainly not worth it.
Had a few hair raising moments, but with a bit of luck, I managed to win the 1800 scenario in 4 years plus a fifth to put down the last resistance in Spain.
Don't think it has a whole lot more replayability however, to be honest. Might try the gottdamerung equivalent scenario for fun later.

Victory and glory is based on the board game by the same name.
As a huge board game lover. I felt the need to try it.
In summery the game is pretty simple and can feel redundent.
Its very different from risk so I'm not sure why everyone in the review keeps saying its risk?
Since the game does feature a basic tactical battle, navies and limited attrition.
The game has a set of event card which are used for the politics in the game. In short frances lets them add territories to the french empire which makes all the major nations mad at france. Englands lets them get other nations to declare war on france as part of the coaliton. A few cards als give you troops.
On a strategic level the game is about momentum. As france you need to knock enemies out of the war faster than they can join it. If you cannot you will be overwealmed.
Battles are fought in a tactical kind of way but they can be rather redundent with players using almost the same tactic ever battle, making them not much better than just strait dice chucking.   Slitherine made a decent AI for this game,  it seems to be able to hold its own with people, which is excellent even in a simple game like this.
All in all this is not the board game to computer conversion of a board gamers dream. It at best is a superior option to computer solitare.

Simple Napoleonic era Grand Strategy game that feels and plays like a boardgame.
The game does not straight jacket players into rigidly following any kind of historical course of action  but the positive aspect of this is that the player has a lot of freedom,
The AI seemed pretty reasonable (often a fatal weekness in fluid strategy games).
When and if nations declare war is dependant upon the play of the cards and use of political influence points won by defeating enemy nations. Other historical events are triggered by a card system that fits well within the system and adds an interesting historical veneer to the game and also add unpredictability.
It captures the mood of the era and of the scale represented  I think.
2 reservations though currently:-
played it through once on fairly high difficulty after a number of poor starts learning the system and then started a second playthrough before getting distracted., how replayable it is currently for its price. Probably something easily rectified with additional cards though if the developer continues to support the game.
Naval warfare is not very good....if you play it as intended the Royal navy is practicaly unbeatable so you may as well ignore the French navy...if you 'game the system'  though its easy to turn it around.
The developer has promised to improve this aspect, it should be an interesting part of gameplay rather than a dead loss or something to exploit. But it should have been there from the outset, not as a DLC as the developer has suggested.
Nothing else that I know about fills a similar niche at the same kind of complexity and playthrough time.
Reasonable game but expensive for what it is.

Wow what a great game. Don't let the simple-looking interface fool you - this is hours and hours of fun and is as thoughtful a period grand-strategic simulation as you'll find. It beautifully captures the military, naval, geopolitical and international dynamics of Napoleonic history like no other game I've played.
The game effectively balances the military prowess of France against the political power of England and Europe's balance-of-power politics. France's armies are great and you will win battles, but England is always on a mission to build a new coalition to oppose you. And if you think you will just blitzkrieg Europe to conquest you will be frustrated by the major powers just as quickly alligning to take you down - thoughtless military aggression will lead you to your own personal Waterloo. Instead, careful strategum, divide-and-conquer politics, and opportunistic empire and kingdom building will be your path to Victory.
Battles are simulated on a tactical map, and reflect the linear (left flank, center, right flank) nature of Napoleonic battles. Hammer the enemy with your Grand Battery? Send forward swarms of skirmishers to disrupt his defences? The enemy is weakening on the left - commit the Imperial Guard now? The enemy has retreated - is your cavalry fit to pursue and hack him down?
I've seen some reviews critical of Britain's substantial naval advantages, and the Royal Navy is truly superior! But if you think Napoleon's navy could just fight the Brit's on even terms, you should ask Admiral Villenueve about that... Instead, use a long-term strategy. I waited until I could distract England with a war in America in 1812, then built my Dutch and Danish navies while augmenting my own, hit the Brits with storm and mutiny cards, and I was able to achieve naval superiority and landed Nappy in London for an epic victory.
Politics are much more realistic than, for example, another favorite, the Total War series.  In Victory and Glory, a defeated enemy will not attack you again the turn after you sign a peace treaty (I hate that in TW!). You will have a passive neutral for not less than a year. Even then, it will take the Brits' political pull and your own aggressive actions to turn them into active enemies.
Build the Kingdom of Naples and the Duchy of Warsaw! Form the Confederation of the Rhine and recruit Germans like crazy! Slaughter Spanish partisans! It's all there and more - if  you love the Napoleonic Wars like I do, this game is the best strategic simulation I've seen.

I have now played this game through once on Adventurer, and twice on Survivor. Here are my thoughts.
Since FarSky is tagged as "survival", "adventure", "indie", "sandbox", and "crafting", I'm obligated to compare and contrast it with Minecraft, which I also have played extensively. This game is not Minecraft. Its crafting system is much simpler. It has a goal, whereas Minecraft does not. It has an end; you can "win". The randomly generated world, while being large and immersive, is finite. The movement mechanics are much different as you're under water. The terrain cannot be deconstructed, but minerals can be mined from it.
The graphics are relatively simple, yet work quite well. All the plants and animals under the sea have convincing movements. The enviroment itself is very well done, between the day/night cycles, and the way it fades into a blue haze at a distance.
The game mechanics were fun. I could get around without any trouble. The combat system is not overly complex. It can be difficult, especially at night in the first days of the Survival mode, but becomes effortless later on.
The premise is that your submarine broke into 9 pieces during a dive, and you are marooned on the bottom of the ocean floor. You must survive, equip yourself, and find the 9 pieces of your submarine. Once you do, it will assemble, and you can ascend to the surface, thereby winning the game. The game itself is relatively short. I have been everywhere, done everything, and beat it 3 times, for a total of 25 hours.

It's an interesting concept and game play seems simple enough to catch onto quickly. The scenery is pleasant from my short time playing. I would spend more time with it, but the game spans my dual monitor setup in both full screen and windowed mode making all the center game action fall on the gap between my two monitors. There seems to be no adjustment for window size and I've been unable to find any tips or tricks in the forum to overcome this shortcoming. There seems to be very little activity in the forums from the dev and forum chatter is that the dev is done with this game and is/has moved on to something else. I do feel cheated, as I could not play the game in a suitable way and there may never be fixes.
Maybe this game and other projects like it should have a Steam category like: Temporal, Short run, Test bed, etc. Something identifying such projects as something with short lived dev updates and support. The price for such games should have a cap as well. I realize original titles like Farsky take much effort to bring to market, but if it's meant to be a short lived project, then don't soak players, because we will be less likely to buy games from that dev again. It is bad pulic relations.

Ever think that Skyrim would be a lot better without the clunky combat system and the inability to hold any titles that have any power beyond giving you a cool name and a suit of armor?
Mount & Blade: Warband is perfect for you then! Apart from the combat, which is still super clunky, this game manages to do what Skyrim could not: make there be a purpose behind becoming the head of the magic college, or the Companions, or the Dark Brotherhood, etc. In this game, you play as a completely customizable character that is thrust into the world of a time period in history. Depending on the background you choose, your character will have varying degrees of difficulty gaining enough renown to have your own territory and build larger and larger armies. Each battle you win, or lose, gains, or loses, you renown and experience. See that city sitting on the hill? Want it to be yours? Done. If your army is big enough, and equiped well enough, then consider it yours! Just be prepared to face the consequences, cause the king who owned that piece of land is going to want it back.
To sum everything up, this game is really clunky, but is really detailed and is for the people who think Skyrim could have had a lot more stuff in it.

TLDR; It's a great WW2 game with lots of potential. It features both realism and arcade simultaneously, and does it well.
First, let me start by saying that there aren't many games left in the category of multiplayer ww2 fps.
This game is among the best in that category, and I think that it is has tons of potential.
I've played RO2 and I think that I prefer H&G over it, as this game provides a more arcade-like feeling, don't get me wrong, it's still pretty realistic, it's just that RO2 is over the top realistic.
Now enough comparing H&G to other games. H&G lets you live out your ww2 fantasies. You can fly a plane, drive a tank, just be a regular soldier among the masses, and you can even be a paratrooper if you want.
Pros/Cons
+Gameplay variety
+RTS style campaign map, cool for people who want to feel like a general commanding armies, please note that it's not complete, for the time being
+Physics engine can be a bit silly but it adds humor to the game
+Variety of weapons/vehicles for each faction
+Hard work pays off, more expensive/hard to get weapons/vehicles are actually good
+Well-made maps
+Ability to have multiple soldiers for each faction, and choose any career for each soldier, with the option to switch at any time
+Everything can be bought with the base currency in the game, including veteran membership
+Active devs who host a livestream every Friday as well as releasing updates every couple of weeks
+From my experience, the community is great. You meet some really cool people who are either a. hilarious or b. really into history
-It can feel pay to win/pay to enjoy at times, as there is a bit of a grind to get better gear and to level up, especially if you don't have veteran membership. As a result , this is one of the few games that get me frustrated, although I'm a pretty impatient person, keep that in mind
- Starting weapons. I understand that the starting weapons should not be amazing, and it justifies buying better weapons, but there is literally no reason to go back to them once you unlock the respective faction's smg's or assault rifle. It's a shame for some people who like the M1 Garand, Gewehr 43, or SVT-40 in real life but find them inefficient in-game.
-Lack of some key factions at the moment, like Great Britain, for example
-Lack of some destruction features, I feel like a ww2 game, or any war game, needs destructable buildings and other objects in order to feel authentic
-Little to no voice acting, watch the "Soviets Are Coming" trailer. That's one of the things this game needs.
-Latency issues if you're using wifi
+- Graphics. They're pretty good, but the game does not look like the screenshots on the steam page...I wish it did.
+- Maps. There are a decent amount of them, and the assault maps can be played in numerious different ways due to the randomness of capture lines, meaning that one map can play a few different ways because only some portions will be available in any given battle. However, they each have kind of a similar feel to them, I just wish each map had some specific thing to make it stand out more.
Overall, I recommend this game. Don't be disheartened by some of the cons I've stated about this game, it just goes to show how much I like this game if I can take the time to write a review and think of pros and cons.
