Get this game.. Its already good, and by mid-late 2016 it could be getting real good. This game is much better than the year old reviews i read on this thread. I was thinking that it would be some sort of run-of-the-mill colony building, griefing, hero based RTS, no no no no ... The game is a survival shooter, you set out into the wilderness and theres a 70% chance you'll be dead if you get greedy or aren't smart.. You are afraid of dying unlike a lot of games.. You can build yourself a Terraria style base in the middle of nowhere and it will persist forever, your own little wilderness secret stash spot,. Phew, finally you can get 1 minute without stressing.. but dont worry about building anything until you somehow survive long enough to save cash without 3 straight failed missions.. expensively repairing your gear in shame... Griefing or player killing? Unless you're dumb enough to build near a public drop zone, you're lucky to even see another player, hell, youre excited to see someone else because the world is so enormous and you're so alone, so very alone..
PROS:
- Survival is hard and fun, you earn everything you get, returnign to base is a pleasure, not a chore
- Desolation, you feel very alone and vulnerable,
- Game concept is ambitious and new.. a giant sci fi shooter open world with sandbox survival elements. though in early stages right now.
CONS:
- The combat seems ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and basic in the tutorial but enter the game and you soon develop your own tricks to fight      and survive in the wilderness and you stop noticing the crap early 2000's style shooter mechanics because you're always 20 seconds from near death.
- missions diversity is low, only a few available right now, probably the last thing on the Devs minds until the game is fleshed out more
- not much player interaction. This is where the "colonies" concept wont play a role until the player base has grown post-release where i think the intention is to group together to ppol resources and make areas of control. An ambitious idea at such an early stage, but could be big if it works.

I have to be honest, when I first bought this game months ago, this port was so bad I wanted to write a negative review of it.  I played it with a decent PC but the framerate kept stuttering, froze sometimes, there was input lag, and unnecessary slowdown (when the game enters slowmotion due to too much chaos on-screen at once) that shouldn't even be in the game.  I couldn't understand how DotEmu screwed up the port so bad, there was no excuse a modern PC can't run it smoothly.  I've tried emulating it in the past using WinKawaks and it was flawless.
Months later, I decided to reinstall it on a crappy laptop to see if the performance has gotten any better.  To my surprise, it did, really.  The slowdown, stuttering, and input lag were all gone.  The game still froze, but rarely, and for about a fifth of a second, anyway.  If this low-end laptop can finally run Metal Slug 3 on Steam, then any kind of computer can, if it's not made in early 2000's.  The sound emulation still kind of sucks, though, most noticeable when you see the "GO!" icon and when the game counts your rescued prisoners.
But enough with the port performance, we all know it's dealt with.  This game is the Metal Slug we all know, and if you don't, I'll fill you in, anyway.  Run 'n' gun, fight General Morden's troops while dodging their bombs and bullets at the same time.  One thing to keep in mind: you're a one-hit-kill and you will die a lot.  In order to
die, I'm afraid you just have to.  It's how you'll learn what to expect so you can play better, that's what I went through.
You'll be fighting more than just Morden's army, but that I'll have to keep a secret if you've never played Metal Slug before.  The weapons come in a nice variety, a Heavy Machine Gun, a Rocket Launcher (or
), the devastating Shotgun, the Enemy Chaser that fires homing missiles, and much more.  The slugs, vehices you can board with mounted machine guns, are nice, too.  Depending on the routes you take, you'll find the signature Metal Slug: Super Vehicle 001, the two-legged Slugnoid, a submarine, and even an ostrich or a camel.  Most slugs have health, which is helpful in a game where you can die in one hit, but others simply don't have that luxury.
The controls are great, complete movement with a D-pad or analog stick and three buttons for Fire, Jump, and Grenade.  But since this is an arcade port, it lacks the wider controls configuration and Vulcan Fix the console versions have.  I have to discuss the Metal Slug Attack, which caused me so much frustration in the past, wasting so many slugs during boss fights.  When you initiate this attack, you sacrifice your slug by charging it into the enemy, triggered by pressing
at once.  Since you'll shoot and jump a lot, you're bound to trigger this by accident, so avoid pressing Fire and Jump at the same time if you can help it.  So DotEmu, if it's possible, I hope you add the option to rebind the Metal Slug Attack command and add Vulcan Fix.
Oh, and there's online play through friend lobbies, so you can get a friend to die with.  I should know, I had a blast years ago with the Metal Slug Anthology on the PS2.  It can be loads of fun with someone else, maybe even easier just hope they'll make good use of that Rocket Launcher they found.  Make sure both parties have a stable connection, otherwise, you'll be plunged into performance stutter or even worse, desynchronization.
If you like side-scrolling run 'n' gun games, this one might be for you.  For a first-timer challenge, set your credits to 20, not Freeplay, and see how far you can get through the game with only 20 continues.  There's also Metal Slug X, remake of 2, on the Steam store for an easier and more straightforward experience.

Summary:  Good in concept, poor in execution.
The game is Air Conflicts: Vietnam and it is exactly what it claims to be.  It's an arcade flying game where you use various aircraft types and styles to partake in the Vietnam war.  Your initial and very quick "tutorial" is based on checking out your flight controls to ensure they function properly.  It's a good way to "hide" a tutorial, but one problem exists that plagues every single mission in this game.  Let's talk about it...
Most modern military games like those of the Battlefield series are limited by the size of map it's possible to have, and Air Conflicts: Vietnam is no different.  To keep players on the map they institute map edge boundries that will warn you first and then proceed to "kill" you if you remain off the map.  In most games this is kept tactfully in the map display as to not ruin the immersion of the player.  In this game, however, that map limit is visibly gridded in the sky and even changes to red when you get close to it.  I constantly felt like I was performing air combat inside a box rather than fighting in Vietnam, and a small box to be sure.  That's my next complaint.  For a game where FLIGHT is the main form of travel, the map areas are EXTREMELY small.  I found myself having to climb and then dive at bombing targets because there really was no way to setup a decent bombing run.
The graphics, sounds, and other things in the game are really nicely done.  I really liked how the ground was laid out, with trees, camps, and proper texturing of the foliage.  It was very well done in that respect.  Sadly you rarely got to see any of it because you were constantly avoiding running into the walls in the sky.  If I could say one thing to the developers it would be to enlarge the maps.  Everything else is beautiful, but the small map size turned me away from this game in under 15 minutes of playing (4 missions completed).
Because of that, I'm sorry to say, this is one game I can't recommend and am glad I got it as part of a bundle.

Ahhhh, Morriwnd.
Even since 2002 (wow, it's been 12 years already), it's been a beautiful, immersive world (especially to me, who started the Elder Scrolls series with Morrowind) where story and sidequests are equally as enthralling to each other as the strange sense of magic you feel when exploring the vast, ash-barren countryside of Vvardenfel.
Although while in today's standards, the graphics do appear to have suffered some, that only adds to the pure nostalgia for those of us who have played this when this was the cutting-edge of RPG and sandbox production.  Sure, you don't have many options for hair or face, and yes, the sluggish walk and dicey combat system can be a bit off-putting.  But past it all, when you've finally gotten to that comfortable place where you can run faster than a slug on a Sunday and hit more times than you'll miss, you begin to appreciate the game as more than just a piece of software.  You really do begin to see it as an adventure into a foreign land.  A place where you've never been before, but will surely uncover its secrets in due time.
And thanks to the good people of the Internet, mods have been created that help with issues in game, such as the overall graphics (especially NPC and player models, such as the Better Bodies mod) and whatever else you might consider to be a problem or upgrade-worthy factor.  The fact of the matter is, that when the dust has settled and all is said and done, Morrowind still remains one of the cornerstone RPGs of yesteryear, and I certainly know that it'll forever be one of the defining games for the RPG genre.

The Gold Standard of open world RPG. The mother of all RPG games to come after it. Morrowind revolutionized the idea of an open world game. There is depth to the world that is unparalleled in both games released before this as well as afterwards. The game is dated, so there is something to be said about how smoothly the game runs and looks and feels, but there are many mods that can be used to remedy those issues
.
This game begins with you as a prisoner. No history, you can become whatever you want to be. You can create a character who does anything you want. The depth of the character development allows you to become anything you want. You can choose follow a pre-built class chosen from a list of 21 including classes such as: sorceror, thief, and warrior. Or you can be something new and creative by creating your own class. If you want (and I did this), you can be a walking tank with a two handed battleaxe wearing plate armour imbued with the blood of demons. You can choose to be one of one of ten races, each with their own characteristics, each with their stereotypes that generate responses unique to that race from NPCs. You can even choose to become a vampire or (with the bloodmoon expansion included in the Game of the Year edition) werewolf!This means you will have a unique experience in your game that nobody else has quite experienced.
While the character creation system is very powerful, it can be confusing for a starting player. The key is you don't have to worry about it. The system has very specific things you can do to optimize your character, but you can enjoy the game just as well without employing those strategies.
In playing this game, you find yourself planted in a world, complete with history, religion, science, and anything else you would expect and more. You can find books with conflicting religions. You can worship demons known as daedra. You can read about Vivec ascending to godhood and the religion surrounding them. There are several religious texts in the game that you can read. It is quite a project to learn about the world, sometimes I wonder if I know more about the Elder Scrolls universe or the outside world.
The province of Morrowind is in a time of peril. The longstanding religion of worshipping AlmSiVi, the tribunal, is wavering. An old enemy is rising again. You have complete control over what you do with the world. You can completely ignore the world's issues and go to set out to just explore caves, crypts, and other areas on your own. You can go join a guild and rise through those ranks, You can even kill people who are essential to saving the world. You can save the world, or you can just as well doom it. The game is whatever you want it to be.
This game is the gold standard of RPG for a reason and all current open world RPGs are based off of this amazing game. If you enjoy any open world RPG,  it is a must to come back to the roots of the genre and play the amazing game that really started it all.

Welcome to the a world full of dreams and nightmares. You play as Pankapu, a guardian being known as a Dreamkeeper who guards this world from the nightmares. Edit: I’ve now updated my review for Chapter 2. Chapters 3 and 4 will be released as a second game.
This is a side-scrolling action-platformer that hearkens back to the platformers of the 90’s, but also brings in modern sensibilities. It’s difficulty level is akin to 90’s platformers as well, but checkpoints are fairly common, so you won’t be losing too much progress when you die. Pankapu’s controls are tight, and he handles really well. He starts out with just a basic horizontal attack that has little vertical range. This is fine on level ground, but makes it tricky to hit enemies on a slope or in the air. Also, attacking in the air gives you a bit of hang time. This takes a bit of getting use to, but get used to it you will. As you progress, you gain additional abilities, such as the ability to throw your sword to hit nightmares at a greater distance, and eventually entirely new Aegis’ that completely change Pankapu’s play style from melee to ranged.
The key gameplay hook that sets Pankapu apart from other games in this genre is the Aegis system. Pankapu starts with the Bravery aegis, which gives him access to melee based attacks and a shield to block incoming blows. Part way through the first chapter he gains a second aegis, Ardour, a new form which is more like a ranger class. He’s more vulnerable to damage and cannot block, but has a ranged attack and can dodge and double jump. You can freely switch between the different aegis’ with the press of a button, but during chapter 1, I found myself mostly sticking to his new aegis, only switching back when the situation needed it. Towards the beginning of chapter 2, you get his third aegis, a mid-ranged type mage-type class that can glide and freeze time. The new levels are structured so that you need to switch between aegis’ much more often to progress past the obstacles and defeat enemies. I was having much more fun switching forms, but it also took more concentration to not switch to the wrong aegis.
The second chapter picks up where the first one left off. I was a little daunted, jumping back into this after over a year’s break since the first chapter was released. The difficulty had been fairly high at the end of the first chapter, but thankfully it had been toned down a little for the beginning of chapter 2. On the other hand, there wasn’t any attempt to refresh me on the finer points of the story. This won’t be a problem for people getting the game now, but it would have been nice to have a quick story recap for anyone returning after playing chapter 1 when it was first released.
Pankapu looks and sounds great. The environments are vibrant and varied, while the music conveys the dreamlike feel of  the world brilliantly. The animation of Pankapu, his allies and his enemies are clean and snappy. One slight criticism is that the levels are often designed around straight walls, floors and slopes which can give the world a blocky look, despite the organic look of the backgrounds.
The game recommends that you use a controller, and the game is correct. The game doesn’t natively support my PS2 to USB adapter, but few indie games these days do so it’s not much of an issue anyway because it’s easy enough to use an Xbox controller emulator. And as a nice touch, the game has the option to display PlayStation controls which suits me perfectly. I haven’t seen this in a PC game before.
There were a few minor cosmetic and interface bugs at launch, but most of those were patched out within a few days of launch. I am however having an issue with my controller. I find that if I’m holding one of the face buttons and tilt either joystick vertically, it’s like I’m rapidly mashing the button instead. A similar thing happens when I’m holding one button and press another. This makes blocking difficult and can cause unintentionally small jumps and double-jumps. It even sometimes skips in-game dialogue. I don’t think it’s really the fault of the game because I’m using a Xbox controller emulator, but I’ve used the same emulator with Bastion, Dust: an Elysian Tale, Terraria and Life is Strange without any problem. I ended up switching to a PS3 controller driver, which didn’t have these problems.
All in all, the first two chapters of Pankapu is the beginning of a wonderful game and I look forward to the release of the latter chapters. I’ll probably get the soundtrack once all chapters are released.

is a fantastic little game.
In a time where "retro" 2D-platformers are a dime a dozen on Steam, this game truly manages to stand out from the rest.
Stylistically it's simple and clean, yet full of charm and originality with all it's little touches.
A beatiful and completely unintrusive soundtrack rounds out the package in the best possible way.
The magic is in the details, as they say, and what
presents is vivid and thematically consistent throughout.
That said, it's obviously the gameplay that truly matters, and I am happy to say that the game is equally solid on this front.
There's a certain quality to 2D platformers that seperates the good from the bad, and it's all in how they
to play.
In the best games of the genre you're not afraid to make a blind leap of faith every now and then, because you're so completely in control that you just *know* you will be able to land the jump.
Fall velocity, responsiveness, accuracy, arc and float of your jumps are all equally important in an equation where even one tiny "off" detail can severely hamper the experience - and
nails all of it.
I'd personally prefer it if you didn't "hang" in the air while attacking mid-jump, but it's such a minor detail.
The game's progression system is also quite interesting - and while there may be some concerns about lenght, given that only the first episode is out for now, it's not super-short by any any means.
You start our on a world map, divided into several levels - and as you progress you'll further open more paths, levels and worlds as you go.
All with a strong degree of "Metroidvania" progression involved, as you'll find yourself going back to revist older levels to further explore them as you gain new skills and abilities later on. Some times just to find some hidden collectibles that were previously unattainable, other times you'll be able to reach new exits that will in turn uncover alternative paths on the map.
In this sense, it's less
and more
- which isn't a bad thing in my book.
On the technical side of things, the game is fine.
The graphics options are limited, but that's to be expected given the nature of the game.
It should run on a toaster and also does have PC-typical settings for high refresh rates, rebindable gamepad layouts and such, so nothing sticks out as sorely missing.
All in all, the game is very enjoyable and absolutely worth a try.

As an indie game dev I really wanted to like this game. I do remember seeing the kickstarer and feeling hyped about the project, however upon finally playing the game I have to say-- I'm severely disappointed.
I only played the game for 15 minutes and encountered so many mistakes that I felt strongly enough to request my first steam refund. First and foremost, the game mechanics for simple combat are terrible. It's a bit of a mix up between tile based combat and and free combat. In other words, when you move your character, enemies around you move as well one step. This is awkward because the controls are a bit too free, often times accelerating actions that you might not have necessarily wanted to take.
The next issue is that the controls are all over the place. I used the arrow keys to move, but WASD and QEZC are also used for diagonal movement. Only 2 buttons that I saw were labeled (f and b) and there was 0 explanation on the control scheme in the game at all. In addition to this, I found I could also use the mouse to click - to -move and battle / interact. In all I just felt like  it was too much space to cover for navigating the game.
The major issues I had with the game where bumping into objects literally every two seconds. The maps were much to small, not enough space for moving, whether it was trying to walk about outside, or inside, the maps were cluttered with unncessary dense objects like rocks and trees. Having to smash them was a chore, and in town you get penalized for doing so.
Poor level design is the root cause of this, after all one of the bare minimums should be that you can walk freely without obstruction in an adventure game.
it may seem minor, but from my perspective it seemed like this game didn't have very much development / play time otherwise these issues would / should have easily been fixed. This caused me to think the rest of my experience with the game might not be so great. It looks great, sure , but the game play doesn't do the graphics justice.

Imagine you're at a party. In this case a party for top down, tile-based RPGs. You see this kinda weird looking chick, but you get a really stronghearted vibe from her hearing her talk and interact with others. Yeah, you are a creepy stalker in this review, just like all gamers today are when following a game's development, but not as abusive as most of them. And then it's your turn, you see her idle, you walk up to her and try to start an easy conversation. The conversation goes nothing like you imagined, nothing you could've mentally prepared before talking to her would be of any use. She's quirky, a strong woman, but quirky. The first minute basically was letdown to you and you think of just parting ways. But then there's this kinda magical moment that makes you feel like a wuss for already leaving her, so you start playing along with her weird ways. And after a few minutes you get her and you kinda start digging her. Yeah, you'll probably not invite her over right away, but every time you meet her this magical vibe starts getting stronger and stronger.
This is the only way i am able to describe my experience with this game on a sentimental level. And if my weird thought experiment would go on it would finish with "...and then they married and lived happily together ever after." Alongside the PC and PS4 i also play the PS Vita version a lot, because on the go this is great for short sessions, while PC for me is great to play the story mode on. I wouldn't recommend trying to grind this game for many hours in one go, because it's combat mechanics will eventually get to you in very negative ways, which is the reason for so many negative reviews. The combat mechanics are interesting, maybe even implemented in the best way this basic idea couldve been realized in a game, but still they are very frustrating, making the game unnecessarily hard to master. I'm speaking of everyone only moving when you do - and this in a tile-based system.
I love this game as you can guess by all the versions of it i bought for so many platforms, and i'm neither payed nor a backer of the kickstarter. If you love random generated worlds and monster placement, standard top down, tile based RPG mechanics paired with an interesting twist, this game is for you.
I'd also recommend checking out "Little Viking How To Play Dragon Fin Soup" on YouTube to give you 100% insight on the game's basics.

Once upon a time, Bruce Willis dressed up in some power armor, and went on an interplanetary joy ride in a UNSC shuttle.  It got shot down over a strange planet infested with bugs and giant floating jellyfish that shoot lasers!  What did he do next?  This is his tale.
Colonies Online is a top-down MMO shooter - in my experience, completely unique - where you shoot stuff and build outposts.  I didn't play it very much, because it's horrible.  You're about to learn why.
First, the game is redeemable.  The visuals are OK, and the basic controls generally make a degree of sense.  I didn't have too much trouble using my character.
The laser on the weapon helps the player understand where they're shooting, which is a very nice touch in this sort of game; specifically it helps you lead enemies who are moving tangent to where you're trying to shoot.
I didn't get past the first planet (the one you crash on), because I didn't really want to.  A lot of things contributed to this.
First, the UI is completely horrible, from a usability standpoint.  Pretty much, the UI just doesn't make sense - I couldn't figure out how to
that I bought in the crash site, for starters.  A little later, at Camp Delta, I found a storage chest with armor in it, but I couldn't equip it for some reason.  Long story short, the UI is just plain broken.  I don't honestly know how people play this game; I assume there's some way of circumventing the UI.  I recommend they rethink the UI from the ground up.
Second, even with the lengthy tutorial text (there's a lot) I didn't know really what to do.  What the tutorial text told me to do, and what I actually could do, were nearly always completely at odds with one another.  The tutorial was useless because it made no sense.
One thing I was looking forward to was the base building and crafting.  I really enjoy crafting in MMO games, when I'm not bashin' skulls and splittin' noobs.  However...for the life of me I could not figure out where to begin.  Sure, killing monsters gives random drops, but I couldn't figure out how or where to do any crafting.  There were no indications of how to take on a tradeskill (if those even exist in this game), or anything else.
Additionally, the base construction is well-hidden as well.  Since crafting is well-hidden from players, I can only assume the developers don't yet want people making stuff, because when I found the base part vendor in Camp Delta, I couldn't figure out how to get even the least expensive parts to set down to make the foundation of a base.
I gave this game a chance, and it failed, horribly.  Pretty much, this game is awful.  It
be great, but it's not - the UI fights the player at all opportunities, preventing them from doing anything worthwhile.  It's not worth $14.99.  It's not worth two hours of game time.  I've already requested my refund.
This game isn't ready for Steam, or for the public at all.  The developer has some
work to do on this game.

I've been playing this game casually for quite a while now. I've had nothing but good experiences with this game. The depth, and scale is amazing, and the player-made "Foundry" missions provide an extra layer of depth to the already story-rich gameplay. Playing Dabo on Deep Space 9, flying around the Risa Summer Resort with my floater rental, and generally exploring the galaxy are a few of my favorite things in this game.
I chose to disregard the negative reviews I saw before trying STO out, and I'm glad I did. This game is fun for Trekkies, AND everyone else that loves a content-rich MMO.

CAUTION: I haven't played enough of the game to know if the free to play part is really worth it on mid or long-term, but for what I've seen (lvl 10) it's pretty okay for the most part. So this is an early impression on the game.
I don't really know a lot about Star Trek, aside from the 4 or 5 movies I saw from the original cast, NG and the recent ones. But as far as I can tell, the game does a good job at representing this universe. The presentation falls right into the science-fiction protocol-loving nerdiness of the lore, which is great. The characters talk to you in the appropriate way and there seem to be a lot of (good) fan service, especially with the ships and outfit stray from the different iteration of Star Trek...if you are ready to pay for most of it. The game still lets you have a lot of free stuf to start of well.
The graphics are find as far as MMO goes, even though I wish the aliasing was less protruding even on highest settings. The models are fairly done, the effects and animations do the job, and some of the skyboxes are simply well made. The only real gripe I might have technically speaking would be the lighting effect that aren't the best. A little bit more god rays and atmospheric lighting would make the cool art direction even better justice. Overall, it's not fantastic, but it can be pretty at time thanks to the art direction.
But what I wasn't expecting really, was the gameplay. The mechanics on land are your classical MMORPG stuff, WoW-style. They tried to had a third person viewpoint to the mix but it doesn't help much: it still is devoided of energy or any kind of excitement in the gunplay. I just don't get why they wouldn't go for a basic TPS approch for that part...You simply click on a box and the character execute the action. Boring. The space "naval combat" on the other hand, takes the same basis, with powers and cooldowns, but put it in a new context. It feels like FTL weirdly meets ACIV: Black Flag. You have to manage your power with different gauges (weapons, shields etc.) prioritizing the task you want to accomplish now, and at the same time you use special abilities from your 1st officers, while maneuvering with your ship, exposing certain parts of your shields, and choosing to fire certain canons while others are in a cooldown...it's pretty fun! I have a lot of fun with that part of the game! And it feels new in that genre.
I hope the game stays good at mid and end-game, and just with the ship combat system, I think there is a lot of place for challenging and fun combat. It's free, it's pretty faithful to the series. A nice scifi f2p to try out!

In MX vs ATV Reflex, you get to race a whole load of vehicles, but it's really all about the motorbikes!
To start with, I definitely recommend a controller for this game!
When you first play this (The motorbike that is), you might be put off by the control system...because it's not like your usual car game where you use one stick for steering. In MX vs ATV you use both. One stick is your steering and the other is your body placement, allowing for full control of your angle when taking a tight corner.
Don't let this put you off...stick to it and be patient with learning it, because once you have, it reveals what a satisfying racing and game play experience this title offers.
You aren't limited to wining an A to B race, you can throw in awesome tricks (easily pulled off by pressing your left button and moving the right stick mid air), to gain more money allowing you to tweak your rides (better tires, exhausts that affect performance), and looks (both vehicles and rider).
Once you've won a race or two in career mode, and tweak your bike with better stuff, your ability to pull off crazy tricks in a race is raised!
You don't only get to race against others...there are exploration modes where you motocross your way to different markers on huge maps, and take some challenges. These vary from Hill Climb events, to jump accuracy events and so on..
Personally I am glad I purchased this title (got it cheap) but honestly it's enough fun to recommend at full price too.
Personal Rating: A fun engrossing racer, with good graphics and satisfying gameplay. Good Graphics, Lots of Mud, and hilarious when you get a stunt wrong and end up face planting into a tree!
Percentage Rating: 85% Not for people wanting a quick arcade fix, this is nearly the perfect balance between arcade and simulation!

This game is calm, inoffensive and free of major bugs. It is also essentially a tech demo.
I cannot recommend it, mostly because there isn't much to it. There's no story to follow, the environment doesn't invite exploration, and the combat is unchallenging (although I appreciate the fact that it can be avoided almost completely). None of these is obligatory - if the game had just one strong feature, it would be enough. Sadly, it has none. The game's mood lasted for about ten minutes.
There is no interesting activity involved in finding resources, mining, or crafting - these systems exist in the game in a bare bones, token form. Base construction is essentially pointless: you may need to expand a bit in order to make room for crops, but that's it. You don't get to build anything pretty or impressive. Exploration is minimal: there are three "depth levels", each with its own look, but there's no constant re-discovery, like in games that actually manage to generate interesting landscapes. Everything looks the same here, and there's no storytelling through decorations. Pacing is non-existent, save for increased danger during the night. The winning strategy is to hide in the base until sunrise, which means you spend a few minutes doing nothing (you cannot "go to sleep" and jump forward).
Unless you're specifically interested in performing a series of simplistic tasks in an underwater setting without thinking about it too much, this game has nothing to offer.
Frankly, the basis of the game is pretty idiotic. But that being said, they did alright with it. It's a good time-killer.

The best way to describe my experience with HuniePop:
I enjoyed it.
I was surprised that I did - it was something I picked up on sale (after much prompting from my Discovery Queue and recommendations from friends). Having heard what it supposedly was, I kinda just dismissed it as some weird fetish game that somehow has a Match-3 gameplay...?
Entering the game, I got just what I expected but the important thing here is how they delivered it. HuniePop in its essence is polished and very well-executed.
You'd think the cast of some dating game like this would be super stereo-typical and/or trying hard to be unique, and in a way, that's exactly what it gives you: many different girls that dont particularly overlap in character or development, have very distinct personalities and likes/dislikes, and overall a new and refreshing relationship each time. For an archetype of game that objectifies and sexualizes women, these are very well-rounded, developed, and explored characters. In a way, they managed to break the mold by adhering to it in a specific way that I've only seen done here; I surprised myself when I picked who my favorite character was, since I normally steer away from that type of character from the get-go (if you are curious, my favorite here is the 'mega ♥♥♥♥♥', Audrey - for her sincerity or some reason not usually associated with that character type, and it's actually odd to explain why).
The feel of the game adds to the effect; it can switch from sincere and sweet to witty and funny without missing a beat. The art and visuals just make it so nice and vivid, from the innocuous outfits and environments to the more raunchy scenes. Somehow, the way everything blends together forms the right atmosphere for the situation.
But the amazing part here is how they managed to integrate the puzzle minigame and not have it out of place. I mean, sure it's odd to represent dating as a Match-3 type game, but - and I dont know how! - it works. And it has that surprising level of balance that allows players who're in it less for the game and more for the characters (and *ehem* what you do with them) to get through it without suffering much preamble, while those who are up to the challenge are actually put to the test - after a few runs of the game, I was actually just trying to clear the puzzles to get the achievements, and it was a grueling fight (at least I had the girls there to cheer me on).
Good humor, good style, and for the most part, in good taste; I'd have to say that this game managed to land itself in my Favorites list, for being a good game overall (props to the developers!) and for surprising me and showing me just how wrong I was in my opinion of it.

- The plot moves at glacial pace with repetitive filler quests out weighing plot quests almost 5-1. To be honest the plot feels non-existent. Tetris moves at a faster pace.
- Game breaking levelling bug. Every once in a while the loading screen freezes and I lose 3 levels (and nothing else). But the enemy doesn't. Since your foes level with you this is incredibly problematic since grinding to recover those levels is impossible.
- Crafting is the only reliable way to get good equipment but is buggy and disorganized. I have 10 duplicate recipes for leather and none of them are sorted. Seriously why? And why can't I add "animal hide x3" instead of "animal hide x3", "animal hide x1" and "animal hide x1"?
- The flanking bonus you get from the pets is awesome. The fact that you can't interact with them is not. You can't heal them or stop them from running of and dieing against some random creature. This means that all the pets end up several levels below you and are OKO'd at later levels. This gets worse with the leveling bug.
- Combat isn't tactical and it's so slow you can't even call it a button masher. I can hit the attack button 4 times before Robin makes 1 attack, while enemies can make 3 and cancel the move you just started. Can you imagine trying to reposition and attack when facing a boss? Good luck.
- The humour starts out funny, like an ill-timed fart, but gets old real fast. Most of the humour comes from the randomly generated names and quest dialogue. So you'll see the occasional funny combination and a exponential amount of repetition.It's trying waaaay to hard.
I hate leaving things unfinished especially stories, but this is just painful. I'm done. Good luck to you poor souls who try the game.

This one is interestig, in a good way.
Mount & Blade places you in a far away medival land with nothing but your wit, a horse, some weapons and some clothes.
There are some factions you can join and fight for, but the point of the game is that you don't NEED to.
There is no finite goal.
Want to become the king of the land and rule the entire map?
Sure can do.
Want to be a bandit king and stike fear in the hearts of trade caravans?
Sure can do.
Want to be a lowly soldier in some army and fight for the money?
Sure can do.
M&B is a sandbox game, a damned good one too.
The combat is easy to learn, yet hard to master and very satisfying, and also very adjustable to your preferred playstyle.
Blocking is a challenge in itself on higher difficulties, and fighting multiple enemies at once can be really hard if you are alone. Being outnumbered can end up with you taken as a prisoner (you can't die in battle or be sold to slavery, you will escape sooner or later and have to start from scratch), but luckily, if you don't like that sort of thing, you can set the enemies to only do half or a fifth of the damage that you can do.
The only negative thing that I have is the AI.
When you are travelling across the map, the AI will attempt to follow paths DESPERATELY. Even if that means that you will run into an enemy and get slaughtered, all for a measly 0.5 speed increase for walking on roads.
Similarly, the combat AI is also not the greatests. Your allies will not attempt to hold a strategic position, such as a mountain, but rather charge right into the enemy.
Oh yeah, and the graphics suck. Low quality textures and an extremely low amount of polygons per model.
It works, don't get me wrong, but it is not pretty. The trailer is very accurate when it comes to graphics.
The sound design is very nice, good and fitting music and neat combat screams.
You can even extract the music from a folder and ctrl-c ctrl-v them somewhere else so you can listen to your favorite soundtracks whenever you want to.
With mod support this one is easily worth the money, maybe wait for a sale and get it with all expansions for around 20$/€. Thats what I did.

First of all: This is indeed an Early Access game. I bought it while being fully aware of that fact. I don't get the people who expect a finished game when they buy early access items.
That being said, i think colonies online has a lot of potential. I bought the game pretty soon after the steam release, half a year ago. There has been ongoing development ever since - which is an important aspect to an early access game.
What can you do now: Fight monsters and other players, grind money, buy better equipment and build your base. The basebuilding is quite solid, it supports placing (and re-replacing but not re-packaging) of components, turrets, doors, and several special constructions like mines or a surgical station used to quickly replenish your hp.
Basebuilding is by far the most interesting part of the game right now, it's lacking in other areas (pve is quite repetitive) but the sandbox character makes up for it.
So should you buy this game? If you like sandbox games, which allow for big base building with a lot of pieces to choose from, you will be happy in this game...keep in mind however other players can attack your home, so defend it well and build it up in a remote area ;) Also, shooting huge alien bugs is fun.

An incredibly fun Run ´N Gun game in both single player and Co-op. If you haven’t played this before expect to die every three seconds but the chaos on screen and barrage of death is actually part of the fun!
If you are wondering whether to get Metal Slug 3 or Metal Slug X my advice would be to wait until they are on sale and get both! They are both very good games and it really just depends on what mood you’re in and how much time you have as to which game to pick.
Metal Slug 3 is a longer game overall and a slightly more difficult one too. It has a little more variation in the type of enemies that attack you, at least from level to level and there are branching pathways to explore. There is more variety with some flying and underwater levels and a greater amount of craft and animals to get in/on to mix things up. This along with more actual levels to fight through at the end stages bulks the game out more.
Metal Slug X is a more streamlined game that takes less time to complete and is a little easier overall. It has a more linear level design and more opportunity to pilot the Metal Slug tank itself. This perhaps gives it a bit more of an early arcade experience and possibly provides a little more flow to the feel of the gameplay. This is also good if you’re looking to squeeze some side scrolling Shoot ´Em Up action into a busy day or don’t feel like spending a great deal of time playing.
Both games have enough differences (as well as positive similarities) in level design and feel/vibe to warrant buying/playing them both if you like this genre of game and it really is more down to what frame of mind you’re in to which particular one you feel like playing. They are such enjoyable, well designed games to play it’s hard to say which is better. I do suggest you get both but I guess if I had a Heavy Machine Gun pressed to my head and I had to choose only one then Metal Slug 3 might come out on top by a (POW´s) whisker but I would miss playing X too.

Sadly you can only Refine 8000 Dilithium on 1 Charakter each Day so would need to play around 100 Days before you can buy a Ship that Way .....  you can get around that by creating 3 Charakters ( 1 of each Career ) and buying a Cruiser-Type Ship , those are Jack of all Trade Ships that ever Carreerpath can use.

I'm only *just* barely edging on the side of recommending the game.  It would be a wonderful $10 game.  But it's being sold for $15.  The game engine is great.  The graphics are pretty and smooth.  The crafting aspect is fun.  The survival aspect is fun.  It just doesn't have enough length of play, and it's not early-access where you can expect to get more content later.  The developers have decided that this short game is the finished product.
You can finish through in about 8 hours of play (or less, depending on skill, but it definitely won't take more than that.  I finished in 4.5 hours first time but that was with constant nonstop play.  If I'd put it down and come back later I suspect it would have taken longer overall as I'd not have kept the player skills as fresh in my head.)
It also has a sandboxy survival mode which I haven't tried yet, but the main adventure game is a bit short.
Don't get me wrong.  The shortness of play is the only thing about it that's not so great.  Other than the duration, everything else about it is wonderful.  It's defnitely very pretty.  Visually it's great to look at, especially in the late game as you go deeper and see lots of bioluminescent life forms.  It's a bit like minecraft but without the ability to alter the terrain - you just gather things and build stuff to add on top of the terrain, trying to make the necessary equipment to survive the adventure.  (For example you'll have to go down deep to finish, but your starting scuba suit can't go deep enough to get to the lower layers, so you'll have to construct a better scuba suit to be able to finish, as well as making better weaponry to survive the monstrous stuff down deep.)

An interesting game that is about undersea survival. As a diver whos submarine just crashed and its components scattered around a procedurally generated underwater landscape you are to recover the lost components and rebuild said submarine.
Before you do, however, you need to find shelter in abandoned seabed stations (and build more, modify, repair or destroy them, they are concidered yours), grow or hunt (or be hunted) for food and mine for minerals. One should also keep an eye on the depth and air meter, as the diving equipment worn is limiting max depth, breathing time, and armor.
The sealife is interactive in that it tries to swim away if its frightened by you, ignores you if it doesn't concider you a threat or hunts for you if it does or you are leaking bodily fluids that simply attract predators.
One of the even more interesting points is that you will find underwater stations that have been damaged. When you are close enough the engine kicks in and starts flooding these stations. Repairing them will reverse the damage but will cost you some iron. As of yet I have not actually seen a base being damaged, but I suspect that the squids or sharks will pound a station if a hunted player enters them for shelter.
As this game is still in active development I have high hopes. The game seems done as is, and is well worth the full price.

This one is interestig, in a good way.
Mount & Blade places you in a far away medival land with nothing but your wit, a horse, some weapons and some clothes.
There are some factions you can join and fight for, but the point of the game is that you don't NEED to.
There is no finite goal.
Want to become the king of the land and rule the entire map?
Sure can do.
Want to be a bandit king and stike fear in the hearts of trade caravans?
Sure can do.
Want to be a lowly soldier in some army and fight for the money?
Sure can do.
M&B is a sandbox game, a damned good one too.
The combat is easy to learn, yet hard to master and very satisfying, and also very adjustable to your preferred playstyle.
Blocking is a challenge in itself on higher difficulties, and fighting multiple enemies at once can be really hard if you are alone. Being outnumbered can end up with you taken as a prisoner (you can't die in battle or be sold to slavery, you will escape sooner or later and have to start from scratch), but luckily, if you don't like that sort of thing, you can set the enemies to only do half or a fifth of the damage that you can do.
The only negative thing that I have is the AI.
When you are travelling across the map, the AI will attempt to follow paths DESPERATELY. Even if that means that you will run into an enemy and get slaughtered, all for a measly 0.5 speed increase for walking on roads.
Similarly, the combat AI is also not the greatests. Your allies will not attempt to hold a strategic position, such as a mountain, but rather charge right into the enemy.
Oh yeah, and the graphics suck. Low quality textures and an extremely low amount of polygons per model.
It works, don't get me wrong, but it is not pretty. The trailer is very accurate when it comes to graphics.
The sound design is very nice, good and fitting music and neat combat screams.
You can even extract the music from a folder and ctrl-c ctrl-v them somewhere else so you can listen to your favorite soundtracks whenever you want to.
With mod support this one is easily worth the money, maybe wait for a sale and get it with all expansions for around 20$/€. Thats what I did.

So let me just say that you should never release a game even as an "Early Release" if you can't even get past the tutorial. It took about 10 mins just for one of the tutorial tips asking me to kill things and loot them to change (after NO ENEMIES EVER SHOWED UP!) into "This is how you use your weapon and reload it." Well, normally you would do those things and the tutorial tip would move on to the next step. No, spent the next 20 mins killing enemies that FINALLY showed up along with some other players, and the tool tip never moved on. Still couldn't loot anything either by the way, so the previous step was a complete bust. Also, the framerate was entirely unacceptable for this day and age. Felt like I was playing on Dial-Up. Yeah, I'm THAT old.
I like the idea here, but so far it is FAR beyond even playable. "Early Release" should never mean we just began developing and threw some shoddy pieces of a game together just so people could "feel" like there might someday maybe perhaps be something worthy buried underneath all the crap. That's more like a "Hey we have this really cool idea we'd like money put into so we can develop it. Heres some early stuff we did, pay us so we can keep developing." That's a Kickstarter problem, not an "Early Release" deal. I like what Steam is doing to help the gaming community, but let's not polish a turd and call it gold, let's be honest about what you're selling. If it's not "about to be released" or "almost ready", let's not call it "Early Release", let's call it "Early Development." Otherwise, you're just wiping turd all over our gold.
I will revise this review if and when this game is ready to call itself playable, and if I ever bother to play it again. Thanks for your time, but I have other things I could be doing than spending 30 mins NOT getting through a tutorial.

Air Conflicts: Vietnam is disappointing to me seeing as I really liked the previous Air Conflicts games. The previous games were all about fast arcade-style air-to-air and air-to-ground combat in large open arenas, and Vietnam basically gets all of those points wrong. The maps are very small and often obscured by low fog, so you're constantly going past the map's walls. The controls are fiddly and strange, nothing at all like the fluidity of Air Conflicts: Pacific Carriers (which I think is the high point of the franchise).
By far the worst thing about the game is that it interrupts gameplay to deliver cutscenes after the completion of each goal, and these interruptions are frequent. Your goal might be to take out three AA emplacements — which you'll get done within 1-3 minutes since the maps are so small — and then you'll sit through a 20 or 30 second cutscene with hammy voice acting. This will happen about five times per mission.
Give this a miss and try out Pacific Carriers instead. Secret Wars is okay too. I regret buying this game.

When it comes to arcade-style sidescrolling shooters, there are only two games I recommend: Broforce and Metal Slug 3. Now, I spent most of my time playing this game on the XBox, stoned, with my cousin, but the only reason we didn't fire up the NES to play Contra instead was because of the obvious level of dedication the makers of this game.
Originally, this game was meant to be put into arcades and munch quarters, and by jove it did its job well. So well, in fact, that it's made its way to consoles and PC. Now, there's not much to a sidescrolling shooter. You walk to the right, you shoot stuff, you get to a boss at the end of the level. Any company can slap that formula together for a mild hit, but SNK took that to the next level.
Not only do you get
different settings to blow up and conquer, but they even went so far as to make sure that every piece of every level fit when it came to setting, difficulty, and variances in gameplay. It's like the dev's would actually sit around and play the levels they just made and had whole meetings about, "Hey, wouldn't it be cool if....?"
For instance, Stage 2 is the zombie level. If you get hit with zombie puke, you don't die like you would in any other level.
Then, you get to trudge around slowly, hoping you find the drop that turns you back into a human. Oh, and your bombs? Those turn into screen-wide blood barfs. Every level has weird minor-mechanics that make every level memorable, without feeling overly-gimmicky.
The only downside to this game is that you're mainly going to be shooting the same, vaguely nazi-ish soldier MOST of the time. That's not to say that there isn't any variety to the enemies, but for being a cabinet game, it's feasible to assume that those soldiers get re-used due to the limited memory available at the time the game was created. One look at the detail that they put into
, and the notion emerges into the realm of possibility.
On the up-side, however, these enemies only really seem to be used as filler between set-pieces where you will encounter unique enemies that are specific to each level.  Also, there seems to be some AI differences between the levels that keep even these filler enemies feeling fresh and appropriate to the setting.
In tradition with keeping everything else about this game tight, the controls were no exception. You've only got a few skills to master, like: jump, shoot, aim, and throw bombs. Actually, that's it in a nutshell. And the glorious thing about it is that there's
learning curve. The first time you do any of those things, you've got it down, and it even
like it's working perfectly. There's no guessing on jumps. There's no wondering if that bomb is going to hit right. It's like putting your socks on before you put on your underwear; it just feels good.
On top of all of this, the developers realized that when the game is ported, the main goal isn't to eat quarters anymore. So, once you beat a level, you can start from there if you happen to "Game Over" in the next. Of course, you don't get to keep your score, but if you have a favorite level, or you just want to see what comes next but can't do it from all the way at the beginning, you can pick up anywhere you want - assuming you've at least beat the level once, of course.
This is a game that SNK
put their love into - and it shows. It's challenging for all of the right reasons, the graphics and sound are a perfect fit, the controls feel like you've been playing for years from day one, and the best part is that it's only eight bucks. Thirteen if you buy the two-pack. With over 300 games in my Steam Library, there are few that I would label as a staple. This is one of them.
If I had to choose two games to play for the rest of my life this would not be one of them.

First things first, don't let my play time fool you.  I've been a player of Star Trek Online for about 5 years now and I gotta say; it's not getting any better.  That said, let's start out with the good...
(TLDR At Bottom)
You can't talk about a Star Trek game without talking about immersion.   This game does draw you in and make you feel like you're a part of the 24th century universe that began with Christopher Pike and continued for decades after.  You feel like you’re a  part of an ever growing galaxy, doing missions to better the life of those around you.  That said, it’s only good immersion for one pass through.  Starting a second character on the same faction finds you instantly bored and upset with having to perform the same exact story over again.  Thankfully there is more than one race, which means more than one story.  If you want to stay the same race though, just take a different route (Assault/Science/Engineering) you’ll find yourself performing the same story over and over again.  In addition, the additional content that is added after the 3 main storylines is pretty much identical no matter what race you are.  Thus, you only get one playthrough of the additional content before you're repeating it with your other races. Anyway, back to the good stuff…
Sound and graphics are well done in this game.  Arguably the best Star Trek experience yet.  Game play adds to that experience as well.  Large ships, while having more firepower and armor, actually feel bulky and slow while smaller ships are much faster and more maneuverable.  You have to customize your equipment/ship to the style you play or you’ll quickly find yourself in a lot of trouble when an enemy race locks its weapons on you.  There are also a HUGE array of ships you can use, of all classes and sizes, bringing a high level of variety, sort of...
Now let’s get to the bad.  This game is distributed by Perfect World.  That means the game is free, but not really.  The game has been slowly converted from a very balanced system to what exists today, a heavy “pay to win” system.  The best ships are only really available on the marketplace and every new ship has a higher price than the last newest ship.  Now, I’m not going to say I haven’t purchased my share of ships, because I have.  But it gets extremely frustrating when a ship you paid good money for is suddenly made inferior by the next ship released, with that ship then being made inferior by the next, and so on, and so on, and so on.  This has quickly become the biggest money grab in the history of MMO’s.
Today, if you want the latest collection of “Tier 6” starships (9 in total) you’ll have to fork out 12000 Zen (the store currency) for the bundle, which equals around $130 of real cash.  Believe it or not, that’s actually a deal!  Buying just the tripple bundle for a specific race costs 6000 Zen ($70, roughly).  Buying each ship individually for 3000 Zen would be an astronomical $315!  For virtual ships in a game where said ship will probably be inferior in less than a couple months, that’s a lot.
In all honesty, the pay-to-win scheme has literally destroyed this game.  On top of all the crap available in the market, which includes inventory expansions, expanded ship storage, upgrades, clothing, bridge layouts, shuttles, and so on, you start to hate looting ships/people because of all the drop boxes you’ll collect.  Of course, the drop boxes are locked and require you to purchase keys (from the market) to unlock them.  I remember, at one time, having my inventory filled with nothing but drop boxes.  Like an idiot I paid for about 30 keys (can't remember the cost, but it wasn't cheap) and got what I expected.  The boxes either had absolute junk or items that would become useless within a very short time.  There was always a very rare chance of getting a starship in a drop box, but I never did.  That said, I've heard of people spending hundreds of dollars on keys just to get those rare ships.  (Maybe Perfect World isn't stupid, because people are)  After my 30 keys were used I started dumping the drop boxes in the garbage, as selling them on the auction is totally useless.  Trust me, if you go to the auction and type in the name of any drop box you’ll have no less than 50 pages of already existing auctions at stupid low prices.
Some players might argue that you can trade in-game dilithium for Zen, and it’s true.  That said, all this has done is pushed the cost of the items in the marketplace higher.  In addition, you can only convert so much dilithium every day, and the exchange doesn’t guarantee how much your dilithium is actually worth.  Honestly, it’s worse than gold farming in other MMO’s.  Not worth the time or effort you’ll have to put into it.
TLDR :
So, do I recommend this game?  Absolutely not.  The pay-to-win scheme has pretty much destroyed this game and the massive amount of drop boxes you’ll end up looting will annoy the hell out of you.  It’s got a fairly good story, which continues to expand, but the game just feels like a Ferengi designed it.  So no, I don’t recommend it.  Why then is my play time is as high as it is?  Not really because I enjoy the game.  I was one of the saps who got suckered early into sinking money into this P2W pit of decay, before we saw it for what it was, and I wanna be sure I get my money’s worth before the final nail goes in the coffin... That's why.

Spore has left me with very mixed emotions.  I LOVE going through the Cell stage and then playing through the Creature stage (4.5 out of 5 stars to that point).  The first night I downloaded the game, I had planned to only play a half hour or so before bed, which turned into 3+ hours and having to be harrassed by my husband to finally shut down the notebook.  I was starting to become an addict already!
And then the Tribal phase happened.
There is a very natural flow between the Cell and Creature stages, with a little more complexity added when you begin to move the camera around.  The game is entirely at your own pace and you aren't penalized for taking your time to explore, look for additional parts, or make more friends.  It's truly a casual game.  And then Tribal turns the game entirely into a Tower Defense game where you have to control multiple units and every minute you spend trying to build a strategy is held against you as the other tribes start to hate you more, attack your village, and steal your food.  To add to the fun, the interface is confusing and unintuitive.  At that point, the game fell to 3 out of 5.
I've made it through Tribal once and into the City/Civilization stage.  And that is as far as I'll ever go in this game.  The Cell and Creature stages have lots of replayability, which is why I can still recommend the game despite my obvious dislike of the rest of the stages.  I bought this game when it was on sale so I feel like it was a pretty good buy for the parts I enjoy.

EDIT! Well it's been just shy of two years since I wrote this review, and I decided to pick up the game again.
The playerbase is still cancerous levels of toxic, cooperation simply doesn't exist, infantry have zero penalties for just camping tanks the entire game, and there is no way to exit the spawn area of some maps without immediately being zerged.

Shorthand:
Pros:
-The combat is often engaging, and very fast paced
-Good variety of weapons, even if unlocking is a chore
-Weapon upgrades for most play styles (accuracy/RoF/Damage, etc...)
-A lot of customizability for players, vehicles, and weapons.
Cons:

-Long wait times for matches, depending on criteria

For the remainder of the review, you'll see me citing historical accuracy... This is because the devs use the expression "historical norms" in patch notes, even when they do not apply.
AND NOW THE LONG BORING PART THAT NOBODY EVER FINISHES!
Heroes and Generals... What a game. There are aspects of the game that are fantastic, and others that make a seasoned gamer like myself go insane with keyboard-smashing rage. I picked up the game a while back so that I could get into it with some mates of mine as a time-killer. At first, the game was rather enjoyable, as all of us were terrible, and it was about the laughs more than anything. Then we started to realized the problems the game suffered from.
Combat:
The combat is fairly straight forward; point and shoot. Names aren't displayed above enemy players, so there is a bit of realism in that you can't use a nameplate to spot. Most weapons rely on Iron sights, which can be bothersome at times due to inaccuracy problems, and handy at others. A few of the weapons have rather preposterous muzzle reports, which throw off some of the realistic aspects.
Certain weapons have an uncanny knack for landing precision shots where it would normally be impossible (The Thompson and the PPSH at 25+ meter ranges, for example). Whereas others completely blow beyond historical norms, emptying magazines almost instantly.
As you might have put together, the game also involves vehicular combat, with infantry vehicles such as jeeps, ranging all the way up to heavy tanks, such as the famed King Tiger, or the Pershing. In some instances, the tanks are balanced, such as light-on-light combat, where mobility is more important than stopping power. In other instances, tanks are beyond out of balance, such as the case of the M-24 Chaffee, or the M-18 Hellcat. Both are capable of accelerating to break-neck speed in less than 30 feet. whilst historically possessing very light armor, both vehicles require more shots to drop than most other tanks of a similar calibre.
Customizabilty:
While the game is not strictly "pay to win" paying is considerably faster than the grind-fest needed to gain access to the higher teir equipment, or even leveling up to unlock new classes. While I normally have a lot of patience for grinding (Vanilla WoW veteran here... ) this game takes it a little too seriously. It would be much more tolerable if the other aspects of the game didn't also need a lot of work.
That being said, a lot of the item costs have become absurd, with an average game's worth of grenades often costing more than the game would yeild. AT weapons are essentially the player's only counter against tanks, save for Panzerfaust scattered throughout the maps, and are absolutely cost prohibitive with the exception of one or two rounds per game. (at the time of writing, I haven't used either AT weapon in some time, this might not be the case anymore.)
Player Base:
Mostly♥♥♥♥♥♥ regrettably. I've encountered 50 horrible players who are just as likely to TK me for playing cautiously, or for targeting their target, for every 1 friendly player who was actually there to enjoy the game, or played using a team aspect. There are also a fair amount of language barriers, as there is only the 1 server. A lot of players will outright ignore strategic advice, and even go as far as to do the opposite out of spite. I suspect this is mostly because of dev neglect of players resulting in sour moods, but that's neither here nor there.
All in all:
It's a free game, so if you can stomach the laundry list of faults, the game is at least somewhat enjoyable, but it's looking more and more like one of those early-release games that is stuck as such in perpetuity.

This game is…meh. It’s something to play if you are bored. Would have made an excellent cell phone game.
Positives
Very easy to pick up and put down
Many creative weapons and equip able items (can’t see them on character though, which is probably a good thing considering some of the items)
Pretty graphics for a simple game
Negatives
All missions are the same, or at least they are where I am at. You either have to find a certain number of items/people or kill a certain number of enemies/boss. Not that thrilling.  There are the crafting and fishing missions, but if you aren’t in a spot where those supplies are at, you aren’t going to be able to work on them.  There isn’t any incentive to level up, because the enemies level up with you.
Bugs! Bugs! Bugs! Turning off that special graphic thingie (very technical, I know, but I don’t remember what it was) helped immensely. But the main map freezes still. Thankfully there is an autosave function every time you enter a new room.
Crafting- it’s fun, until you realize that you just spent a good 10-20 minutes, creating the ingredients for the weapon you want, only to realize after you have created that special weapon that you are too under leveled to use it.  And don’t even get me started on finding the crafting ingredients. The digging is very random, so if you are trying to make a particular item, it’s going to take you a lot of digging to find it. Which I suppose is realistic, but I’m playing as an alcoholic red riding hood. I’m not going for realism here . Though I wouldn’t mind the shovel being more like a real shovel. I don’t understand why the shovel is a consumable item.
Graphics- weather events can obscure them, which makes it annoying.
Storyline-not that great. It’s not very storyline intensive, as far as I can tell. It’s definitely not humorous. I don’t remember laughing at anything in this game actually.
You will do the same things over and over and over again.

The idea of this game is sound.  With a combination of base building, monster hunting, looting, exploration, PVE and PVP the game really could pack a punch.  However that is the idea of the game, not the actual game in its current state.
The "shell" on offer is very limited.  Walking, shooting, looting, basic base building are all there.  But that's it.   With limited features, repetitive situations, and no real feeling of accomplishment, this game feels more like being stuck in a plain cardboard box rather than a space aged adventure.
I bought the Dreadnaught pack to get an extra copy so my brother and I could play, and I have to admit that this is the first time I regret buying a game on steam.
Keep an eye on this game though.  It could turn out well.  However, that would require the investment of the developers, who at this stage, have promised a show, sold the tickets, but ran off with the cash.  I will of course update my review, should my opinions change with future updates.

Disclaimer: I need to state that I do not work for the company, I am however an avid space/scifi player and a game like this was one I could not pass up testing. With that being said here is what I have found:
Overall rating: 7/10 (Has great promise but needs a lot of attention).
1. Pros
* Free roam and exploration. (This game is a sand box), And each planet is MASSIVE. Area wise.
* Colony building (Currently in a rudimentory form but shows promise once they develop and add crafting and other managment abilities and structures such as a player run market system.) You can however build your colony anywhere you like, Although the limitation of where you can deploy an ILU (Individual Landing Unit, which is basically an item that allows you to travel to other planets and other sectors on a planet. You can walk across the entire suface unhendored if you want of a single planet, but they are huge, and it is much easier to simply travel via your ILU)
* Quests are straight forward, though can be difficult to understand your objective "location" wise. As there are no markers. However this is countered by the fact that there are few, as this game focuses on the player, and is about you. The quest in generally simply serve more as a "Tutorial" as you play the game giving you tips on occasion, the any real quest purposes.
* Gear is fairly easy to aquire and upgrade (though you will have to aproach it intelligently in order to get anything quickly, It's mostly about farming mobs currently and searching for special drops to sell for Armor and gear "Until the crafting system is in place").
* NOT PAY TO WIN. The stuff you can pay for with real money (Pyromanser, Dreadnaught, and Citizen packs), are of Medium gear levels. The armor is 6/8 (8 being the highest current protection level in game), and the weapon does about 300 - 375 DPS with varying ranges (Where as the best weapons in game do 500-700+ DPS).
The pyromancer pack has a Flamethrower which is really nice for a new player, but has a very short range which can cause killing some of the mobs to be more difficult (Many of the mobs are quite a chalenge to kill and range is a tactic). The Citizen pack and Dreadnaught pack both have long range weapons.
- The only difference between these pack Weapons/Armor and the Medium level gear you can get in game is that the weapons have a larger ammo clip (About double that of the normal medium in game weapon of the same veriety). The best weapons and Armor in game however,  can only be obtained through playing the game.
* Updates it seems are done 1-3 times a month. And Major issues are generally fixed soon.
* Game is decently pretty to look at with many differnt environments, graphics are not too shabby either, though they could use some work.
* Open world non restricted PVP, (With recent updates even your colony can be set to shoot other people :D )
2. Cons:
* The game is a bit laggy server wise, and Rubber banding can cause you to die on occasion which can be a bit anoying. Your weapon wont relaod correctly and it will lag out and the Mobs will kill you. Or you'll simply rubberband back into their line of fire at times. I caontribute this however to the game being new. Overall this should not interfere with your playtime.
* There are no Guides so to speak for the game or real tutorials or information on how to do stuff, and the website is not very active. So figureing stuff out can be difficult at times, but hey some would actually count this as a Pro, rather then a con.
* Occasionaly your game will crash while killing a Queen. You'll still get the loot (Thankfully) but you'll have to relog in or restart the client.
* When loading to another planet or loading in general, the game can get stuck on the loading screen, In my experience it happens about 3/10 times. And you ahve to restart the client. (Again thankfully, you don;t need to load very often at all as you can just walk everywhere once your on a planet).
* The game is set in a top down slightly angled view, much like the original fallouts. Not being able to tilt the camera and look at your suroundings is a bit anoying. You can however, unlike in fallout 1 and 2 and tactics, turn the camera, you just can't tilt it. I count this as a con because the game worls is really pretty in a lot of ways and it's a shame you really can't look at it all from different angles. But maybe they will add that later.
Conclusion:
Overall I think this game shows great promise, I can contribute many of the cons to being in early development, Mining and Crafting and research are supposed to be added soon, and I can;t wait for them.
Over all, the largest issue with this game currently are probably 3 things:
* Crashes
* Stuck on Loading
* Rubberbanding / Lag
But it is in early develoment and release and currently sits are a Mid alpha, Pre beta form. So depending on your ability to deal with some of the cons above, it may be a great idea for you to give this game a try. Or not.

In the jets, C-123 etc, there isn't even an independent rudder/aileron control that I've found-so if you pull up then want to roll, it ends up sending you in some crazy direction of its own devising. The maps are tiny (so tiny that in a jet, I went from out of bounds to out of bounds in less than 10 seconds while trying to kill a MiG) and the voice acting is corny at best.

This game could be the single reason I may never pre-purchase anything again.  While this developer has put out some VERY nice work in the past Air Conflicts: Vietnam isn't one of them.  There are two huge flaws that are pretty much impossible to overlook.  The first one that really hits you in the face are the small maps.  Imagine trying to fly a jet inside the airspace of a tennis court.  Then imagine trying to fight a battle in that same cramped space.  its not very practical.  So you spend much of the game flying out of bounds which is no fun and I would say makes the game unplayable.  Second are the graphics.  They didn't look that stellar in the trailers but I will normally ignore minor graphic issues in exchange for good game play. Unfortunately the graphics are far worse than in the trailers.  Jaggy beyond redemption is probably the best term to describe it and no GPU or tweaking is going to fix it.  Air Conflicts: Vietnam would need a complete overhaul of its graphics and maps to be reasonably playable.  Hopefully the developer will eventually roll out some patches to make this a more enjoyable game.  It could happen, I guess, but right now the game isn't ready for prime time.

The bad:
* Boring repetitive gameplay.
* Bad AI.
* Tiny maps.
* Awful quality of maps (ground textures are ugly, lack of objects).
* Graphics are not good (it may looks good on screenshots, but it ugly in motion) - trees and clouds are just plane sprites (reminds me of 2000th).
* Lack of achievements.
* No replay value.
* No simulator control scheme for gamepad.
* Dead and pointless multiplayer.
* Story. Your alter ego is muted. Why Thompson fight for so long? For what? There is no answer.
The good:
* Soundtrack.
* Relatively long campaign.
* About 20 authentic planes and copters.
* You can control up to 6 various aircraft at single mission and switch them freely.
* Random rescure MIA pilots from your squad are interesting for first 1-2 times.
Some additional thoughts:
This game has somekind of historical accuracy: Americans are bad - bombing civilians, spreading agent orange, napalming villages. But if you don't like to be bad, you don't like to play this game. Well, if you American - you may like such "patriotism".
It is the worst game of the Air Conflicts series.
If you want to get flight arcade game look at HAWX1-2 (better graphics, better gameplay, better replay value) or Ace Combat (fun gameplay).
I think it is very mediocre - this game is surely not my best buy.

This is the first game I have played where you can "choose your own adventure" and I loved it. So, for a little bit in this review lets rewind back twelve years ago in 2004 (when I first played it, and look at it then). In 2004 the graphics are amazing and everything about this game is flawless. The story is great, the game play is great, everything is great. This is a great game. Now, in 2014 and compared to Skyrim, the graphics aren't good, the story is boring, the combat is terrible (I swear I hit that Cliff Racer ten times, not only once) and it requires you to have a ton of patience and a lot of hours has to be put into it; I have done around 12 hours and I don't think I'm half way done with the main quest! However, it is still a wonderful game, even though I perfer Skyrim and Oblivion over Morrowind.

If you're coming to Morrowind after playing a newer ES game, particularly if you've only played Skyrim, a word of caution. This game is significantly different from the other games of the series. It's harder to get good at, glitchier, and more unforgiving. The magic system is confusing compared to the simplicity of Skyrim, the combat is a wreck (even though it still works) and the animations are horrible.
That being said, this is still a very close second to Skyrim in my opinion. The story in this game is unpralelled in the ES series. The sense of mystery surrounding the world you inhabit is second to none.

Although it has various annoying problems, Farsky is absolutely incredible.
Yes, your oxygen does continue to run out in the submarine, forcing you to go to the surface or back to your base quickly.
Yes, you can drown while in the submarine and occasionally that may be over extreme depths, causing the chest with all your items to spawn where you can't go without dying.
Yes, the various chests around the game world can't be moved and thus your OCD flairs up.
However, yes - you can kill sharks and fish and rays and barracuda with knives, harpoons and turrets. Yes, you can die in terrifying ways. Yes, the gameplay doesn't get old and thus you can play forever without getting bored.
And finally, yes the environment is extraodinary.
So, while it has faults that could be easily fixed, it also is the type of game that is worth the $15.00.
(And if you get it on sale, like I just did, then you'll be more than happy with your purchase.)
