Winter Voices is some kind of a strange game.. I wanted to play it just by reading the hashtags: female protagonists, independent RPG, adventure.. plus, it's the only game published by Inner Seas here on Steam - by the way they're a French studio and they're working on the sequel of Winter Voices (that hasn't still a date, I think like late 2018). They're from Paris and they also publish poetry collections and books in French too.
As I said, you'll control a girl who has lost her father on her way through this RPG which has lots of visual novel/narrative elements (well, it's a lot introspective) and a turn-based system derived from other more famous RPGs, set though in a tactical world with the usual grid (I'm not citing any big name like.. Final Fantasy Tactics shh.. no, but that's the idea XD).
I have to agree with other players who pointed out more the narration and the story in this game rather than the gameplay aspect, 'cos for what concerns gameplay and graphics it should have been way more worked out. So well, take a peek to videos on Youtube to get an idea on both the gameplay and the "way of moving" of your main character in the winter world so that you can have an idea.
I emphasized the psychological aspect of the game 'cos all the leveling up system of the girl (who's your only party member, but the battles you'll see that aren't the core aspect of the game..) is related to her story of depression and introspection.
Anyways I found the narration great even though it's obvious that it's been thought originally by foreign (French in this case) developers and not English (well, you can play it in French of course but I played it in English).. it's been a good work in my opinion and well, you have to be prepared 'cos you'll have lots of lines to read and less battles to fight.
Talking to other players, they told me about the bugs that this game had during its release period and some of the fixes that have been done - I experienced bugs not yet solved, but now the game is playable. Anyways, the main problems that you can experience now regard mainly the movement and the fact that the combat grid of the tactical turn-based combat stays the same in the main world, but of course you won't see the squares on the ground. And so you'll often have to deal with blocked roads from other NPCs or other movement issues.
Yeah, it has many problems and going on with the chapters the game tends to become hard for what concerns missions, battles and upgrades but still, nothing unplayable in my opinion.
Probably it's because I played tons of RPGs of any kind, but I managed to move myself without many problems even in the later chapters.
You've got to be prepared, since it will be a long journey and it will mostly deal with narration and not with combat and such. And this is why this is a RPG, but this can not by any means be classified as strategy/tactical RPG since if you look at awesome games in that fields (just think of the Banner Saga, one of the greatest series in the latest years in my opinion) well, there's lots of narration but the core of the game are the positioning of many units (not only one or a few), choosing the most important ones for that particular battle, looking for terrain differences (can I cite Advance Wars for this aspect, that here is completely absent? XD), and well fighting turn by turn until you emerge victorious, and then go on with your adventure.
Here there's little of these aspects, 'cos even the battles are linked to the emotional and introspective narration of the chapters and the main characters' story. And some times you'll be asked just to endure the fight, survive, or flee.. of course, you'll se why.
So, coming to a conclusion, bear in mind that this game was released in 2010 so be aware if you read reviews from those years 'cos many things have been fixed, at least as of the last half of 2017; still, you have to be prepared to get involved in the story and to deal with a slow game with its own beauty in the narration rather than in the combat system (which will still require some time due to the number of upgrades and so on) and the gameplay.
I'd suggest you to download the demo and/or to watch Youtube videos before buying it, and if you think it can be your genre well, it's worth a try bearing in mind that it's an indie RPG and it's the first game that this French studio created (with Adobe Air) so it has still many flaws, not too many though to negatively review it :)

After playing 12 hours of this. I can say this game is a must have in your library. Mount & Blade: Warband. Offers something different for the RPG gamers, like myself and makes it a fun experience, but sadly tends to drag out in some areas. While also makes it extremely challenging.
First and Foremost, know what you are doing. Play the tutorial a few times, read a few guides, watch a couple of Let's Plays and get a good idea of what you want your character to be like. Because depending upon your background origin, the world will react to you in many, many different ways. But also will either make it a painful experience or a thrilling one.
Also level up properly, if you don't level up properly this will become a *dare i say it?* An Elder Dark Souls Scrolls experience with the Mount & Blade name slapped right on it.  And what do i mean by that? Well in an Elder Scroll game, you play who you want to be, with either the worst leveling up system or the cheapest (depending upon your point of view) Where the Dark Souls experience comes in. This game is heavily trial by error. You have to learn from your mistakes and/or think really hard as to what you want to do next. There are no second chances unless you quicksave it first.
There is no manual save, or autosave (Well I shouldn't say that. The game will save at certain points). The only real buttton you have to rely on in that area is the quicksave. It is important you also remap your keys, the way the "default" layout is. It's a bit wonky and sometimes unforgettable or extremely frustrating in a win scenario for you. But instantly makes it a Losing scenario. Why? Because the default controls are abysmal.
Depending upon what expanison you are playing (Napelon, Vikings Conquest). You will get more or less of the main game itself (Warband).  Vikings Conquest, seems to be the more "funner" since you can be your own little lord or king, and/or just be a regular character. Just be aware being lord or king can be challenging at times. So be sure to look up on those guides and/or ask questions within the community or checkout a few Let's plays.
Also there seems to be random crashes at certain intervals. There is no real solution for that (However, if someone does find a solution. Please post in the comment section, so i can edit this part of the review).
Despite the funky controls, random crashes, and a sluggish pacing mixed with the feels of rage quitting. This game is really deep in terms of actions, consquences, characters, etc. Everything and anything to what an RPG is. If the community invests in the modding scene a bit more. Then this game in the long run. Will still be a fun experience.

When I first took a look at "Manhunter" (around the time I purchased "Manhunt", oddly enough), I saw all the negative reviews that said all the same thing. "I stopped playing after the first ten minutes". Well, I'm glad to know YOUR habits, but what exactly about this game sucks? Well, everything, but that's beside the point. Wait, actually...
The first thing that sucks about this game would probably be everything. The sound is just standard gun sounds. Nothing special. The voice-acting is sub-par (Especially John's voice actor- and you hear him 90% of the game!). And the graphics literally want to look bad in this game. I kid you not! The game lags more than a Windows 95 trying to run a full Mincraft server with 64 people on it. And, to put things in perspective, I can play BioShock, Mass Effect 2, and The Old Republic on my computer just fine. No lag. No framerate issues. But this game is just... It's basically like a neurotic mother-in-law that can't make up her mind about anything? Will this level have a good framerate? ... No. Will this level have good sound? Sure! Will this level have clunky animation? Yes, to all of them!
Probably the most noticeable flaw (the one, I assume, that turned off gamers after ten minutes into this game) is the walking. And jumping. And sprinting. And interacting with the world, really. It just all sucks. When John walks, it feels like he's walking on rubber legs and has to fling them out one at a time in order to properly move. When he jumps, it looks like he does a normal jump then out of nowhere, just farts and gets an extra boost on his jump. And John basically sprints like a fat kid during his first day at gym school. You can sprint for a total of... 5 meters. Or less. And then John will pant like a dog into your headphones for the next 30 seconds. Lovely. And the actual animations of the NPCs are just... unnerving. They move like programmed robots. Like Davies at the beginning of the game (and the *koff* "citizen" at the end of the game (even though it's just Davies again)) walks in cutscenes with his arms oddly spread out and pointing down. And enemies will die in unnatural manners, flinging in very specific directions after you snipe them.
And you will snipe. A lot. I mean, if you're the only intelligent being in this game, you will snipe enough- since the only way to kill the waves of enemies fast enough it to hit them in the head, and the only gun that can do that properly is your sniper rifle. And the game seems to focus heavily on it's sniper rifles, since it'll give you TWO at the beginning of every stage and each one will be filled with TWO HUNDRED bullets. But the sniping (really just the shooting as a whole) is monotonous and uninspired. The game will show you the wind when you zoom in on your scope, but that only mattered once in the entire game when I had to snipe trucks... that would explode in one hit. But whenever you point your scope at an enemy the reticule that shows you where your bullet will hit and would be off to whatever direction the wind blows it, just happens to lock right on your enemy.
This game is all about walking, running, and sprinting. There is no variety or creative level design to pace out the experience more. And the story compliments it's perfectly by being the exact same thing. You'd think the game would end after you finally kill the RIGHT hit you were originally supposed to kill, or perhaps when you disable a ruddy bloody rocket! But the game just ambles on, and only ends when it feels it's padded itself to a long enough point. And I had no reason to care about the story of the characters. Max and John are the only main characters in the whole story and all their dialogue amounts to is-
MAX: John, do this!
JOHN: Roger that. (x500)
What else sucks? Well, I did say everything, so what about the AI? Yeah, that sucks. Just like the game itself, the AI is programmed to be either "Stand here and keep shooting, and never take cover." Or "Flank John at the worst possible moment," because when I'd hang behind my cover for just about 7 seconds to heal (which takes forever to do in this game)- a random baddy would either spawn behind me or run around on my side and start shooting me. And I've even seen some enemies hide behind foliage, which I found oddly smart for the otherwise ignorate AI. And all your enemies are either Russians or Middle Easteners, so you already know the game's view on relationships with people outside their own country.
The music is also very limited. There are only two different tracks that play during shoot-outs and that's it. There is no music beyond that. And whenever you finish a shoot-out, the music will cut off awkwardly. And this isn't a glitch (even though this game is filled with those), because during the 5 hours I played this game- this would happen every time I killed the enemies in a room (which would be hilarious if I killed a guy in room, and the music would only pause for two seconds, as I'd open the door and new enemies would come out.)
The levels are very straightforward and pretty easy to grind through to get to where you want to get to. But the game is a bit too linear. If you deviate even a little from the course (or want to try swimming) you have 4 seconds to retrace your steps or you are screwed. And the save points in this game suck, because of how poorly dispersed they are. I don't like manual saving because it makes a game easier, I like manual saving because it makes a game less repetitive- something that Manhunter wouldn't hurt to not have. It's INCREDIBLY frustrating when you step out for two seconds, accidentally get blown to smithereens by the enemies, then get teleported to fifteen minutes earlier in the game. It's the biggest leash-yanker in this game.
I'd say this game is trying to make a commentary on triple-A FPS's like Call of Duty and Battlefield, by saying if their gameplay was the same as Manhunter, they'd be considered just as bad because of their poor stories. But, I think that's a bit too deep for anyone to get out of a game like this. Manhunter is a definite must-not-play. If you just bought this game and looked at my review, take my advice and refund it that very second! It is one of the worst games on Steam!

The Misadventures of P.B. Winterbottom -PC-
The Misadventures of P.B. Winterbottom is the “Dr. Seus” of 2D platform gaming. It plays well, it has a fun “indie” artistic style, and it narrative overlay is cleaver and witty. While it lasts, these misadventures are a great fun, unfortunately I plowed through this game is just a couple short hours. I would have liked to have seen a full scale adventure, but for what you pay for, it is well worth it.
In the game your objective is to try to get your character (who is a mix between Yogi Bear and Scrooge Mcduck) to collect all the pies on the screen.  The premise sounds simple, but it will soon become apparent that some of these pies are tricky sons of a gun to collect.
The levels are separated into sets of levels. At the beginning of a set, the game will introduce to you a new game mechanic, and for the rest of the levels collecting pies will be become increasingly more complex. Collecting pies has never been this hard before! The game mechanics are fresh and intuitive. I will not give any of the game mechanics away, for it would ruin the whole mystique. The new game  mechanics really set The Misadventures of Mr. Winterbottom apart from other generic puzzle side scrollers. I applaud the high standard of creativity.
Almost every puzzle is set in a static screen, there won’t actually be much side scrollin’ action in this game, only in the later levels you’ll be able to side scroll. I think this was because of the nature of these puzzles. They can get really tricky, and it is helpful to have the whole puzzle right in front of you at all times. I do prefer the classic side scroller, and many times the levels in this game felt like a puzzle level from “Tetris Attack” or “Yoshi’s Cooke”, I still enjoyed it.
As you run around as Mr Winterbottom, he controls reasonably well. He is not perfectly precise, but you rarely if ever will be punished for not being exact; your objective is to collect pies and as long as any part of you guy touches a pie, you’ll collect it.  The whole game is based on puzzles and not perfectly executed maneuvering (even though some levels trick you into thinking so)
The story and narrative are reminiscent of popular children books. The phrasing rhymes, and come 2 lines at a time. There are still pictures that accompany every described location. I looked forward to the narrative as it came and I read and enjoyed every line.
The only real problem with The Misadventures of Mr. Winterbottom is that it is too short. I completed the game fully in less than 4 hours. Given, I am a wizard of sorts, but there just isn’t as much content as I would have liked. I can’t really complain cause I got the game for like $5 off of a Steam sale.
The Misadventures of Mr. Winterbottom is a great diversion with plenty of re play-ability: weather it be in attempts to get a better score / time or to watch someone else solve the puzzles for the first time, it is plenty of fun. I have suggested this game to a number of people, as I think it can be fun for a very broad # of people. Go and play you some Mr Winterbottom!
Written September 2010 for website allgamesplayed given a 4 out of 5

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

What makes a good horror game, in my humble opinion, is all about suspense and atmosphere.  And this game has both in spades.
First is the sound design.  In this game you hear your character's heartbeat (and she has a diminished stamina bar for running away) when you get too close to a spirit.  Add to that the ambience and the enemy groans and snorts, and you're in for a creepy ride indeed.
Second is the visual design, and the art for this game is on par with the likes of Silent Hill or Zero/Fatal Frame.  A lot of the spirits are not downright menacing, but rather strange and curious, and it really captures the right feel for such ambiguous creatures.
The story is pretty minimalist as well, with a very basic outline that gets your character motivated to explore the night.  But that's really all they need.  I think leaving the nature of the enemies a question was a good story decision.
So overall, I'd highly recommend this game if you're looking for something spooky and atmospheric.

The game's aesthetic is the main thing it has going for it, and that's really what will keep you playing. The gameplay could stand to have more variety to it (different ways of sneaking/running past enemies would have made for a dynamic experience), but the game was still fun.

Through the streets angered spirits of all kinds chased me, with jagged jutting fangs and gaping black sockets for eyes. Their fast pitterpattering along the asphalt and heart-crushing presences followed and filled my vision with spectacular redness. My heart pounded its way through my fragile little ribs, leaving me to waddle away.
Stone dogs popped out of bushes to snap down with a barking surprise. Floating backpacks grabbed my arms and split me in two. Starfish with burning eyes chased and splattered the streets. Marshmallow tufts lead me down paths only to meet towering puffmen to slaughter me the same. All around no spirit would let me be, no spirit would let me find my big sis.
But then there was that walking statue in the school courtyard, reading his granite book and stiffly stepping with his hard rock sandals. All he did was pace back and forth, reading a single engraved stone page. I stood in his way and he continued forward, carrying me with him. I felt my heart slow to a calm, silent beat and snuggled up against his slim, rough thigh.
Not all spirits are so bad after all.

Rogue Operatives, in case you have somehow looked at the trailer and not understood, or perhaps read the description and are still baffled, is an online, multi-player hide & seek game (Or, as I believe you Americans tend to call it "Hide & Go Seek").
One party plays the Rogue (or hider) and the other plays the Operative (or Seeker), and the aim of the game is either hide, or seek! The hider gets to choose one of the in game assets, which are in keeping with the surroundings (at present there are three maps - a farm, an ice world and a space station). For example, in the farm, you can choose a bale of hay, or a shovel. The Operative (seeker) is tasked with finding as many Rogues as possible in 15 minutes.
Finding the Rogues isn't all that easy, but you are armed with a presence detection device, similar to a radar, which tells you when you are close, and your trusty gun. The gun is for you to tag the Rogues... or eliminate them, if you will. Once eliminated they will join the Ops team to close in on other hidden Rogues.
This game is in Early Access and still has a way to go before being considered a full game, but what is there presently is VERY fun, especially with lots of people.
We have played 1V1, 2V2 & 3V1, and playing with four people, with voice chat is very funny. Presently there is only text chat support, but no doubt the devs are working on voice chat. In the mean time, try Skype or TeamSpeak.
There are minor issues with the game presently, such as spawning bugs which will see you not alternating teams, or assets showing incorrectly, but this is what Early Access is for, to help identify these issues and help iron them out to make the perfect game!
We love the game and our rather long video of multiple 1V1's show how much fun there is to be had in this cracking little hidden gem.
The dev's are SUPER COOL too and will often hop into your game with you to help fill up the game.
I will be checking in on this regularly as it is a game I fully love and hope grows in popularity, content and ideas.

I've only recently gotten into Morrowind but this is hands down one of the best fantasy RPGs I've played in a long time. If you're expecting something like Skyrim or even Oblivion you'll be very pleasantly surprised.
I've always played Oblivion and Skyrim on and off, but it was only this summer that I decided to sit down and power through them for real. I had a lot of fun with Dawnguard and a good deal of Dragonborn, but what really got me hooked was reading through all the extra material, which eventually lead to stuff like TESLore posts and UESP surfing. The Elder Scrolls series has such a rich mythology that's easy to get sucked into.
Eventually I thought I'd take a break from Skyrim (still need to finish Dragonborn) and bought Morrowind because it was on sale. I'm not the kind of gamer who lets graphics get in the way, so Morrowind being dated wasn't an issue.
The game's mechanics are based around classic RPG number/dice-rolling elements. This may turn some people off, but I personally really like the way it functions within the world of the game and how it affects your character. Unlike Skyrim or Oblivion you don't start off the game feeling like the special chosen one. What Morrowind does extremely well is making you feel small, weak, and insignificant. No one holds your hands, you aren't given special powers, and the guards (and frankly any innocent bystander) can thoroughly beat your♥♥♥♥♥down. I'm only level 6 but I can actually feel myself progressing and getting stronger.
The game's immersion doesn't come from flashy spectacle or realistic graphics. In fact, a lot of the primitive aspects actually help towards it. What Morrowind relies on is the player's imagination. The text without voice-acting, the lack of quest markers and fast travel, and the varied environments allow you to fill in the gaps on your own and draw you deeper into the world.
As for character customization, there are many archetypes that you can build after that the game supports (i.e. spellsword, thief, monk, ranger, archer, etc.). Some builds are better than others, but the game allows enough freedom for you to play how you want. I'm running a straight sword-and-board knight and I'm having loads of fun. (Fair bit of warning though: the bowplay is iffy in this game, since it relies on dice-rolls and numbers. Skyrim has it beat in this regard.)

The bunkers add upgrades to your character for the FPS portion of the game rather than actual base building. First Impressions Video:
Bunker Punks is a super fast paced rouge-like shooter set in a dystopian future run by mega-corporation. You work as a band of rebels tearing up corporation buildings to try to destroy the corporation forever. And, I'll tell you, this game is super fun.
The gameplay is similar to old school shooters like Doom. You have a character with a gun who shoots evil robots with guns. Simple, genius, the best. Your character moves lightning fast and is super responsive. The guns fire dead on point (with expected spread of course). These, combined with rooms filled with enemies, makes for a super fast paced game.
The rouge-like qualities are pretty decent. Your game will be divided into runs where you work your way thorugh a map of different buildings trying to get to the last one, and the shops between runs. In the runs you fight robots, upgrade your bunker (to give your dudes extra perks), and get killed (because you gonna die). The shop areas in between give you new punks, bunker rooms and upgrades to help you on your future runs. This gives the combo of great rouge-like combat with persistant progression.
Now, it all sounds fine and dandy, right? What, you might ask, is lack luster about this game? The game doesn't feel like it has a ton in it. I've trounced through many levels and only found very basic weapons of every class. I feel like I've seen every piece of armor that you can loot out of buildings and I've fought every type of robot (and I'm only 3 hours in). This being said, I still want to play more. There is a decent number of enemies (around 7 or eight types), each of which has their own niche. The guns and armor does end up making my runs feel samey in terms of strategy, but there's always new situations to shoot your way out of.
In addition to this, there is the elephant in the room. The graphics. There are some graphics purests our there that can have nothing but ultra realitstic, 4k 1080Gigapixel graphics. And i say, thats legit, good graphics are pretty sick. If that's you, you won't like these graphics. They are pixel art, and pretty good pixel art at that. I never stopped and thought that anything actually looked bad. In fact, I quite enjoyed the aestethic.
So, all in all, Bunker Punks is an awsome game. It's tons of fun to play, even is it's lacking some depth at the moment. It's definitely worth picking up, or at least keeping on your radar.

When first getting the game, I expected a cheap Left 4 Dead clone that I expected to be fun but soon be finished with. I love the Left 4 Dead formula, Vermintide certainly takes clear inspiration from it but it's far more than a clone. The most notable, though contentious point is the loot system.
It can take time to get some high level gear, but there is a vast assortment of different weapons that have unique play styles and traits. Difficulty and special feats factor into what loot you can get, although it sometimes does feel stingy or too reliant on dice rolls. The levels themselves are very well constructed and are incredibly replayable. There are a lot of small tricks and secrets to master for each character and the Skaven are an extremely fun opponent to face.
Though some of Vermintide's influence is clear, it expands and in some ways improves on an existing formula that is very much worth exploring!

Winter Voices is focused on reading and text choices but it also has unique RPG system that acts as an extension of storytelling rather than generic combat. It has relatively complex stat and skill system but there are no items, equipment, looting or inventory. This is an episodic adventure so I highly suggest trying the demo or first episode.
I would compare my experience with this game to reading a book about RPG game instead of actually playing one. That may sound negative but it is weird to a point where I enjoy it. If you not a fan of text walls you already hate 80% of what this game is about.
So you cannot directly attack enemies in this game. The hole "combat system" seems to be metaphorical representation for fighting your own emotions, memories, and thoughts. In a nutshell RPG system here is all about staying alive as long as you can. To complete "battles" you commonly have to survive several turns or move to a location. However, there are many other objectives that can be hidden in a clue ( for example you may need to kill yourself on purpose )
Really "RPG system" here is more like a puzzle game. For the most part, you trying to pick the safest route to complete your objective while using the grid to your advantage. Many of your spells are designed for stealth, distraction or pushes.You can actually skip a lot of the battles if you can't complete them but you will be losing Experience. There are some battles you can't skip that are tied to the story or boss fights.
About 15 hours into the game you do get a way of attacking enemies but it will be a part of specific objectives and not your own skill. You have to get on a tile that gives you attacking skills for 5 turns as part of puzzle solving.
You can absolutely lose the game by poor skill management. Well, it would not be your fault because you don't know what kind of objectives you will come across. The skill system is very extensive so it is hard to say what is useful and what is not. On that note, I really wish this game had a skill reset system because you can put yourself into unwinnable situation deep into the story.
Skill System like everything else in the game is a mental extension of your character. It is actually very cool and creative design which is the best part about the whole thing (advance stat crunching) There are many passive effects, heals, summons, active buffs, debuffs and stealth just to name a few. I think I counted 12 different skill paths so there are many ways of playing the game.
Another cool thing is that your Stats sometimes have an impact on text choices. Humor can unlock new dialogue options for example. I got couple passive effects to increase humor and I seem to get more joke options while I talk.
Love the music. For the most part, it is ambient but it fits the game and adds to hunting atmosphere. You can customize your character a little bit even though this game really did not need that feature. Even the Skill art is neat because it is all inspired by character's mind. It is not exactly a gorgeous game but it looks different in a good way. The only problem I have is lack of environments (you will often see same types of backgrounds)
The game has a lot of deep writing which overloads my imagination. It deals with emotional interpretation so you can find your own plot here. About 15 hours into the game you will finally get the idea of why things are happening. Without giving away spoilers I will just say that Winter Voices does a good job of tackling a very sensitive subject which few games would be willing to undertake. Although I was too lazy to read all of the conversation I was interested in the conclusion. Voice narration when used in few parts is pretty fantastic .
You can also meet new party members and build relationships that will unlock skills for them. I am at 40%+ In romance with a crow ( a bird damn it )It is hard to say on how much impact your choices actually have. I think it's possible to not get some of the party members by talking crap to them but I did not try it.
.There are a lot of problems with gameplay and glitches but the unorthodox gameplay and good writing make it very different kind of experience. I think many people will hate it because they expect traditional RPG game.  In its core, this is very expanded text game with choices where "battle system" works more like a puzzle game that complements a text story. If you look at this game from a writing and storytelling perspective it is a good game for what it is .

I really, really wanted to love this game. But.....this was a game that just didn't click with me at all. I felt that it had too many shortcomings that I couldn't really recommend it to anybody else.
I got up to to the third season in the game before I felt that I had spent enough time in game to know all the ins and out of this game to review it.
first, let me point out the best parts of the game:
1) plenty of mini-games. some mini games you even earn in-game currency if you win. and the fishing mini-game can be fun too, once you get the hang of it.
2)Plenty of sidequests and some collectables like collecting new clothes to wear on your avatar, etc.
3)Some of the artwork in the game is really great!
But.... here comes the negatives:
1) it feels like a very small world in game. The amount of places to explore is very, very limited to the point where some places almost feel claustrophobic, espeically with all the trees and stuff taking up space and getting in your way when you're trying to explore the map. games like stardew valley often got around this limiation by allowing you to interact with the enivorment, by doing things like cut down the trees, etc... as well as giving you goals like unlocking new places to explore. World's dawn doesn't have that at all.
2) the start of the game can be so boring. As seeing there's such small spaces in each area of the map, there's not much that you can forage to get your money up. And your starting farm is so clean and tidy that you don't have anything to work on. In other simlar games out there, you started on a run down farm so the first thing you'd do is clear out all the weeds, etc so that you could have a space to grow your food. In world's dawn, You don't really have any goals for your actual farm itself other than upgrading your house and collecting all the kitchen appliances. unlike in other life/farming simluation games you can't upgrade much of anything else or even build new buildings on your farm.
The start of the game try to get around this by giving you a goal of meeting everyone, and also the side quest of giving the eldery mayor his favortive homemade stew. But the start game is still so boring.
3) I know that I said that some of the artwork was great... but the other aspects of it is pretty mixed. You got your generic-looking rpg maker sprites, but then the trees and the character avatars look like it was hand-made. The trees look so cartoony in that cute way, but then you have the animal sprites which look very realstic (sorta). It feels like three or four artists  with all very different art styles got together and worked on this game... it's just a mismash of different art styles.
so because of that, the game doesn't feel as polished as it should be.
It feels like somebody's very first indie game, and it kind of shows too.
Gud.

I expected this game to be about the contrast between the extremely cute and the horrific, but Yomawari does much more with it than just juxtaposition. It is, at every level, the journey of an innocent little girl, at the age where everything in drawn in crayons and you don't really understand anything about the world, through fear, pain, and death. It's not the darkest game out there, but it's definitely pretty damn grim for a game where you are a cute lil' girl.
The ghosts are really creative, and if you're into horror for of the grotesque and creative aesthetics, Yomawari delivers. Hallucinations are few and far between, but most creatures are a treat of Japanese horror.
You know this problem horror games have when they're scary the first hours and it progressively de-escalates as you become familiar with the game? Yomawari is different. It's not really a survival game, in the sense that you're going to die, easily and a lot, but it's rarely very punishing. It is in essence a die-and-retry. But while it never really inspires dread, the gameplay makes it tense, consistently and until the end. The only thing you can do against the spirits is avoiding them. Stealth very rarely works, you have to zip past them. Only, the game gives you a limited stamina bar, which depletes faster and faster the closest you get to a ghost. What this means is that you generally have juuuuust enough time and stamina to dodge the spirits. It's actually pretty neatly calibrated, and it makes it so that basically you can never feel safe. Especially not with those nasty ghosts that come rushing at you for behind. You probably won't be scared, but you will be on edge.
That's of course the weak spot of the game, a short four hours to finish the main story, with optional events and collectibles scattered across the map, with a free roam mode to get them all after the story ends.
Overall, plenty to like if you like sad, tense games and J-horror aesthetics.

Nippon Ichi's second Vita-released horror game after the disastrous htoL#NiQ: The Firefly Diary, Yomawari was directed by Yu Mizokami, who worked on graphics and level design for The Firefly Diary, but is a very different, and better, thing altogether. There's not much in the way of mechanics, but it does a lot with what it has, especially the flashlight, which has a limited range of movement and is your only real defense, aside from hiding, against the spirits and spectres in this charmingly-presented Japanese countryside town. With fantastic sound design (your heartbeat is used to alert you to spirits getting closer) and superb presentation throughout, it's a tense experience that does not outstay its welcome (around 4 hours) and made a serious impression on me.
There are a few areas to criticise- some enemies, especially in the final stretch, can be a bit flaky when it comes to hit detection and can get stuck on walls to make things even harder, there's a few monsters that are much, much faster and appear with little time to react to appropriately, and it is a little jumpscare-heavy, but overall, this is a solid game, one to play in the evenings over the course of a week, with earphones on and the lights out.

Cuteness and horror go together like chocolate and orange; not everyone is going to appreciate the combination, but those that do find it delicious. I’m not talking about an adorable doll coming to life and murdering people, I’m talking about adorable characters struggling against adorable antagonists. Cuteness doesn’t take me out of the moment, instead I find it enhances that key element of horror where you are faced with something familiar or comforting that has been corrupted in some way. Yomawari: Night Alone does just that, taking charming doodles and drawings and teaching you to fear and distrust them. It might also teach you to hate them, but with enough patience you’ll find a fine tale of terror here.
Your button-eyed, bobble-headed protagonist is out walking her dog one night in a place she very obviously should not be. A sharp, tragic shock follows that leaves the little lass all alone in the night, searching for her missing family. Her search takes her all across her darkened neighborhood and the surrounding rice fields, forests, factories, and other haunted places. She’s not really alone though, because on this particular night there are more spirits out than munchkins on Halloween. And these are out for blood, not candy.
The game plays out over seven chapters, each one starting from the relative safety of the little girl’s home. She’ll decide a goal for herself, usually following a lead into a specific part of her town, and then you’re left to guide her. The map is quite open, moreso as you get into later chapters, so there’s plenty of exploring to do if you’re up for finding weird monsters and collectibles. In addition to the dozens of items you can find, there are certain spirits you can only encounter in specific places or under special conditions, as well as ones just hanging around to creep you out.
This gets at what’s so special about Yomawari, and why its atmosphere is so effective. The open map allows you to go wherever you feel like and see what you want to see, and early on it’s going to be confusing and terrifying. The narrow, twisting streets of rural Japan can hide all sorts of secrets, with mysterious shrines and suspiciously vacant lots right in the middle of neighborhoods. When you find a new place or encounter a new spirit, you’re not going to know how safe you are or what you might uncover if you delve deeper. Hostile spirits are often obvious but others might simply stand around, staring at nothing, or vanish without a trace. They’re as mercurial and unpredictable as you might imagine ghosts would be, at least until you learn their habits.
The game mechanics support this feeling of unease, but can also turn it into one of frustration. When you get near a spirit you’ll hear your heartbeat, rising in intensity as you draw closer. You have a generous sprint meter for scooting around town but it drains faster the closer you are to monsters, making escape a difficult proposition if you get too close. You can also hide in bushes and behind signs, obscuring your vision and leaving you to judge when it’s safe by how hard your heart is beating. And then you have usable items like rocks and salt which can distract or slow enemies to help you slip away.
All of this is great, but it’s not applied in a very well thought-out manner. Most of your usable items are hard to use effectively and some are only effective on one or two enemies. Some enemies can be evaded or juked easily while others will pursue you relentlessly. And sometimes the rules themselves break down, with no heartbeat for spirits that charge out of nowhere, or pounding heartbeats for ones that are completely benign (as far as I know). These outliers produce memorable moments of terror or dread, but can frustrate when they lead to death. If something catches you, you die and head back to the last shrine you stopped at or checkpoint in story-heavy areas. One-hit kills are always a recipe for aggravation, and a few of the “boss” spirits can be extremely hard to avoid until you get totally familiar with their encounters after a dozen deaths or so.
There were a few spirits, the Grudge girl (of course there’s a Grudge girl) and the factory thing in particular, that made me consider giving up on the game. But these moments of frustration are surrounded by creepy hikes through the Japanese countryside, skirting past drowned spirits and human-faced dogs to find cryptic notes scribbled in crayon. The bizarre, otherworldly appeal of Silent Hill and Siren is here in small places, obscured by the soft shapes of your doll-like protagonist and the sketchbook weirdness of the spirits after her. It’s hard to tell if you’re wandering a haunted town or haunted by your own demons, and that uncertainty is what draws a lot of people to Japanese horror in the first place.
I was honestly surprised at how often Yomawari could startle me, with spirits bursting out of alleyways and narrow escapes being far too narrow for comfort. But I was also surprised at how often it could frustrate me, when I had to repeat those escapes a dozen times or retrace steps over and over. You have to approach it with the right mindset, one ready to learn the quirks of quirky horrors and comb the streets for lost shoes and dolls. With a warm and inviting art style and delightfully sharp sound design, it’s a great package to spend hours wandering around in. Yomawari features some quality weird horror from Japan in a dark, colorful world to explore, and that’s plenty to keep me poking around.

It comes across a tad creepy at first, but HuniePop is one hell of a game!
At first glance, it seems like a generic dating sim that might get old after a while of bland dialogue that you don't have much control over. But once you get into the swing of things, its an awesome game!
Every female is different from the last in this game. Each one having a much different personality than the last, completely different backgrounds and all of them requiring a different tactic when it comes to dates. For example, Audrey enjoys flirtation during her dates whilst Nikki enjoys talent, but Aiko isn't too impressed if you go for talent. Meaning you have to focus on matching different tokens than others, depending on who you're dating. For me, this puts HuniePop on top of other games like Bejewelled or Candy Crush, where those games don't put much focus in what each little jewel or candy can do.
The strategy in the game is phenominal, but the dating sim aspects tends to be lacking in comparison. When you meet each girl for the first time, you can choose any of the lines given to you, and you'll still get to go on a date with them (in which they never turn you down), regardless of how suave or how stupid you may come across. It's worth noting that there are two forms of currency in the game: Hunie and Munie.
Munie (as the name suggests) is money that you use to buy gifts, and of course, every girl likes different gifts. But some gifts can give you "date gifts" which can affect the tokens during dates, and can be used in as many dates as you like (Which is pretty nice!).
If they accept gifts outside of dates, you gain Hunie. Hunie are points that are used to upgrades tokens in the main strategy form of the games, which is especially useful. Talking to the girls gives you Hunie as well, usually by answering questions about themselves, or by answering questions that you think they'll like. However, this is as complicated as it will get for the dating sim section of the game. It's worth noting that you can have sex with these girls at night after about three or four successful dates, but doing so is just a mini-game followed by a raunchy picture afterwards (Boobs and panties only though).
The main menu that you use to navigate and utilize your hunie and munie is essentially a smartphone called the "Huniebee", which is given to you by Kyu, a love fairy. The Huniebee is used to "track" the girls so you can talk to them, which CAN come across as creepy, but the girls themselves don't seem to mind you talking to them as long as they're available from the travel options. They can also reject alcohol if they think that drinking is a terrible time to do so. So it's great to see that the girls have control over how you play the game to some extent. Alcohol is used to gain more Hunie from talking, and can give you an advantage during dates. This can seem a little dark as well, but it's not completely needed in the game.
Do I recommend HuniePop? Absolutely! If you can overlook a few aspects that could be misconstrued.

I've only recently gotten into Morrowind but this is hands down one of the best fantasy RPGs I've played in a long time. If you're expecting something like Skyrim or even Oblivion you'll be very pleasantly surprised.
I've always played Oblivion and Skyrim on and off, but it was only this summer that I decided to sit down and power through them for real. I had a lot of fun with Dawnguard and a good deal of Dragonborn, but what really got me hooked was reading through all the extra material, which eventually lead to stuff like TESLore posts and UESP surfing. The Elder Scrolls series has such a rich mythology that's easy to get sucked into.
Eventually I thought I'd take a break from Skyrim (still need to finish Dragonborn) and bought Morrowind because it was on sale. I'm not the kind of gamer who lets graphics get in the way, so Morrowind being dated wasn't an issue.
The game's mechanics are based around classic RPG number/dice-rolling elements. This may turn some people off, but I personally really like the way it functions within the world of the game and how it affects your character. Unlike Skyrim or Oblivion you don't start off the game feeling like the special chosen one. What Morrowind does extremely well is making you feel small, weak, and insignificant. No one holds your hands, you aren't given special powers, and the guards (and frankly any innocent bystander) can thoroughly beat your♥♥♥♥♥down. I'm only level 6 but I can actually feel myself progressing and getting stronger.
The game's immersion doesn't come from flashy spectacle or realistic graphics. In fact, a lot of the primitive aspects actually help towards it. What Morrowind relies on is the player's imagination. The text without voice-acting, the lack of quest markers and fast travel, and the varied environments allow you to fill in the gaps on your own and draw you deeper into the world.
As for character customization, there are many archetypes that you can build after that the game supports (i.e. spellsword, thief, monk, ranger, archer, etc.). Some builds are better than others, but the game allows enough freedom for you to play how you want. I'm running a straight sword-and-board knight and I'm having loads of fun. (Fair bit of warning though: the bowplay is iffy in this game, since it relies on dice-rolls and numbers. Skyrim has it beat in this regard.)

Any true Elder Scrolls fan will tell you that this game is the best in the francise and I must agree. However the gaming engine of this game is rather dated which you will notice as soon as you leave the docks to Seyda Neen, the first town you discover. You will find that the game is not voice acted save a few generic lines of dialogue from NPCs, a few monologues from the Daedric Prince Azura (kind of your guardian angel), Daedric prince Hircine, and tribunal member Almalexia.
The game is truely a bridge between the archaic elder scrolls games and newer titles such as skyrim and oblivion. Morrowind introduces 3 dimensional graphics replacing 2d sprites. The story line, in my opinion is much more in depth than previous installments. However, this game has a few problems. Morrowind uses a chance based combat system in which you may actually find yourself not hitting enemies at point blank range with a mace and or other melee weapon. This is the same for all skills whether lockpicking, weapon maintenance, magic, speech or otherwise. This factor of the gaming engine becomes less of a problem as you level up. Morrowind does not have a fast travel system, the fast travel system was a novelty which would be reserved for TES Oblivion. There are virtually no unkillable NPCs in Morrowind, however there are essential NPCs which upon killing you will recieve a message basically telling you that you can no longer complete the main quest. Morrowind is a very unforgiving game like its predecessors, Arena and Daggerfall. Overall it takes a lot of time investment and research and reading for this game to become actually fun for the average gamer. It is for these reasons that many attempts have been made to update Morrowind to a newer engines including the Oblivion and now Skyrim engines.
If the reader should purchase this game I emplore you to either invest a lot of time in the game before making an obnoxious opinion or consider using the mod known as Skywind (which is Morrowind on Skyrim's engine). I do not think Skywind is finished yet but in either case be patient this game gets very very good especially mid to late game.
I recommend it to people who aren't so snobby about graphics. The story is amazing, and that's really what the game is about. That's what I love about it, anyway.

This game has been a disappointment. While it has a unique style and gameplay, it's unplayable. The pace of the game is horribly slow, it tries the patience. Your character walks slowly, it is extremely loaded in text and every action you take is slow. That aside, the game runs slowly too. It has trouble keeping up with each spell you cast, areas take a long time to load, etc. If the previous two points weren't enough, the frequent glitches in the game had me reloading constantly, making any sort of progress painstakingly difficult.
The difficulty is also very problematic. While most encounters are very simple to get through and will allow for many different approaches and a variety of skill set, some are near impossible. I can count half a dozen encounters that I had to either retry 30 to 40 times, give up or win through sheer luck. I had to give up at a certain point in the epilogue after my 20th attempt at a 5-part encounter that you have to retry
every time you fail.
Simply interacting with the environment is annoying. The only way you can interact with the environment is by walking to certain areas. This poses many problems: it takes ages to reach any point, the areas you need to walk to are not indicated, NPCs can get in the way (especially your companion), certain interactions block others, etc. The fixed camera means that half of the map at any given time is not visible, which means getting around and aiming at enemies is very difficult­. It's also often unclear on what tile an enemy is standing, it takes a lot of getting used to and even then, you still make a mistake every now and then.
I could probably criticize this game further but I'm sure my point is clear by now. All in all, what could've been a great experience was ruined by the poor construction of the game. I got this game for a few dollars during a sale and regret purchasing it and spending as much time as I did on it. It is most definitely not worth the full price.

Winter Voices is an indie text heavy RPG a bit akin to Planescape: Torment, but also very different. Its strongest point is its fairly linear psychological and existential story centred on some of the darker aspects of us humans, but ultimately it's an experience of struggle, development, hope and growth; made with psychological insight. Next its "combat" encounters and its weakest the free roam hub-sections like the starting village. The game has a lovely artistic vision and ambience created by its hand-in-hand art direction, soundscape and writing. Which all have a wonderful poetic feel and are tied into the "combat system" beautifully. Plus if you are fond of metaphorical writing in works like "Thus Spoke Zarathustra" by Nietzsche, then you're bound to find the dream sequences interesting, as they employ metaphors to great effect. That said the English translation can be a bit iffy, so play it in its native French if you can.
The game is set in a fictional universe at the start of an industrial revolution in a Western country. The plot unfolds in a little remote, primitive and snowy mountain village, which lives by and practices a variant of Old Norse religion, whether the game is set in a Fantasy setting, or employs Magical Realism is up to interpretation, though it isn't at the core of the narrative outside of the dreams. You play a young and fragile twenty-four year old woman whose father has just died, it fairly quickly becomes apparent that you, the protagonist, have an abnormally hard time dealing with this death (wink wink), which propels you onwards on a journey of self-discovery within your dreams and the real world.
RPG mechanics
There are three classes to pick from Huntress, Weaver and Völva (a shamanic seeress). All of which favours one the six stats (Humour, Willpower, Memory, Perspicacity, Charisma and Intuition). These stats represents your strengths and weakness in your psychological profile. You get, primarily,  XP points to level them up from completing quest, "combat" and speaking with people. Separate from this you also gets Skill Points  as you level up. You can use them in a giant 2D-snowflake-formed Skill Tree with a total of 90ish skills to choose from enveloped by twelve different main paths (Negation, Metamorph , Pride, Social, Support, Composition, Ex-nihilo, Acceptance, Resilience, Resistance, Protection and Dispersion. ) to pursue, as you start out in the centre of it. You won't be able to learn all the skills in one play-through. Each of the twelve paths represents different ways, more or less gamey centred, human beings can deal, reflective or not, with grief and loss, whereas the "sub skills" are mixed between human traits such as creativity, perfectionism etc., and more culture specific things on the other hand such as: Song: Voluspa and Void Walker.

"Combat" encounters. The combat encounters take place in the dreams of our protagonist. Troubled dreams that portrays her struggles to come to terms with her father's death and her past. They are turn-based puzzle-like encounters on a grid that represents her fight with her inner demons.  Overall I found the combat encounters interesting and varied enough in their different puzzles in my play-through as a Völva. Though an occasional freezing bug of the entire game was annoying in some of the longer key encounters, especially as you couldn't save in between them.
In fact it made me put the game aside for around a year before returning to it once again. Though I am glad I did, as I really, really loved certain parts of the narrative :D

Very fast paced dungeon shooter. Graphicswhise it pays tribute to the early days of 3d gaming but it fits and positively sustains the simple gamplay mechanics. There is no zoom or ironsights just cirlestrafing and quick aiming against ever increasing numbers of enemies.
Each level consists of a number off floors which the player has to clear in order to finish the level and get to safety. If you die, you have to start over again and lose all your progress. Throughout the levels you can collect different loot which is either weapons, types of armor, money (used for upgrading the stats of you character as long as s/he is alive) and tec-credits (which can be spent on permanent improvements for the upcoming games at the end of you characters life). Upgrading your stats is fun and adds a little resouce management character to the game.
However there is still room for improvement. Music is a bit repetitive. I hope they add more tracks to the different levels, same goes for the graphic design. It would add more individuality to the various locations you visit. Another good idea would be to make the overworld map so that you can only advance towards the final goal without visiting all levels. This way you would need to make choices which loot you need the most and therefor decide where to go next.
The verdict: Solid straight forward shooter, if you love Quake, Doom an the like, definitely give it a try. If you grew up with more modern shooters (COD, Battlefield), you might still like it and get it on a sale.

Generally speaking, I feel like this game misses the mark. The writing is deeply irritating and pretentious nonsense, which is fine. I'd be happy to suffer through a little irritation if the "game" parts of Winter Voices weren't just as deeply irritating. Simply put, the "combat" is terrible.
Firstly, it would be inaccurate to call this combat. It technically is a tactical RPG combat system, but what you're doing isn't fighting so much as avoiding damage for an arbitrary number of turns (one of the popular "win" conditions is Last 10 Turns) or reaching a certain tile on the tactical grid. When I read about it, it impressed me as a novel way of representing the game's protagonist dealing with nightmares and emotions and such, and it is, but the implementation is clunky and amateurish in the extreme.
The art's very attractive, the setting is intriguing, the UI is effective (as you can tell from the screenshots) and while I personally find the faux-Proustian pretentiousness of the writing insufferable, it's entirely possible that it gets less so in the later episodes, but the combat system drags it all down into the mud of disappointment and unplayability. I feel like this would've worked better as a more traditional story-driven adventure or even visual novel-type experience than trying to cram it into tactical RPG shoes.

You start as a 24 years old woman who lives in small village and looses her father. Everything is suffocating her in her hometown, so she decides to travel to a distant city where her father used to live.
It has a unique graphic presentation, nice soundtrack and interesting theme however gameplay and some design choices are trying really hard to repel any person willing to give this game a chance.
The protagonist struggles with a depression after her parent's death and this is quite visual as her fears take on physical form and throw you into the battle. Why would you need to fight a dragon while you have your inner horrors to fight? Battles are turn-based and usually require some planning.
You also improve by leveling when you access skill tree in a form of snowflake and pick an ability which manifests how the character decides to deal with the reality (tough up - persistence +, cling to friends - heal allies, etc.). I like the whole idea quite well.
On the other hand, the game fails to explain gameplay mechanism. Sometimes you find yourself surrounded by enemies, the text hints some a mechanism is being introduced and then you have to figure out what it is.
It would be fine but combine it with slow pace (mostly thanks to slow movement of everything on screen) and the will to experiment leaves you.
It brings me to another flaw in the game and that is general slowness. Controls are responsive but moving across mere 3 screens (1 screen = a short path next to a 1 bedroom house) can take up to a minute.
There is also nothing to explore. You can either walk around, click on a person you wish to talk with or participate in a battle. No clickable objects which is not a flaw but I think it is good to mention.
I played the prologue and a bit of episode 1 because I decided it is not worth it to keep going. I am not excited enough about the story to spend time mostly watching character crawling around.
This game is certainly not for everybody, try demo to decide for yourself.

I tried to like this but it really fights with me, for every good there is a bad and the Reflex system just leads me to ask "Why?". In short I want my five dollars back. MotorCross madness is rolling over in its grave, shame Rainbow, shame. To think of the games these guys made and to have it come to this. I can only guess some pencil pusher shoved this stupid system on them and forced it by leveraging funding for the game, why else would they do it. At first I wasn't super excited.  I felt some of the portraits for the characters were meh and the world wasn't very pretty.  Also, I didn't like that you only had forty plots of land to plant in.
After sinking a few more hours in though, the game just started to appeal to me.  Running around gathering ingredients to make cocktails, playing the lockball minigame, and meeting all of the villagers just made me enjoy the experience.
But to make things simple let's just make a pros and cons list.
Pros
Cute characters
You can sprint
Nice variety of achievements (that you actually get rewarded for ingame)
Music isn't annoying to hear on a loop
Easy to keep track of what people like as gifts
Villagers move around instead of staying in one spot
Festivals are enjoyable
Cons
It costs more to buy a chicken than it does to upgrade your house
Only forty plots of land (I don't mind it too much since you can only plant four crops each season)
Catching one fish takes an hour
If you don't have enough money to buy something from the home shopping network, you have to wait until next year to purchase it
Lack of dating options (there are four girls and four boys, but it just seems strange that you can't marry someone like Indigo)
Once someone hits four hearts, they'll have a chance of coming to your house and ask if you like them or if you don't.  There is no, "let me think about it" option or anything like that.  It wouldn't be that much of a problem if you didn't have to pick one person so early.  I like to get to know the options as much as I can and then pick, like in other Harvest Moon or Rune Factory games.
But honestly, I don't feel like the cons ruin the game as much as they are inconvenient or slightly annoying, with the exception of the confession thing which is moderately annoying.  If you still aren't convinced that you should get it, then just wait to get it on sale for like, four dollars.

Very similar to Stardew Valley, but stream-lined and much simpler.  There are fewer things to do, each task is less complicated.  For example, the mine has only five levels and no enemies; farming is limited to 40 squares; only two kinds of animals; marriage is a possibility, but not kids, and the candidates only have limited back stories; etc.
That being said, the game has few bugs, some clever ideas, and is very solid implementation of the genre.  So if you like Stardew Valley, or other Harvest Moon-style games, you will almost surely get enough fun from this little town to get your money's worth.

I really liked Stardew Valley and wanted something like it. Unfortunately, compared to Stardew Valley absolutely everything about World's Dawn is second rate.
The controls are... creative. Every button is different from what you'd think it should be. Esc doesn't bring up the save/load/exit/options menu like it does in nearly every other program in the world. Here, it brings up your inventory. The (a) button on the xbox controller... that's usually your go-to button. Whatever the most important function is, it's usually done with a. Here, it's x. a makes you run. If there's a way to bring up the map of the area, I couldn't find it. With no map, I had trouble even finding my own farm when it got dark. And if there's a way to re-map the controls in-game, I couldn't find that either. I exited by hitting f5 to window the game, then clicking the X in the upper right hand corner with the mouse, which is kind of odd but seemed like the easiest way to do it.
The graphics are second rate, and from the limited interaction with the characters... like, in Stardew Valley, you could get a broad idea of what the person was like very quickly, from both their appearance and from their introductory statements. You knew right away that Abby kept to herself, that Haley was shallow and snobbish, etc.
In World's Dawn, all it tells you upon the first interacion is what the person does and who they live with. And it doesn't show you those things... it tells you:  "Herp Derp lives with his sister and mother and works a little bit on the farm with them". There's not too much in the appearance of the characters I met, either. They all looked like kind of generic, loosely anime styled people. There was nothing about their look which intrigued me, showed me personality, or made me think, "I'm going to work on getting this person to like me".
I could take the time to look up the control scheme and learn it. That alone wasn't a game breaker. But there was nothing about the game that pulled me in enough to make me want to put in that effort.
If you've never played a game like this, do yourself a favor and buy Stardew Valley. If you've already played Stardew Valley and are really desperate for more of the same, World's Dawn isn't going to scratch that itch.

If you liked Harvest Moon, you're in for a good time. This is a romp of nostalgia for me and I love it. The music is soothing, playing this game relaxes me in a way that is so familiar and I really missed experiences like this. Stardew could become very cluttered, too much to do and not enough hours in the day, too many things that felt important. World's Dawn, however, is a very zen experience for me. The days are calmly paced and there is enough to decide to do without it feeling overwhelming. The events so far have been pretty fun, too.
The controls feel pretty intuitive. The characters are charming and cute, I am having such a hard time deciding which one I want to marry, because I legitimately really like all of them. And a lot of the non-marriagable cantidates are just real fun to interact with as well. What I can see of the plot so far is very Harvest Moon-esque (if you've played more than one, you get the general theme), but it seems interesting and I'd like to know where it is going. And the side quests are interesting so far as well, I can't wait to dig into this game more!

A very good cutesy horror game about a little girl trying to find her pet dog and older sister who go missing when their town is suddenly infested with spirits.
Some things to note is the game doesn't really tell you some very important things, one being that the Shrines you can "save" at by donating a coin to aren't really "saves", they're actually temporary checkpoints that you will respawn to when you die. To actually save, you need to pause the game and press the button to return home and save at your diary. If you DO NOT do this, and before you head off, you instead save at a Shrine, you will lose all your progress!
It is okay to die in this game, that's what the Shrine checkpoints are for, you are going to die a lot in trying to figure out puzzles and how enemies work, and all the items you pick up are still with you when you die. So don't be afraid to die!
Also, there is a button to turn off your flashlight, it's the Back button on an Xbox Controller, and B (I think) on keyboard.

Good, but not exceptional, and pretty dang short. The time-clone mechanic isn't that original (or at least, isn't anymore, probably wasn't when this first came out either) but they do put a lot of spins on it, every chapter past the first has a gimmick or two to it to make things more challenging/varied. The difficulty curve is strange though, world 1 is pretty easy but worlds 2-5 are all about on an even plane, and it never really gets too hard. There's some platforming and some puzzling involved, especially platforming in the bonus levels where you're on a time limit. Not too intense in either direction though, it finds a good balance. There's not a lot to do though, some 50ish levels in the main game and 30 bonus ones, but none are particularly long, and I 100%'ed the entire thing pretty easily in 4 and a half hours. I wouldn't say it's a bad game though, most of the puzzles are pretty decent and there are some nice aha! moments in them. Some of the bonus puzzles are a little cruddy though, especially the ones that are just "threw stuff in a room, go collect it all".
Wouldn't go around praising its name or anything but, if you want a solid, enjoyable enough puzzle-platformer, go for it, it's not too expensive anyhow.

I like the puzzle aspects of the game, using clones to press buttons and flip switches and so on, but this game quickly lost my favor with its emphasis on timing-based challenges. I've played games like this before, where you had to use the cloning mechanic to have a copy of you at the right place at the right time in order to collect all the doo-dads and reach the exit door. But this game puts a damper on the fun by arbitrarily restricting how many copies you can make in each puzzle, and by requiring you to execute the solution to the puzzle in a strict target time set by the developers (i.e. the pies disappear if you don't gather them fast enough). The time-limit problem is only compounded by adding timed doors/switches into the mix. Finally, the game requires you to strike your clones to launch them at high/far pies, but once you strike them, it breaks them out of their loop, so they disappear. This means if you are trying to execute on a puzzle that requires striking a clone, and you don't pull it off, you have to set up all of your clones again. So yet another puzzle game that requires you to reset a puzzle to its start position over and over and over again when you ALREADY KNOW THE SOLUTION and are JUST TRYING TO EXECUTE IT. Irritating.
Also, while I like the art / atmosphere of the levels, the constant cinematic cuts/intros are interruptive.
Want to play a game that uses this exact same mechanic, but doesn't have all of the annoyances, is way more fun, and is absolutely free? Search for a browser-based game named "Chronotron". You're welcome.

Culinary quandaries never quite quashed this game's crisp quality!
After Braid, what do you do with puzzle platformers? Time's been conquered, cerebral symbolism that only Blow knows bombarded the chances of others, or so it might seem! However more can play at that game, especially when you decide to go off your rocker with time and clones all in the pursuit of the pinnacle of primal desires...Pie!
Yes, the great quest of Mr. Winterbottom is the pursuit of pie, regardless of the consequences of Bakersburg or spacetime, as you make your way through puzzles after a mysterious mystical pie. You duplicate yourself to satisfy your gluttony, but as you play, you must satisfy that of your clones too to proceed, much to your dismay. With the ever-increasing complexity of your pie predicaments, the game almost begins to feel a little finicky, but the solutions remain satisfying to figure out, and rarely leave you perplexed.
The cream atop this curiosity? A distinct visual style and cheerful soundtrack to keep you intrigued and entertained as you try to gather every last pie and incidentally resolve other situations in Bakersburg at the same time. The game's story isn't terribly fascinating, but the writing is fairly amusing at times. If I had to guess, I think there are a few spots that suggest the origin of Mr. Winterbottom tucked away into the tale, and if correct, it works surprisingly well to explain the perpetual misadventures of Mr. Winterbottom.

The EC exchange currency has been devalued to a point where anything useful is unobtainable without saving for months, or possibly years, due to the lack of ability to collect valuable loot because no one does pve ques.  The crafting system will take years to complete without any money invested, or you could throw money at the game and it will still take a year and a couple thousand dollars, just to allowed to have the random chance at something that may or may not be useful.
Many more examples exist, but to sum up the problems:  Lack of players makes a grindy game an impossible grind.  If you've never played before, don't waste your time.  If you haven't played in a while, it's more waiting for the same thing you've done already.
